Possible photo lead: archive.org item casbcfm_001261 (Sept 1955), licence not checked, not added.

Register number conflict, not resolved: the NHLR page for this lookout prints US 594, CA 65 (kept in the record). The firelookout.org California list (fetched from cache) shows NHLR US 883, CA 93 for Sierra Buttes and US 594, CA 65 for a Sierra Peak in Orange/Riverside, so one of the numbers may be wrong. The brief's conflict note says the two share a number. The Forest Service trail page also shows a phone line with 'Open by appointment only'; that appears to be a district office contact, not the lookout, and was not used. Current staffing and visiting rules are unverified: the last dated staffing source is 1992, and the 2024 Ukiah article is a visitor account. The 1954 storehouse loss is not the lookout itself. The 1926 report relied on telephone messages and is hedged in the event note. No photos added.

One source read in full (FFLOS detail page). The record gives no build year: it says the station was 'likely' built in the mid-1930s, so there is no built event with a year. The brief's kind 'ground' fits a building rather than a tower, and the register says no primary lookout was built on the summit. No staffing, fires or access information found; AllTrails returned 403 and was not used. The site map image was not read. No photo URLs were added.

The record's 12.2 m height comes only from the 1964 newspaper item; the register and Angeles Adventures say 30 ft, so the facts use 9.1. Staff names come from Angeles Adventures, not the register. The Bee Canyon fire item (Valley News, quoted on Forest Lookouts) spells the station 'Sierra Polona'. No new photos added; the record already has six.

Brief height_m 18.3 is unsupported and is proposed for removal. Build year: NHLR says 1931, the 1986 bulletin says the steel tower came in 1934; both are in the story. Access is unknown: no source read says whether the public may visit, and the brief's access field was left unset. The 2019 Cal Fire notice proposed removing an abandoned residence and a communications tower; the Forest Fire Lookout Association California list (source 7) shows it as Standing, and the 2020 and 2025 notices show it in use, so the tower's current role is clear but its visitor status is not. The Sierra Vista weebly page has many 1931 press clippings; only the three quoted in the story were read. Elevation: NHLR 2,785 ft (849 m) is used by the brief and not repeated in the story. No photos added.

Current status is the main gap. The newest dated source is the fire-lookouts.org page updated March 1, 2013, which contradicts its own 2010 and 2012 entries. The Yosemite.com listing is undated and the Peakbagging photo caption is from 2002. Check the Sierra National Forest before publishing. The county correction is a spelling fix. The brief's 'built 1951' is the present cab, not the first structure; consider noting the 1900 origin in the record.

Built date conflict, unresolved: the July 1931 Searchlight item (quoted on the Forest Lookouts page) says the new Sims Peak station was completed; the Hmdb CCC marker says the Sims camp crew built three lookouts including Sims and that the camp lasted six years. Sources do not say whether the crew rebuilt an older station. Location: the record point (41.04302, -122.36142) lies roughly 2 km south of the Sims Flat marker (41 3.664 N, 122 21.634 W); the peak site itself was not verified. Agency: the record says Shasta National Forest, which is the name used in the 1931-1962 clippings. The Forest Service Sims Flat page sits under the Shasta-Trinity National Forest; the sources do not say which unit administers the peak today. Consider a correction once confirmed. No removal date found. The Living New Deal Sims CCC camp page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Two web searches used.

Read: the Forest Lookouts Slate Mountain page (1932 newspaper items as quoted there, 1944 and 1945 mentions, and the 1953-54 NGS station description and recovery note); the FFLA California list (Trinity row: Tower, Gone, no register ID); the OSM node (tags and edit note only); and the FFLOS page for the El Dorado County Slate Mountain (US 1893, CA 88). The El Dorado site is a different lookout and is not used for any fact here. Open items: (1) height: 26 ft in the 1932 Searchlight item versus about 45 ft in the 1953 NGS description; the record's 7.9 m (26 ft) is left out of facts and is not settled. (2) Agency and forest name: the 1954 note says property of the California State Forest Service; the September 1932 Dunsmuir News item says Shasta National Forest (the Searchlight item names no forest); the record says Trinity National Forest. No source here explains the change. (3) Status: 'gone' rests on one FFLA list row with no date, cause or register ID. No source describes the site today or whether it is open. The record's osm=standing conflict looks like an over-read of the OSM node. (4) Newspapers were read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the originals were not checked. A Peakbagging California lookout table appeared in search and was not read; it may give a status or note for this site.

The brief says the chapter learned of the 2003 removal afterward and believes FFLA was not informed. That sentence does not appear in the 2012 report or the pages read, so it is not used. The 2012 report's entry sits under the Eldorado National Forest heading. No fires or access details were found. The 6.1 m height is the 20-foot tower named by FFLOS; the cabin's total height is not given.

No source read states the lookout's status or staffing after 2019, and the camera post is undated in the cached text, so current status rests on it plus the 2019 register entry. The firelookout.org California list has a 'Gone' status on the row just above Slater Butte, but that row's coordinates (41.00268) are not Slater's (41.85805) and Slater's own status cell is cut off in the cached text, so it was not used. The Gaia GPS road listings (1.7-mile road) were seen only as search snippets and were not used. The register numbers (US 1378, CA 201) match the brief. No access or visit information was found, so no access or visit key is set. No photos added.

Brief's 2003 'restored' is not supported; sources say reopened and rededicated. Cab size conflicts (14x14 ft in NHLR vs 365 sq ft in ANFFLA); the blog's 365 sq ft is the whole structure. Brief omitted the 1980 closure and 1970 helicopter delivery. Access 'public' is inferred from the hike-only trail and volunteer staffing; no official Forest Service access statement was found. Staffing as_of is the hiking guide's update month, not a staffing schedule. Photos not added.

Access, staffing and current condition are not in any source read; the access key is omitted rather than guessed. The FFLA Southern California list (firelookouthost.org/southern-california) has a Smith Mtn row, but its columns are jumbled in the cache, so it is not cited. The 1964 Built field and the 1944 BC-301 caption conflict with the description; the story flags both. Height 18.3 m in the record matches the 1931 60-foot tower plan, so it is proposed for removal. The status key was removed: no source read gives the current condition, and the story says so. Pending a Cal Fire San Benito-Monterey Unit or Los Padres NF source for access and status. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'best-known item' claim was removed as unsupported.

Two Smith Peak lookouts exist: this Tuolumne tower (Stanislaus NF) and a separate Plumas County tower near Lake Davis. The brief's source page smith-peak.html is the Tuolumne page and is correct for this record. The Plumas story (us-ca-smith-peak-plumas-national-forest) states that the Tuolumne tower burned in 1987; this record confirms that from NHLR, the Forest Lookouts page, and the 1988 Merced Sun-Star item it quotes. Staffing evidence is dated 2012 (PDF) and undated (NHLR, present tense); the 2024 visitor report describes the access road only and does not confirm staffing or visiting rules, so current access is unverified. The Roaming Civic page was read only for the access-road passage. Photos on NHLR are credited but no licence was seen, so none added. The 2012 report is the only source for the catwalk and roof work.

Record source_pages includes smith-peak.html, which is the Tuolumne Smith Peak; proposed correction above. The register says the cabin sits on a '9 foot enclosed timber tower', which is unclear and was not used in the story. Current staffing ('staffed as_of 2020') rests on the register; the Sierra REC article has no date in the cached text. Pages about Smith Peak near Groveland (the 2024 Roaming Civic post and a 1931 'administrative site' claim in a search snippet) concern the Tuolumne tower and were not used. No fire events attributable to this tower were found in the newspaper items read.

No access or visit information was found in any source, so facts.access and visit are omitted; the record's access 'unknown' stands. Height was not found. The no-rental line comes from an undated citlink.net copy of a CAL FIRE list; confirm on a current Cal Fire page. Peakbagging and the register disagree on the forest (Lassen vs Plumas) and on staffing; the story reports both. The July 2026 fire report says near the lookout, not at it. The register's photo credit (Ron Kemnow, 2008) is noted but no image URL was found, so no photo entry.

Thin record: one January 1922 newspaper item (via the Forest Lookouts page), the Forest Fire Lookout Association row, and the Forest Service wilderness page. No build year, design, staffing or removal date found. The FFLA row gives coordinates as Undetermined; the record point (39.38127, -122.77277) came from West US Lookouts and was not checked here. Do not merge with the Oregon Snow Mountain lookout (Grant County, Ochoco/Malheur National Forests, station noted in 1915: https://oregonlookouts.weebly.com/snow-mountain.html), which is a different tower. Two web searches used; no current source for this site was found beyond the wilderness page.

The 1974 record date is correct for the current tower; the first station dates to a CCC build in 1934 (Redding) and a 1920 mention. Height 6.1 m comes from a 1977 NGS description of about 20 feet, converted; the register gives no height. The 1947 discontinuation is known only from a reprint of a Weekly Adin Argus item on the Forest Lookouts page; the original paper was not checked, and the closure may have been seasonal. Access is 'public' per the register, which is undated; no recent visit or staffing report was found. No fire events were found in the sources I read. Grokipedia says the station dates to the 1920s; it is an AI-generated page, so I did not use it. Photos are credited on the register (Ron Kemnow, 2008; Fred Johnson) but no image URLs were found, so no photo entries.

Status is disputed and not resolved. The register says the tower remains, the FFLA California list marks it Standing*, which its key defines as a tower with the cab no longer in place, and the FFLA 2012 chapter report says the site no longer exists and is a repeater site. The register's text is internally inconsistent about the cab: a 732-6A cab tops the tower with a repeater antenna attached, yet the cabin and storage structure are said to be removed. The FFLA key therefore adds a cab-gone reading that conflicts with the register's 732-6A entry; the sources do not settle it. The 1977 newspaper item predates the 1982 build date, so an earlier lookout may have stood here; the sources do not say. The access note is from 1991. The site carries high RF exposure; the story advises against climbing. One web search added only CEQA notices and a repeater reference.

Fire name disagreement is not resolved against a fire record; the web search budget ran out before one could be checked. The brief's 1999 event was labeled staffed; the Register wording is refurbished and reopened, so it is relabeled restored. The 1960 Sandy DeLapp clipping is not counted because it does not name this tower. No source in this pass describes the site today or public access. Photo credits on the Register page not added.

No public access or visit information was found, so facts.access and visit are omitted; the record's access 'unknown' stands. The record's kind 'two_story' is not stated by any source; the register describes a 14 by 14 ft cab on a 10 ft brick base, so the kind may be a shorthand worth checking. Height was not found. Builder (CCC vs district) and base material (brick vs concrete block) disagree across sources; the story reports both. The conversion to a communications facility is undated. The register's 1949 photo credit (Los Angeles Times) is noted but no image URL was found, so no photo entry. The 1974 end-of-staffing date (district history) and the 'at least 1962' register line are consistent, not in conflict. The Forest Fire Lookout Association list is a chapter page; the 'comms fac.' row is the only source for conversion.

Two conflicting histories (register vs. Plumas history quoted by a 2012 trip report) and a closing-date dispute. The Plumas history is only quoted second-hand through a blog; the book itself was not read. Do not confuse with the Oregon Spanish Peak lookout, which turned up in search results. Staffing names come from Forest Lookouts newspaper transcriptions. The record's kind 'ground' and material 'wood' are consistent with the sources.

Thin record: one register entry, one listing with an unexplained 1933, and one 2018 trip report that mentions no lookout remains. Staffing, fires and removal date are not in any source read, so none are stated. The register's 'Stag Dome Lookout - courtesy of Viola Parker' photo was not downloaded. Brief elevation (2328.7 m) matches the register's 2,329 m. Agency and boundary conflict left for the editor. The brief's access 'unknown' was replaced by 'public' from the 2018 trip report; no closure found, but the visit is a single 2018 account, so an editor may want to downgrade it. Web searches found no further lookout history.

Build year: register says 1930's, compilation says 1936; the brief's 1930 is not in the register (see corrections). The 1936 year comes from a compilation of newspaper items, so it is secondary. Staffing and 1940 fire items are secondhand newspaper quotes on the compilation page; the 1964 Crystal Bay tower is linked to Stateline only by that compilation. Access is upgraded from unknown to public based on 2026 and resort listings; the Forest Service recreation page fetched did not give readable detail on this site. Climb sources disagree (about 100 ft vs 335-400 ft). The Marin 2008 walk and the 2026 guide are the only sources describing the site today. Worth a human check: current Forest Service signage or rules for the gate and parking.

The first-tower dispute is the main issue. The Mountains Foundation (1922 80-ft tower on the peak; 1934 damage and replacement) conflicts with the 1933 newspaper transcriptions (80-ft wooden tower at Grass Valley collapsed January 1933; steel tower on Strawberry Peak begun May 1933) and with the register's 1933. The newspaper text comes from a transcription page quoting The San Bernardino County Sun; I did not check it against the original paper. The corrections proposal depends on that. Access is set to public because the Mountains Foundation says it was open for the 2025 season, but the Forest Service copy showed a temporary-closure notice and a winter closure, so re-check current status before publishing. The staffing as_of date is undated because the register page is undated.

Brief height_m 95.4 is wrong; the tower is 30 feet (9.1 m) per NHLR and the 1930 plan, so the record is corrected. Access is unknown: no source read confirms whether the summit road or the lookout is open to the public today, so no access level is set and the story says to check with the Modoc National Forest. Staffing has no current source; the last mention is a 2007 photo note about possible summer volunteers. The 2025 Cal-North report says forest staff and the report author discussed relocation or restoration; no decision is recorded. The 1929 fire is named for Sugar hill, but the sources read do not say whether it reached the summit. Facebook group posts found in search were not used. No photos added.

Thin record: one register page and one county staff report. The register gives no staff names, fire events or dated photos beyond 1937. A Facebook group post gives 1937 as the build year; it was not used. The Forest Lookouts Sugar Pine page has no lookout text beyond its header, so it is not cited. The county report does not give coordinates, so whether its radio site stands on the old lookout footprint is open. The record's 1930 build year is replaced with a 1930s range. Height 24.4 m comes from the register's 80-foot figure.

The 1931 build date rests on the NHLR 'Built' field; no second source gave it directly. Web search results pointed to Girard Ridge Lookout (Shasta-Trinity, 1931) and to Washington State Sugarloaf lookouts; those are different towers and were not used. The record's material 'wood' came from the design and is not stated by any source read; the register describes only the 8 ft concrete tower. The FFLA list has a separate Tuolumne 'Sugarloaf' (enclosed tower, gone) that is not this lookout. No source read gives a current access level, so access is omitted. The staffing 'no longer staffed' is inferred from the 1954 closure clipping, which says closed and does not explicitly say never staffed again.

The brief's status 'gone' is supported only indirectly: the register lists it as a former site with unknown removal date, and the June 2020 blog describes rocks and metal, not a tower. No source gives a build or removal year. Elevation 1,507 m (4,944 ft) and coordinates match the register. The brief's kind 'tower' matches the register's description. The Forest Service recreation listing (recid=11468) read this session is a general forest page with no Summit Valley entry, so it is not cited. The 2020 blog is a personal hiking account and is the only description of the site today; the story says so by describing only what it found. Access is marked public on the strength of the trailhead and NRA trail description, not a closure notice; the summit route's status is unverified. Two WebSearch calls and four distinct page reads (register, Forest Lookouts, Smith River Alliance, blog) were used, with the forest recreation page as a fifth read that yielded no site data.

Dates conflict. (1) Build: a 1920 district newsletter item (via the Forest Lookouts page) describes a working lookout and cabin before the 1921 date given by SummitPost and the Tobias history. (2) End: SummitPost and the Tobias history give 1935 for the switch to Tobias Peak, but a June 1936 item names the Sunday Peak lookout, so 1935 may be early. (3) Burn: 1954 per SummitPost and the Tobias history; a trail guide says destroyed in the 1950s. (4) Elevation: the trail guide gives the summit as 8,295 ft; a 1934 report gives the lookout as 8,200 ft. Record kind 'tower' matches the FFLA row and the trail guide, while the 1920s newspaper items describe a cabin. The Kern River trail update is dated June 2022 and the Wilderness Portal page is undated; check current trail status before recommending a visit. The Living New Deal Tobias Peak page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Two web searches used.

Brief's 1972 build date corrected (see corrections). Height conflict left open: 30 ft (NHLR) vs 50 ft (1934 newspaper). No public-access or visiting source found, so access and visit keys are omitted. Staffing evidence ends at the June 2008 CAL FIRE list. Brief's agency wording matches the weebly header.

Built 1927 is consistent across the three history sources. The 1928 Horn item says he had been stationed there for two years, which would predate the 1927 build; the story does not use this. Removal year and fate differ (register 1974 transported; Angeles Adventures 1975 demolished). The HikingGuy page mentions the 2021 Antonio Fire along the trail, not the summit. A 2024 fire was seen only in a search snippet and is not used. No page describing the current site condition was read beyond the register's 2013 photo captions. The brief's height_m of 15.2 appears to come from the 1915 50-foot plan.

Thin record. No build date, designer, staffing history or removal date was found, so the story leaves those out. The 1943 item is the only dated source and does not name a lookout. Peakbagging's 2023 table lists Swain Hill without the (LO site) label it uses for removed buildings; its key does not say what an unlabelled entry means, so this is not treated as a conflict with the FFLA's Gone. Not checked: the Feather River Bulletin archives (fth.stparchive.com, cdnc.ucr.edu) for dated coverage of a Swayne Hill lookout. The record's other_names entry matches the page header, so no correction.

Thin record. No build date, designer, staffing history beyond the 1924 mention, or current description was found. The NHLR Pilot Peak page (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/ca/pilot-peak-lookout/) says the first Pilot Peak cabin was built in 1916 and rebuilt by the CCC in 1935; that does not sit easily with a 1931 'station established' item, and it was not used in the story. The Plumas County lookouts blog (plumaslookouts.blogspot.com) has a Table Mountain heading but no text in the cache. No photo found.

District: the register (OCR 'ldyllwild') says Idyllwild Ranger District and the Forest Service page says San Jacinto Ranger District with an Idyllwild office; the story uses the Forest Service name and cites both. Closure status is the main open question: the Forest Service page (temporary-closure notice, closed-for-the-season banner, posted hours) and the Mountains Foundation (currently closed) are both undated copies, and the record says public. The access level is set to closed; re-check before publishing. Elevation disagrees across sources: register 8,752 ft (2,668 m; the record's 2,667.6 m comes from here), Mountains Foundation 8,828 ft, Forest Service 8,846 ft. The record is left unchanged. The 77-year figure is not explained by any source. It would be close to 77 years if counted from the 1917 cabin, but that is my inference only. The 2017 chapter report spells the peak Taquitz, and it says America Core kids (the record says youth crews); the story says young helpers. The register text has typos (ldyllwild, suppports) that I left out of quotes or copied as printed.

Access: the record says unknown and no source states current access, so facts.access is omitted. A 2019 post (updated December 2025) says a National Defense Area may affect access; check with CalFire or the land manager before any access level is set. Coordinates: the record's 32.57961, -116.68867 matches the firelookout.org row for this site; the FFLOS page gives N 32.579350, W 116.683330, about 0.5 km away. Not changed. Register numbers: the firelookout.org row for this site lists FFLOS US 521, CA 7 and also an NHLR US 382, CA 43 line, which the NHLR California index assigns to Needles Lookout, so the record's note that the two sites share a register number is not confirmed. Elevation: the record's 929.3 m matches FFLOS (3,049 ft, 929 m); the FFLA page says 3855 ft / 1175 m. Unresolved; the story does not use elevation. Height: 6.1 m is the 20 ft in the sources converted to metres. The 1938 and 1966 items are read through the Forest Lookouts reprints; the original newspapers were not checked. A search result lists an SDG&E P25 radio site named Tecate Peak (radioreference.com/db/site/45710); I did not open it, so the story does not claim any radio facility stands there today.

No source read says whether the site is open to the public, so no access key is given. The Register names the county fire department as administrator. A search for Tejon Mountain turned up only Tejon Ranch history pages, which do not mention the lookout, so none are cited. The build date is unresolved: the Register says prior to 1922, while the county annual reports describe a tower erected in December 1936. Confirm with a newspaper or county report before publishing a firm year. The Angeles Adventures link to the Sawmill tower move is not confirmed as the Tejon tower.

Only the register and Forest Lookouts were read, and a search for the site today found nothing, so the story says no source describes the site now. The height is unresolved (60, 70 or 75 ft), so the brief's height_m was left unchanged. The closure reason differs between sources. The 1936 and 1937 annual-report quotes are near-identical text; the 1937 year matches the register. Forest Lookouts quotes a 1935 article naming a Temple City location; the register puts the site on California Street, north of Arrow Highway.

Only three pages were read. The Forest Lookouts Thomas Mountain page has only a location line, so it is not cited. The geocache page for the site returned just its title when read, so it is not used. The 1935 and 1938 build dates conflict; the story reports both. No source describes current road or gate status. The brief has no height, so height_m 18.3 (60 ft) was added from the register and Hundred Peaks.

Record built year 1931 stands as the start of construction; the completion year (1931 or 1932) is worth a human look. Radar end year is disputed (1967 vs 1970). Peakbagging's claim that the lookout was used in WWII for enemy plane spotting is unsourced and left out. No source found confirms staffing or road status after 2012; a 2024-25 search returned only general fire-season news. A Lassen News item on the Thompson Peak Initiative (a Cal Fire grant) appeared in search results and was not read.

The 1936 build date rests on one Peakbagging photo page ('probably'), with no second source. The 1939 fire account is a reprint of a California Ranger item, quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; we did not read the original. Not used: two Calisphere and UC Davis photos titled Thompson Peak Lookout near Janesville and near Susanville, which appear to show the Plumas County site; and a Stanislaus NF Facebook throwback post about 1938 (not readable in the cache), plus a comment there suggesting the tower burned, which is not a source. A reviewer could check the Stanislaus NF post or Forest Service history for a build or removal date.

Built year 1933 comes from the register only; the August 1934 newspaper item calls the lookout new, which fits. 'Still standing' is the Forest Service's own line on an undated trail page. No source read says whether the cab is open to visitors or climbable, so access level and climbability are left out of facts. The Ojai Valley News hiking column returned HTTP 429 and was not read. Record name, coordinates and elevation match the register; no corrections proposed. The weebly page spells it Thorne; the register and Forest Service use Thorn. No staffing after 1958 was found.

Staffing and removal are well sourced from the register and the Forest Lookouts page (which quotes a 1988 book). Today's condition rests on one undated trip report, so the remnants may have changed. The 'federal property' remark in that report was made at Alder Peak, so it was removed from this story and access moved from 'restricted' back to 'unknown': the land went to the Army, but no current rule was found. The trip report places the lookout on the south summit, not the highpoint, which matches the remnants it describes.

Built and staffing dates rest on 1930-1932 newspaper clippings as transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page; the originals were not checked. The FFLA county list prints FFLOS US 1872, CA 67 on the row before Three Sisters; in the firetower.org list that number belongs to Three Peaks Lookout Site, so it is not attached here. No removal date or site description found; a Colusa County or Colusa Herald archive search would be the next step. An earlier draft named a site author; the cached page text does not name one, so the source no longer does.

No page I could read says whether Timber Mountain is staffed now or open to climbing, so the story says so and no access or staffing keys are set. A search snippet hinted at Forest Service staffing and a 2022 blog visit, but snippets were not read pages and are not used. The 1912 platform is 'may have' per NHLR only. The 1932-1945 history comes from one compiled history site quoting newspapers and Forest Service records; not checked against originals. The 30-foot height is the NHLR's tower height; the total height of the cab on it is not given. The brief's build year (1966) and elevation check out.

Only one detailed source: a 1943 San Bernardino County Sun item transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page (original not checked). Built date, design and removal are not in any source read. Tip Top is not in the cached firetower.org former-site list for California (matched on the name). Do not present the 1943 staffing as current. Check San Bernardino National Forest records before publishing anything about the site. An earlier draft named a site author; the cached page text does not name one, so the source no longer does.

Coordinates and elevation disagree. The record (from the register) has 35.849955, -118.572367 and 8,218 ft (2,505 m). Fire-Lookouts.org gives 35.5101 N, 118.3421 W and 9,292 ft; peakbagging.com also says 9292 ft. The 1937 and 1946 newspapers give 8,200 and 8,550 ft. Left unchanged; a map check is needed. Staffing: the 2025 brochure says a Forest Service employee resides in the tower; Fire-Lookouts.org (undated) says it is no longer staffed, and in the same paragraph says it is currently staffed. The access level 'restricted' is my reading of the gate note; check current gate policy with the Forest Service before editing. 1947: the register says not in active service, but a July 1947 newspaper item names two lookouts on Tobias. 1936 (Fire-Lookouts.org) and 1937 (newspaper, 'will be manned June 10th') differ on when manning began. District: the register and Fire-Lookouts.org say Hot Springs RD; the 2025 brochure says Western Divide RD. The 1954 burning was Sunday Peak Lookout, not Tobias. The 1947 item names Etha Rice and the 1951 item names Bea Rice; the story keeps each name with its own date and source. The story now states the fire-lookouts.org staffing conflict in full (no longer staffed, and staffed 5 days a week in the same paragraph).

Build year is circa 1940 (register) and believed 1940 (Tehachapi News); the California lookouts history page quotes a June 1936 notice planning a Tollgate lookout, so the first plan may predate the 1940 build. Staffing status is 'unknown': no page states today's status. 'unstaffed' would only be an inference from the Tehachapi News wording that staffing ran until the 1970s. The 1954 fire is quoted from a newspaper transcription on the California lookouts page (Bakersfield Californian), not the original paper. The preserve acreage differs between sources. The article's own date is not shown in pages read; the 2022 dates come from the register's photo captions.

The 1973 closure rests on a single visitor's comment on the NHLR page, so it is marked as one account. The 6.1 m height is the 20 ft tower alone, per the NHLR description. Current access is not documented in any source read; the 1973 'long, dusty dirt road' comment is historical and not used as current access. A web search summary mentioned a 2015 trip report describing the lookout as locked and shuttered; it was not fetched and is not used. Wikipedia's Tomhead Mountain article has no lookout history. The only survival source is the NHLR page; no second source for the South Fire damage was found.

Height is disputed: the register and a July 1938 newspaper say 20 feet, a June 1939 newspaper and Carey's quote of a 1945 forest history say 30 feet. The record's height_m 9.1 matches the 30-foot figure and was left unchanged; it is not in facts. Access level 'closed' rests on Carey's 2012 post (public access prohibited since 1959); no current Forest Service notice was checked. The FFLA California list marks this site 'Standing*' and the meaning of the asterisk was not found. Newspaper quotes come from the Forest Lookouts compilation, not the original papers. Used 1 WebSearch and about 8 page reads, two over the per-tower budget, to get the access and height evidence.

Built date, design and the graffiti-covered base are well sourced. Removal date and owner conflict across sources. The brief's access 'unknown' is now 'public' based on the trail guide and islands.com. No staffing names or fires are sourced, so none are given. Height 9.1 m is the register's 30 feet converted; it describes the tower only. The removal year 1972 was dropped from the events list: islands.com gives 1972 as the end of operations, not a demolition date.

The 2026 Six Rivers project page does not mention a lookout; the link between that project and the old station is a name match only and is not asserted in the story. Clippings are transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page (originals not checked). One clipping spells the carpenter's name Wyllie and another Wylie, so names are left out. No construction date for the first station is in the sources; the 1931 staffing is the earliest evidence. Not in the cached firetower.org former-site list for California (matched on the name). An earlier draft named a site author; the cached page text does not name one, so the source no longer does.

Gone lookout; the brief's 'built 1934' and 'removed 1960' were both incomplete. The station dates from 1930, and removal is late 1960s with no exact year. Today's condition rests on the register's photo caption and a satellite-image description; no source describes the site after the 2018 fire. Access 'public' is from a hiker's undated account and the Santa Monica Mountains NRA location, not a rule.

The NHLR page gives the tower as 41 ft and the CCC build as 1934-35; I used those. A web search summary mentioned a 45-ft tower from a trail guide and a Groveland office phone number; neither was fetched or verified, so neither is used. The sources do not say whether the 2009 cabin restoration and the 2012 rental plan are the same work, and no source read confirms the current condition or whether the public can visit. The record's 'abandoned' is from the 2012 report and is dated to that year. The height 12.5 m is the tower only, converted from 41 ft.

Sources disagree on height (80 ft register vs 100 ft 1937 press) and design wording. The sequence of 1937-38 towers is unresolved, so no 1938 event is recorded for this site; the July 1938 report describes a moved and rebuilt tower plus a second new one at the peninsula, and a May 1937 report describes the headquarters tower being moved to Upper Klamath Lake; no source says which tower became the register's tower, so the story flags this. The brief's 1937 build date is supported. A 1940 memo about a water tower for the peninsula cabin is not about the lookout and was left out. The register's 1964 photo credit (courtesy Tulelake NWR Headquarters) has no image URL, so no photo entry. No access information found; the story says so.

Brief height_m 12.2 is wrong; NHLR gives a 60-foot steel tower, so the record is corrected to 18.3 m, with the 1937 65-foot figure noted. Elevation 2103.1 m matches NHLR's 6,900 ft. The Forest Lookouts page has nothing after the August 1937 item, so the story is thin on 1938 to today; the 2002 photo captions are ambiguous about whether the lookout was replaced and no date is given. Access is unknown: no source read says whether the public may visit. Blog and trip-report pages found in search were not used. A further search for post-1937 Turner Mountain history (tower replacement, the 1913 house, current use) would be the next step. No photos added.

Status 'standing' is from the record and the 2026 news reports (which call it a 30-foot tower); I did not visit the site. Height 30 ft converted to 9.1 m. Open question: the 1932 station versus the 1966 tower. The sources read do not say whether they are the same building; the built-1966 event cites only the 2026 news report, not a source that links the two. The Feb 2026 photo caption said the cameras would soon go in, while the 31 Mar 2026 report says they are active; the story gives both. The Forest Lookouts clippings are a secondary compilation of old newspaper items; I did not check the originals. Access changed from the record's 'unknown' to 'private' on the register's wording. Registered date from the register page (Feb 2, 2020). Fact-check 2026-10-08: the 1932, 1935, 1938, 1956, 1989 and 1990 dates were confirmed on the Forest Lookouts page and added to the evidence quotes.

Staffing 'staffed' as_of 2019 is the register's undated present-tense text, taken with its 2019 registration date; no current staffing schedule was found. The Forest Service district page I checked had no lookout listing. The 14-ft tower height is converted to 4.3 m. Access left out of facts: the sources read give no current visiting rules (the only visiting statement is from 1971). The 1934 CCC date is from the register; the Forest Lookouts page repeats it from a Klamath NF history volume that I did not read directly. Record fields other than these were not checked. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the 1951, 1961, 1963 and 1971 dates were confirmed on the Forest Lookouts page and added to the evidence quotes; the story now says 'an earlier lookout' because the register says 'earlier', not 'first'.

Bear Basin Butte record should carry the Camp Six relocation: NHLR lists it as US 288, CA 21, registered January 6, 1999, nominated by the Gasquet Ranger District, and available for rental. Peakbagging.com says it moved its own pin after Dean Gaudet located the site; check the FFLA coordinates 41.81861, -123.86333 against that. The 1916 tower and the 1934 CCC lookout may be different structures. The 1950 event year is a placeholder for 'the 1950s'. No access or visit information for the original site was found.

Thin record: no build year, staffing, fire history or present-day description found. Ownership is state: the 1993 CEQAnet notice names the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) as the public agency, and the agency field is set to match. Peakbagging.com lists the site with elevation 1214 ft and prominence 480 ft; not used because the table cell carries no quotable label.

Only the FFLOS register gives substance; the Forest Lookouts page for Valley View has a heading and county but no history entries, so no staffing or fire history is reported. The brief's osm=standing conflict is a misreading, since the OSM node carries no status tag. The 4.3 m height is the 14-foot tower named by FFLOS. The 1968 photo is a caption on the FFLOS page; the image URL was not captured, so no photo entry was added. No source describes current access.

Brief's record matches the register for elevation, height (20 ft = 6.1 m), built 1934 and removed 1970; no corrections proposed. Agency is ambiguous: register administers via Shasta NF but locates in Klamath NF; the story reports both. Today's condition rests on one 2012 photo caption (footings beside a weather station) and a 1948 survey description, so the site today is not well documented. No source found says whether the public may visit; access is left unset rather than marked unknown in facts. The compilation's 1936 incident is from a 1936 California Ranger report quoted on the page, so it is secondhand. Brief's source list did not include the Wikipedia Long-Bell Lumber Company article: the cached version does not mention the lookout, so it was not cited. Worth a human check: current Klamath NF records on the site and any road or closure notices.

Two fetched sources only. The story says nothing about the site today because no fetched page covers it. Unverified leads from search snippets (not fetched, so not cited): a 2005 climber report and a 2011 trip report describe stone foundation remains on the summit; a 1998 Ventana Wilderness Alliance article (ventanawild.org/news/ws98/dclook.html) reportedly dates the end to a mid-1960s lightning fire, which conflicts with the 1976-77 burning dates. That URL returned no text from the cache. A search snippet also reports the Forest Service main trail (2E04) closed for the 2026 Timber and Plaskett fires; not verified. firelookout.org's CA index lists Ventana Double Cone under FFLOS US 2040, CA 146, which differs from this record's US 1873, CA 68; possibly a duplicate record. The brief's 2019 registration date was not re-checked.

Record height_m 121.9 (about 400 ft) is not supported by any source I read; it looks wrong for a peak lookout, so I left height out of facts. Please verify before publishing. Record 'standing' is not confirmed by any text read: the register photos run to 2017 and the page does not say whether the cab stands now. The 2026 status is unknown, so the story does not say the cab stands. Access: the Forest Service describes the roads but says nothing about the cab; access level was left out. Sources disagree on forest administration at the summit: the register names the Tahoe, while the Forest Service route page places the road at the Tahoe-Toiyabe junction. Search snippets (not fetched) mentioned an early-1930s first lookout, a boarded-up cab, and differing summit heights (8,431 to 8,455 ft); none was used in the story. The 1958 clipping is from the Reno Evening Gazette as cited on the Forest Lookouts page. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the 1986 survey date is in the register text and now appears in the evidence quote; the 1958 date and Reno Evening Gazette attribution were confirmed on the Forest Lookouts page; the Forest Service page does not use the word 'dirt', so the story and trail note now say OHV routes.

Two minor date conflicts (build year 1935 vs 1937, and burn month August vs September 2009) are noted in resolved_conflicts; both resolved toward the more corroborated/specific NHLR figures. Did not verify current-day staffing schedule beyond the 2023-era Edison article, which may be slightly dated.

The record's KRCR link (krcrtv.com/news/butte-county/construction-underway-for-new-vina-helitack-base) returns HTTP 404 in our cache; drop or replace it. The record's kind two_story is not confirmed by any source read. No source read gives lookout staffing or fire history, so none is stated. The register's 'open to visitors' note is dated 1991 and predates the 2018 rebuild; no source confirms public access today. The 1954/1955 start date is unresolved. A Corning Observer article on the base's aircraft returned HTTP 429 and was not read.

No build date or structure description found. Staffing evidence is a single October 1940 item (dated October 25, 1940). The 'today' description rests on the Forest Service trail guide, which calls the spot a site and does not describe any remains. The spelling differs by source: the FFLA list says 'Virgin Creek Butte', while the Forest Lookouts page and the trail guide say 'Virgin Creek Buttes'; the story keeps each spelling for the source that uses it. Peakbagging.com lists this as Virgin Creek Buttes (LO site), elevation 4760 ft; not cited in the story.

History rests on the register page and one Forest Service crew history; no staffing or fire records were found within the search budget. The FS page calls the 1930s camp a California Conservation Corps camp, and the story uses that wording; no other source was checked. The register says Vista Grande Fire Station and the FS page says Vista Grande Guard Station; not reconciled, so the story names each as its source gives it. The register photo caption (c. 1920s, courtesy Cleveland National Forest) has no image URL in the cached page, so no photo entry was added.

Only two pages describe this tower. The Forest Lookouts page has a 1951 heading and then an image where the rest of the entry would be; the image was not downloaded, so the story may be missing its construction history, and a human could read it. The FFLA California list is the only status source and gives no removal date. The Department of Defense line may name the owner rather than an operator; the agency fact rests on that single line. Three web searches found nothing else about the tower. Access is unknown, and no visitor note is included.

1934 build date rests on the registry alone; no newspaper or Forest Service record was read. The 1969 smoke report is quoted second-hand on a hobby page. Access is inferred from one trail report (6.5-mile fire road); no official rule found. Height corrected to 20 ft per registry and trail report. Status 'Demolished' on Angeles Adventures conflicts with the rest; kept as standing (cab gone). The brief's 'unknown' access replaced with 'public' on the basis of the trail report and no closure found. Staffing 'not staffed' as of 1987 comes from the registry's wording.

Register and Forest Lookouts page carry the main facts. The Forest Lookouts page is a compiled set of newspaper clippings and survey notes, not a primary record. Current status (2026) is unverified: the newest visit report is 2011, and no current staffing, open-to-visitors or rental source was found. Access level left unset because no source says whether the tower is public. The firelookout.org California list shows Weaver Bally as a standing tower under NHLR US 1060, CA 105. An earlier FFLOS number, US 1790, CA 36, sits on that list's Warm Springs Mountain row (Los Angeles County), not this lookout, so it was removed at fact-check. A WebSearch returned AllTrails and Peakbagging pages, which describe the road as needing a high-clearance 4WD vehicle and give elevations of 6,990 and 6,971 ft; these were not read and are not cited.

Only three sources, and the 1934 build date and the WWII cabin rest on the register alone. The 2018 blog is the only source on the site today; it is a personal account, not a survey. The Forest Lookouts page gives location only. A search snippet (not fetched) cites a 1955 Refugio Fire history (ResearchGate PDF) that names West Big Pine among lookouts to get radio telephones; its text is garbled and was not used. The same snippet says the forest was called Santa Barbara National Forest until December 3, 1936; not verified. The register lists the site as US 2017, CA 134. firelookout.org's CA index shows an NHLR US 1060 near West Big Pine; not checked. No closure or access notice was found, so no access level is recorded. The 2018 blog says the lookout stands on a peak it calls West Big Pine Lookout, and that the higher peak to the east is 'properly' West Big Pine Mountain; the register places the lookout on West Big Pine Mountain, so the story keeps the register's identification and reports the blogger's view.

Three sources only; the fate account differs (burned 1969 vs demolished before 1980, no date) and the story says so. No staffing or fire records were found. The 1989 LA Times article about lookout cabins at Mt. Vetter and South Mt. Hawkins was read but does not cover this lookout, so it is not cited. The Angeles Adventures dates (1936-1960s) are not explained on the page.

Proposed corrections are for human review, not applied. The record's NRHP 78000295 and other name point to the Prospect Peak Fire Lookout in Lassen Volcanic NP; Wikipedia and the 1977 nomination both describe that structure as abandoned on Prospect Peak in the park. Unresolved: Wikidata Q14683716 puts its coordinates at the West Prospect site (40 35 38 N, 121 22 45 W) and records a 1981 'structure relocation' for the NRHP lookout, while Wikipedia gives 40.573 N, 121.345 W for the park lookout. Check the NRHP location and any move before accepting the registers correction. Current status and access are not verified: the search also returned an ALERTCalifornia camera page and a syncrosafari page saying the tower is still in service, but neither was read (page budget). The weebly header says Shasta-Trinity NF; the register and 1955 inspection say Lassen NF and Hat Creek District. The record's kind 'two_story' was not checked against the register's 'enclosed timber tower' with a cab on top. The story now says the NRHP listing 'appears' to belong to a different structure, because the Wikidata coordinate conflict above is still open.

Possible duplicate records in project data: FFLOS 'West Verdugo Mountain' (US 2103, lat 34.2202, lon -118.28959), FFLA 'Verdugo Peak' (lat 34.2152, lon -118.28, status Gone), FFLA 'West Verdugo Peak' (no coords), and the Forest Lookouts 'Verdugo' entry. Not merged here. The brief's note that the site 'shares a register number' could not be checked; the other record was not seen. Summit identity is unresolved: the register puts the site at 2,983 ft, and Wikipedia's infobox gives 3126 ft for Verdugo Peak, the range's highest point, so the lookout may stand on a different summit. A search snippet (not fetched, not cited) credits the City of Glendale with a 60-foot tower on Verdugo Peak in 1934 and a shutdown in the mid-1950s, which conflicts with the county attribution here. firelookout.org's CA index also lists NHLR US 1351 beside 'Verdugo Peak'; not checked. The FFLOS 'Date Registered' and the brief's 2025 date match.

The 1959 account is quoted second-hand from The Arizona Republic on the Forest Lookouts page; the original article was not read. Today's condition rests on a 2012 blog and a 2022 trip report, both personal accounts. The AllTrails page returned HTTP 403 and was not used; its search snippet mentions radio towers, but that is unverified, so the story says only towers. The access level comes from trip reports and a gate, not an official notice, so check before publishing a firm access claim. The register spells the peak Whitaker; the Forest Lookouts page spells it Whittaker.

Four online sources. The Gazette piece is subscription-gated and undated; only its opening paragraph was read. The 1935 and 1936 newspaper items are reprinted on the Forest Lookouts page and were not checked against the original papers. Access today is not described by any source, so the story says nothing about visiting. Elevation 977 m in the record matches the FFLOS and NHLR figures. Do not confuse with the Idaho Williams Peak lookout (a 1932 L-4 cab in Payette NF), which is a separate record. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the Gazette's 2017 Detwiler Fire account conflicts with the NHLR removal wording, and the story reports both. The events.removed correction (2017 to 2017-2018) is still pending human review.

Identity unknown. The OSM way (1477386021) carries name Wilson Tower, emergency=fire_lookout and tower:type=observation, but no ownership, height or date. No register, Forest Service or news source found for a Wilson Tower at these coordinates. Two web searches (Siskiyou and Shasta-Trinity; Wilson Mountain). Search results surfaced other places named Wilson Mountain or Mount Wilson (Los Angeles County, Arizona, Virginia) and Shasta-Trinity lookouts (Girard Ridge, Little Mt. Hoffman, Hirz Mountain) that do not carry the Wilson name. The name may be local or informal. A human could check the Klamath and Shasta-Trinity ranger districts or search for a nearby peak name.

Location conflict is not resolved. The register says the building stood right next to Highway 32. The 2017 Chico article puts the Windy Cut Bridge, which lies below the site, six miles down a dirt road from Highway 32, so the lookout may have stood far from the highway. Record said removed 1986; the register gives only a range, so the removal event was dropped (see corrections). Register captions a December 1961 photo credited to Meriam Library, California State University, Chico. The image URL was not captured, so no photos entry was added. A firelookout.org Tehama list row near Windy Cut carries a number (US 1327, CA 150) that matches another lookout on the NHLR; not used. Site access is not described in any source read; the bridge reopened in 2017.

Record's built 1917 and gone status hold. No present-day description found in one search. The Lane County, Oregon Windy Peak (Siuslaw NF) is a different tower and is named in the story so readers do not conflate them. The 1916 guard mention predates the 1917 build date; unexplained. Elevation differs slightly between sources.

Height 32.9 m is converted from the register's 108 feet. The register also mentions 29-foot towers of another type, which we did not attempt to reconcile. Staffing as_of is 2015 because the register's staffing line is undated; the 2015 Cal Fire post is the newest dated item read. The Placer County lookout page returned HTTP 403 and was not used. Access level is not stated in any source, so none is recorded. Verification 2026-10-08: the 1947 date is now worded as the register's own account (materials stored until 1947, when manpower was available to build), not as a confirmed completion date; the climbing advice was removed because no source supports it.

Current access and rental status are not stated in any source read. The NHLR entry is dated 2017 and the Peakbagging photo is from 2011, so the status is at least several years old. The 1962 hire is known only from an Oakdale newspaper as quoted on the Forest Lookouts site; the story now says she took a summer job as a fire lookout, which is the newspaper's wording. The rental finding is negative: the FFLA California list (checked 2026-10-08) shows ten rentals, none at Woods Ridge. Staffing as_of is 2017, the NHLR's status date. Verification 2026-10-08: the advice to ask the ranger district and not to climb the tower was removed because no source supports it.

Record's built 1914 and gone status hold. Access rests on a Santa Maria Times column about Zaca Lake and its trail, not a survey of the summit, so access is public with a caveat. No source describes remains on the peak. Figueroa Mountain, the 1917 successor site, is not covered here.

Dates rest on one register description, which says 'possibly' for the 1957 build. The FFA list only repeats the Removed status. Material corrected from steel to metal; height_m 9.1 is converted from the register's approximately 30 feet. No access source, so access is omitted. The staffed-for-a-few-years statement has no year, so it is not an event. Nothing describes remains on the site.

Very thin record: no build date, design, staffing or removal year appears in any source read. Two searches and about six pages checked; the Colorado/Utah FFLA chapter site was linked from the register but not separately fetched. The 1948 abandonment is for the Alta mining town, not the tower; it is in the story only as context and the event is not tower-specific. The register's coordinates (37.885220, -107.854060) and Wikipedia's townsite coordinates (37.88583, -107.85167) are roughly 200 m apart by our reckoning, which is why the story says 'a short distance away'. Source conflicts: forest name (San Juan vs Montezuma), type (tower vs tram house), and status wording (taken down / abandoned / removed). The ghosttowntrails.com page was not used: it covers the townsite and is a membership site. Worth a human check: a current photo or Forest Service record of the tramway and whether the lookout site is open.

Only three pages were usable and none gives a build date, design, staffing or fire history. The Southern Ute Indian Agency link comes from one line on the Forest Lookouts page and no other source confirms it, so verify it before publishing; the brief had no agency. The FFLA list shows the tower as removed with no register number. Wikipedia is used only for the location; its 1996 wildfire on the mesa is unrelated and left out. A YouTube search snippet claims a 1936 build, but the video was not read, so that date is unverified and not used. Two web searches found nothing else.

Brief record checked: lat/lon and elevation match the FFLOS detail page; no corrections. The FFA list gives 39.04917, -105.51278, about 30 m from the FFLOS point. Build and removal years rest on one FFLOS description; the other two sources say only removed. No staffing, fire, access or remains information in the sources read, so those keys are left out. The 1958 FFLOS photo has no image URL in our cache, so it is not in photos. Wikipedia's peak article was not used.

Build decade comes from one FFLOS line; Forest Lookouts and the FFA list say only removed. Conflict left open: the San Juan handbook (fire records from 1909 over 33 years, so roughly early 1940s) says lookouts were planned for Baldy Mountain, which may or may not be this peak; if it is, it sits badly with a 1920s tower. The brief lists kind as unknown, but FFLOS calls it 'This tower' and the FFA list says Unknown type; the editor may want kind=tower. No access, staffing or fire information found, so those keys are left out. Two WebSearch-style lookups and one San Juan Forest page read were used.

Only the FFLOS detail page gives any description (built in the 1910s, taken down in the 1920s); the other two sources say only removed. Brief lat/lon and elevation match FFLOS to rounding. The brief lists kind as unknown, but FFLOS calls it 'This tower'; the FFA list says Unknown type, so the editor may want kind=tower. No staffing, fire, access or remains information found, so those keys are left out. The site's register entry and the San Juan National Forest are the only place-level sources.

Brief's 2022 entries for the cab door and stair treads: the 2022 report gives no year ('last summer'), so the event year is the report year. Brief's 2021 solar date is supported ('As of 2021'). Staffing is as of the 2020 article; current staffing unknown. Material (wood vs steel) and gate location disagree across sources and are flagged, not resolved. The Dangerous Roads guide is third-party; confirm the gate and winter closure with the Dolores Ranger District. Pages read: 6 (NHLR, Forest Lookouts, the 2022 PDF with two greps, the Journal article, Dangerous Roads). Searches: 1. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the register puts the gate 0.3 mile below the tower and the story now says so; the 2019 batteries were being replaced and the story now says so; the 2020 article is dated only by its 50th-anniversary reference, so the JSON no longer gives a month.

Only two sources, a register entry and a state list. Neither gives a build year, a design, staffing or fire history, so the story leaves those out. Two WebSearch runs returned other Blue Mountain lookouts (NY, MT, WA, Victoria AU) and the Eightmile Mesa lookout in Archuleta County, which is a different site and was not used. Brief record checked: status, elevation, register number and coordinates agree with the register. The Colorado list coordinates differ from the register by a short distance; the story reports both.

Only three thin sources; no build year, design, staffing or fire history in any page I could open, so the story leaves those out. Search summaries (not opened, not used) point to a firelookout.org/cohost-co/burro.html entry that gives a 1910s build, a 1914 photo and an Old Montezuma National Forest label; that page returns 404 in the cache under both http and https, so verify it before adding any build detail. The 1947 forest consolidation sentence (source 4) is context only; no source ties this lookout to the old Montezuma forest. Brief elevation (3541.8 m) and coordinates match the register.

Newspaper items are read from a lookout-history site's transcriptions, not scanned originals. Elevation differs by source: 10,974 ft for the register's site, 11,434 ft in the 1919 guidebook, and about 11,305 ft for the peak on Wikipedia (not used in the story). Staffing rests only on 1919-1921 newspaper items. The brief's agency field (BLM) is supported by the register and left unchanged. Nominator name from the register is kept in the 2011 event note.

Access, visiting and rental status are not in any source read, so no access or visit keys are set. Staffing is from the 2019 Register review only; no current staffing source. No fire history found. Record kind 'platform' is proposed as 'tower with open cab'. The NPS page is for an ancient tower with a similar name and does not mention this lookout. Park Point Lookout, the park's other lookout, was not researched. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story no longer calls the Forest Lookouts summary 'earlier' (its date is not given) and says towers were mainly built in the Classic period, rather than 'around' those dates.

The record's kind 'two_story' is kept: the register describes a one-story stone base with a wooden cab, and the Association lists a '2-Story Cab'. No change proposed. The 1970 removal year is a stand-in for 'the 1970s'. The register's 'closed to the public' line has no date, so the story does not state current access beyond the Forest Service tour dates. Staffing is not in the sources and is omitted.

The register gives no build date, so the record has no built event; the 1963 newspaper item is the earliest dated mention. The 1967 removal year is the earlier of the register's two probable years. The 1963 item names a summer employee; the name is left out of the story and the research record. Both sources are short, and no photo or later description of the site was found.

No independent source beyond NHLR and the FFLA Colorado list was found in the cache or a quick check; both agree on name, location and standing status (FFLA uses 'Deadman Mountain'). The NHLR page is unusually detailed for a short tower (CCC predecessor, 2004 visit narrative, 2019 condition note, Sprint cell-site encroachment), so confidence is medium rather than low despite having only one substantive source. Worth flagging: do not confuse with the unrelated 'Deadman Mountain Lookout' in Wyoming, which also appears in the raw cache and is a different structure.

No source I read describes staffing, fires, current access or the site's condition beyond the footings, so the story leaves those out and the facts carry no access entry. The register's 30-foot figure is converted to 9.1 m for height_m. Coordinates: the brief's point (37.28419, -107.27622) matches the Colorado register; firelookout.org lists 37.28442, -107.27596, about 35 m away, the same site. The brief's elevation (3,027.3 m) matches the register. One web search was run. A core.tdar.org record titled Devil Mountain Fire Lookout (a 1996 assessment of Colorado national forest properties) appeared in results but was not opened; it may hold construction detail.

Stair count: Wikipedia gives 143 stairs for the last stretch of the trail; the NRHP nomination counts 243 steps up the whole stairway. Staffing: the first documented staffing is Helen Dowe (1919-1921), so the story no longer says staffing began with the 1912 station. Built dates: the NRHP nomination (first station 1912, 1919 tower, 1951 present lookout) and Wikipedia agree; the register's 'constructed in 1912' for the cab conflicts, and the correction proposal relies on the nomination. Wikipedia gives the NRHP listing as both 1991 and June 13, 2003; the NPGallery record supports 2003. Elevation differs: register 9,702 ft (2,957 m; the record's 2957.2 m), Wikipedia 9,748 ft (2,971 m). Visitor numbers in the register differ (over 15,000 a year in one passage, about 40,000 a season in the 2019 note). The 2025 chapter report says the lookout was not staffed in 2025 and will not be in 2026; the staffing record is updated accordingly. Whether the cab is open to visitors is not established by these sources, so the access note stays cautious. Both sources give only the 1930s for construction, so the events list has no build entry (the schema needs a year); add one once a dated source is found. Search summaries (not used): a USFS assessment, Administering the National Forests of Colorado, Table 5, suggesting a CCC F-53-C Lone Dome crew, and a local researcher's topo-map pin. Two registers agree on design and dates. The access statement rests only on onX, a trail-guide site, so confirm with the San Juan NF Pagosa Ranger District. No staffing history or notable fires found in the sources read. NHLR Lookout.aspx?id=915 returned HTTP 500 and was not used. No rental listing found. A search result about a prescribed fire on Eight Mile Mesa was not read and is not used.

Build date disagrees across sources and is left open: NHLR detail gives 1911, its description gives 1912, and Forest Lookouts gives plans c.1907 and construction 1908-09 under Ranger Jack Cammann. Staffing also disagrees: Forest Lookouts gives 1910-14 with abandonment, but a 1919 guidebook it quotes describes a man stationed there in dry periods; the abandonment year 1914 is the end of that range. Record items not found in pages read and left out: the $500 FFLA grant (2008), the 2015 restoration and removal from the high-risk list. A search summary of Wikipedia mentions a 2015 cupola rebuild by Historicorps; not read, not used. Access rests only on the 2019 survey; no current closure or rental notice was read. No photos added: NHLR mentions a July 2024 photo by Ian Roberts but no image URL was retrieved. Budget: six page reads and two web searches used.

Coordinates (38.040996, -105.012697, elev ~2252m per OSM) fall in the Wet Mountains near Greenhorn Mountain/St Charles Peak/Lake Isabel, San Isabel National Forest area, but no cached or web source ties a named lookout to that exact point. Checked every cached NHLR and FFLOS Colorado entry's coordinates (both index pages) and none are within a reasonable distance of this node. Three WebSearch queries (generic coordinate/region search, San Isabel NF fire tower history, named Wet Mountains peaks) turned up nothing specific to this structure. Possible the OSM 'Fire Tower' label is generic (e.g. a different kind of tower, or a genuinely obscure/undocumented lookout) rather than a proper name — worth a human look if better aerial/historic-map sources become available.

Sources are short register entries. None gives design, height, staffing, fires or site condition, so the story omits them. Nothing found describes the Glade site today. The NHLR Benchmark page (as of 2019) mentions a locked gate installed after vandalism; that belongs to Benchmark's own record. Search budget was exceeded by one websearch.py call (three used). A Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook post about a 1941 Glade photo was not in the cache and was not read.

Core history (1908 stone shelter, 1933 damage, 1939 rebuild, c.1942 enlargement, 2014-2017 restoration, 2018 vandalism) is consistent across the NHLR, Forest Service, Historic Routt County and Colorado Preservation pages. Open points: the NHLR elevation (10,759 ft) differs from the 10,839 ft given by the agency and two other sources; the exact year staffing ended is not recorded; the History Colorado page (which gives about 1947) returned no text when fetched, so it is not used. The cohost-co firelookout.org page listed in the brief's source_pages returned a 404; dropped from sources. No specific named fires found in available sources.

Core history rests on NHLR and the West Lookouts newspaper quotes. The 1915 end of staffing and the lightning abandonment come from one 2014 hiker blog, so treat them as medium. No rental listing for Leon Peak found; the Next Summit article's rental lookout is a different site.

Only status and registration are sourced. Register calls it a tower site; the FFLA Colorado list calls the structure a platform. The FFLA list spells the county 'Sagauche' (typo, not used). Exact height_m and precise CCC construction dates beyond 1940 were not found; RIDB only says 'built in the 1940s' while NHLR gives 1940 specifically, so I used 1940. No conflicting built-year sources requiring a resolved_conflicts entry. Two sources. The register gives the 1942 build, the temporary building, the purpose caption and the elevation, but has no removal field. Access is from OuterSpatial and the summit road status may change seasonally, so the story says so.

Three sources agree the tower is gone; none gives a build year, design, staffing or fire history, and none describes the site today. Do not link the August 2009 Narraguinnep Fire to this tower: the Benchmark Fire Lookout (a different tower, westlookouts.weebly.com/benchmark.html) is the one reported evacuated. The record's photo file name hints at June 1940, but the register page gives no caption, so it was not used. Public access unknown.

Only the register gives construction and removal, and it gives the removal only as 'the 1970s' (stored as 1970 with a note). The 4x4 guide is undated and may be out of date on access. No staffing or fire sources were found. The access road is public forest road; the story does not say whether any part of the lookout remains at the summit, because no source says so.

The brief's kind 'ground' may be wrong. The brief's events omitted the 1916 build and the 1948 end of use; those are added here as events, not corrections. The platform's history is absent: no source gives a build date, design, staffing, or fire record, and the Wikipedia article has no lookout history. Two thin sources. The 1931 item is quoted second-hand on the Forest Lookouts page; the original newspaper was not checked. The FFLA gives type Unknown and no NHLR or FFLOS number. Only two sources located: the NHLR detail page and the FFLA Colorado list. Unresolved: builder (Wikipedia says CCC labor, Conservancy says local contractor) and last year of use (NHLR and Conservancy say 1969 or late 1960s, Wikipedia says 1978). Thin record. No source read gives a built date, design, staffing, or history; the FFLA gives the point no type or status. Removal year conflicts (1976 vs 1996) and the story reports both. The tower stood on Starr Peak per SummitPost and the Daily Camera, while the FFLOS record is named for the mountain. Four sources disagree on the replacement and removal years (1949, 1950, 1953; 1969, 1976, 1977); the story reports the spread. The NRHP nomination is a PDF with later amendments. Two short sources only. Thin record: only the register entry and one Forest Lookouts entry were found. No build date, builder, staffing, fires or removal date were found in any source read. No source read gives a build date, staffing, agency or access for the Mount Parnassus lookout. The only status source is the Forest Lookouts 'Removed' label, undated. No build date, designer or owner name is confirmed. The only build claim is an unverified forum reply (2008). No source gives a removal date, so no removed event is recorded. No staffing or post-1938 fire history was found. Assumes the register's 23' is structure height (height_m 7.0). Removal date rests on the association's pages ('between 2002-2006'); no state or agency record was found, and the State Police hand-over has no date. No build date, designer, cost or design history for the tower was found in two searches and about five page reads. No build date, design, height, or staffing found in the two sources read. The NHLR 'Elevation' of 27 ft (8 m) is ground elevation, so the brief's elevation_m 8.2 is not a tower height. Thin record. Neither the register nor the Forest Lookouts page gives a build year, staffing history, fire history, or access rules. The FDACS page describes the forest's wildfire history but does not mention the tower. The OpenStreetMap point for the tower was checked but is community-edited and not cited. One page read ran over the per-tower budget because the first grep pass was partial. The register prints the elevation as 133 ft (41 m); 133 ft is 40.5 m, and the story uses the register's printed figure. Verification 2026-10-08: the steel-tower description is now attributed to Forest Lookouts, which is the only source that says steel; 'northern Baker County' was corrected to Baker County in northern Florida; the advice to ask the Florida Forest Service and not to climb was removed because FDACS does not support it.

Every tower fact rests on one register entry (FFLOS); Forest Lookouts adds only the county. No build date, design source, staffing, fire history or access description was found. The 1950 removal year is a placeholder for '1940s or 1950s'. Two searches and several page reads found nothing else for this site. Wikipedia is used only for the community's location, not the tower.

Register page is the only substantive source. The brief's 2017 News-Press article (news-press.com, story 99520472) returned HTTP 403 and is not cited; the register links to a 2017 article under a 'Their watch has ended' title, but nothing shows it concerns this tower. The register gives no build date and says the tower may have stood in one or two earlier places, so 'standing' applies to the 2024 site only. A web search for Golden Gate turned up an unrelated Naples tower (a 2000 antenna structure from a tower database, not read and not used). Brief elevation 5.5 m matches 18 ft in the register. Access is omitted because no source describes it. Photo captions were read: two captioned 1990s and credited to the Florida Forest Service, one captioned 2024 and credited to Brad Eells, and several more credited to Eells without dates. Image URLs were not captured, so no photos array. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the story no longer says nobody recorded the build date, and its photo sentence now covers only the captioned photos.

Height (85 ft, 25.9 m) and the 1936 date come only from a blog quoting a Water Atlas PDF that was not opened; verify before publishing a stronger claim. NHLR's '52 ft (16 m)' is labeled Elevation, so it is ground elevation, and the brief's elevation_m 15.8 is that figure. Climbing status of the tower is not documented. Page reads: 7 (one over the cap), because some pages were re-read to get full text.

Thin record. NHLR is the only tower-specific source: location, elevation, registry number, registration date and administrator. The Forest Lookouts page is a stub with name and county only. No build year, designer, staffing, fire history or access/visit information was found. The Scribd history (a user upload of a 2006 Division of Forestry compilation) is general context on the 1930s tower network and does not name this tower. Florida Memory image pages (items 140289 and 106202) returned HTTP 403, so any photo captions there are unread. Wikidata has a bare label only. The NHLR Florida index shows no rental or visit data for this tower. Recommend a Florida Forest Service or regional newspaper check for the build year before a fuller history. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the register never uses the word standing; the story now attributes only the present-tense placement to it.

Thin record. NHLR is the only tower-specific source: location on SR 20, elevation, registry number, registration date and administrator. The Forest Lookouts page is a stub giving name and county (spelled 'Putnum'). Wikipedia supplies only community context. No build year, designer, staffing, fire history or access information was found. Do not use archive.org item casbcfm_001263 ('Hollister Division of Forestry headquarters', 1956): it is a San Benito County, California photo, a different place.
