The Scribd history is general context and does not name this tower. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the register never uses the word standing; the story now attributes only the present-tense placement to it.

Thin record. NHLR is the only tower-specific source: site description, elevation, registry number, registration date and administrator. Conflict to check: the same NHLR entry uses present tense for the tower yet calls its site a former Division of Forestry site, and the sources read do not say whether the tower itself remains as described. The Forest Lookouts page is a stub with name and county only. No build year, designer, staffing, fire history, access or rental information was found; the NHLR Florida index has no rental or visit data for this tower. Wikidata has a bare label only. The Scribd history is general context and does not name Homosassa. Tampa Bay Times and Lakeland Ledger tower articles returned empty or HTTP 403, so they were not used. Recommend a Citrus County or Florida Forest Service check of the current condition before any status is assigned. Fact-check 2026-10-09: status moved from standing to unknown because the register never uses the word standing.

No build date, staffing schedule or public-access information was found in the sources read; access is omitted rather than guessed. The Register's 100-foot figure is used for height_m, following the convention in other records. The booklet is a Scribd copy of a Division publication, not checked against an original; it is cited only for the Dixie County background, and its text never names Jonesboro. Site described as mostly abandoned by the Division, with the tower still used occasionally. Abandoned has no year, so it is left out of events. The footnote 2 title follows the Scribd page heading.

Single source: the NHLR entry was the only page read that gives a build date and design. The NHLR 'Elevation' of 103 ft (31 m) is ground elevation, not tower height, so the brief's elevation_m 31.4 is ground elevation. The Lakeland Ledger 2015 article on Polk's aging towers returned HTTP 403 when fetched; its search snippet suggests the tower near Lake Pierce was 'barely hanging on', which would change the status. Check it before publishing. The FL DEP Broussard Catfish Creek Preserve plan says park access is from Firetower Road south of Lake Hatchineha Road, but it does not confirm the tower's location, so it was not cited. Page reads: 6.

The 2005 purchase year is inferred from a January 7, 2006 article saying one year ago, and it is shown as inferred. The News Bulletin 2015 article is paywalled after its first paragraph, so only the registration sentence was used. No design or height is given in the sources read. No dated source confirms the tower's current condition beyond the undated city page calling it the fire tower beside the center. Climbing access is undocumented.

The record's point (29.115192, -80.948894) is not described on the OSM page itself. No NHLR or former-site entry matches it, and the OSM entry gives no name or history. The Florida tower list at tnlandforms.us (revised 2016) has no tower within about 6 km of the point; its only nearby entry is labelled 'gimlet' with no lookout attached. The OSM entry (way 264235672) was last edited about nine years ago (changeset 48449176). Suggest checking aerial imagery or the Volusia County GIS to see what structure is there. If it is not a lookout, the record should be removed. The Tiger Bay Road drill tower is a county training structure, not linked to this entry. The story is short because there is nothing more to tell.

One detailed source (Forest Lookouts, quoting the Bradford County Telegraph for 1939 and 1942) plus an OSM point. The page's 100-foot height is used for height_m (30.5 m). The OSM ele value 64 is a map elevation, not tower height. Waymarking pages for this tower exist, but their text did not cache and were not cited. A WebFetch summary of one page mentioned a May 2023 visit log but no condition, so it is not used. Today's condition and access need a Florida Forest Service contact or a recent site report.

Single-register history: every built, design and registration fact comes from the NHLR page; the Eastern US Lookouts page has no details for Magnolia. The Florida Memory and Lakeland Ledger pages returned HTTP 403 to fetch_text, so they were not read. Who holds the land is unclear: the register says ownership reverted to adjacent landowners and names the LDS church as administrator. Access is marked private on that basis; confirm before publishing. The register gives height only as a 100 to 120 ft range, so no height_m is entered. The record's county, agency and 1933 build year agree with the register.

Thin record. NHLR says little is known. The only substantive source is an urban-exploration photo tour (Abandoned in 360, August 2025) that uses hedged language ('likely', 'perhaps') and gives a 1953 completion, a Florida Forest Service builder and a guessed 100 ft height; those are attributed in the story and not put in facts as verified. The mid-2000s closure (the article's only dated support for it is a wall map marked Spring/Summer 2008), the 1999 tower count and the staffing narrative in that article are not used as facts; the story attributes the closure to the photo tour. The link between the NHLR 'Marion County Airfield' tower and the photo tour's Dunnellon Ranger Station is inferred from names and location; no page says they are one structure. Museum of Florida History returned HTTP 500 and floridamemory.com returned 403; not retried. Access, visit and staffing are unknown and left out of facts. NHLR credits a photo to David Viero, but the image and licence were not checked, so no photo entry was added. Two web searches were used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: story now says registered (NHLR 'Date Registered', not accepted), gives the Dunnellon Army Air Field as the name the field was known by, and attributes the mid-2000s closure to the photo tour without implying a record.

Every fact here rests on one Register entry. No build date, staffing, fire history or access information was found in the two searches and page reads. The record's standing status has not been checked against anything newer than the 2016 rehab. Height_m uses the Register's 120-foot figure, following the convention in other records. No photos were located.

Brief record is correct on height (100 ft = 30.5 m) and design. The article's column text is jumbled; quotes were taken from the cached text. Its paragraph about land bought in 1944 and a tower built in 1945 by International refers to another tower (probably Wacissa), so it was not used. The Forest Lookouts page gives no staffing list. No post-2009 source was found; the site today is unknown. OpenStreetMap node 358719663 still maps a tower point at the location, which does not show that anything stands there.

Thin history. The NHLR entry is the substantive source: it gives the 80-foot height, the standing-since-1935 date, the Indian Mound location, the USFWS administration and the 2014 nomination by Brian Pippin, but no build date, builder, staffing or fire history. The Forest Lookouts page has little more than a header. The OpenStreetMap node gives height 25 (units assumed metres) and ele 2; facts height_m 24.4 is the NHLR's 80 ft converted, and the OSM tag is not used as a fact. The refuge fact comes from the FWS page (refuge establishment, 1931) and is not tied to the tower in any source. The Friends of St. Marks history timeline has no entry for the tower. The floridamemory.com item on a St. Marks refuge fire tower was not readable (HTTP 403). Access, visit and staffing unknown and left out of facts. The NHLR photo is credited to Brian Pippin; no photo entry added. Two web searches and about six page reads were used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: story now says registered (NHLR 'Date Registered', not accepted) and describes the Forest Lookouts page as carrying little more than a header.

One register page carries the substance; Wikipedia is used only for the county disagreement. Two web searches found nothing on the tower's build date, builder, staffing, fires or public access. Story is short (about 160 words) because the record is short. No photos found.

The WPTV report carries no date in the copy read, so its 50-year figure and the drought-season staffing read are undated. Staffing is coded 'emergency', the closest schema value, for the severe-drought watch described; the report gives no schedule for other seasons. The Register and the report use different agency names (FDACS and Florida Forest Service); neither source says how they relate, so both are reported as written. No build date found. Access is omitted: neither source describes public visits.

The 1931 build date and Forest Service credit come from the NHLR page and the Eastern US Lookouts page, which agree. The HMDB marker's CCC claim conflicts with that date and is unresolved; the story says so. Current climbing access is not confirmed by any official source. The only climbing statement is in a Komoot trail listing, a third-party app whose text may be generated, so verify with Osceola National Forest or Florida State Parks before publishing the access level as public (floridastateparks.org returned HTTP 403). The marker's listed coordinates are within roughly 15 m of the register's, so the marker sits at the tower. The record's height_m of 30.5 agrees with the register's 100 ft, but the register does not say whether that is to the cab floor, so it is not restated as a fact. A USFS page on the Olustee Experimental Forest timed out and was not read.

Two cached sources agree on Lee County, the 100-foot Aermotor design, the 1961 assembly or erection, the Florida Forest Service role and the 2024 registration. Both News-Press articles (2015 and 2017) returned HTTP 403 from fetch_text, so they are not cited. Search snippets from them mention the 1961 acquisition and that this is the only standing fire tower in Lee County; they need a cached copy before staffing, fires or the SR 80 location can be added. The brief's 'built 1961' is kept, but the sources describe assembly or erection in that year, not an original build date. Access is omitted because no source states a visiting rule.

Thin record. The brief's source starfl.com/news/20181108/toppled-by-michael returns HTTP 404 from the cache, so that article is unread. The register page links to 'Toppled by Michael - Photos' (target not read). Two web searches found no other coverage of this tower. No build date, design or height appears in any source read, so none is recorded. The 1988 item is reproduced on the Forest Lookouts site and attributed there to the Panama City News-Herald; the original newspaper was not checked. The 1988 'staffed' and 'fire' events rest on that one reprint. The brief's elevation (3 m) matches the register's 10 ft (3 m) and is an elevation, not a tower height.

Very thin: a short Forest Lookouts entry (county and agency) and an OSM height tag. Two web searches and a Wikipedia check (Palmdale, Florida) found no tower history. The 60.96 m height is a volunteer map value, not verified. Contact the Florida Forest Service before publishing the status or height as fact.

Only two thin sources, and the build date and builder are unknown. The register's WPA claim is the nominator's own belief ('I believe'). A Florida Memory catalogue entry titled 'Gate entrance and tower at CCC camp in Pine Top' (floridamemory.com/items/show/62708) appeared in search results and points the other way, but floridamemory.com returned HTTP 403 to fetch_text, so it is not cited; check it by hand. The 1957 article's state-built line covers the headquarters buildings and does not say whether the tower was one of them. Access is marked restricted only because the tower sits at a forestry station. Note for the team: the 'A Legacy Remembered' CCC marker (hmdb.org m=55674) surfaced in a Pine Top search, but its coordinates and text place it at Olustee, not Pine Top, so it is not used here. The record's ownership 'federal' is the main correction proposed; the agency field already reads Florida Forest Service.

Single readable source: the NHLR detail page (cached). Unresolved conflicts, not in the story: (1) A Waymarking page (wm5GXN_Punta_Gorda_Lookout_Tower_PID_AD7808) cites a 1982 Florida DOT description of a steel tower about 110 feet high, about 8.5 miles southeast of Punta Gorda on the northeast side of US 41 northbound. That conflicts with NHLR's 100 ft and forestry-station siting. fetch_text could not read the page body (only the title was cached), so nothing from it is quoted; a human should check whether it is the same tower. (2) The record's news-press source (2017 Lee County fire-towers article) returns HTTP 403. A search snippet describes the Caloosahatchee Forestry Center tower in Lee County, so it is probably not a Punta Gorda source; not cited. (3) The Forest Lookouts Weebly index lists PUNTA GORDA under Glades County, but only in navigation text with no body, so it is not used. Not verified: construction date, builder, fire history, staffing, public access. The record's ownership 'federal' is contradicted by NHLR (correction proposed). No photos added; the record's NHLR photos are all rights reserved.

Thin record. The 1958 fire item is quoted from The Evening Independent on an enthusiast site; the page dates it October 12, 1958. I did not check the newspaper itself. The 2005 bid appears only on that same site (dated September 14, 2005); I found no buyer, sale record or government auction listing. The 2015 report excerpt is headed '2015 & beginning 2016'. It lists Salem #268 (standing) and #318 (removed) but names no county, so it is not known whether either is this Taylor County tower. The status 'standing' in the record comes from the OSM and eastern lookouts records; no dated source I read confirms it. The FFLA Florida caches in data/raw/ffla have no Salem entry. The title and publisher for source 2 come from the URL and search results, not the document cover. Suggested checks: a Florida Forest Service public-records request for the 2005 sale and tower history; the Florida lookout association about Salem #268 and #318; OSM node 10012727105 (tagged tower:type observation). No corrections proposed.

Facts rest on one register entry plus the Forest Lookouts removal note; no build date, design source, staffing or fire history was found. The register says likely under 60 ft, so no height_m is recorded. Wikipedia is used only for the community's location. The anyplaceamerica 'Salt Springs Tower (historical)' listing returned 403 and was not read. Not checked: whether the register's site location is inside the Ocala NF boundary.

Thin record. The FFLOS page gives the footings statement, the 2020 registration, the nominator and the administrator. The Forest Lookouts South Tower entry is only a name, county and forest. Two searches found no build date, design, height, staffing, fires or access information. A 1957 photo caption from a Historic Florida group (seen in a search snippet only; not fetched or cited) mentions a South Tower Recreation Area in the Ocala forest; worth checking in a state or Forest Service archive. The brief's access 'unknown' is left unfilled because no source states an access level.

Original build date is not in any source (register gives no year for the State's build). Brief's access 'unknown' corrected to closed. The Weebly Flagler page (Wadsworth record) attaches a 1959 Southside rename to a Flagler County tower; that conflicts with the park history. The Florida chapter report asks whether the Jacksonville Heights tower was re-erected as Southside; unverified, not used. No new photos added.

One map feature and no other record. Status 'standing' in the record rests only on the map point; no photo or second source confirms it stands, so verify before publishing that status. The name is generic. No owner or operator identified, and I did not trace the mapper's edit history. Firehouse report (2010, Lake County) is background only and is not linked to this structure. Searches for 'The Fire Lookout Tower' in Lee County found nothing. Visit: private, nothing to visit.

Only the NHLR page describes this tower in text. The 2015 Commons photo is matched to the register's location by our own comparison of coordinates, not by its caption, so treat it as likely rather than confirmed. No build date, staffing or access terms were found. Florida Memory item 326330 (a Florida Forest Service building and fire observation tower) returned 403 and was not read. The photo's upload path was confirmed to resolve (image/jpeg, HTTP 200).

Construction date, access and agency are not established. The register has no visit reports. The Weebly Flagler listing may describe the Jacksonville tower under this record (see us-fl-southside-forestry); its 80-foot height and 1959 rename are not used as facts. The Florida chapter report says the Jacksonville and Palm Coast towers were both once called Flagler Tower. A News-Journal 2012 article on the Wadsworth tower returned HTTP 403 and was not used. Brief's elevation (13.4 m) and coordinates match the register (44 ft; 29.534523, -81.262412).

Thin record. The NHLR page gives the design, the 1931 build, the Columbia County location, the 135 ft elevation and the 2013 registration, all matching the brief. Forest Lookouts confirms 1931 and the Forest Service erection. Not found: staffing, fires, access rules, and any condition report after 2013, so the standing status is unverified. The Tebesir article is a generic travel piece and is weak evidence; it is cited only for its past-tense wording. A Florida Memory item about the three Osceola towers returned HTTP 403 and was not used. Height 30.5 m is 100 ft from the NHLR. The brief's record needs no corrections. Fact-check 2026-10-09: 'at the top' removed (the Register page does not say it); 'accepted' changed to 'registered' to match the Register's Date Registered label; the status is now unverified to match the story; the camp sentence says 'fire lookout' because the page's only 'tower' matches are the names West Tower Hunt Camp and West Tower Equestrian Trails.

The brief's blow-down date, registration and agency check out against FFLOS. The history rests on two 1940s-era newspaper items and a 1964 NGS station description, all read through the Forest Lookouts transcription rather than the originals. The 1948 and 1964 accounts conflict on material and distance (see resolved_conflicts). A 2014 News Herald article (search snippet only; the fetch returned 403) says a Youngstown forest ranger still went up the Bay County tower when alerted; if it can be read from another route it may support a staffing sentence. The brief's access 'unknown' is left unfilled; no source states an access level.

Thin record. The NHLR page gives the description, 2022 registration, nominator and maintaining agency. The Forest Lookouts Becker page is a single line with a Rayonier Corp entry that is not explained. No build year, staffing, fire history, visit reports or access rules were found. Two searches returned no news coverage of this tower. The County Insider item is about a different tribute tower at the Wildlight development and is cited only to tell the two apart and to describe Rayonier's timber history; it does not connect Rayonier to this tower. The Florida Forest Service page does not say whether the agency runs this tower. Height 30.5 m is 100 ft from the NHLR; the brief had no height. Fact-check 2026-10-09: 'newer' removed (the item does not say the tower is new); 'accepted' changed to 'registered'; 'local news item' changed to a Nassau County publication, since the item is written from the county's side; the Florida Forest Service sentence now follows the FDACS page; the status is unverified to match the story.

No build date, design, height, staffing or fire history was found in the sources read. The Commons file title says GA216, but tnlandforms assigns GA216 to Fargo (Clinch County) and Baker to GA272. The file's camera position is about 75 m from the Baker coordinates, so the match is likely but not confirmed. The photo url is the Commons file page, not a direct image URL. The brief's register numbers BLL US 41122 and GFC US 209 were not confirmed by the sources read (tnlandforms shows BLL-41122 and gfc-209). The 2006 Savannah Morning News article returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

Thin record: only the Georgia list and one OpenStreetMap node. No build date, staffing or fire history was found in NHLR, FFLOS, Wikipedia, or two web searches (no GFC, newspaper or NRHP hit). The story is short by design. OpenStreetMap says demolished but gives no date. The brief's elevation (198.4 m) comes from the Georgia list and was not checked against a second source.

Ownership conflict: the record is headed Ware County - Georgia Forestry Commission, yet the county sold the structure in 2006; brief's ownership 'state' was not changed. A GovDeals auction listing ('FIRE TOWER used by the Georgia Forestry Commission', located 1.3 miles west of the Bickley Fire Station) appeared in search, but govdeals.com returned HTTP 403 and it is not cited; it may date the sale and show the site, so worth a manual check. A 2006 Savannah Morning News fire-tower article also returned 403. No photos on Wikimedia Commons for this tower.

Best-documented of the three: the NHLR page has three visit reports (Jan 19 2014, Oct 4 2014, Nov 25 2018) covering staffing, locks, the road and condition. The 1949 build date matches NHLR and Georgia ForestWatch. The willhiteweb page is a hiker's history site; its paper-sign CCC attribution and 1938 map line are reported with attribution and not treated as established. The NHLR description calls the tower a '33' metal tower' with a CL-100 series cab; no height is recorded because the figure is unclear. The Oct 2014 'mile hike' and the 0.4-mile AT detour are different routes, not reconciled. A mountainquailpress.com result for Black Mountain describes a tower in California (San Jacinto Mountains) and was excluded. Access is recorded as closed because the tower is fenced and locked; no source says the public may climb it. The 2018 visit report is the latest condition evidence. Fact-check 2026-10-09: 'on the summit' removed from the lead (neither the Register nor ForestWatch says so; the hiker's site only mentions the summit in passing); the repeater sentence keeps the Register's 'it appears' hedge; 'accepted' changed to 'registered'; 'other users' replaced by the groups the hiker's site lists; the Register names no builder, which is a negative claim checked against the full page.

Four sources, and none gives a build year or designer; a Chattahoochee National Forest history or a Blue Ridge Ranger District contact is the next step. Elevation differs by source: register 3,060 ft (933 m), N2Backpacking 3027 ft, and a Georgia tower list 3016 ft; the record's 932.7 m follows the register. Staffing is undated (Mountain Travel Guide). The closed status rests on the 2019 register entry and two undated web guides, so confirm with the Forest Service before presenting it as current. The record's access 'unknown' is now 'closed'.

One detailed source (the register entry with a May 2018 visitor report) and one tower list. No build year, design, staffing or current access status found. The visitor's note on public or private ownership is unresolved; a Gordon County or Georgia Forestry Commission contact is the best next step. Treat the 'standing' status as last confirmed in 2018.

Current public access/climbing status is not documented in either source; worth a follow-up with the Chattahoochee National Forest or GFC. Build-year and NRHP-listing-year conflicts between the two sources are noted but not resolved.

The register gives only a range (late 1950s to early 1960s) for the build, so no built event is recorded. The register's coordinates place the tower at the forestry office rather than on a summit. Elevation: register 1,721 ft (525 m), tnlandforms 1715 ft; the record's 524.6 m is consistent. Visit terms (staff escort) and the 'no longer in active use' status come from the March 2019 register entry and are undated; confirm with the Lumpkin County forestry office before publishing.

Core facts (1953 erection by the Georgia Forestry Commission, 100-foot Aermotor steel tower, 7 by 7 cab, staffed until the 1990s, now used for communications) rest on the NHLR entry and are corroborated by Forest Lookouts for the year and design. No source gives the staffing end year, fire history, or access or visit rules, so those are left out of facts. Elevation: NHLR gives elevation 100 ft (30 m), which matches our record's elevation_m 30.5, but tnlandforms.us lists 103 ft for the west bainbridge site, so the two sources differ by about 3 ft; not a record error category, so not in corrections. Record height_m 30.5 matches NHLR 100 ft. West Bainbridge identity: tnlandforms GA261 coordinates (30.91725, -84.59683) match the NHLR site (30.917480, -84.596030) to within about 0.001 degrees, so the two entries describe one tower. Photo: a Wikimedia Commons file (Forestry Commission Tower, Decatur County.jpg, CC BY-SA 4.0, EXIF author name Michael Rivera, uploader Mjrmtg, GPS date 15 July 2017) was found but its direct image URL was not fetched, so no photos entry was added; the editor can add it. Its caption places a Georgia Forestry Commission tower on Dothan Road in Bainbridge; the caption does not name the Decatur County Fire Tower, so the link to this tower is inferred. Two web searches and about five page reads were used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the photo sentence now says a Georgia Forestry Commission tower and uses GPS date wording.

One register page carries the tower facts. The statewide blog is context only. Two web searches (Early County tower; Georgia Forestry Commission history) returned no tower-specific pages, and local city and county history pages had no mention. Access, fire history and current owner are not in any source read, so they are left out of facts. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. The record's 86 m elevation is the NHLR site elevation, not tower height. Story is at the low end of length because the evidence is thin.

Current status rests only on NHLR's present-tense 'located on' line; no source describes the tower's condition. Access marked private from the NHLR line that the tower is privately owned; no source read gives the owners' visiting policy. Staffing is not in any source. The brief's agency entry is the private owners, which NHLR names as administrators. The two Forest Lookouts pages agree with NHLR on the 1952 and 1973 history. A 100-foot 1952 line on the Georgia list sits under a different heading, so it is not used. Searches for the owners' own site found nothing usable. The brief's 218.5 m elevation matches NHLR's 717 ft.

Current status and staffing rest on the NHLR line that the tower remains in active service; the NHLR description carries no date, and no GFC or news source on current use was found. The Vanishing Georgia free text stops at a subscription paywall. It calls the tower very relevant in the same passage as the Bugaboo fire threat but does not explain the link, so the story does not claim one. Wikipedia says Bugaboo Fire; Vanishing Georgia says Bugaboo Scrub Fire. Access marked restricted is an inference from the ranger-station location, not a stated rule.

Thin record: NHLR is the substantive source and the Forest Lookouts Georgia list gives only county, agency and design. Status and access come from NHLR's 'appears to be abandoned' line and its note about removed steps; no newer source was found. The brief's standing status is kept with a status_note added. Two searches found no news or GFC page on this tower. Worth confirming on the ground that the tower still stands before any public use is suggested.

Replacement question is open: Weebly says the current tower is a replacement, but NHLR and Wikipedia date the tower to 1941 with no replacement mentioned. Access 'restricted' is my reading of the locked gate; no climbing rule in the sources. The 1960s event is coded as 1960 (decade only). The register gives 3,315 ft elevation, matching the brief's 1010.4 m; the tnlandforms list gives 3449 ft and was not used. Register coordinates match the brief. No new photos added.

No staffing, fire history, or rental information in any source read. Elevation sources disagree (3,511 ft NHLR vs 3,694 ft list and trail guide); the record's elevation_m 1070.2 follows the NHLR. Access rests on an undated trail guide and a 2014 trail report, so recheck before giving visit advice. Do not confuse with us-ga-glassy-mountain (the NHLR itself warns of this). A Forest Lookouts page mentions an August 1949 National Archives photo; that photo page was not read, so none is listed under photos.

The 1957 article gives Lowery's retirement (last year, at 82) and also says he was allowed to stay on for the new tower; the story reports both without choosing. Steel tower height and date of its removal are not in any source; the only fate word is 'Removed'. Single 1957 newspaper article, reprinted on Forest Lookouts; original Rome News-Tribune not found. The 1956 'built' event in the brief is really the replacement tower; the first lookout dates to 1930 per four sources. The height of 41 feet (12.5 m) follows the majority; the register's 30 feet is recorded in the story. The Forest Service post is a Facebook repost of a Forest Service history; part one (the 1930 story) was not fetched. The Facebook post's oral history dates the removal to 1984 and the post itself does not settle the date. The brief's registration event (2022) was not verified in the fetched page, so it is not added. Photo credits (Fire Lookout Museum; Nez Perce-Clearwater archives) come without image URLs, so none added.

Brief design L-4 confirmed by three site pages. Brief access 'unknown' kept; the Drive Up tag is the only access signal and is not a current-condition claim. The 1922 staff predate the 1930 L-4 tower, so the listing may refer to an earlier structure; the story says the sources do not say. Elevation 5910 ft is in the story but has no facts key. No photos added.

Brief height 18.3 m (60 ft), county and build year (1929) confirmed. The current-condition account is a single page note dated August 19, 2025, so treat it as a snapshot. A reader comment on the same page about a 1944 staffing is left out as unverified. The page's photos are credited to the Bert Russel Collection, with no image URLs or license given, so none were added.

Built years 1919 and 1935 agree across three sources. The Idaho Fire Lookouts page carries an unsigned reader comment saying the fire was purposely set; it is unverified and left out. The 2019 photo caption is the only source on remains, and no source here covers public access. The brief's firelookout.com listing was not read. Web search budget was used up before this tower could be searched further.

Sources agree on the 1921 development, the 1923 cabin and the 1934 east-point L-4 tower. For the west-point tower, Firelookout.com, Idaho Fire Lookouts and the Forest Lookouts 1934 entry all give a 100-foot pole L-6 built in 1934. The Forest Lookouts page also quotes a June 1944 note about poles for a 110-foot tower which it says was erected on the west point. The height and erection date of the west-point tower are not settled from the sources read. The TPA annual reports (1957-58, 1961-62) are known only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the originals were not read. Idaho Fire Lookouts labels the site Drive-Up (Drive-Up Destroyed), recorded in facts.visit, but no source describes the site today or says whether it can be reached now; the brief's access unknown stands.

The brief record had no events; the sources supply the c.1918 camp, the 1920 cabin, the 1945 named lookout and the 1957 end. The sources agree on the dates but differ on the wording of the 1957 fate. Idaho Fire Lookouts credits the 1945 name to the Forest Fire Lookout Page, so it is firelookout.com's record. A genealogy search turned up only family-tree pages, which were not used. The Forest Lookouts page also lists a federal survey station named Beaver Jack (PID QZ0635) reached by helicopter. That is a survey mark on the highest ridge top, not the lookout, and its description does not mention the lookout, so it is left out. No source describes the site today or its access. Do not confuse with the Beaver Peak in Shoshone County (us-id-beaver-peak).

Do not confuse with the other Beaver Peak in Shoshone County, on the St. Joe National Forest (T43N R8E sec. 23, 3 miles west of Red Ives RS, destroyed 1953; firelookout.org lists it at 47.05694, -115.42511). That one is at idaholookouts.weebly.com/beaver-peak1.html and firelookout.com/id/beaverpeak267.html. The brief record (47.9872, -116.17042, Coeur d'Alene NF) matches the sources used here. Unverified lead, from a search snippet only, not read and not linked to this lookout: a Forest Lookouts Shoshone County page mentions a December 1928 lightning death of a Coeur d'Alene TPA lookout, Clair Corey, on an unnamed mountain. No source describes the site today or its access. No source calls the 1928 tower the first lookout, so the story does not say so.

Dates trace to the Kresek data via Forest Lookouts; the other three sites repeat them, so they are not independent. The FFLA list carries a second Beaver Peak in Shoshone County (47.98720, -116.17042, Tower Gone); its Idaho Fire Lookouts page (cda-region/beaver-peak/) is a different tower and was not used. No photos found. The brief's status gone, design L-4 and 1953 destroyed match all sources, so no corrections proposed. None of the first three sources gives coordinates for this lookout, so the story no longer assigns either FFLA Beaver Peak entry to it.

Core dates agree (1922 cabin, 1963 current cab, 2009 registration), but the base is disputed: the register, firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts say concrete; the Forest Lookouts (weebly) page says cinder block. The record's height_m 3.7 and kind two_story are not supported by any page read and were left out of facts. No rental listing found in one search; access is only the drive-up note from Idaho Fire Lookouts (July 2025 article). The weebly page's 1919 material is attributed to a Nevada State Journal item it quotes; that original was not checked.

Location: the record point (46.51124, -114.67897) is an Idaho-site map pin on 'Beaver Ridge Lookout Road', about 19 km from the register and index point. Correction is proposed, not applied. Cab type disagrees: flat cab (register, Idaho site) vs two-story (Forest Association index); story reports both. Staffing: Idaho site says every fire season; firelookout.com says summer. No fire, rental listing or access rules found. Record id ends in -2, so another Beaver Ridge record may exist; not checked. The University of Idaho Keeping Watch page repeats the register coordinates but was not cited.

The 1937 newspaper item is quoted only on the Forest Lookouts page; the original was not checked. The 1938 date is repeated by three sites that share the Kresek source. Idaho Fire Lookouts credits two photos (Stan Meyers Collection; Bonner County Historical Society/Chuck Peterson collection) but gives no image URL or licence, so none were added. The brief's status gone and 1966 destroyed match the sources. Fact-check 2026-10-10: every footnoted claim was found on its cited page; Bonner County (firelookout.com) and the 1938 L-4 cab (Idaho Fire Lookouts) are now in the evidence list.

Story is about 109 words, under the 120-word floor, because the sources offer only the 1930s date and an undated abandonment; nothing was padded. An earlier draft said no source says whether the site is open to visitors; Idaho Fire Lookouts' Hike-In label contradicts that, so the story now states the label instead. Thin record: no source gives a year for the abandonment, so no events are listed. No staffing, fire or site-today information in any source read. Forest Lookouts gives the land location as 45N-8E-23. The brief's status gone is not supported; the proposed correction to abandoned is for human review. No photos found.

The 1963 build, the Anderson staffing, the 1998 last-staffed year and the 2014 demolition agree across three amateur lookout sites. The present state rests on one climbing guide updated September 2020 (antennas, road, land mix); no recent photo or BLM record was read. A BLM NEPA register entry (DOI-BLM-ID-T030-2014-0012-CX) appeared in search results but was not read; it may cover the 2014 work. Access is drive-up per the guide and the Idaho Fire Lookouts header; check current BLM land status before any stronger access claim. Brief coordinates differ from the weebly page by about 0.0001 degree, which is negligible.

Construction and staffing dates agree across sources, but several come from one Idaho lookouts page and its Kresek-based inventory. The 2013 evacuation comes from one source (idaholookouts.weebly.com). Access wording rests on firelookout.com plus a 2019 climbing-guide recon, not a current agency notice; the story says so only by quoting them. The record's access 'unknown' could be updated to closed by a human. No record corrections proposed. The 1963 date in firelookout.com's heading is unexplained.

Built and abandoned dates agree across all three pages, but two of them cite the same Kresek inventory, so the agreement is not fully independent. Summit elevation differs: 6,099 ft (firelookout.com) vs 6,349 ft (Idaho Fire Lookouts). Location: the record point (48.33799, -116.08378) is about 1.9 km from the FFLA list and firelookout.com point (48.3254, -116.10125); a correction is proposed for human review. Staffing: no documented staffing history on any page, so none is stated. The Idaho Fire Lookouts page has a 1970 photo caption (Stan Meyers Collection) naming Forest Service staff from the Clark Fork Ranger District; the caption does not say the photo shows this tower and no image URL was captured, so no photo is added.

Built date is disputed: 1928 (association's 1947 report), 1930 (firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts), 1931 (association's 1946 report; a 1931 aerial photo shows the lookout). The 1935 100-foot steel tower appears only on firelookout.com and the Idaho site; the association's reports describe wooden lookouts until 1947. Replacement is 1947 per the association and 1948 per the Idaho sites. Removal date is unknown in every source. height_m 22.9 matches the 75-foot post-1947 steel tower; the first pole tower was listed at 85 feet, so the record height may refer to the later tower. Archives West (A.B. Curtis collection) has item-level records of this lookout: a 1931 aerial view, a 1936 oblique aerial view (116th Photo Section, item A 1352) and a 1954 color slide. Rights statements were not checked, so no photo entries are added; footnote 4 points to the collection page, not the item page. The Idaho site and firelookout.com abbreviate the association as CPTPA; the full name comes from the weebly page.

Two corrections are proposed: the build year (1918 per four sites, not 1919) and the height (12.2 m for the 40-foot L-4 standing until 1976, not the 20-foot platform tower's 6.1 m). Access is marked public on the strength of the Farragut State Park trail routes and WillhiteWeb's drivable-summit remark; no closure or gate rule was found, so confirm before publishing. The 1967 Kinzel first name differs between sources. The FFA Historian's Facebook story about 1967 appeared in search results only and was neither read nor quoted. The Chad Kinzel story linked from Idaho Fire Lookouts was not followed. Photo credits (Fire Lookout Museum, Dave Bula collection, National Archives) come without image URLs, so none added.

Brief access 'unknown' stays unknown: the 2025 post says the site is right off the road, but no source gives access rules. No staffing history is documented, so no staffing fact. firelookout.com places the tower relative to Quarles Lookout; a Quarles record would help locate this site. Brief status 'gone' is supported.

Many dates conflict and are reported as such in the story: current steel tower 1955-57 work, 1958 (Kamstra, Idaho Fire Lookouts) and 1959 (register); lightning death 1931 (register, newspaper) vs 1932 (Idaho Fire Lookouts); fall death 1964 (newspaper, association report) vs 1966 (register); elevation 5,477 ft (register) vs 5,520 ft (other pages). Record height_m 12.2 (40 ft) matches the 1933 pole tower, not the current 54-56 ft steel tower; left unchanged for a human decision. Record design L-4 describes the 1933 tower; current cab is 14 by 14 feet per the register. Access is set to restricted because the tower is owned by a timber association, used for emergency detection, and a 1958 report limits visitors to the observatory platform; no current rules were found. Idaho Fire Lookouts lists a 1918 tower and a 1923 glass-cabin tower as separate; sources do not settle the sequence. Staff names on Idaho Fire Lookouts were not reproduced. Checked 2026-10-08: the story no longer credits Mable Gray with the first watch on the strength of Idaho Fire Lookouts, which gives only the 1902 perch detail; Kamstra calls her the first lookout here. A 1955 association report (Forest Lookouts) dates the L-4 tower to 1934, against 1933 elsewhere; the story notes this. Only the association report calls the 1964 death accidental.

firelookout.com places the tower on the southwest point of Tungston Mtn, but the record uses the Bethlehem Mountain name and coordinates (48.90021, -116.28798). Check which peak the pin is on before publishing. The brief's 1950 event is corrected to the 1950s. Naturally North Idaho is a local history post used only for trail-era context; it does not name the tower's trail.

Built and replacement dates (1924 cabin, 1959 R-6 cab) agree across the register and Idaho Fire Lookouts; firelookout.com says 1925. The forest is disputed: the Forest Service trail page lists the Salmon-Challis National Forest while three other sources say Boise. Staffing is recorded as unstaffed/undated by inference from emergency status; the last known staff was 1983. firelookout.com's '10' treated timber tower' is ambiguous (tower or cab dimension), so no height is recorded. Current cab access is not established. Keeping Watch has coordinates only. Search results also pointed to a Facebook group post and a Boise National Forest history PDF; neither was used as a source because they were not read or did not mention Big Baldy in the cached text. The 1924 cabin and 1959 replacement are already in events, so the earlier '1959 built' correction is applied and the corrections list is cleared.

Brief status 'gone' and kind 'ground' are supported by the Forest Fire Lookout Association list. No source gives the date the cabin was abandoned, so there is no abandoned event. Brief access 'unknown' stays unknown; the hike-in label is the only access detail. The Forest Service list has a note about lookouts still standing; the plain-text extract does not show which rows are highlighted, so this site is not treated as standing.

Brief's build year 1963, removal 2013 and FFLOS registration (March 25, 2020) are confirmed. Today's condition is unverified: the 2021 climbing guide mentions the road and probable electronic installations at the summit but not any lookout remains, and the BLM visit page it links was not read. Elevation disagrees across sources (7,523 ft register vs 7,560 ft Idaho Fire Lookouts); the register figure is kept. The 1962 newspaper quotes are read through Rex's page, a secondary copy. No photos added: the register's 2012 photo has no image URL in the crawl text.

Gone tower; no source we read describes the site today. Brief record (L-4, 50 ft, gone, Clearwater NF) matches the sources, so no corrections. The 1932 vs 1934 build year is unresolved. The 'Drive Up' tag comes only from idahofirelookouts.com and does not say whether a road reaches the site now. No photos found.

Thin record: one platform, three short listings, no staffing or access detail beyond the hike-in tag. The brief's gone status has no source behind it, so the proposed correction is unknown. Elevation 8,094 ft is from idahofirelookouts.com. The section/township/range reading of '21N-14E-20' is ours: the Forest Lookouts page carries no label, so the story says 'we read' it. The Forest Service list writes Big Horn Point as 'Sec21 T38N R8E', which fits that reading, but it is a different source and does not confirm the Forest Lookouts code format. No photos found. Current state needs a Payette NF check or a site visit report before the status is changed again.

The brief had no design or height; L-4 and 30 ft (9.1 m) come from firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts. No source documents staffing. Elevation 4,659 ft is from firelookout.com. Hike-in access is from idahofirelookouts.com only. No photos found. Proposed status and agency corrections are for the editor to accept or reject.

Three sites agree the crow's nest and camp date to the 1920s and were in ruins in the 1980s. Nothing read describes the site today, and no photo from after the ruins was found. The only current-state statement is the hike-in tag. Idaho Fire Lookouts says it has no documented staffing history, so the story leaves staffing out. The brief's kind 'platform' is not contradicted, but no source calls it a platform. Record us-id-big-meadows-2 (Kaniksu NF, 47.9895 -116.2031) cites the same Forest Lookouts page used here, whose listing is Bonner County at 59N-5W-33, so that record is probably a duplicate with wrong coordinates; flag for merge. Photo already on the record (idahofirelookouts.com 2025 upload) was not re-added.

Record height 9.1 m matches the 1921 30-foot tower; the 1932 L-6 tower was 45 ft (13.7 m), proposed as a correction. Destruction date conflicts (1940s vs 1950s) and a 1956 aerial observation are both reported, not resolved. No source found describes what remains at the site now. Access 'public' is inferred from the hike-in label and national forest land; no closure is mentioned. Tower sequence (Big Rock vs High Springs) is tangled across sources. No photos added. Budget: 2 searches and 5 page reads used.

Brief's 1934 build year is supported by the register but disputed by Forest Lookouts and Rex's page (1937 L-4 cab); both are recorded. Brief's design 'L-4' is supported by two sites but the register describes a groundhouse. The 2018 fire is supported only by the two Idaho-area lookout sites: two web searches found no report naming this lookout in a 2018 fire. The 1946 staffing item is a newspaper quote via a secondary site. No photos added: no image URLs were in the crawl text.

Height is disputed: 72 ft (Island Park Historical Society, 2026) against 100 ft (Idaho Fire Lookouts, firelookout.com). Abandonment is 1985 on Idaho Fire Lookouts but no longer used by 1981 per Island Park Historical Society. The staffing as_of 1981 is the last date sources give for use. The register page is undated, so its staffed=No answer is not used as a date. No photo with a stable URL was found. A Forest Service social-media post and an Instagram repost describe the 72-foot tower, but their text could not be read, so they are not cited. Access is hike-in per Idaho Fire Lookouts; the record does not say whether the abandoned tower may be climbed, so check with the Targhee NF before publishing any visit advice.

The Idaho Press article has no publication date in our cached copy, so the takedown plan's timing is unknown; confirm with the refuge before publishing the fate. The 1937 build date and fire-lookout purpose rest on that one article. Roaming Civic says the tower is not on the NHLR. No staffing or fire history found in the pages read. The Idaho Press fetch returned HTTP 429 on earlier tries and succeeded on a later retry. Brief access 'unknown' is now closed per the 2024 visit.

Record design 'L-4' is the cabin type; the tower is L-6 per firelookout.com and the 1939 item's cabin note, proposed as a correction. Height 26.2 m (86 ft) is kept from the 1939 item; the 1942 report and later pages say 84 ft. Build year (1937 vs 1938) and 1962 fate (removed vs destroyed) are reported as conflicts. No source describes the site now, or whether it is open to visitors. Lead, not used: a 1950 photo titled Billings Point lookout tower in the Potlatch Lumber Company collection at the University of Idaho (https://www.lib.uidaho.edu/digital/plcphotos/items/plcphotos721.html). Its license was not checked, so it is not in photos. Its coordinates (46.636, -115.804) are about 4 km from the record's point. Budget: 2 searches and 4 page reads used.

Record height 12.2 m (40 ft) matches the 1920s pole tower; the 1934 Aermotor was 80 ft (24.4 m), proposed as a correction. Design 'Aermotor' is kept, with the two-tower history noted in the summary. The Newport Hill page lists its 40-foot tower as removed, so neither site has a standing tower per these sources. Newport Hill's height (40 ft) conflicts with the 80 ft given for the moved tower. No source describes remains at the original site. Access 'public' is inferred from the hike-in label. Budget: 2 searches and 5 page reads used. The naughtyhiker.com 'footings' passage was checked and is about Cooks Peak, not this site, so it is not used.

Brief's 1932 build and 1959 loss are supported by all four sources. The brief's 'destroyed' wording is supported by three of four sources; the register says removed. The 2016 Clearwater list gives a 35-foot pole where the others give 40 feet. Neither the Forest Service list nor the search summary says how the tower came down. The 2016 list shows one photo for the site, but no image URL was captured, so no photo is recorded. The Idaho Fire Lookouts page names the 1932 staffer and gives no later staffing.

Build year (1937 vs 1938) and tower height (72 ft vs 84 ft) conflict between NHLR and the other two sources; noted in the story rather than resolved. NHLR's own record page says the tower is 'available for rental,' which conflicts a little with the record's access.level of 'unknown' -- worth a look, but I left access as unknown in facts since no source confirms public climbing access, only rental/standby status.

The tower record's 'rental' block and the 'Lookout Butte Lookout' alias both appear to actually describe a different, separately registered lookout (NHLR US 769) about 40 miles northeast of Black Butte on the same forest -- see the two proposed corrections. If that's confirmed, Lookout Butte Lookout likely needs (or already has) its own record with that rental data. Core build-history facts about Black Butte itself (1925 camp, 1928 cupola cabin, 1970 Region 6 Flat Top rebuild) are corroborated by two independent sources (NHLR and firelookout.com) and match in every detail, so confidence in those is good. However, current status is genuinely disputed: NHLR and FFLA (firelookout.org) list it as standing, while a separate, uncached Idaho Fire Lookouts page for this exact lookout (same coordinates/elevation/build history, in their Selway-region listing, source 6) marks it 'Abandoned' with no further detail. The original research checked only idahofirelookouts.com's West Central region page (source 5, which covers an unrelated same-named lookout) and missed this direct conflict. Confidence is capped at medium because of this unresolved status conflict and because the access/rental story still needs a human to verify and fix in the live record.

Brief coordinates: the ffla pair (44.82013, -115.7892) matches Keeping Watch and was kept. The brief's idaho_fl pair (44.80462, -115.79623) did not appear on any page we read, so it was not used. The elevation is in the story only because the facts schema has no elevation key. No source states the access level or whether the public may visit, so access is omitted. The 1944 staffing is a single newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. No source describes the remains today. No photo was found.

All three pages agree on the 1932 L-4 cab, 1952 base and 1972 R-6 cab, and on the 7,077 ft elevation. Record height_m 3.0 is close to the 10-foot base (3.05 m), not an overall structure height; left unchanged. Record kind two_story is consistent with a cab on a 10-foot base; not changed. Access is only the hike-in and staffed notes from Idaho Fire Lookouts; no visiting rules found. The AllTrails trail page returned HTTP 403, so no trail length or route was verified. The Idaho Fire Lookouts staff list was read only as far as its visible portion (to 2009); staff names were not reproduced.

Restoration status conflicts: the Boundary County Historic Places page calls the tower complete and awaiting rental inclusion, while Campflare says restoration work is still required. The record's coordinates (48.61354, -116.24767) are almost identical to the NHLR listing's coordinates (N 48.613497, W 116.247753), but the NHLR says the tower moved about half a mile ENE in 2019, so the coordinates may describe the old site; verify before relying on them. The FFLA 2019 report gives the chapter's refurbishment support but no restoration details. No photos added; the Idaho Fire Lookouts page carries an unlicensed photo credit, not used.

Describes the same tower as us-id-black-mountain-at-black-mountain-ridge (both cite NHLR US 1464); consider merging the two records. The record coordinates (48.61038, -116.2577) nearly match the NHLR listing, but NHLR says the tower moved half a mile ENE in 2019, so the point may be the old site; verify before use. Campflare and Boundary County Historic Places pages are undated, so the restoration status may have changed. A search snippet mentioned a 1997 rental placement and a 2002 magazine rate; neither page was read, so neither is used. No photos added (the Idaho Fire Lookouts photo credit is unlicensed).

Three Black Peaks appear in these sources: this St. Joe site (6,258 ft, camp and patrol point in the 1930s); a Kootenai National Forest Black Peak (6,548 ft, cabin 1929, destroyed 1968; source 3); and a Sanders County, Montana Black Peak listed as Ground and Gone on firelookout.org's Montana list. The record's coordinates 47.18264, -115.27246 were not checked against any source page, so confirm the match before relying on them. Firelookout.com names St. Joe and Lolo National Forests; Idaho Fire Lookouts names only the St. Joe. The record's status 'gone' is not supported; sources say abandoned in the 1930s. No photo found.

Brief status gone and coordinates 45.11868, -114.41677 agree with the climbing guide (45.11859, -114.41639), so no correction. The 1924 14x14 house and the 1935 two-story cabin are both reported; the sources do not say whether they are the same structure, so the story does not claim it. The 1950s burn is a decade only and is not an event with a year. Weebly's single 'Removed' label has no date or explanation. Access: the climbing guide describes a 4WD road but no source states public status, so access is omitted. No source describes the summit today. No photo was found.

Brief record (gone, L-4, tower, Nez Perce NF) is consistent with the sources, so no correction. Heights conflict (25, 28, 40 feet), so none is recorded in facts. No staffing source was found, so staffing is omitted. In the Forest Service list the 1950s entry is a photo year, not a staffing year, and is not used. Forest Lookouts includes a 1960 Idaho State Journal item about an unrelated shooting near the site; it is left out. Firelookout.com and the Forest Service list credit a Nez Perce NF photo, but no image URL was found, so no photo is recorded. No source describes the site today or public access.

Built year 1934 and the 1940s abandonment agree across three sites; the 1940 event year is a placeholder for the decade. Record fields checked and consistent: L-4 design, gone status, St. Joe National Forest. No source gives a removal date, a current access rule, or what remains on the summit, so access is left out of facts. Second search turned up nothing new.

The 1929, 1932 and 1934 build sequence and the gone status agree across the register, Idaho Fire Lookouts, firelookout.com and the 2016 Forest Service list. Open points: the direction from Powell (firelookout.com says northeast, the Forest Service says northwest), Idaho Fire Lookouts' 7218 ft elevation (likely a typo, but we did not confirm it), and staffing (no staffing history; one undated photo caption names George Bradley). The 2016 Forest Service list notes one photo of the site credited to Luke Channer, but we had no image URL, so no photo was added. The Idaho Fire Lookouts page is dated 2023 by its post date, not a visit date. The weebly Blacklead page has only an index entry and was not cited. Brief's record was accurate on all points checked.

Decade-only dating: the sources say 1930s (Forest Lookouts with a question mark), so there is no built event. No source names a staff member, and Idaho Fire Lookouts says none is documented. Forest Lookouts and the Forest Service list both draw on Ray Kresek's Fire Lookouts of the Northwest, so they are not independent confirmation of each other. Name clash: Blacktail (Frisco Peak) is a separate record (FFLOS US 1172, ID 11, 46.20829 -115.10781). Its pages say a 1926 cabin stood atop Blacktail Butte; the Forest Service list gives that cabin to Frisco. Unresolved, and the story keeps the cabin out of this history. The brief coordinates (45.89062, -115.99708) fit the Forest Service location (T30N R4E Sect. 31, 6 miles ESE of Grangeville). Brief record checked (county Idaho, kind tower, gone): no correction. Not read: the Kresek book, Nez Perce NF district files, any photograph. Today: no source describes the site.

Construction (1932) and destruction (1941) agree across three sites. The Painter and Stobie staffing rests on the Idaho writers' own identification, and the Painter link is stated as a belief, not a record. Record height_m 3.05 is the sourced 10 feet converted to metres. Access is left out of facts: sources call it hike-in and describe visits, but none states current public access or closures, so the story says so. A Facebook post by the Idaho writers (not read) and the Priest Lake Museum photo captions (search snippets only) were not cited.

Record checked: ground kind, gone status and coordinates match the Idaho list. Record events list only 1939 abandoned; the 1935 cabin date is added from all three lookout pages. The 1927 Blanchard lookout line is unexplained: a human could check the Idaho TPA annual reports for what stood there. A Facebook group search result mentions a two-storey 14 by 14 foot cabin one mile southwest of Blanchard at 2,858 feet, which may be a different structure; it was not read or cited. Access is left out of facts because no source says whether the site is public today.

Thin record: a 1936 name and an undated 1930s crow's nest. The record's status 'gone' is not supported; both lists say Abandoned, so the correction is proposed, not applied. Location: the record's 48.97342, -116.88601 matches the FFLA list; the Idaho Fire Lookouts map uses a different point (about 48.977, -116.832, from the site's map data, not from the page text we quoted), so the two sites disagree on the spot. Record kind 'platform' fits the crow's nest. A bchistoricplaces.org blog post mentions a 1929 fire near Blue Joe Creek but not the lookout; not used. No site description or current condition found in two searches.

Record is a lookout, but every source describes only a camp c.1930; the design value should not be read as a tower. Gone status comes from two directories; no source gives a removal date or describes remains. Access 'hike-in' is from Idaho Fire Lookouts only. The Bitterroot Star item is an opinion column about the wider area, not the site. Two searches found no Forest Service inventory entry for the site. Brief county 'Idaho' corrected to 'Idaho County'.

Staffing entries for 1920-1924 predate the 1934 build date given by NHLR and firelookout.com for the current structure; no source explains whether an earlier lookout post existed on the site before 1934, or whether the staffing survey's dates are approximate. Flagged in the story as an open question rather than resolved. No rental/reservation information found; access described from the volunteer survey's site-visit notes only.

Three names for one station: Bird Peak (Idaho Fire Lookouts), Bird Point and Bird Creek (the 1929 letters and the npshistory editor's note). Identification rests on the shared 1929 keeper, plus firelookout.com's placement 2.5 miles east of Shefoot Lookout, which the listed coordinates roughly fit (Shefoot Mtn is 47.30660 -115.68510). The Dave Brown 1930 entry rests on one source that cites Swiftwater People, which was not read. Built date is only 'L-4 cab' in the 1930s, so there is no built event. Dates: 1925 camp (three sources agree), 1969 destroyed (two sources agree). Brief record checked (county Shoshone, ground, destroyed 1969): no correction. Not read: Swiftwater People, other Guntermann letters in the same npshistory series, Forest Service records, any photograph. Today: no source describes the site.

Thin record. Three sources agree on the 1935 L-4 cab, the 1956 loss and the patrol tower two miles south atop Dominion Point. Identity risk: a Bonner County Daily Bee article of 31 January 2026 (https://bonnercountydailybee.com/news/2026/jan/31/group-seek-to-identify-honor-fire-lookout-crews/) describes a concrete footing at a former 'Dominion Mountain Lookout' and a 1933 lookout named Charles Nelson. That is the Dominion Mountain / Dominion Peak site on the state line (46N-7E-4, FFLOS 47.36733 -115.57757), not this Bluff site (44N-7E-12, 47.17809 -115.51969), so it is excluded. No staffing is documented for the Bluff anywhere read. Brief record checked (county Shoshone, ground, destroyed 1956): no correction. Not read: the Dominion Point patrol entry (listed on the Shoshone County page without detail), Forest Service records, any photograph. Today: no source describes the site, and the 2026 article concerns a different site.

Built 1932 and destroyed 1973 agree across the four history sources, but two of them (FFLA and the FS list) draw on the same older records, so the agreement is less independent than it looks. County conflict unresolved: Shoshone (FFLA list, brief) vs Clearwater (Forest Lookouts index); the story names no county. Distance of nine miles comes from the FS list row, where the number sits on a wrapped line ('R11E 9 / miles N of / Powell RS'). The 40 ft figure is treated as the pole height and converted to 12.2 m. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from the gate; no source states the land's rules. Staffing: the Idaho page says no documented staffing history, so no staffing facts are recorded. Fire cause: no source gives one; the melted-glass remark is a 2025 visitor's inference and is cited as such. Today: only the July 2025 Idaho Fire Lookouts post describes the site. Brief record: no field errors found beyond the county question.

Brief event '1955 destroyed' confirmed by all four pages; the brief lacked the 1934 build date, now added. Brief county 'Shoshone' matches the FFLA page ('Shoshone County, Idaho'). Staffing rests on one name from the Idaho Fire Lookouts page, which cites a 1934 Wallace Press-Times item; the newspaper itself was not read. Site today: described only in the Idaho Fire Lookouts post (posted July 4, 2022); no source gives the land's access rules. Height: 30 ft converted to 9.1 m. Weebly index lists the township 50N-5E-6, not used in the record.

Location conflict left unresolved: the record's point (46.86827, -115.87455) comes from firelookout.com, while the FFLA list gives 46.59890, -115.79500 for the same name in Clearwater; no correction made. The protective association is abbreviated CPTPA on firelookout.com and CTPA on the Idaho Fire Lookouts page and in the Archives West caption; the Forest Lookouts table names the Potlatch Timber Protective Association. The story uses the name from the 1953 report quoted there. The 1953 rebuild appears only on the Forest Lookouts page. The record's county is null; the sources give Clearwater County. No staffing source found in two searches.

Correction: brief event '1960 abandoned' proposed as 'removed'; sources say 'Gone 1960' and 'Drive-Up Removed', and none says abandoned. The 1930s build date is a decade only, from two history pages; no single year is documented. No staffing or fire history on any page; the Idaho page says it has no documented staffing history, so no staffing facts are recorded. The Forest Lookouts index gives the station a Kaniksu NF township (61N-1E-4) and no history. No firetower.org record for this station turned up in the cache or the search. 40 ft converted to 12.2 m; the source gives the tower as '40' steel tower' without saying whether this is pole or total height. Today: no source describes the site now; access level not recorded. Idaho page dated September 16, 2025.

Two web searches found no Forest Service, NRHP or newspaper record of Boston Mountain; the two lookout-history pages may share a source, so their agreement is not independent. The 1980s crow's nest remark on Kamstra's page is unexplained and is reported as a disagreement in the story. No staffing or fire history was found, so none is written. Record elevation_m is null while the sources give 7,648 ft (about 2,331 m); suggest filling it. Status gone matches the record, so no correction is proposed.

Three sources agree on the 1915 camp, 1927 cupola cabin and 1935 accidental fire. Record kind 'ground' fits a cupola cabin; the sources do not name a tower. Coordinates conflict in the brief: 48.75127, -116.99501 (firelookout.org list) vs 48.75992, -117.02495 (Idaho list). The second pair sits almost on Little Grass Mountain in the firelookout.org list (48.75990, -117.02470), so it may be a copied point; the story does not use coordinates. Two searches found no other account of the 1935 fire. Firelookout.com credits photos to the Fire Lookout Museum and USFS but gives no image URLs, so none are recorded.

Design and dates match the brief (L-4, 4.6 m; 15 ft is about 4.57 m). Destroyed-year conflict (1965 vs 1966) is left open. Search leads not read: a 1990 Payette fire history with a 1944-1989 fire list, and a 1968 Payette history manuscript (Hockaday); either could settle the year. No staffing history is in any source, so none is recorded. No photo URLs were found; firelookout.com credits the Richard Holm collection and USFS without links.

Only hobbyist and association listings. The 1931 build and 1962 destruction agree across three sites, but none gives a cause or a source for the dates. Idaho Fire Lookouts says no staffing history is documented, so staffing is left out. The brief recorded only the 1962 event; the 1931 build is added. Do not confuse with the Idaho County Boundary Peak (46.36913, -115.52358), a separate record also marked gone.

The build year (1934) and location agree across all sources. The fate does not: the Forest Service list says burned in 1954 while the two lookout-history pages say abandoned in the 1950s and gone by 1964. Two searches found no further record. Record elevation_m is null while the sources give 5,243 ft (about 1,598 m); suggest filling it. Do not confuse with the Kootenai Boundary Peak at 47.81440, -116.32418, which is a different lookout. Status gone matches the record, so no correction is proposed.

The record's gone status comes from the Forest Fire Lookout Association list, which actually reads Abandoned; the brief's note that idahofirelookouts.com says gone does not match the page, which says Abandoned. Kamstra's 'Still there' has no date, and no recent photo or visit was found. Two web searches found nothing else. Holm's 2010 Payette fire lookout book is listed in the Idaho Bibliography Project but was not checked. Suggest a recent photo before any status is published. Record elevation and kind (platform) are consistent with the sources.

Sources disagree on the last staffed years: two listings say in use into the 1970s, while Idaho Fire Lookouts also lists Mr. and Mrs. Kirkpatrick in 1981; the story reports this without resolving it. Agency naming differs across listings (Clearwater-Potlatch TPA vs Clearwater Timber Protective Association); the brief's name matches only Forest Lookouts. Brown Creek #2 is a separate record and is not covered here. A Clearwater National Forest history PDF (foresthistory.org) quotes a memoir about a 'Browns Creek Lookout' staffed by a woman from Weippe, but the text does not say which station or year, so it is left out.

Location conflict is unresolved: the FFLA list gives 46.32278, -115.82422 (the record's point); the brief also cites 46.31556, -115.80472 from Idaho Fire Lookouts, but the fetched Idaho page has no coordinates, so that second position could not be checked; the story gives only the FFLA position. 'Browns Creek Lookout' appears in The Clearwater Story (npshistory.com, chapter 3; undated visit, a woman lookout from Weippe who had worked since the war) and in TPA annual-report quotes on the weebly Brown's Creek #1 page. The sources do not say which Browns Creek tower is meant, so those mentions are left out. Brown's Creek #1 is a different tower (1910 crow's nest, 1934 100-foot steel tower, torn down 1999) and must not be merged. The 1913 log cabin is listed on the same entry; no source says whether it stood on the same spot as the 1934 tower. No staffing history is documented (Idaho Fire Lookouts). Destruction is known only to the decade.

The 1963 destruction date appears on two listings; Forest Lookouts gives no destruction date. The Clearwater National Forest lookout list PDF (fs.usda.gov) has Destroyed 1963 rows for other sites, but no Browns Rock row turned up in it, so it does not confirm the date and is not cited. Current site is described only as a gravel pit by Idaho Fire Lookouts, a hobbyist listing. The brief recorded no events, so the 1923, 1931, 1934, 1939 and 1963 events are new.

Sources agree on the 1932 build and the gone-by-1959 date. The record's 'abandoned 1959' (from idaho_fl) is recorded here as removed, because the three pages read say gone and do not say abandoned; the record's status 'gone' is consistent. Access level left unset: the sources give hike-in only. No staffing is documented by any source read; Idaho Fire Lookouts says so, and it is left out of the story. firelookout.com credits a photo to Harold Coffman, but no image URL was in the cache, so no photo is added. One web search found no other Bruin Hill source.

Disputed: the 20x20 log lookout is dated 1929 by the register and Idaho Fire Lookouts but to the 1930s by Forest Lookouts. The 1982 cab is described three ways (concrete and wood on rubble base; wooden on concrete slab; cinder block and wood frame). Administration is unresolved: the register says the timber association administers it, while the resort calls it an active Forest Service lookout. Elevation is 7,569 ft in the register and 7,552 ft on two sites. The register says Valley County; firelookout.com says Valley/Adams. The 2025 staffing as_of comes from the Idaho Fire Lookouts page dated March 26, 2025. The tower record's built=1919 (firelookout_com) describes the earlier house, not the current cab. Leads not read and not cited: a University of Idaho 1990 report on Payette NF fire control history, and a 1933 Idaho Statesman item in the McCall Public Library collection. Recommend checking current staffing and public access with SITPA or the Payette NF before publishing.

Build date conflicts: the 1920s log cupola cabin (firelookout.com, which also says 1940s pole platform still there) versus partly complete in August 1929 (Pend Oreille Review, quoted on the Forest Lookouts page) versus built in the 1930s by the CCC (1962 Sandpoint News Bulletin, quoted there). Not resolved in the story. The dates also differ on use: the 1962 report says not used since 1950, while the site pages date abandonment to 1962. Location conflict on the record: FFLA point 48.5622, -116.14932 versus idaho_fl point 48.5641, -116.16046, about 850 m apart; the record point is kept and no correction is proposed. The web search returned a Wikipedia article titled Buck Mountain Lookout Tower that was not opened and is not used here. No staffing dates beyond 1933 were found.

Unresolved conflicts: pole tower height is 30 feet on firelookout.com (1931 entry) and 30' also in the Idaho Fire Lookouts page's 1931 entry, versus 20 feet on the Forest Lookouts page citing Kresek. The record's height_m 6.1 equals 20 feet; 30 feet would be about 9.1 m. Not proposed as a correction, because height is not one of the correction fields. The 1934 tower's distance is 1/4 mile on two sources and 1/2 mile on Idaho Fire Lookouts. The crow's nest year is 1929 on firelookout.com and c.1929 on the Forest Lookouts page. The record point (47.85057, -116.60907) is about 50 m from the idaho_fl point, so no location correction. No staffing history is documented by any source read. The Idaho Fire Lookouts timeline (cited in the story) also gives the 1931 pole L-4 tower as 30 feet and the destruction as 1955, so all three cited pages agree on the 1955 date; the 1931 height is 30 feet on firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts against 20 feet on the Forest Lookouts page citing Kresek. The Faset Peak and 2023 fire-map results are not this site.

Thin record. All three listings are hobby sites. Only the Forest Lookouts listing says where its dates come from (all three to one source, Kresek), so those dates are not independently checked. Location conflict is unresolved: the record's point (48.85216, -116.79134) is about 1.7 km from 48.83736, -116.79745, which the firelookout.org index gives (its firelookout.com listing agrees per the brief). Neither point was checked against the sources' text or a map, and the story gives no coordinates. No staffing, fire or access history in any source read, so access is left unset; 'Hike-In' is the only access statement.

Three listings (firelookout.com, Idaho Fire Lookouts, Forest Lookouts) agree on the 1931 platform and the 1933 L-4 tower. Three date the end to 1975 (Idaho Fire Lookouts, Forest Lookouts, Spokane Historical), and firelookout.com says removed that year. Two open points: the second tower's year (1959 vs 1960) and destroyed vs removed. Staff names come from Idaho Fire Lookouts, which credits Kellogg Evening News and the Forest Fire Lookout Page; the 1944 spelling differs between sites. No source states public access, so the access level is left unset; the drive-up listing is the only access statement. Photos on the listings are credited to the Fire Lookout Museum, Pete Miles and the USFS with no licence stated, so none were added.

Thin record: four sources repeat the same 1920s crow's nest and camp, abandoned and ruins. The 1920s date is decade-only and no abandonment date is given, so no abandonment event is recorded. The brief's status 'gone' is corrected to 'ruins' per both site pages. Idaho Fire Lookouts states no staffing history is documented; nothing is written on staffing. Spelling differs (Burgdorff vs Burgdorf). No photos were found with image URLs. Coordinates in the FFLA list match the brief. A better source would be Kresek's Fire Lookouts of the Northwest or a Payette National Forest lookout history; a University of Idaho catalog item (cccidaho1229) was found but its full text was not located. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the story no longer says no source describes what remains, because both site pages describe ruins. The 1920s crow's nest and camp sentence no longer cites the FFLA list, which gives no date or camp.

Rental status is not confirmed. A reader comment on the Idaho Fire Lookouts post points to recreation.gov, but no listing was read, so the story says nothing about rental. Idaho Fire Lookouts' Drive-Up Abandoned tag is its own category and is not treated as a current status. Photos not added, though University of Idaho Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness History Project items (sbw019, sbw087; 1938 photographs) surfaced in search and could be checked for license and use. The 1930 cabin date is consistent across three sources.

Height is unresolved: 10 feet (firelookout.com) vs 15 feet (Idaho Fire Lookouts; Idaho County listing crediting Kresek). The 1915 staffer named by Idaho Fire Lookouts predates the 1933 tower; the source gives no explanation, and an earlier post on the knob is possible but unproven, so the story only states the dates. A different Burnt Knob (NHLR-registered, standing, Selway / Nez Perce, 45.70271, -114.99109) must not be merged with this record. A 1936 photo caption from the Archival Idaho Photograph Collection appeared only in a search snippet for idaholookouts.weebly.com/burnt-knob1.html and is not in the fetched page text, so no photo entry was added. firelookout.com credits a photo to the Fire Lookout Museum but gives no image URL. Nothing is written about remains because no source describes the site today.

Destroyed year is 1955 in two listings and 1956 (tower torn down) in the Forest Lookouts listing; both are in the story. The Forest Lookouts listing cites Kresek only for the c.1939 cabin date, so its 1956 entry is not attributed to Kresek. The 50-foot figure and height_m 15.2 come only from the Forest Lookouts listing, which does not say whether that is total height or height to the cab floor. The record's 'ground' kind may be wrong (see corrections). The photo on the Forest Lookouts listing carries 'Permission for use required' (Kenneth E. Carpenter collection), so no photo was added. No source describes the site today, and no access level is set because none states one. No staffing or fire history appears in any source read.

Location is ambiguous: firelookout.com and the FS list describe a patrol lookout two miles southwest atop Big Creek Point, while the record coordinates are for Burpee Mountain; the story says so. A Big Creek Patrol listing on idaholookouts.weebly.com (seen only as a search result, not read) places a patrol lookout two miles SW of Burpee Mountain; worth a read if someone wants to settle it. The photo url is the UIdaho item page, not a direct JPEG link; the image itself was not located. About six pages were read, including a 404 on a guessed weebly URL. No source describes the site today. The UIdaho photo caption and firelookout.com both say 16 miles south of Elk City, while the USFS list says 16 miles SE; the story uses the USFS figure and does not reconcile the two.

The brief's height_m 4.3 is not supported by any page read; it matches the 14-foot footprint, so a correction proposes removing it. Elevation (6,844 ft, 2,086 m) and the 1933 build and 1967 abandonment agree across sources. Staff names come from firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts; Idaho Fire Lookouts adds Larry Johnson (1935) and Mr. Malcom Smith (1945), which firelookout.com does not list. Spelling of the design name differs ('Nez Perce' on firelookout.com, 'Nez Pierce' on WillhiteWeb). The Idaho Fire Lookouts page includes reader comments, which are not cited. Access and trail details come from a hiking guide and a personal site and are dated 2021 to 2023, so check current road and trailhead conditions before publishing. Photo credits (Tyler Nyman, Carol Elam collection) have no image URLs, so no photo entries were added.

Thin record. Two lookout histories agree on 1935 and 1955; the Idaho register says Removed with no date. No staffing, cause of loss or present-day site description found. Only one search was run.
