Only two sources. The register gives no build date, height, design, staffing or access, and the Columbia caption (July 2025) is the only evidence it still stands. The Forest Lookouts Kentucky list has only 'RENNOX, Metcalfe County' with no detail page. A Facebook 'Abandoned Kentucky' post about an abandoned Metcalfe County tower is not tied to this lookout, so it was not used. The Columbia 'Great Wooded South' series by Billy Joe Fudge may have another piece on this tower; worth checking. No photos recorded: the register and Columbia photo credits have no clear license.

Single source: the register page is the only source read, and web searches found nothing about this tower beyond it. Dates are decade-only in the register (1930s built, 1980s removed), so no built or removed event is recorded. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from current use as a communications site, not from a stated rule. The register shows a 2017 photo credited to Robert Wittenback, but no image URL was in the cached text, so no photo was added.

Height comes only from the 1936 item (some 80 feet), so it is an approximate figure. The campground sources are current; they do not say whether the tower spot is on campground ground. The Dyrt is a commercial campground guide, used only for the tower's location near the entrance. The Register's December 2023 photo credit (Linda and Robert Wittenback) has no image URL in the fetched text; no photo added.

Demolition rests on the NHLR and FFLOS registers, which are the same organization's two sites, and is dated only 'as of 2024'. The 2016 newspaper is the only independent source. The 1934 build is supported by three sources. No lookout names, staffing dates or notable fires were found. The 'abandoned' step has no year, so it is left out of events. Brief status 'standing' is corrected to removed.

Elevation not in facts. The brief gives 384.4 m, but LEX18 says the highest point in Bath County is 1,388 feet (about 423 m); the two should be checked against a survey before either is used. The 1959 rebuild comes from one source (Eastern lookouts history) and is worded as 'half the original height' without detail. The tower 'fell out of use in the 1970s' is a decade only, so no event year is given. NHLR 'Staffed? No' is undated, so staffing as_of uses the check date. The USFS recarea page in the brief (recid=70728) does not mention Tater Knob, so the 2008 Forest Service statement is taken from its quotation on NHLR. Read budget ran over (about 7 page reads) because the first two fetches were low-yield.

Register is the main source. The UK Coal Camp Project record conflicts internally on dates (see resolved_conflicts) and is used only for camp context. Its coordinates (37.208333, -84.070833) differ from the register's (37.198532, -84.071221) by roughly 1 km; the story uses neither. The brief's 'removed 1970' is corrected to 'late 1970s' per the register, and no removed event is recorded because no exact year is given. The 'gone' status rests on the register's account; no photo or site visit report was found.

Brief status 'gone' is right for the original site but wrong for the tower: moved around 1964 and standing as the Bald Knob Tower (FFLOS, NHLR). NHLR gives separate coordinates (36.78, -88.058) for the Bald Knob Tower, which presumably mark its current site; FFLOS coordinates are the original site. No source found on public access or climbing; check with Land Between the Lakes. Nothing found on what remains at the original site. Search summaries mentioned foundation piers and a Golden Pond visitor-center location; these were not verified and are not used. No photos collected (NHLR photo captions not extracted).

Thin evidence and no build date. The Wikipedia row for Abita reads Still standing; adjacent rows in the same table read Torn down, which is why the first grep was misleading. The 100-foot figure is ambiguous (cab or whole structure); height_m 30.5 follows the 100-foot figure. OSM tags it as an observation tower with lattice construction at 9 m elevation. The record's agency 7N is a survey location, not an agency. One web search found nothing on Morgan Road or the tower's use. The story is short by design; do not pad it.

Build year is supported by two sources (1929 newspaper, 1941 NGS description). Staffing is only a 1929 plan; no later source says who manned it. Rain totals are from 1955 and 1957 newspaper items as quoted on the Central US Lookouts page; not checked against the original papers. Fate is uncertain: Wikipedia marks it torn down with a question mark. The Wikipedia location (northeast of Jena) and the 1929 report (near the La Salle Parish line) are not reconciled. No current site description found. The firetower.org Louisiana register lists six registered sites and none of them is Aimwell.

Thin record. No build date, staffing, fires, or removal date found in the sources read. Torn-down status and the 2012 USGS label come from Wikipedia; the 1949 map is a Pastmaps reproduction, not checked against the USGS original. The survey text on the page is undated; its bench mark is stamped 1938, which does not date the tower itself. Not on the firetower.org Louisiana register. Community Facebook posts were not used.

Thin record. No build date or builder found. The 1984 staffing and the 1957 rain totals come from newspaper items quoted on the Central US Lookouts page, not checked against the original papers. Wikipedia gives the location as Pollock, Grant Parish, and the brief's coordinates match. Do not confuse this with the Catahoula Lookout Site (US 855, LA 2), a different Kisatchie tower in Grant Parish (us-la-catahoula). The Kisatchie National Forest site page was not read. No photo found.

No source read gives the tower's construction date, builder, design, height or staffing, so the story has no built or staffing section beyond the 1915 state context. The Forest Lookouts page is mostly site navigation; its Athens content is the agency, county, township/section, status and an NGS station block. The NGS listing has two rows for PID CQ2989, coded XX (surface mark reported destroyed) and NN (no geodetic control), each for horizontal and vertical control. The listing's own legend defines both codes, but nothing in it says which row is current. The firetower.org six-site list was read in full and does not include Athens. The 'nothing to visit' claim was removed from the story; access stays unset. The brief's coordinates (32.6576, -93.0597) match the Wikipedia point to four decimals, but the Forest Lookouts page gives no coordinates, so the record's location source label may be wrong. Ownership 'state' in the record is not stated in any source read here. Access was not set because no source supports an access level and there is no tower to visit. The NGS name 'Athens Fire Tower LFC' could be added as an other_name.

No source read gives the year the Louisiana National Guard removed the tower, so the story and events leave the removal undated. Search results did not settle it: the Wikipedia Louisiana list's 'Catahoula' entry is a parish heading for a different tower, and the 2011 Louisiana chapter report only records the site's registration. The record has no built event; the register gives 1933 and it is added here. The NGS datasheet itself was not read; the description comes via the Forest Lookouts page. No source describes access or remains at the site today.

Parish conflict left open, not resolved. The Forest Lookouts list says Grant Parish, which matches the brief's record; the FFLS register page says Sabine Parish. The story reports both. Editor to decide which the record should show. Brief's coordinates and elevation (78.6 m) match the register's 258 ft (79 m). The register's 100-foot height gives height_m 30.5. The removal date is only 'early 1980s' in the one source that gives it. The 2011 report mentions historic photos that accompanied the nominations; no photo URL was found, so none is listed. A Wikipedia Louisiana list page that was read has no row starting with 'Clear Creek'. A search snippet points to National Park Service material on CCC towers at Kisatchie; it does not name this tower and was not used.

The 1993 move to a Bentley tourist attraction rests on one line on the Forest Lookouts site. A Facebook group post titled 'Fire Tower in Bentley' turned up in search, but it could not be read, so we have not confirmed it is this tower. The 1936 build date, 1942 handover and 1983 permit come from the register description only. Nothing we read describes the attraction, the tower's condition or any visitor access, so access is left out of the facts.

Single source (the FFLOS register entry). No build year, builder, staffing or demolition year found in any source read. The demolition is given only as 'the 1990s or 2000s', so no year-specific removal event is recorded. A search for a Forestry Commission link found nothing and none is assumed. The Wikipedia list of Louisiana fire lookout towers has no De Soto or Grove Hill entry. The nearby-sounding Dolet Hills Power Station (DeSoto Parish, closed end of 2021) is not linked to this site by any source and is not used. No access level recorded: the register does not state one.

Single source: the Wikipedia Louisiana list, which gives the status 'Still standing/Inactive', the note 'Damaged', and the coordinates that match the record (30.665, -92.995). No build date, builder, design, staffing or access information was found. Two web searches returned only generic Dry Creek pages; the Beauregard tourism page and the Dry Creek community article did not mention the tower in the parts read. Guessed Fire Lookout and NHLR URLs returned 404. The Wikipedia reference for the 2015 item has no URL in the cache, so it is cited through the list. A parish or Louisiana Office of Forestry check would be the next step for build date and condition. Budget used: 2 websearch.py calls and 6 page reads.

Very thin sourcing. No entry for Fields Fire Tower in the cached NHLR or FFLOS (firetower.org) Louisiana registers, and no mention in the cached centraluslookouts.com Louisiana page beyond a bare county-header photo callout with no text. Wikipedia's own citation for 'still standing' points to a USGS GNIS feature-detail page (geonames.usgs.gov, Apex app); it is JavaScript-rendered and returned only the generic USGS/Board on Geographic Names homepage when fetched, so it could not be used directly. One WebSearch and two page reads were spent (this Wikipedia page plus the dead-end GNIS fetch); stopped researching rather than spend more of the budget chasing a page that would not render. Builder, construction date, design, height, and managing agency are all unknown and should not be guessed. A human with access to LDAF's Louisiana Statewide Forest Resource Assessment and Strategy PDF (cited elsewhere in the same Wikipedia list, pp. 36-37) might find more.

No build year, first-staffing date, or move/alteration history was found in the sources reached, so the story says so. The record's elevation (27.1 m) is consistent with the register's 89 ft. The 33.5 m height is converted from the register's 110 ft. Access is unknown: no source reached says whether the public may visit, so no access or visit fact is written. Use wording conflicts between the register (very high fire danger days) and Wikipedia (high wind days); the Wikipedia asterisk is unexplained. Do not confuse with a Gordon tower in Wisconsin (a 1935 Aermotor listing seen in a search result, T.44N-R.12W); that is a different structure and was excluded. An OpenStreetMap node (358380019) tags it as an observation tower of lattice construction at ~26 m, but that was not cited. Search budget: three websearch.py calls, one over the two-per-tower budget.

Thin on the tower itself: the register page is the only source about the tower; the 2010 NRHP nomination and the NPS page cover the recreation area and say the CCC built the tower only 'likely'. No staffing, current access or post-2011 condition was found, so access and staffing are left out of facts. The firemen's dwelling dates (1935-1958) belong to the cabin, not the tower. The register says 'CCC Troop F-6' and the NPS page says 'Company 5407, Camp F-6'; the story flags this without merging them as fact. Not used: the register gives the recreation area's NRHP listing as December 2011, while Wikipedia gives December 7, 2010 citing the NPS weekly list; this concerns the recreation area, not the tower. The nhlr.org Lookout.aspx?id=906 page returned HTTP 500. Used about 10 distinct pages, over the 6-read budget, because the tower has few sources.

Unresolved conflict: the register says a 99 ft 9 in Aermotor LX-25 built in 1933 (with a 1934 USFS photo and a 1952 stair change); the central Louisiana lookouts site says an 82-ft steel tower with a 7x7 cab was erected in 1951-52. It may be a replacement or a different tower. The Forest History Society PDF 'A History of Kisatchie' was searched by keyword and did not yield a Kisatchie-tower entry. No source found on current access or climbability; the access level is left out of facts. The Wikipedia 'active use' status is undated. The record's height_m 25.0 conflicts with the register.

The record coordinates (30.92639, -90.72917) match the Wikipedia list exactly, and the list status is 'Still standing/active use', so the record's standing status is confirmed. The list's location column reads Greensburg (the parish seat) rather than Liverpool, so the place name and the tower name differ; the story says so. No build date, builder, design, staffing or access information was found. Searches returned nothing specific to this tower. Guessed Forest Lookouts, Fire Lookout and NHLR URLs returned 404. The Forest Lookouts index and the FFLOS Louisiana page were checked, but the FFLOS table was cut off in the read, so its absence of this tower is unconfirmed. Budget used: 2 websearch.py calls and 6 page reads (including the 404s).

Only Wikipedia's Louisiana list gives this tower any detail, and it gives nothing on construction, height, ownership, staffing or use. The list's note that it looks disused or retired sits beside a note that it is visible on Google Street View; neither is a dated record. Two web searches returned no tower history. The local NHLR crawl has no page for this tower (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/la/lorraine-lookout-tower/ returns 404), and the FFLA Louisiana cache does not name it. A Fire Tower Rd in Ponchatoula (Redfin address listing) is not linked to this tower and is not used. Worth asking the LDAF Office of Forestry or the Louisiana chapter of FFLA for records, and a photo would be the main gain. The story is short by design; do not pad it.

The register's only removal date is 'by 2021'. Wikipedia's Merryville row estimates removal between 2015 and 2016 from old aerial imagery; this fits 'by 2021' but is not confirmed, so no removal year is certain. No built year beyond 'early 1950s', so no built event was entered. No staffing, fire or access information found in the sources read; the Central US Lookouts Merryville page is only a heading. The record's status 'standing' is contradicted by both registers and Wikipedia (proposed correction). The Wikipedia 'Torn down.' quote is taken from the Merryville row of the list.

Two independent sources (the NHLR register and a lookout-hobbyist history site) agree and complement each other, but neither confirms what happened after the 2006 disassembly: whether restoration was completed, where the tower now physically stands, or whether it's accessible. The tower record's coordinates are tagged 'exact' from NHLR but almost certainly predate the 2006 move. Worth a human follow-up with the Catahoula Ranger District or a recent visit report before treating location/access as current.

Only the 2017 NHLR entry and two quoted newspaper items cover this tower. The 1920s build date is 'believed' per NHLR, so no built event is recorded. The 212 ft figure is the site elevation, not tower height; no tower height found. Access restricted is inferred from the removed lower landings, not an official rule. Four searches, including the Wikipedia Louisiana list, found no LDAF tower record for Caldwell Parish. The 1957 entry is a rainfall report, so treat it as a weak mention. The page prints the newspaper as 'The Monroe New-Stars'; the story uses Monroe News-Star.

Thin evidence. Wikipedia's list is the only source with substance on this tower, and it gives no construction date, height, owner, staffing or use. TopoQuest is a gazetteer entry: it gives the point elevation (167 ft MSL) and map name, and it calls St. Helena Parish a county, which is a terminology slip, not a correction to the record. Search results also surfaced a 213 m cable-stayed mast and an 89 m CAPLINE tower at Pine Grove; both are communications structures, not lookouts, and are not used. The local NHLR crawl has no page for this tower (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/la/pine-grove-lookout-tower/ returns 404). Records most likely at the LDAF Office of Forestry or the Louisiana chapter of FFLA; a photo or a dated record would be the main gain.

Height (100 ft in the register, about 112 ft in the 1941 survey) and build year (1937 in the register, 1936 in the byway guide) disagree. The move to Fort Sill, Oklahoma comes only from the register; we did not find a second source for it. Public access is inferred from the byway guide listing the site as a stop, not from a visitor rule. The guide's publication date was not visible in what we read.

Thin evidence. Wikipedia's list gives status and a 1945 map note; the USGS page gives the station name, interpolated coordinates and an empty data list. Neither source gives a construction date, height, owner, staffing or fire history. The USGS station name links the gauge to the tower but does not prove a shared site, and the two coordinate sets differ by about 1.3 km. The 'active use' wording is Wikipedia's and undated. Records likely at the LDAF Office of Forestry or a Washington Parish library or historical society. The local NHLR crawl has no page for this tower. A dated photo or owner statement would be the main gain.

Thin record. The only status is the undated Wikipedia list entry 'Still standing.' (its Street View note is not a dated check). The Central US Lookouts page lists the name only. No build date, builder, height, owner or access rules were found. Sunny Hill does not appear in the cached NHLR Louisiana index or the cached FFLOS pages we searched. anyplaceamerica.com and mindat.org refused fetches (HTTP 403), so their tower pages were not read. Access level left unset. Suggest asking the Louisiana Department of Agriculture and Forestry (Office of Forestry) and checking a recent photo before any change to status.

Unresolved height conflict: 175 feet per the NHLR, the Town of Woodworth page and the Forest Lookouts header, versus 176 feet in a Kisatchie National Forest Facebook post seen only as a search snippet (the page returned a login stub; not cited). That snippet also calls it an MC-40 model and 'the tallest active lookout in North America'. No page read names the model, so the facts omit it. The Forest Lookouts page is a header plus one line, so the 1954 camera note rests on that single line. No source read gives current staffing or climbing rules; the Alexander State Forest Wikipedia article and the Louisiana Department of Agriculture and Forestry were not read. Confirm current status before publishing. No corrections to the brief.

Thin record. Two sources agree on the 1937 CCC build replacing an 1918 tower, and the NHLR registration date matches the brief. No staffing, fire or access sources were found. The Forest Fire Lookout Association Massachusetts chapter Facebook posts describe a 67-foot Aermotor MC-39 and say the 1918 tower moved to Georgetown; I could only see search snippets (the pages would not load), so the 67-foot figure is unresolved against the NHLR's 60 feet and is not in the story. The brief's OpenStreetMap height tag of 18.3 m agrees with 60 feet. Worth checking the FFLA posts or a Bureau source before publishing any height beyond 60 feet.

Two sources. The 1911 to 1913 detail, the Thomas Buxton staffing and the deputy-warden meeting rest on the Willhite page, an independent history site; no state record (Massachusetts DCR or Mount Greylock Reservation) was read. Elevation conflict: 3,491 ft (FFLOS) versus 3,487 ft (Willhite); record kept at 1064.1 m. The brief's status 'gone' is kept: the cab is gone, but the steel tower's fate is unknown. The Veterans War Memorial Tower is described only in the Willhite page; its build date is unverified and it is not confirmed to stand on the 1911 site. No photos collected.

Good on the 1959 tower, the 2016 and 2024 condition reports and the access situation. Missing: when staffing ended, whether it ever spotted a notable fire, and who built the 1959 tower. Forest Fire Lookout Association Massachusetts Facebook posts (about the 1920 tower and a 2017 roof replacement) could not be read, so they are not used. Recommend a Massachusetts local-history search for Bureau staffing records. Access is private land; the story advises against climbing. No photos recorded because license terms were not clear.

The brief's agency 'Alander Mt' is a mountain name and is proposed for correction. The access 'public' fact describes Beebe Hill State Forest, where the moved tower stands, not the Alander Mountain site; an editor may want a narrower note. The main open question is the tower's condition today: Wikipedia (late 2024, unsafe), the register (2025, restored) and the hobbyist page (restored, open) disagree. The register links beebehill.info; check it or NY DEC before publishing a 'today' claim. Elevation: the brief's 653.8 m matches the register's 2,145 ft (654 m); the hobbyist page gives the summit as 2240 ft and is not used. A search snippet from a Forest Fire Lookout Association Massachusetts chapter Facebook post gave 1932 for the Washburn re-erection; the page was not opened, so the story does not use it.

The 1924 tower and the current access status rest on Wikipedia's Ward Reservation article, which cites a 2017 Andover Townsman piece by Gail Ralston, 'Holt Hill Part 2: The fire tower'. That article returned HTTP 429 to both fetch_text and WebFetch, so it could not be read; retry later, as it is the likeliest source for staffing history and notable fires. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Massachusetts Facebook post calling 1970 'the year it was built' could not be read and is not used. The Mass.gov page is undated and does not name Andover. No photos recorded.

Brief said access unknown; set to public because the summit is conservation land crossed by trails. Sources disagree on the build year (1916 vs 1917), height (40 vs 48 ft) and phone line length (1 vs 2 miles). No source describes the footings today. Forest Lookouts is a compilation of newspaper and state-report quotes; Wikipedia is used for its own statements. Unread lead: ffla.org/lookouts/ma/ashburnham.htm. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the 1913 newspaper item names the company as Crocker, Burbank & Co. and gives no location, so the story no longer calls it local. The 2002 buyers are from the full Wikipedia sentence.

Only the register page could be read, so the history rests on one source. Facebook posts by the FFLA Massachusetts chapter could not be loaded (login wall). Their text appeared only in search snippets, which say the tower stood on Peter Hill and give a different staffing span (1914 to 1916, or 1914 to 1918). Not verified and not used in the story. Those snippets also mention remnants on the hill; also unverified and not used. The brief lists kind as unknown; the register says wooden tower, so kind could be set to tower. Staffing end and any surviving remains are not covered by sources read.

Good sources for the layout of the site (NHLR, FFLOS, Forest Lookouts, Brush Breakers), but the dates disagree and no source gives current access. Conflicts to check: (1) present tower built 1947 (NHLR; the Shoot Flying Hill tower removed 1947 per FFLOS) vs relocated to Clay Hill in 1948 (Brush Breakers). The record keeps 1947. (2) Steel tower 1912 (NHLR) vs 1914 (FFLOS, Brush Breakers); height 48 ft (FFLOS) vs 50 ft (passage quoted on the Forest Lookouts page). (3) First wooden tower 1897 (NHLR, FFLOS, Brush Breakers) vs 1890 (Forest Lookouts summary). (4) Site elevation: NHLR 66 ft (20 m, matches record elevation_m 20.1) vs Brush Breakers hill elevation around 200 ft; the story does not use either elevation. Correction proposed: the FFLOS US 35 registration belongs to the former site, not to the standing tower. Access and ownership today: not found in any page read; the story says so. Status standing is from the 2014 visit and an undated Brush Breakers page; not verified after 2014. Not fetched and not cited: Forest Fire Lookout Association Massachusetts Facebook snippets describing the 1947 tower as built late summer 1947 and as still standing on Clay Hill. Worth checking before adding any access level. No photos added (the FFLOS page lists photos but none were read). Unknown: notable fires at either site; none found in the pages read. Checked 2026-10-08: the 48-ft and 1947-removal claims come from the firetower.org former-site page (cite 2), not the Forest Lookouts page; the 1904 date for the Benson article is the page's own claim and conflicts with its 'last year' wording, so the story attributes it to the page. The 1911 selection item is the Sandwich Observer (October 31, 1911) as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the 1922 item is the Barnstable Patriot (May 15, 1922).

Brief said access unknown; set to public because the Appalachian Trail passes over the summit. Build year is disputed (1913, 1914, 1915). The Willhite page is a personal trail-lookout site; its footings claims are repeated by the AT hike description, and firetower.org agrees that footings remain. The AT page heading reads 'Hike Description' (checked 2026-10-10), so the source title was changed to match it. Willhite's other account (built 1914, stored, rebuilt on Lair Mountain in 1915) conflicts with the 1916 move; it is noted here and not in the story. No staffing or fire information found.

Status correction: the brief's 'gone' contradicts the register (2015) and the 2018 chapter post, both of which say the stone structure still stands. No source newer than 2018 was found, so current condition is unconfirmed. Use period conflicts (1939 vs briefly in 1938) are unresolved and both are reported. The build date of the stone structure is not in any source read, so no built event is recorded. The Lowell Sun text comes through a compilation site (easternuslookouts.weebly.com), not the original newspaper. The horse-barn and horse-paddock details are from a chapter post and a personal blog, so treat them as reports, not checked facts.

The Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook post on this tower returned only a login wall, so its search-snippet claim that the cab was replaced in 1967 is not used. The Section 15 text read shows no publication date and describes this tower only by location. The only visit report on file is from 2006, so present condition and access are unverified. Build history rests on one register entry. No photos recorded.

Build date not found in any source read; the register's Goat Peak comparison (built 1928) is not a date for Bray. Unresolved conflict: the register calls Bray one of two official lookout towers, while the Mt. Tom Range viewing-tower page names two viewing towers (one overlooking Westhampton, one on Goat Peak) and does not mention Bray; a Holyoke tour listing includes Bray Tower. The Westhampton tower is not named on that page, so it is not assumed to be Bray or the Visitor Center tower. Not established that Bray was a fire lookout; the register and story say lookout tower but no source says it spotted fires. A Facebook photo search snippet mentioning a Mount Tom tower was not used because the page could not be read. No photos recorded.

The 1949 build year rests on the NHLR page alone; no second source for the build date was read. Location (Nickerson State Park, Deer Park Road) is confirmed by the Cape Cod Fire Department listing and the Mass.gov review. Conflict to flag: the Mass.gov review says the tower is atop Deer Park Hill, but also that Brewster and Wellfleet are not located on hills. Administrator: the register names Mass. Bureau of Forest Fire Control; the Cape Cod Fire Department listing calls it a DCR District 1 fire tower. The sources read do not say which office runs it today, so the story gives only the register's name. Record coordinates match NHLR (41.760220, -70.041520); the OSM node in the record (41.758097, -70.035366) is roughly 500 m away and was not cited. The record's 'restored 2015' event is better described as stair platforms replaced (a repair), so the event is recorded as modified. Staffing, access for climbing, and condition today are not in any source read; the NHLR page has no visit reports for Brewster. The Mass.gov review is undated (its citations include a 2011 work), so it is not evidence of current status. No photos added; the Mass.gov review refers to photos in an appendix that was not read. Checked 2026-10-08: the NHLR page as read is 936 characters with no staffing or visit-report section, which supports the story's absence statement; the register's own text says 'Built 1949' and 'Mass. Bureau of Forest Fire Control' for administration, while its description names the Massachusetts Bureau of Fire Control as builder. The story now says the state review is inconsistent about the landform, rather than that the sources disagree, because the register also places the tower on Deer Park Hill.

Built date conflict: FFLOS says 1912, the state heritage report says 1911. Not resolved; the story gives both. Elevation conflict: NHLR gives 1,202 ft (366 m) for its point; FFLOS gives 1,100 ft (335 m) for the tower site. The brief's elevation_m (366.4) follows NHLR. Coordinates differ by about 0.9 km (NHLR 42.142033, -72.224251; FFLOS 42.14972, -72.22444); not resolved. The brief's status 'standing' is kept, with a status_note explaining the loss of the cab and platform. The current owner of the tower structure is not confirmed; the report names Turnpike Authority ownership of the fenced site. The date of the reconnaissance report is not stated in the fetched text; the mass.gov path suggests 2016. No staffing roster was found; the 1915 item names no lookout. Two WebSearch summaries mentioned a Pioneer Valley profile and a Turnpike Authority fenced site, but those were not read, so they are not cited. The Massachusetts Historical Commission 1982 survey and a Brimfield town copy of the report returned 403 or duplicated text, so they were not used.

Unresolved: the older tower's move and build dates differ (firetower.org 1918 and 1930; FFLA post 1919 and 1932), so both are given. The FFLA post places the older tower along Lower College Pond Road, while firetower.org gives SW Line Road; treated as the same older tower because both record the 1986 closure and 2002 move. NHLR says 80 ft; a second FFLA post seen only as a search snippet says 85 ft, not used because the page could not be read. The FFLA posts about the 2000 and 2017 photos returned only a login wall, so no post-2014 condition is confirmed. A 1957 Carver forest fire appears on the Carver Fire Department history page, but no source read ties the tower to it, so it is omitted. No photos recorded.

Brief status 'gone' and kind 'tower' look right: the site is gone and the tower was moved to Minnesota in 2002. Two dates conflict between the register and the chapter (1918 vs 1919 move; 1930 vs 1932 replacement), and both are reported. The Minnesota farm's location is not given in either source; the Minnesota fire tower history page checked did not mention Carver. The register's SW Line Road and the chapter's Lower College Pond Road are both recorded, as the register and chapter give them. A second chapter post (search snippet only, not loadable here) also says replaced in 1932; not used. No access level is recorded: neither source states public access to the spot. The NHLR Carver Fire Tower (US 733) is a separate record and is not covered here.

Disputed: first tower 1917 (registry, 1917 state report) vs 1918 (FFLA); height 48 ft (registry, FFLA) vs 50 ft (1917 state report); current tower 60 ft (registry, Forest Lookouts) vs 68 ft structure height (FFLA). FFLA credits the US Forest Service with supplying the 1939 tower. Elevation: registry 574 ft (175 m, matches the record) vs FFLA 1075 ft, which looks wrong, so it is not used. State tower number is 15 on the 2016 state listing and 26 on the FFLA page. Current access and rental are unverified; the only current signal is the 2016 listing and an undated FFLA page. A search summary claimed a 1951 68-foot replacement; no page I read supports it (the 68-foot 1949 line in the Forest Lookouts index sits under Deer Park Hill, Brewster), so it is not used. Ask the Bureau of Forest Fire Control to confirm current status and access before publishing any visit guidance. The 2015 report publisher is inferred from its firelookout.org host.

Today's status, staffing, access and rental are unverified. No source read is later than the 2019 blog post, and the record's access 'unknown' is kept (no access facts added). Record fields (county Dukes, elevation 32 m, kind tower, status gone) check out against the Forest Fire page; no correction. Disputed: current tower 75 ft (registry) vs 68 ft structure height (FFLA); the 1914 structure's 60 ft height comes only from the registry. Brief height_m 58.5 corrected to 68 ft (20.7 m). Origin conflicts between the Register and New England Defenses (the latter cites a 1989 newsletter); not resolved. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook search snippet (not read in full) gives a third origin, a West Tisbury tower; not used. No page read gives visitor access, so the story says so. Living New Deal page refused the fetch (HTTP 403). FFLA Massachusetts Facebook posts (not fetchable, search snippets only) describe an 'International Derrick 1933' tower and say it was dismantled in 1951. The Long Lines page is undated and its 'inactive' label may be out of date. Summit access is not established by any source read. SEMRECC's building page does not name the site its headquarters occupies, and the story does not name one either.

Several dates and sizes conflict. First tower: 38 ft (FFLA) vs 30 ft (registry), first used 1912 (FFLA). The 40-foot tower: built 1917 (registry) vs a 40-foot Acushnet tower moved in 1938 (FFLA). Current tower: 1969 (registry and the record) vs 1970 (FFLA); 70 ft (registry) vs 68 ft (FFLA). Elevation 347 ft (registry) vs 353 ft (FFLA); the record's 105.8 m is close to the registry's 106 m. State tower number is #27 on the 2016 state listing and #19 on the FFLA page. The FFLA 'private property' note is undated and may describe the original 1912 arrangement, so the access level 'private' should be checked with the Bureau before any visit guidance. Current access and rental unknown. No staffing history found. Search summaries stated more detail (1938 and 1944 changes, 1970 date) that I checked only against the FFLA page, so only page-read facts are used.

The 1928 build date rests on the register page alone; no second source found. Searches surfaced a 1928 Goat Peak lookout in Washington State, a different site, so do not conflate them. Sources describe recreation and hawk watching only; none says the tower was built for fire watch, so the brief's kind 'unknown' is left as is. Current access comes from the DCR hike guide and an advocacy site. A check with the DCR Mount Tom office or MACRIS would settle the 1928 date.

Height and cab design are unconfirmed. A search snippet from the FFLA Massachusetts chapter gives 68 ft, but the Facebook post could not be read, so it is not used. The register names the older Bureau of Forest Fire Control as administrator; the 2023 Gazette names DCR, so agency is set to DCR and the record's agency field may need updating. Staffing: the register's 'Staffed seasonally' note is undated; the 2023 staffing item is a plan. The closure comment is undated (photo April 2016), so current access should be confirmed. Climbing rests on one 2020 trip report. No fire credited to this tower was found. The Eastern US Lookouts Moores Hill page yielded only navigation text.

Record fields (Hampden county, 443.5 m elevation, gone, tower) match the sources; no correction. The 2005 footings finding comes from the Forest Fire site alone. FFLA Massachusetts Facebook posts about Sweetman Mountain (remains, a 1950s observer photo, a removal post, a recovered photo of the tower) appeared in search results, but fetch returned only titles, so no claims from them are used and no photo is added. A lead for the editor: the FFLA post titled as a recovered photo of the Sweetman Mountain tower may carry a usable image, if its license can be confirmed. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the earlier story said the site did not make clear which structure stood until 1962; the page says the 65-ft tower was staffed until 1962, so that sentence was corrected. The phrase 'stood above Granville' was removed as unsupported by the sources.

The 2004 register is the only official source. Trailspotting (Aug 2026) describes the steel tower as still staffed during fire season and says visitors were invited up by the operator; this is one secondhand account, so confidence stays low and public access is not established. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'no later source' sentence was contradicted by the Trailspotting page and was rewritten; the 1940 Lowell Sun item was missing from events and has been added.

Brief status 'gone' is only partly right: the 1851 structure and 1861 addition survive as the summit house, but no source says whether the lookout room was in that part or in the 1894 annex that was demolished. The FFLA Massachusetts Facebook post on this lookout (Prospect House used as a lookout 1911-1918, now a museum) would not fetch, so it is not cited. No staffing, fire or room-access sources were found. Kind 'tower' in the brief is consistent with the register's 60-foot tower. Story names him Joseph A. Skinner because the sources spell his first name Allan and Allen. The 1821 guest cabin is now also an event in the JSON, with the fuller source quote.

Height conflict unresolved: the register says the first tower was 48 ft, and the State Forester report (via Forest Lookouts) says 50 ft. The present tower is 70 ft per the register. A search snippet from a fire-lookout site that returned 404 gave 68 ft, a 1913 first date and a 1936 radio date; none is verifiable here, so none is used. The Pelham record should read: move 1920, report published January 1921, height disputed. The Pelham register page does not mention Hanson. No current access, staffing or visit data found; access left unknown. Height 70 ft converted to 21.3 m.

Only the register is specific to this tower in the cache; the other two sources are statewide. Staffing and public access are not established, so no access key is set and the story says so. Lookout-site pages found by search (ffla.org and firelookout.org) returned 404 from the cache and were not quoted or used. Their search summaries say the tower is on Pinnacle Hill, gives 68 ft rather than the register's 70 ft, gives October 1, 1921 as first operation, and calls it an active state tower; none of that is in the story. The 1969 build year and the 1921 replacement rest on the register alone. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 3 readable page reads plus failed attempts.

The Hingham register lists its location as Prospect Hill, Plymouth County, and the Norwell entry describes a 48-foot iron tower on Prospect Hill built in 1916, so both records describe the same hill and the same height. Neither names the other, so the story says the Norwell tower appears to be the same tower. The FFLA Massachusetts Facebook posts that mention the Hingham tower could not be fetched and are not cited. The brief's kind 'unknown' should probably be 'tower' per the register's 48-foot tower. No access, staffing, fire or present-day site sources were found, so those keys are omitted.

The register's 'Mount Tom Hotel' is read as the summit house rebuilt in 1901, which stood on the summit until the May 1929 fire. No fetched source ties the 1914 lookout to that building by name, so the story flags it as likely. The FFLA Massachusetts Facebook post on the old summit house (upper room used for fire detection in the 1910s) would not fetch and is not cited. The brief's kind 'unknown' should be 'tower' per the register's 60-foot tower. Last year of lookout operation and staffing were not found. The site has a foundation, not a standing lookout, so status 'gone' matches the sources.

Built and replacement dates are well sourced, but the register dates the present tower to 1956 while the FFLA post's height (68 ft) differs from the register (75 ft). No source read gives current condition or staffing after 1945; the 2004 register entry is the latest tower-specific record. The 2017 FFLA post was readable and is cited for the 1916 height, the abandonment, and the 68 ft figure. The Town sketch gives the logbook watch's purpose as watching Kingston Bay for suspicious activity and does not call it a fire watch, so whether the WWII watch relates to the fire tower is undocumented. Camp Nekon is town conservation land; whether the tower is open for climbing is undocumented.

NHLR is the main source; the Forest Lookouts history is built from newspaper clippings. The 2026 trail guide is the only current source. The brief's height of 24.4 m conflicts with the register's 68 ft (corrected). Elevation differs slightly between NHLR (2,126 ft) and FFLOS (2,123 ft); not used. Search snippets about a 2003 rebuild plan and a steel frame were not fetched and are not used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: every story claim was checked against the cited pages and matches. The pending corrections (status) are left for human review as STORY_GUIDE.md requires.

OpenStreetMap-only record. The tower carries tower:type=observation and no emergency=fire_lookout tag, so it may not be a fire lookout at all; the kind 'tower' is still safe. Mapcarta labels it Essex while the nearby reservation is in Ipswich, so the town needs checking before any change (it may sit near the Essex/Ipswich line). Neither the cached NHLR nor the cached FFLOS Massachusetts index lists an Essex or Ipswich entry. The archived copy of the OSM source PDF (web.archive.org, 2014) did not load, so the current Mass.gov copy was read; the refuge observation tower it mentions is not tied to these coordinates. Status, build date and builder are unknown.

Three sources, all read. The NHLR page is the substantive one: 2002 registration, cab history, and an April 2016 visit report. Current access and staffing rest on that 2016 report; no newer source was readable. AllTrails (HTTP 403) and the Roamful and MyHikes listings appeared in search but were not readable, so none is cited. The brief's 2015 'restored' event is proposed as 'modified' in corrections. Not verified: whether the tower has changed status since April 2016, and whether the public may climb it. No photos added.

Conflict unresolved: the register dates a 70-foot iron tower on Burrill Hill to 1926, while the Friends of Lynn Woods flyer says Burrill Hill's earlier towers were wooden and that the first steel tower went up on Mount Gilead in 1929. Thin record. Staffing and current access are unsourced: the Wicked Local 2005 article returned HTTP 403 and FFLA Facebook posts returned login walls, so none was read. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 3 readable page reads plus failed attempts.

Only two pages were read: the NHLR register entry (no visit reports, no staffing) and an OpenStreetMap node that gives the 1972 start date. The FFLA Massachusetts Chapter Facebook post on this tower could not be fetched (login-blocked). Single register source for the tower's history; the Harvard Forest page only confirms the museum name and a 1930s diorama scene, not this tower. The brief's record puts the FFLOS registration (US 1548, MA 55, March 27, 2014) on the Pine Hill tower, but that entry is the former Manomet Hill site; see corrections. FFLOS and NHLR agree on the 1911 state-built tower on Reservoir Hill. Neither gives a removal year. No visit report, access information or photo found.

The 1940 Quabbin Lookout Tower is a different structure and should not be merged with this record.

Five sources read. The early history (1911 fire watch, 1912 and 1915 items, 1923 observer change, 1961 status) comes from the Forest Lookouts newspaper excerpts. These are transcriptions on a hobbyist site and were not checked against the original newspapers. No photos added.
