A web search hit on a different Long Hill (Wetipquin, Wikipedia) was ignored. No photos were added.

Thin record: the FFLA entry is the only source naming a tower here. Two searches found no fire-lookout history for the Kedges Straits site. The Wikipedia article mentions a 1984 peregrine nesting tower on the refuge; it is not a fire lookout and is not treated as the FFLA structure. The FFLA coordinates are close to the refuge's Wikipedia coordinates but not identical. Access is set to closed from the USFWS page; the brief's 'unknown' is replaced. Wikipedia is used only as a lead for the refuge; the peregrine tower line is its own claim. Recommend confirming with FFLA or refuge staff what the entry refers to.

Brief status_note matches the FFLA list but omits the state report's wooden-deck account. A 1929 Forest Worker item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page places a 120-foot tower at Millville, Worcester County; not reconciled and not used. No visiting information found, so access is set to restricted. No photos added.

Thinnest of the three. FFLA is the only source naming a tower at this point, and its entry carries only the name, county, coordinates and the word 'unknown'. TopoQuest identifies a cape of the same name in Kent County, at coordinates that do not match the FFLA entry. Two searches found no tower history, owner or access note. The 2007 DNR report's list of towers has no Kent County entry. Proposed corrections: remove '(unknown)' from other_names, and reword status_note because the FFLA page does not say details are uncertain. Recommend confirming with FFLA what the entry refers to before keeping it as standing.

The brief's status 'gone' rests on the undated Maryland list (source 2); the 2017 NHLR entry only says removal was planned, so the removal date is unknown and the story does not give one. The brief's elevation (12.8 m, from NHLR's 42 ft figure) is not a facts key and was not used. No source found on staffing, fires, or the site today. Read budget exceeded (about 12 page reads, many dead ends: Wikipedia, MHT survey PDF, DNR poster, a Powellville fire company page); 2 searches used. Fact-check 2026-10-09: Wicomico County added as an evidence quote; the DNR paragraph's copied wording was rewritten; the story now says none of the sources checked describes the site, rather than no source.

Two accounts of the build date, height and funding conflict (1931 newspapers via Forest Lookouts vs NHLR 1941/140 ft/federal). Current access to the museum tower is not established: the museum's own site was not read and no visiting hours or climbing rules were found. No source describes what remains at the original site. No new photos found. Three searches were run for this lookout, one over the budget of two.

Brief events said 'None relocated' and is corrected to the 1999 move. Build year (1931 vs 1941) and height (100 vs 140 ft) conflict between sources and are unresolved. Museum hours and whether the restored top can be climbed were not verified: the findcityoffice listing gives only an address, and the search did not surface a museum website. Staffing is from the Register ('last staffed in the 1970s') plus one 1942 newspaper mention. Used 6 page reads and 2 searches.

Brief record (24.4 m, standing) checks out; the FFLA asterisk legend supports 'cab no longer in place'. Access was unknown and is now 'permission' from the Wikipedia and WillhiteWeb text. Sources 1 and 2 are the strongest; WillhiteWeb (4) is a hiking-site history with no citations, so its 1883-1886 and 1923-1964 items are secondary. The 1921 'erected 25 years ago' phrase conflicts with WillhiteWeb's 1886 date and is unresolved. A search-result mirror of Wikipedia said the fire lookout 'has since been removed'; that page was not read, and the cached Wikipedia text says the tower still stands. No current owner or public-access statement was found. Do not encourage climbing.

Only two sources. The 1930 article is a plan, and nothing read confirms that the tower was built, its height, its cab, or who staffed it. FFLA lists it standing with no asterisk, so the cab is presumed in place. The 2007 Maryland DNR Forestry Towers report (https://dnr.maryland.gov/forests/documents/fire/Fire_Tower_Report.pdf) covers towers the state managed as of December 2006 and does not list a Sideling tower, so the tower may be privately or locally owned, or may be gone. The Wikipedia Sideling Hill article has no tower mention. Next steps: a Washington County or Maryland Forest Service archive search for the build date, and a newspaper search for the 1930s-40s. Access left unset because nothing was found.

Record height_m 14.3 does not match the register's 100-foot tower (30.5 m); facts.height_m uses the register. Record agency 'Maryland Department of Natural Resources - Forest Service' is not confirmed: the NHLR 'Administered by' value was cut from the fetched text. Registration year: register says April 23, 2007; Discovery Center says 2009. The 1934 replacement and the 1938 build date are not reconciled. Opening hours come from undated pages; check with Deep Creek Lake State Park.

The DNR report is dated April 2007 and covers towers managed as of December 2006, so the condition finding is roughly 20 years old. FFLA lists the tower as standing with no asterisk, which fits the report. The DNR table gives 80 feet and a good condition. The 1,760 versus 1,685 foot elevation gap is left open. No staffing record or visiting policy was found; the DNR report describes the site as a fenced communications compound, so access is set to restricted. Do not encourage climbing.

Both main sources agree on 1934 and a CCC origin (register says Doncaster Camp crews; MHT says believed). Name: register calls it Welcome Forestry Tower; MHT form calls it Welcome Firetower (CH-752). The MHT form was last updated 2003 and the condition and paint details are old; current condition unknown. The record's source_pages dnr.maryland.gov/forests/firetowers/welcome.pdf returns 404; the eastern-us Welcome page yielded only a header. No staffing or public-access source found, so access is marked restricted without a visiting rule. Height 120 ft (36.6 m) comes from the register only. Record's agency matches the register.

Construction and staffing facts come from two 1935 and one 1944 Midland Journal item reprinted on the Forest Lookouts page; the reprint ends in 1944. Current status rests only on the FFLA list. The Cecil County History blog (cecilcountyhistory.com, post on fire towers) reportedly says the tower still stands, has a 2011 photo, and that the state stopped operating the towers, with seasonal staffing into the 1970s. fetch_text got HTTP 403 for that page, so it is not cited and needs checking. A DNR poster reportedly says Aeromotor built most Maryland towers; no source read names Woodlawn's builder, so none is stated. The brief record had no agency; the agency fact is worded from the District Forest Warden quote. No licensed photo found, so none added. Access level left unset: no source described access.

Record height_m 3.7 (about 12 ft) is not confirmed by the sources read: the April 1924 item gives 12 ft, the July 1924 item 15 ft, and a 1935 item 20 ft; left out of facts. The record's 2015 'destroyed' event is recorded here as 'other' because the sources say the tower blew over and lay on the summit. The 1924-1949 newspaper items were read as transcriptions on the Eastern US lookouts site, not as the newspapers. The 1949 fire destroyed the tower of that date; the sources do not say when the tower standing in 2011 was built. The AllTrails page for the trail returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Access 'public' rests on the Maine by Foot description of public reserved land.

Brief events 2007 and 2008 (Morneault volunteer restoration) are NOT in this JSON: no page read supports them. A search result points to firelookout.org cr-me-2008.pdf (Maine Chapter Report 2008), which was not read because the page-read budget ran out; check it before adding those events. The brief's 'airlifted in August 2020' and 'one of three cabs replaced that week' are not confirmed: the BDN article says only 'recently installed', and the 2020 year-end report says 'reviewed in 2020'. Only the first 3,000 of about 6,200 characters of the BDN page were read, so cost and funding details were not used. Staffing 'not staffed' is an inference from the 'closed' note and the article's past-tense description of observers; treat it as medium confidence. The brief's status 'standing' is supported by the FFLA list and the 2020 article.

Dates: Forest Lookouts dates a lookout station to 1914 and the tower erection to April 1921; we record 1921 for the tower. Two web search summaries say the first tower was 1914 and moved to Dill Ridge in 1927 and back, a 1998 preservation effort, a 1967 reinstallation and a 2021 condition note; none of those pages could be read (the Hilton legacy page returned 404, towerdex returned 403, and a Maine archives link returned 404), so none is in the story or the JSON. Check firelookout.org's Maine record and the Maine Forest Service before publishing a current condition. The 2008 report's 'may be removed in 2009' is a plan, not proof of removal. Brief lacked a build date; agency kept as the brief's Maine Forestry District from the Forest Lookouts header, while the 2008 report names the Maine Forest Service. Access unknown. No photos added.

Very thin record. The Forest Lookouts page and the firetower.org page both give 2000 as the removal date; only the firetower.org page names Connecticut as the destination. No source read gives a build date, design, builder, staffing or fires, so the story has none. The Connecticut town or owner is unknown, so the tower's current location is unknown. Unread search snippets claim a 1946 or 1949 build, a Blackstrap Hill (Falmouth) origin and a 1999 removal; these conflict with the 2000 date in the pages read and were not used, pending a check against Maine Forest Service records. The brief's FFLOS registration date (2008) matches the cached register page ('Date Registered September 15, 2008'); the story does not use it.

Removal date is disputed: the register says before 1932, while a Maine Atlas caption shows a 1932 photo of the standing tower and says removed sometime in the 1930s. The removed event year 1932 is a placeholder. The same caption places the tower on 'Sally Mountain at Attean' and dates a 2,221-foot-mountain wood tower to 1908; the other records do not mention 1908 and this is unreconciled. Brief height 3.7 m matches the 12-foot 1920 inventory. No source found describing the summit today or public access. The twelve-fires item is headed August 1907 but tagged (1905) on the source page; the story flags this. Story wording of the 1905, 1914 and 1916 items was tightened to match the source text. Brief record otherwise checks out: gone, FFLOS US 83, registered 2008.

Height conflict: 27 ft (1919 district report), 36 ft (Daily Kennebec Journal, 1919, quoted on the Forest Lookouts page), 24 ft (1919 annual report and 1920 inventory). Facts use 24 ft, the figure matching the brief's 7.3 m. Location conflict: Lincoln Plantation (district report, register) vs Grafton (Kennebec item). Maine Memory dating conflict: title ca. 1929, creation date circa 1920. The 2004 removal rests on the register alone. No source found describing the site today or public access. Brief record otherwise consistent: gone, FFLOS US 84, registered 2008, agency Maine Forestry District.

Not cited because not read: a Facebook group post and a YouTube video description (seen only in search results) say a Civilian Conservation Corps camp (Co. 1129) built the tower in 1937-39 and that it lasted into the 1960s. That conflicts with the register's circa 1954 removal. Worth checking before publication. The Living New Deal page returned HTTP 403, so it was not read. Do not confuse with 'Washington Bald Mountain' (Maine Atlas caption: a 55-foot tower built 1918), a different site at 45.09818, -67.92316. The Forest Lookouts page for this site has only a location line and adds nothing. The 'tallest in Maine' claim is the Sun Journal's; not independently checked. Brief record consistent: gone, FFLOS US 85, registered 2008, Baring. Brief has no height; 30.5 m comes from the article's 100 feet.

The build date and original builder are unknown. The 1951 move and the 1955 and 1965 details rest on one undated hiker-oriented site (willhiteweb.com); that site also gives the 1941 survey note, which the story paraphrases. The Forest Lookouts page gives only the county and agency. Current status rests on the FFLA asterisk and the hiker site. No Maine Forest Service records found. A search lead pointed to Maine Memory Network photos of Maine Forest Service towers, not checked. The record had no height; height_m 12.2 converts the 1955 'about 40 feet' description and is secondary.

Brief had no height or design; added from the 1934 report (40 ft). No source found on staffing, fires or the site today. Facebook posts by the FFLA Maine chapter show the tower in the 1950s but could not be read, so not cited. The 1934 annual report is read through its quotation on Forest Lookouts [2]; the report itself was not opened.

Staffing conflict is unresolved: NHLR says rangers staff it during high fire danger (present tense); NPS says it has not been manned since 1976. The NPS fire towers page was last updated 2020-10-07. Current 2024-2026 opening status was not confirmed by any source I could read. OpenStreetMap node 358231332 tags access=private, which conflicts with NPS; not used. Wikidata gives elevation 833 ft; NHLR gives 807 ft (246 m, matching the brief). Coordinates match NHLR. Registration date September 16, 1993 is confirmed by NHLR and NPS.

The brief record calls it a tower and gives no height or design; the 1915 and 1920 sources describe a station and a ground cabin, so 'tower' rests on the FFLA listing and the 1920 map title. A 2021 firelookout.org inventory appeared only in a search snippet (reportedly: tower without cab, groundhouse in bad condition, and a steel tower from 1965); its URL could not be fetched, so it is not used. Verify before adding any 1965 steel-tower event. The 1953 Blackmore item is a bear anecdote reprinted from the Biddeford Journal; only the lookout attribution is used.

Build date is disputed (1906 photo inventory vs 1916 newspaper item). Most of the early history comes from the Forest Lookouts page, which quotes old reports and photo inventories; the originals were not checked. Trail Finder's body text calls the trail remote 2-mile, but its length field says 4.00 miles round trip; the story says 4 miles as listed. Two Facebook items seen only as search snippets, not read: a 1967 'Big Spencer Mountain' post saying the tower came down over the 1966-67 winter, and a post saying the cab blew off in a December 2009 storm. Both conflict with the Forest Lookouts account and are not used. No closure notice found; the story does not encourage climbing.

Record kind 'ground' is proposed as 'tower' (see corrections); the Association's list still says Ground, so a human should decide. Height conflict left open: 1917 says 38 ft, 1920 says 16 ft; the record's height_m 4.9 matches the 1920 figure, so height_m is not put in facts. Dates differ slightly: the cabin and foundation are dated about 1960 by Wing and a new tower airlifted in May 1962; both are given as the sources give them. Agency names vary by source (Maine Forestry District, Maine Forest Service, Maine Parks and Lands, Maine Bureau of Parks and Land). Access is not in facts: state ownership in 2011 and Appalachian Trail hiker use are reported, but no source states current public access. The FFLA 2011 report's 'Mount Blue' look-alike tower is a different site and is not used. The Facebook post and willhiteweb pages were not cited.

Brief height 14.6 m matches the 48-ft figure. The Trout Mountain link rests on one Maine History Online caption; the Trout tower standing today was built in 2020 from Alabama parts and is not the Black Cat tower. No source found on staffing, fires or the site today.

No staffing source found: a Facebook post by the FFLA Maine chapter claims about ten years of staffing, but the page would not load, so it is not cited. Opportunity Hill is not placed in any source read; it may or may not be the Opportunity Farm site in New Gloucester, and no source links them. A Facebook group post mentions an 1853 observation tower on Blackstrap Hill; not used. The 47-ft towers mentioned in the 1931 report are not tied to Blackstrap in the sources.

Thin evidence: no source found on staffing, fires, access or what remains on the site today. Build year conflicts (1947 vs 1949) and both are reported. Brief record status 'gone' is correct; no corrections. The ipage.com state listing is attributed to the Forest Fire Lookout Association by inference (it matches the firelookout.org Maine list). No photos added; image URLs were not verified.

Brief name 'Boarstone Mountain Tower Site' and kind 'ground': sources show no tower was needed, so the 'Tower Site' label may mislead; the editor may want a different display name. Access is public per the sanctuary guide, but no source describes what remains of the station today. Coordinates match Wikipedia's summit to about 30 m (inference). The 1913 vs 1914 build year is reported both ways. No photos added.

Brief height 3.7 m corresponds to the 1914 12-ft wood tower; the collapsed tower was the 1937 steel tower (35 as listed, unit inferred as feet). The summit's current state rests on a single 2021 article; the register and the article disagree on removal. Access is inferred from the article's description of the road and trail. No staffing or fire records found. No photos added.

The 1924 build rests on two Daily Kennebec Journal items quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, consistent with the 1925 state map. The brief's access 'unknown' is filled with 'public' only as an inference from a hiking guide that describes a trail in the park; check before publishing. The brief's agency (Baxter State Park) is right for today; the 1924 operator was the state forestry department. A search summary cited a Maine database entry giving 1,792 ft and an installed-1924 date; the database URLs returned 404 so those figures are not used, and the hiking guide gives 1,796 ft. No staffing, fire or caretaker history appears in any source read. The register's 2004-2005 removal range is shown as year 2004 in events.

County conflict is unresolved: the register, Forest Lookouts page and Maine list say Piscataquis; the 1944 state map record says Penobscot (T6 R7 WELS). The story reports both. A search summary cited a Maine database entry (circa 1942, 20-ft wood tower, T6 R7) but the database URLs returned 404, so no build date or height is used. No staffing, fire or access information appears in any source read; the brief's access 'unknown' stays unknown. Consider a Maine Forest Service or state archive inquiry on the county and on the build date.

No build date, height or staffing is in any source read. A search summary cited a 1925 build and a 48-ft steel tower for Carr Pond, but the sources we opened do not say so, and the Maine database URLs returned 404, so neither figure is used. The 1928 map is the earliest dated evidence. Today's condition and access are not described in any source. The register calls it 'Carr Pond Tower Site' while the Maine list calls it 'Carr Pond Mountain'.

Brief status 'gone' confirmed: the structure moved to Green Mountain, Effingham NH. Heights conflict and are not resolved, so height_m is not set: 48 feet in the 1920 report, 47 feet original and 39 feet after 1977 in the NH register, 60 feet in the Laconia account. No access level set: the Maine site is not described, and NH climbing rules were not found. An AllTrails page on the summit deck returned HTTP 403 and was not used. Facebook posts (tower up 1919-1921; move 1922) were not used. Two WebSearch calls and about ten page reads, over the read budget because the moved structure needed New Hampshire sources.

Brief height 4.9 m corrected to 3.7 m: 16 feet was the 1917 partly erected tower; the 1919 report and 1920 inventory give 12 feet. Build dates come from the Forest Lookouts quotes of annual reports and a Daily Kennebec Journal entry. A Facebook post dating construction to 1918 was not used. No removal date in any source read, so no removed event. Access not recorded: the sources place the site inside Baxter State Park and say nothing about visitor access. Two WebSearch calls and about five page reads.

Built 1931 is supported only by the state report as quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page; no primary copy of the report was read. Staffing history and the original design of this tower are not found. Access is recorded as public from a single 2024 hiker's guide with no owner named; confirm land status before publishing a visiting note. A Canaan Historical Society post and a Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter post mention 1931 and aging stairs, but Facebook returned only page titles, so they are not cited.

The summit has no fire tower but does have a communications building and radio tower, per the 2018 and 2021 accounts; both are blog or hike reports, not agency records. The 1917 height (16 ft) and the 1920 inventory (12 ft) disagree. The museum home page lists admission rates ($12 ages 12-65, $10 ages 65+, $7 ages 4-12) and does not mention the tower; whether the tower display is covered by admission was not confirmed. The sister record us-me-chase-mountain-tower-site-at-patten-lumbermens-museum is the moved tower. No new photos found.

Relocation year 2001 is supported by FFLOS, the 1HappyHiker blog and Maine IAT, which may share an FFLA source. Suggest adding a 2001 year to the Patten record's relocated event, which has none. Staffing: no names or dates beyond the 1909-1922 watchman cabin. Access: no source says whether the tower can be climbed; the museum page gives only general visiting details. Photos: a Patten Lumbermen's Museum Facebook post about the tower's removal exists (search snippet only, not read, license unknown), so no photo entry was added. Design height left as a conflict, not a fact.

Thin record: no source fetched gives staffing, fires, or the reason for removal. The 1929 article announces a planned tower; completion is inferred from the 1931 map. A Facebook photo caption seen only in search snippets gives a 1929 erection date and mentions a radio site; it was not fetched and is not cited. Access and current site condition are unknown; the record's access field was left out. Brief's height (7.3 m) matches the 24-foot figure.

Dates 1910, 1914 and 1938 come from the Eastern US Lookouts timeline (citing the Maine Historical Society photo inventory and state reports) and the Maine Memory record; neither original report was opened. The brief's 24-foot height is confirmed (converted to 7.3 m). The cab's removal date is not found; the FFLA legend is the only basis for 'cab gone'. Access is not recorded: no source states ownership or whether the tower may be climbed, and Wikipedia's 'abandoned' is a secondary description. The FFLA Maine chapter Facebook posts mention a 1938 rebuild by the Maine Forest Service and a later observation-tower conversion, but Facebook returned no text, so they are not cited. Staffing after about 1920 is not found.

Thin record. Only the FFLOS detail page and the FFLOS state index are tower-specific. The Maine Atlas page is statewide context and is not tied to Cook Hill's own watch years, so the story does not claim Cook Hill was staffed to 1991. Facebook posts from the FFLA Maine chapter appear in search results with claims that the tower was built in 1949, manned through the 1991 season, and trucked away in 2000 by a private party. The Facebook pages returned only a login shell, so none of those claims is used; they are leads to check against a readable source. Brief record matches: registered 2008 and gone. No access information found.

Thin record. We have only the 1910 listing, the 1920 inventory and a 1918 map. No build date, staffing history, access or closure information. Searches surfaced Facebook posts (a 2006 photo of the Wesley tower off Route 9 / Airline Road, and a 'Days Hill' mention) that could not be read, so their details are not used. Confirm the Day Hill / Wesley Mountain identity and current access on the ground or with the Maine Forest Service before publishing any visit guidance.

Brief agency (Elliotsville Plantation) may be out of date; the proposed NPS correction is flagged but not confirmed by a land-record source. Brief kind=ground and elevation 571.8 m agree with the Register. Park Service elevations (1,942 and 1,950 ft) differ from the Register. Park Service pages carry photos but no license line was read, so no photo is added. The Weebly page (easternuslookouts) was read for context only and is not cited.

Brief's height 3.7 m matches the 1919-20 12-foot tower, not the current one. Register says 60 ft; Forest Lookouts and Red River Camps say 48 ft; the conflict is not settled, and 14.6 m is proposed. Brief's 2016 event was the watchman's camp, not the tower. The November 2019 windstorm rests only on Red River Camps, a commercial site; a state or FFLA source would firm it up. The 2020 cab replacement is confirmed by two sources: the 2020 FFLA Maine report and the Bangor Daily News column. The 1991 closure is a regional statement; no year is given for Deboullie. The brief's agency (Maine Forest Service) still matches the register, though the Bureau of Parks and Lands did the 2016 and 2020 work. No road or trail directions were verified.

The 1926 build date and the 1935 height rest on newspaper items quoted through Forest Lookouts. The 1950 removal is confirmed by two sources. No description of the site today and no access information. The brief's height 11.0 m matches the 36-foot figure. Two WebSearch calls, one of which returned nothing on Deer Mountain, and about four page reads.

No source describes the site today, and no access information was found, so access and visit keys are omitted. Township disagrees across sources: Forest Lookouts quotes 'Twp. No. 18 R. 16'; the Maine Memory record keywords say T14 R16 WELS; a DigitalMaine map title seen only in a search snippet says Township 11 Range 16. Not used in the story. Maine Memory record 19115 has a photo, but no image URL was retrieved, so no photo entry.

Brief record (gone, FFLOS US 104, ME 30, registered 2008) matches. No build date found for the Dill Ridge tower; the earliest dated fact is the 1931 map. The Almanac Mountain facts come from a Forest Lookouts page that quotes old state reports and the Daily Kennebec Journal, not from the state directly. The register says 'moved back' in 1967, which implies an earlier move from Almanac that no source read describes; the story notes this without claiming it. The Almanac Mountain tower is not the Dill Ridge record's own site, and the record does not currently mention it. The FFLOS index marks Almanac with an asterisk whose meaning I could not confirm. No access information found for Almanac Mountain.

Brief record (gone, FFLOS US 105, ME 31, registered 2008) matches. Spelling differs by source: Double Top (Digital Maine, Forest Lookouts) and Doubletop (FFLOS). The removal date is a range in the register; the 1996 event year is only the start of that range. Park status comes from a rare-map dealer's description of the 1919 station, not from a Baxter State Park page; no Baxter source was read. A Facebook post from the FFLA Maine chapter (seen in search results) says a 1972 photo showed the tower inside Baxter State Park with its cab long off, and a 1997 reference to a color photo; the Facebook pages returned only a login shell, so neither claim is used. Those are leads to check. No photos added.

Height disagrees (50 ft in the 1917 report and by hikers; 48 ft in the 1920 inventory). Cab status rests on the FFLA key alone: the Sun Journal and Maine by Foot describe the tower without saying whether a cab is present, so check before stating it in a headline. Land ownership not found, so the access level 'public' is an inference from hiking reports and the lack of any closure notice. A Facebook post seen only in search says the steel tower was erected in 1917; not read. The AllTrails listing was seen only in search, not read. The June 2026 blog is a personal hiking blog. The story advises against climbing because of the missing lower ladder and the tower's condition.

The brief's firetower.org page for the Swan Island location (...-at-swan-island-wma/) returned 404 in the cache and live, so it is not cited. The state page does not mention the former lookout, so the link between the Swan Island tower and this lookout rests on Forest Lookouts, Wikipedia and the FFLA list. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook post seen only in search results dates the move to 2005 and describes restoration; it is not cited. Height and design of the 1931 tower are not in the sources read. Access to the original summit is not confirmed.

Move year conflicts (2002 vs 2005). A travel article (2003) and a Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine Facebook post (2005) appeared only in search results and were not read, so they are not cited. The state's wildlife viewing tower is probably this tower, but the state page does not say so. Read budget exceeded by about two pages.

Sources conflict on current state: FFLA lists Tower Standing with no asterisk (cab in place), while the FSM newsletter (Fall 2025) says remnants of fire lookout towers remain on Green Mountain. The story reports both and does not choose. Unverified leads, not used: an FFLA Maine chapter Facebook post (seen only as a search result, never opened) says the tower was erected in 1920 and was 48 feet tall with a cab in poor shape; a second post names a watchman for 1971-1981. Check both before using. Do not confuse with the New Hampshire Green Mountain lookout on NHLR (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/nh/green-mountain-lookout/), a different tower. No access, visit or staffing data found; those keys are left unset.

Status: the register (firetower.org, registered 2008) says no longer standing; the 2016 chapter report and the Forest Lookouts list say standing, with the cab gone per the list's asterisk legend. Cab removal date not found. The 1916 sources name W.F. Hinckley (newspaper) and W.H. Hinckley (report); we did not decide whether they are the same man. A web search summary mentioned a 2020 'Structure Only - No Cab' entry on firelookout.org and a 1923 Maine State Archives panorama map, and it gave a 75-foot height; none of those pages could be read (firelookout.org/lookouts/me/me.htm returned 404), so none is used. Height is 60 feet per the 1920 inventory quoted by Forest Lookouts, so the brief's 18.3 m stands. Access: no public-access statement found; the only access fact is the 2016 'trip in'. No photos added.

Unresolved: the Forest Lookouts page quotes a 1943-44 forest commissioner's report describing a new 41-foot tower begun on Mount Harris in 1944 and due in 1945. The NHLR and Former Fire Lookout Sites pages say the tower stood in Pennsylvania until 1940 and was moved here. The sources do not say whether the tower removed in 2006 was the 1940 move, the 1944-45 tower, or both. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter Facebook post seen only in search results dates the Harris tower to 1945; I could not open it, so it is not cited. The NHLR text gives the tower as 'a 50 wooden tower' with no unit, so no height is recorded. The NHLR 'Staffed? Yes' field is a question on a volunteer visit form, not a staffing history, and I did not use it. No staffing or fire history was found. No source describes the site today.

Location is not settled. The Site I register entry puts the tower on SR 163 east of Ashland; the Maine Memory postcard and the Site II entry put Haystack Mountain at Castle Hill. The story reports both and does not reconcile them. The brief's FFLA point (46.66695, -68.23208) is about 2.7 km from the Site I register point and carries the same register number, US 76; check whether that point belongs to Site II. The brief says log construction (from FFLA); no fetched source confirms it. A search snippet from an FFLA Maine chapter Facebook post mentions a 1914 log lookout at Castle Hill; it was not fetched and is not cited. No construction date was found, so there is no built event. No access or visit information was found. Staffed 1915 is inferred from the camp for the lookout man.

The remains at the summit (cabin and anchor points) rest on one blog post, not on a land trust, Forest Service or register source. The register says only that the tower is no longer standing. Trail length is 0.75 miles in Maine Trail Finder and about 0.7 miles in the blog. Township 15 Range 6 WELS agrees across the Forest Lookouts page and the 1919 DigitalMaine map. Nothing found on whether the land is in public or private ownership beyond the trail listing; the Hedgehog Mountain Land Trust could confirm the summit's status. No photo entry: the DigitalMaine map has no image URL retrieved.

Removal dates conflict: about 1960 (Maine Memory record and the Maine Historical Society photo inventory as quoted by the volunteer list) versus between 1971 and 1972 (former-lookout register). Left unresolved; a check with the Garland Historical Society or Maine Forest Service records would settle it. The 1944 entry's phrase 'wooden-modern steel ring connector' is unclear, so the design fact stays general. No sources found on staffing, fires or access. One search and about five page reads. Maine Memory record 8832 has a c.1950 photo that is a candidate for photos, but no image URL was captured and the record says images may not be reproduced without permission except for classroom use, so it is not added. Record coordinates come from the FFA list and were not checked against a second source. No corrections proposed.

Built date is not in any source read; the story starts at the 1919 record. Height 3.7 m comes from the 1920 inventory figure of 12 feet (no later height). The 1989 restoration text and the 1999 removal are quoted secondhand on the Eastern US Lookouts page (originally Bangor Daily News), not checked against the original article. Summit elevation differs between hiking sources (1,589 ft vs 1,592 ft) and is not used. The brief's agency field is kept as Baxter State Park with the Maine Forest Service as builder.

Status rests on the FFLA list and its legend (Standing* = cab gone), consistent with the brief. The 1950 date is the Maine Forestry Service map date, not a build date. No build date, height, builder, staffing, watchman or access data found; those keys are left unset. Naming caution: the Rocky Mountain tower in Aroostook (firetower.org/NHLR, US 81, ME 7) is a different site near 47.28 N, far north of this tower's 46.59 N. A Facebook group comment (seen only as a search result, not opened) says Horseshoe and Rocky Brook are synonyms; the story follows the FFLA name only.

Status rests on the FFLA list and its legend (Standing* = cab gone), consistent with the brief. The 1931 date is the map date, not a build date. No build date, height, builder, staffing, watchman or access data found; those keys are left unset. A Facebook group post (seen only as a search result, not opened) reports a short hike to this tower on Oct. 4, 2025, west of Monticello; not used and not verified, and it is not an access source. Do not encourage climbing: treat access as unknown.

Hunt Mountain is the 1924 original site; the structure was moved to Lawler Hill in 1931 and removed there in 1978, so the Lawler Hill record should carry the same chain (its own brief says Tower Gone). No source read describes the Hunt Mountain site or the Lawler Hill site today, and none states public access, so access is omitted rather than guessed. The 1924 facts come from newspaper items quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page (Daily Kennebec Journal), not the originals. The brief's height 14.6 m matches the 48-foot figure. The FFLOS page spells the Lawler Hill location Benedicta, while the 1931 map says Benedicts; the story avoids the spelling. Research read budget exceeded by a few page reads on this record while sorting out the Lawler Hill move.

The 1948 build year and the 1991 end of staffing rest on one 2011 newspaper story, which quotes a commission member. The commission's own blog gives no build year. A search snippet of a Facebook post says 1948 was the last staffed year, which conflicts with 1991; it could not be opened, so it is not cited. The main open question is whether the tower was removed in 2013 or 2014. Check with the Maine Forest Service. The brief record lists ownership as unknown. The 2011 article says the Forest Service owns the tower and two private owners held the land, so ownership could be updated after checking.

Built 1925 is supported by two independent sources (survey and guide). The brief's 2017 modification is confirmed by the FFLA 2017 report. No watchman or staffing history was found. Digital Maine lists Brighton Plt under Sagadahoc County, which conflicts with the Somerset placement; the story avoids naming a county. Facebook posts by the FFLA Maine chapter (1925 build, cab removed 'several years ago') could not be opened and are not cited. The 2026 blog is a single personal trip report; treat its access remarks as one visitor's view and confirm land status before publishing a visiting note.

Build dates conflict: the Maine Memory Network record says 1914 steel and 1926 replacement, the 2010 trip report says 1914 with a 1925 ice collapse, and a 2025 article gives 1926 as the erection date. Tower height is 14 feet in the 1926 record and about 15 feet in the 2010 and 2025 sources; the file uses 15 feet (4.6 m) for the current tower. The access level 'public' is an inference from hiking guides that mention no gate, and the roads cross timberland company land, so confirm before publishing a visiting note. Search snippets of Facebook posts from the FFLA Maine chapter and a regional group say the camp is privately owned and the deck was converted in the early 1990s; they could not be opened and are not cited. The brief record's status note matches the FFLA legend.

Only the register gives a removal year (1978). The volunteer list is the only source for the 1915 build, and it cites the 1914 report, which describes a plan, so completion is not confirmed. No staffing beyond the 1914 mention, and no fire or access information was found. Coordinates from the FFA list (45.76992, -68.43113) were not checked against a second source. Two searches (neither confirmed the 1915 build or the 1978 removal) and about four page reads. No corrections proposed.

Height conflict: 41 ft in one 1914 newspaper item, 36 ft in the 1914 Forest Commissioner's report and the 1920 inventory; the brief's 12.5 m is the 41-foot figure, so a correction is proposed. The removal date is not in any source read; the status is gone per FFLOS only. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter Facebook post, seen only as a search snippet and not readable through fetch, describes the steel tower on the summit as still present in the forest and the watchman's camp as in ruin halfway down. It is not cited and the story does not use it; an editor should check it by hand before anyone says what stands on the summit, because it may conflict with FFLOS 'no longer standing'. The 1914 facts are from newspaper and report text quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page, not the originals. The 1918-1932 map record is an archive copy; the DigitalMaine catalogue carries the same series.

Three sources, and none gives staffing or access. The FFLA legend supports the cab-gone reading. The 1921 Digital Maine item is catalogued as a still image in the Avery Collection (keyword: Map). The word 'panoramic' does not appear on that page, so it was removed from the story and this record. No item-level rights statement appears on the page, so no photo entry was added. The record's 14.6 m matches the 48-foot figure; no correction needed. Brief status note is accurate.

Best-documented of the three, but it rests on one long 1983 Bangor Daily News account reprinted on the Forest Lookouts site. The record's 9.8 m is the pre-1963 height; see the height correction. The staffing entry is unknown after the summer 1983 lookout; no later staffing record was found. The climbing restriction comes only from one travel guide post dated August 5, 2016; check before publishing. A Facebook post in search results claims a first tower opened in Edmunds in 1951; social media, not cited, unverified. No photo added.

Thin record: three sources. The register gives only 'during the 1930s' for removal; the schema needs a year, so no removal event was written. The register calls the structure a tower and the association's Maine list calls the site ground; the sources do not settle which. The volunteer list has a separate 'COBB HILL, Penobscot County' heading with no detail, which may or may not be this site. Two searches (one for the Lee site and one for its removal) turned up nothing dating the site; search leads (Maine Forest Service historical records, Lee historical society) are untested. Coordinates from the FFA list were not checked. No corrections proposed; the record's kind 'ground' matches the FFA list but conflicts with the register's 'tower'.

History rests on two Maine state-archive pages (Maine Memory and the Digital Maine 1919 map) plus the register. No source read describes the site today, so the story says so. The register page gives no coordinates while the Maine list gives 45.45283, -68.71853; the story notes they are rough. Maine Memory photo item 19121 (Forest Service lookout tower and camp, ca. 1920) is noted but its image URL and license were not read, so no photo is added. The register's 'tower' is a 48-foot steel tower per the 1917 replacement. Used 1 websearch.py call and about 5 page reads.

Brief had no built year. The register says 'late 1940s', which cannot be stored as a single year, so no built event is recorded; the story gives the register's wording. Brief's elevation 137.8 m matches the register's 452 ft. No design or height source was found, and no access source was found, so those keys are omitted. The Maine Forest Service page covers the state network in general, not this tower specifically.

Brief events not verified and left out of the record: 2007 winter repair, 2015 FFLA grant ($500), 2016 closure, 2018 engineering assessment, 2019 closure to the public. None of those pages were read in this pass; treat them as unconfirmed. The 1981 and 1985 dates conflict between the register and the Forest Lookouts excerpt. The 2025 report does not say whether the footings were removed, so the story says nothing about remains beyond what sources state. Photos: none added; the Forest Lookouts page has none with a stated license. The register's '24 fire tower' wording is read as a 24-foot tower, matching the 1918 annual-report quote.

Thin: one annual-report quote and one 1932 map. The record's 'gone' status conflict is unexplained; please check where that value came from. The Eastern page for Ararat has no status line in the text we read. A geocache listing (GCHCJD) reportedly describes a 1933, 50-foot tower still standing in 1998, but fetch_text returned only its title, so nothing from it is used. The 1931 report's 'forty-seven foot' stations are not tied to Ararat, so no height is recorded. No access or staffing source found, and no photo added.

Brief's 2011 and 2012 events are confirmed by the 2011 and 2012 Maine reports. Erection year conflicts: the 1931 report describes a fall 1931 program; the 2021 Sun Journal list gives 1932; a Facebook caption seen only in search results (not fetched, not cited) also says 1932. A Facebook caption also says the old tower closed at the end of 1971; unverified, left out. No staffing source found. Wikipedia is undated. The 2011 'Avon' mention is a single report; Wikipedia also places the summit in Avon, and the story says so. No photos added.

Only three sources, all read. Staffing is not covered by any source read; a Facebook caption seen only in search results (not fetched, not cited) says a Levi Walton manned the tower from about 1975 to 1991, so staffing could be added if that caption is verified. Current state of the Lasell Island tower is unknown. The 1931 program quote covers five 47-foot towers; the source links the Mountain Hill lookout to that program, and the 47-foot size rests on the 1935 newspaper item. No photos added.

No access level or visit information was found, so the access key is omitted. No notable fires were found in the sources read. The most recent dated staffing evidence is the 2000 Firehouse article; the NHLR's 'staffed each year' is undated. Facebook posts from the Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter mention a tower steward and past volunteer lookouts. They were not fetched and are not cited. The Sun Journal table row gives the Sabattus date; the tower's 1939 origin rests on that table and the marker's 'moved from Sabattus' line.

Sources conflict on what stood here: the register says a tower was removed in the 1920s, WillhiteWeb describes a ground house and summit observations, and the 1920 abandonment reasons differ (weather versus view and fog). The 1916 Forest Commissioners Report and Hakola's Legacy of a Lifetime were not read directly; they appear only as quoted by WillhiteWeb and a forum post. The forum claim that the lookout ran to the end of the 1919 season is not used as fact. No source gives the cabin's collapse year or the site's present condition. Used 1 websearch.py call and about 5 page reads. The register's 'platform' kind matches only the Maine list page.

Dates for cab removal and the viewing-platform conversion were not found in the pages read, so no events are recorded for them. The 1960s end of use comes from the Maine Trail Finder story alone and has no exact year, so it is not an event. Search snippets (not read as pages) said the tower was used until about 1960 and mentioned the cab; not used. Maine Trail Finder title checked against the page and corrected to Above the Trees - 5 Maine Fire Tower Hikes. The Wikipedia cache for Mount Kineo had no tower matches. The OpenStreetMap node was not read. Brief height_m 19.5 is supported (64 ft); brief status and agency are supported; no corrections proposed.

Access 'public' comes from the Land Trust and the register; the story gives no climbing advice. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine Facebook snippet says the tower was used as a radio tower around 1995 and was not then generally open to the public. It was not fetched, so the story leaves it out. The 2008 Morning Sentinel item is quoted through the Forest Lookouts page and was not read directly. No staffing history or notable fires were found, so those keys are omitted.

Brief record says 18.3 m, which matches the 60-foot height in the sources; no change needed. Cut-down year conflicts between Press Herald (1976) and Trail Finder (1975); the story reports both. The 1943 event year comes from a report covering 1943-44. The 1920 newspaper quote and 1935 height come from the Forest Lookouts compilation, which quotes newspapers and reports; I did not check the originals. The Press Herald article's publication date was not visible in the cached copy. The Maine Memory record is titled 1924 but its subject line says Milton Twp. and its description says Peru. A hiker forum and a search summary mention a mid-1970s toppling; neither was opened, so they are not used.

Removal year conflicts (1994 Central Maine, 1996 Willhite, 1990s FFLOS). The Bolton Hill destination rests only on the FFLOS record; two searches turned up nothing on Bolton Hill, and I did not verify the 'east of Waterville' geography. The 1924 watchman death reported in the Forest Lookouts page and the Willhite page is left out of the story as not needed for a visitor's history; it is a sensitive event. The Central Maine article title was not visible in the cache, so the title here is descriptive. Brief record: height 3.7 m matches the 12-foot 1919 tower; agency matches the Weebly header; access 'unknown' is now public (on the AT).

Single source: the firetower.org/FFLOS entry. The Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine list (https://firelookout.org/lookouts/us/me/) has no Mud Pond entry. Two web searches turned up nothing more on this tower. The brief's status 'gone' is not supported by any source read; the story reports the 1998 local account instead. No access, staffing, fire or build-date evidence found.

No source I could read gives the date of the present tower or the last year it was staffed. A Facebook snippet from the FFLA Maine chapter reportedly describes three towers (1913-1928, 1928-1958, 1958 to present); the page would not open, so the 1958 date is not used. Ownership and public access are not established by any source read, and the summit has five communications towers. Check with the Maine Forest Service or the FFLA Maine chapter before adding visiting advice.

The destination record (us-me-norway-bluff-at-ashland-logging-museum) gives a 'wood cab, reconditioned for the move' design. History is well sourced from the Forest Lookouts page, the 2012 and 2013 Maine chapter reports, the 2012 historians report and a 2013 dedication notice. Current condition and public access are not confirmed. The FFLA list says standing. A Visit Aroostook search snippet mentions climbing the tower, but the page itself does not, so it was not used. Staffing: a watchman's camp existed in 1914; no names or later staffing found. The record's 2012 'relocated' event could take the 7 May 2012 removal date as well. The record's 2012 'restored' note describes a carpentry step, not completed restoration; the 2013 event covers the finish. No photos added; a Maine chapter Facebook post and Ashland Logging Museum pages were seen only as search snippets.

Built 1914 and the 60-foot height rest on the Forest Lookouts page (which quotes the 1914 Forest Commissioner's Report and a 1920 inventory) and a Maine Memory photo. Current standing is from the FFLA list only, with the cab-gone reading taken from the FFLA legend, so no recent photo or site visit confirms it. No access, ownership or rental source was found; access is recorded as unknown. Two Forest Fire Lookout Association Maine chapter Facebook posts describe the tower as standing without a cab, but those pages returned no readable text and are not cited. Maine Memory record 19124 is a candidate photo, but its licence was not checked, so no photo is added. No corrections proposed.

The FFLA list and legend give the current standing (structure kept, cab gone). The state plan says closed and the Maine by Foot guide says a climbable ladder remains; we follow the plan and do not encourage climbing, and the disagreement is stated in the story. The 1935 48-foot height may not describe the present structure, so no height_m is recorded. The 2014 plan calls the trailhead to be developed while the Pinnacle page gives directions to a temporary parking area and is undated, so the current trailhead is unconfirmed. The Forest Lookouts page gives the agency as the Maine Forestry District only. Ownership of the tower site was not confirmed. No corrections proposed to the record.

Read: Press Herald 2019 (built 1933; lower steps removed; trail restored; 6-mile round trip), Maine by Foot (intact tower; TNC warns people not to climb), FFLA Maine standing list (no asterisk, so cab not marked missing). Not found: builder, tower height or design, staffing history, current condition, any visiting rules beyond TNC's warning. Elevation disagrees: 3,186 ft (Press Herald) vs 3,183 ft (Maine by Foot); not used in the story. The Maine State Archives 'No. 5 Mt.' panorama map is for T6 R7 WELS, Penobscot County, a different mountain. Used 2 WebSearch and about 6 page reads.

The main conflict is current status: the FFLA list says Standing, while Maine Memory and its exhibit say the 36-foot steel tower was removed in 1993. Facts record status gone with the conflict in the status note, and the corrections list proposes standing to gone for human review; a recent photo or Forest Service record would settle it. The township is TD R2 WELS in Maine Memory and Township 9, Range 3 in the 1914 report; the FFLA coordinates were not checked against either, and the sources do not reconcile the two. Only the 1916 forest commissioner's report, as quoted by Forest Lookouts, calls the site No. 9 or Bald Mountain. Forest Lookouts gives the 1915 replacement as a log crib tower, but the Maine Memory caption says it was a wood tower, and the sources do not settle which. No access source was found, so access is unknown. The Facebook posts about this site were not read. Maine Memory photos 19126 (ca. 1918) and 19127 (ca. 1920) are candidates, but their licence was not checked, so no photo is added.

Access, ownership and current condition not found in the sources read, so no access fact is recorded. Staffing not found. FFLA lists it as standing with no asterisk. Facebook group posts from 2026 about the tower were seen only as search snippets and a short fetched header, so they are not used. Height: 75 feet from both Maine Memory and Forest Lookouts; height_m is that figure converted. The record's agency line matches the Forest Lookouts header. Used 2 WebSearch and about 5 page reads.

Build dates (1914, 1919) and the 36-foot height come only from WillhiteWeb; no second source was found. A Forest Fire Lookout Association Facebook post gives a July 1959 date and names a different warden, but Facebook pages could not be read, so it is not cited. Wikipedia has no tower content. The Maine lookout list also lists the current record as standing with cab gone, so the brief record needed no correction.

No build date or design found for the Opportunity Farm tower. The Eastern U.S. Lookouts New Gloucester page, which this record links, never mentions Opportunity Farm. The Conway Daily Sun replica article returned HTTP 429 twice and was not read. Read budget exceeded by about two pages.

No build date, design or height was found for the New Gloucester tower. The 1950-51 notes say 'New Gloucester fire tower' and never name the farm, so the link to FFLA's Opportunity Farm entry is an inference. FFLA's coordinates for this site (43.95342, -70.29415) are the record's own. Fryeburg details are in the sibling record us-me-opportunity-farm-at-fryeburg-fairgrounds. The Conway Daily Sun replica article was not read (HTTP 429 in an earlier pass). Maine Memory and Facebook search hits were not used as sources.

Identity: FFLA 'Oquossoc Bald' (44.94354, -70.77553) is treated as the Bald Mountain tower near Oquossoc, because the 2021 Sun Journal calls it 'Oquossoc Bald Mountain, Rangeley' and the 2026 piece calls it the 'Bald Mountain fire tower in Oquossoc'. Coordinates were not checked against a newspaper location. The built date is only '1920s' in the sources read, so no built event is recorded. OpenStreetMap node 7624268161 is tagged disused=yes (version 1, about six years old); not relied on. Preserve Pals says 'climbable and maintained' and 'one adult up at a time', but the same site says the author has not been there; not used.
