No notable fires found in sources read. The 2010 visitor's name is omitted. Height 55 ft converted to 16.8 m.

Only the register and one tower list were readable. No construction date, builder, design or height found; two web searches and no other readable page named the tower. The staffing as_of is the register entry year because the description is undated. Lower stairs removed: the story tells visitors not to climb and does not encourage access. The origin of the name Aycock is not established by any source read.

Height (80 ft NHLR vs 60 ft MyHikes) and elevation disagree between sources, so height is not published as a fact. The 1932 newspaper items describe construction in progress, so the completion year rests on NHLR and MyHikes. Access level comes from a hiking guide and the land is tribal; BIA and tribal visitor rules were not checked. The fire-watch end date is not firm. Staffing is not published as a fact: the 1933 warden watch is in the timeline, but the vocabulary has no value for it and no current staffing source was found. The 1934 CCC road and a 1934 marriage item in the same newspaper page were left out as not relevant.

Built year 1934 is supported by the register and a state report quoted on a lookout-history site. Search snippets (not opened) gave a 1933 date (SummitPost) and a CCC-built 1937 date (Conserving Carolina); the Conserving Carolina page I read has no construction date, so neither is used. Search snippets also mention a padlocked chain-link fence and a 2016 blog on restoration plans; not verified, not used. The tower's current condition is the main gap: contact NC Division of Forest Resources District 9 or Conserving Carolina before publishing. The brief's 1934 build, 14.3 m height and 2008 registration match the sources and were kept.

No source gives a construction year, so the story has no built date. Removal and the final fire are dated only to the decade; 1960 in the events is a decade marker. Access is not described by any source, so no access level is recorded. The FFLOS page's footings photo (credit Victoria Oliver) was not added as a photo; its license was not checked. The Forest Service trail listing does not say whether the trail reaches the site.

The brief has no tower height; NHLR gives only the cab base at 94 feet above ground, so height_m is omitted. The NHLR description and the Charlotte Urban Institute article share nearly identical text, so they are not independent confirmation of the 1936 date or the staffing history. The Charlotte article is dated September 24, 2012, so its staffing and fire-finder statements are 2012-era and are dated in the story. Its 'torn down in the early 1960s' remark is about the King Mountain tower in Eleazer, not Buck Mountain, and is not used. The USFS and FFLA Facebook posts returned only titles, so their claims (CCC build, 'no longer used') were not used. The QRPer post (dated October 2024) says the stair-base door was not locked and that the author reached a platform below the padlocked top floor, without mentioning a permit; the story leaves these details out to avoid encouraging entry and says the sources do not settle whether the public may climb. Access is set to restricted (fenced, gated, padlocked). Current status rests on the 2024 post and 2012-era sources; no 2026 source was found.

NHLR is detailed and includes two dated visit reports (2008, 2020), giving good texture on condition change over time. The build year (1928 vs 1929) and tower height (21 ft vs 20 ft) conflict between NHLR and the Forest Lookouts site; left unresolved. The Earl Shaffer 1948 overnight-stay claim and the 'Viking Mountain' alternate name both come from a single blog post and are not corroborated elsewhere; flagged in the story and as a proposed correction rather than treated as settled fact. No NRHP nomination or newspaper coverage was found for this tower.

The register is the only source for the 1936 build, the design and the 2008 registration. A hiking-map search snippet gives the mountain as 4,498 ft against the register's 2,466 ft site elevation; that page could not be read (fetch returned no text), so the conflict is unresolved and left out of the story. The register's 45-foot figure is a tower height that may not run to the cab floor, so height_m is omitted. The staffing as_of is the register entry year because the 'one of the last active' description is undated. No visit, access, fire or staffing history found; the story sends visitors to the Division of Forest Resources.

Build year (1933 or 1936) and height (30 or 40 ft) are disputed; the story reports both. The record's NGS None is consistent with the Register's registry numbers, which list no NGS entry. tnlandforms.us lists Cowee Bald (NCT045) with a code FB3563; it is not explained on the page, so it is not used. The Carolina Mountain Club page returned 404 and the MyHikes page repeats BusyHiker, so neither is cited. Current access rests on BusyHiker and a September 2020 visit report; no 2025 or 2026 source was found. The Register lists a September 2020 photo credited to Christopher Armenti, but the page gives no image URL, so no photo entry is recorded. The 'late 1960s' and 1960 staffing dates are approximate.

Single source: the NHLR register entry, which dates the tower only to the 1940s or 1950s and gives no removal date for the cab. The record's agency field names the private owner; the story does not repeat the name because it is not needed. The record's ownership field is unknown and could read private per the register; it was left unchanged. Record status standing is consistent with the structure still standing in 2022, but the status_note records the cab removal. Access is private, so the story asks visitors not to climb without permission. A FFLA Aermotor booklet was found but did not yield text, so the LS-40 design is taken from the register alone. Two WebSearch queries and four reads were used.

Access and rental status are not confirmed by any source read, so no access key is set. Staffing conflicts between the 1998 Register and the 2024 FFLA report; the story gives both. The brief's 2008 roof, 2009 grant ($150) and steward details, and the 2024/2025 grant events are verified against the FFLA reports. The brief's tnlandforms.us source only lists the tower with a survey code and was not used. The 1936 CCC build and 1966 transfer come from the NHLR page alone. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the planned-repairs sentence no longer attributes the water-damage purpose to the flashing, and the 2025 return now gives both reasons the report states.

Unresolved conflict: the register gives built 1935 with no source on its page; the 2026 blog says the construction date and builder are not publicly documented. The story reports the register's date and flags that it is unconfirmed. A Facebook video description gives the height as 99 ft 9 in, but it could not be read or cited, so height_m is omitted. The register names the private buyer of the 2018 auction; the story says 'a private buyer' and the evidence quote leaves the name out. The record's federal ownership is proposed for correction to private. Treat as private property; no public access described.

Fate and today are thin: Forest Lookouts marks the tower removed with no date, and the register's 2013 caption calls it a former site. No source describes what remains or whether the site is reachable, so no access level is recorded. Built year is decade only. Do not confuse with the Frye Mountain fire tower in Montville or Swan Island, Maine, which appeared in search results; it is a different tower. No photo was added.

Height (70 ft), 1941 build year and 5,340 ft elevation agree across the Register, Conserving Carolina and the NPS; the metric height of 21.3 m is converted from 70 ft. The county is disputed: the record's Transylvania matches the Register only, while the Forest Lookouts listing and tnlandforms.us (NCT069, Haywood) say Haywood; the record was not changed. The NPS calls the tower 'Frying Pan Fire Tower' and the record uses 'Fryingpan Mountain Lookout'; both names are in use. The NHLR page says 'now used as a radio relay point', which is the only source for current use. The 1990 staffing year is approximate ('early 1990s'). The NPS page has a photo credit ('U.S. Forest Service Photo / Steve Norman') but gives no image URL, so no photo entry is recorded. The Forest Lookouts page is a long index, but the only Fryingpan detail it shows is the county heading.

Build year conflict (1931 vs 1932) is unresolved; the Register and TEHCC say 1932. County conflict (Yancey vs McDowell) is unresolved. The 1996 restoration matches across the Register and two blogs. Current cab closure comes from a blog and an undated wiki revision; verify before publishing. The Forest Service Green Knob Trail page shows a 'Temporarily closed due to storm damage' notice under Current Conditions; no date or scope, so the story now says so. Two blogs say the tower is on the National Register of Historic Places; not verified, not used. Outbound calls the tower abandoned; not used. Facebook posts not cited. Staffing history rests on two blogs; no current volunteer schedule found. Page reads: 7 distinct pages, one over the 6-page budget.

Build year (1936) and height are supported by two sources. The fate after the March 2018 surplus bid notice is unknown: check the NC state surplus records for an outcome, and ask the NC Forest Service about current status and access. No staffing source found, and no access or visit source, so those keys are omitted. The earlier 30.2 m height had no cited source and is now 30.4 m. An undated Facebook post by Steven Ward Smith calls the tower 99'9" and names an Aeromotor MC-39 model; not cited because it is social media and undated. The 'standing' status rests on the 2018 register entry; no dated source confirms it today.

Year of the closure order is not in the text we could read; the News-Topic page is partly paywalled, and the article's date was not visible. Land purchase in the early 2020s is in the article, so the closure is recent, but the year is unverified. The 1927 date is consistent across the Register, the site history page and Wikipedia, but Wikipedia cites the site, so they are not independent. The Dellinger 1987 article PDF is an image scan with no text; not used. A local archives Facebook post shows a 1928 photo of the tower and says its erection date was not found; that post was not opened, so it is not cited. Gate date 'early 1940s' is approximate. No fire history found. Read budget reached: 6 distinct pages and 2 searches. Verification 2026-10-09: the partly paywalled News-Topic text confirms the Forest Service lease, its duty to maintain the private road, and the early-1940s gate. The story now says 'effectively closed' and quotes the site's radio and cell tower line in full.

Built year is disputed inside the record: the Register's Built field says 1942 but its description and two hiking guides say 1952. Story uses 1952. Access level 'restricted' is our reading of a locked gate and a normally locked cab; no official closure notice was found, and the Forest Service page was not reached. Staffing before 1942 and the first staffing year are not in the sources read. 'Maintained for emergency use' is the Register's wording and may be dated.

The 1935 build, its cost and funding rest on one volunteer page that quotes a 1934-36 state report; no independent confirmation found. One search and a fetch of the Jones Lake State Park page found no tower mention. The brief's 30.2 m appears to be 99 feet without the 9 inches; corrected to 30.4 m. The 1937 item may describe another tower. Worth asking the NC Forest Service or Jones Lake State Park. OSM elevation of 23 m matches the brief.

Core facts (1934 build, CCC, two staff members, 1980 retirement, $300 sale, reconstruction at Big Ivy) agree across sources. Removal and re-erection years conflict and are reported as ranges. The record's coordinates (35.76112, -82.43127) and elevation (701 m) may describe the reconstructed tower at Big Ivy rather than the original mountain site, so check which place the record means before publishing. Park hours and whether the tower can be climbed are not stated in any source read. The registry's 'standing' is true only of the reconstruction; the original tower is gone.

Not a historic fire lookout. It is a park lookout tower in Cane Creek Mountains Natural Area that the park says is now open; the editor should decide whether it belongs in the fire-lookout set. height_m 24.4 converts the park's 80-foot climb; OSM's 25 m is close. The June 2025 date comes from the blog's web address, not a date shown on the page. Construction date and builder are unknown. Two searches and three page reads; the Facebook post returned no text.

The record's 1951 build year is the stone structure; the original steel lookout is 1938 per the Register, but a camping blog gives 1936 and 60 feet. Unresolved: that date gap. The blog's timeline (hurricane after a few years) gives no replacement date, so it cannot be checked against the Register's 1951 replacement. A Facebook post (not cited) gives 1949 and an 18 ft 6 in tower. Restoration date not found, so no event for it. Visitor hours not verified. 'Standing' refers to the stone structure, not the fire lookout. Wikipedia calls the summit tower abandoned, which does not match the Register's restored viewpoint; not used for that point.

Access is the main open question: the 2018 blog says fenced, and the undated trail guide says open, but its own May 2018 update says the fence was rebuilt and the tower closed until further notice. Verify with the tribe or the Fire Mountain Trail System managers before publishing. The 1957 build and BIA ownership match across the Register, the 2018 blog and the trail guide. The 1960s end of fire use rests on one blog that cites Peter Barr's book; not checked against the book. Restoration plan (2008) has no later record. Facebook posts that call the tower abandoned, and the Grokipedia page, are not cited. The Wikipedia 'Mount Noble' article is about an Antarctic peak and was not used. Read budget: 3 distinct pages and 2 searches. Height 60 ft converted to 18.3 m.

Beyond the NHLR register page, no newspaper or Forest Service archival material turned up for this specific tower in cached sources or three web searches; a 'Sterling Mountain' NRHP tower that surfaced in search results is a different structure in Orange County, New York, and was excluded. Wikipedia calling the tower 'abandoned' sits a little oddly next to NHLR's description of an open trap door and NPS radio-repeater use -- worth a direct check of current NPS trail/tower status pages. Current staffing and public-access level are inferred, not confirmed by an authoritative current source.

Story sources are 2019 and 2023 items; no 2024-2026 status found, so the access note should be rechecked with the Tusquitee Ranger District before anyone visits. The brief's agency field comes from the Register's administrator line and differs from the Forest Service sources. Staffing and current-use claims conflict across sources; the story says so. Facebook posts that appeared in search results were not used because they were not fetched.

The 18 m height in the brief matches the 1934-36 state report's 59 ft 3 in steel tower, not the NHLR's 50 ft Aermotor (15.2 m), so height_m is left out of facts. The record's 1936 build year is from NHLR and the Journal-Patriot; the 1934 report is quoted second-hand by Forest Lookouts and was not checked against the original. The Journal-Patriot article is partly paywalled, but the quoted lines were readable and the article's own date is not shown. The Wilkes Record column is dated December 10, 2023. A TV item quoting a ranger on a 1936 CCC build was not fetched and is not cited. NHLR's 'restricted for electronics use' is quoted as written; no source explains what it means. Access is set to restricted because the tower is described as unsafe to climb; no official closure notice was found. Staffing is recorded as unstaffed on the strength of the undated Journal-Patriot report.

Build year (1932), location and the 2018 restoration agree across sources. Unverified leads not used: a search summary says public access ended in 2017, and another says a CCC camp manned the tower from 1933; neither appeared in a page I opened. Elevation: the register and Smoky Mountain News give 3,670 ft (1,119 m, matching the brief's 1118.6 m); Romantic Asheville gives 3,643 ft. No post-2018 condition report was found; the travel guide calls the tower in excellent condition but is undated, so verify the current state before relying on access.

No source after 2016 gives the tower's condition or access; the Wikipedia access line is undated. The 2015 report says rehabilitated while the 2016 goals still plan a restoration announcement, so the story says the record is unclear. Staffing history (NPS staffing until the late 1960s, cabin removed 1987) appeared only in search snippets, so it is left out. The record's height_m stays null: the register's 60 ft is the tower height, and the cab-floor height is not sourced. Quotes from the 2013 article come from an archived copy with no named publisher.

Four pages were read: the tnlandforms.us North Carolina tower list (map revised June 2021), the OpenStreetMap way, and the NHLR and FFLOS North Carolina listings. Two searches gave no history for this tower. The name link between Tirzah (tnlandforms list) and Glenns Mountain Fire Tower (OpenStreetMap) comes from the brief's records; neither page names the other, so please confirm it before publishing. The OSM page was not checked for coordinates. The brief's status 'standing' rests only on the OSM map entry. Design, height, build date, staffing, agency and access are unknown and omitted. The NHLR page shows 31 lookouts and no Tirzah, which supports 'not registered' by inspection of the full list. A Mapcarta search snippet placed the tower in 'Mount Tirzah Township'; it was not read, so it is not used. Read budget ran over: about nine fetch_text calls, including one failed NHLR request, and the early reads were partly repeated. Fact check 2026-10-09: the OSM page names only Glenns Mountain Fire Tower and the tnlandforms list does not mention Glenns, so the name link is still the brief's own and no source confirms it. The NHLR North Carolina page was read in full: 31 names, no Tirzah. The FFLOS page names Big Stamp Lookout Site and Frye Knob. The story now says 'lookout register' (both registers are national) and drops 'north-central', which no source states.

The Register page has no visit reports. Current condition rests on a 2016 photo caption, and the staffing end date (late 1990s) comes only from that caption. Access is private land per the Register. Search results from Facebook and a Walker Top group were not used because they were not fetched.

The NRHP nomination PDF (npgallery GetAsset for NRIS 00000164) returned no readable text, so the 1999 Van Dolsen nomination was not read; it would settle the height and staffing dates. A Facebook post from Old Homes of North Carolina reports a 1970 sale by the Haithcock heirs to the state and a spring 1993 end of staffing, but it could not be fetched, so it is not used. No source found on current access or climbing. The 1932 state report is known only through the Eastern US Lookouts quotation.

Current condition is unknown beyond the 2019 Register nomination photos and an undated trail-lookout status line. No closure notice was found. The brief's 1933 build year drops the Register's 1933-1942 range. The access level 'restricted' is our reading of the removed steps, not a posted rule.

The record's 7.6 m height was the earlier 25-foot wooden tower; corrected to 53 ft (16.2 m). The 1935 versus 1937 build date is unresolved; no NRHP nomination or Forest Service history was read. Eastern US Lookouts quotes a 1936 newspaper plan for a 43-foot stone tower, but the built height was 53 feet. The NHLR and Eastern US Lookouts spell the memorial name Bryne; the Forest Service and Eastern's 1939 quote use Byrne. Current climbing rules and hours were not found in any source. The 2016 fire is dated November 23, 2016 by Eastern US Lookouts only.

Built year is disputed: the register says 1936 and Willhite cites a 1934 USGS benchmark note, so both are kept as events. Burn cause differs: register says vandals, Willhite says arson. Material differs: register says metal, Wikipedia says wooden. Deck date: register says 1993, Willhite says early 1990s. The 2016 fire line rests on Wikipedia alone; a Forest Service or news source would strengthen it. Access and climbability come from undated sources. The record's height_m 9.0 (OSM) is close to the register's 30 ft, so it is left as is. The 1948 Shaffer detail is from Willhite only. The story no longer says the observation deck exists today: the only source is undated, so it is attributed to Willhite.

Staffing and notable fires are not in any readable source. A 2002 Wilmington Star-News obituary (seen only as a search snippet; fetch returned HTTP 403) says Willow Atkinson Baker began as Wilmar Fire Tower operator in about 1958. Not used because it could not be read. 2024 social posts call the tower abandoned; not used as sources. Confirm the 2018 auction and current owner with the NC Forest Service or the county before publishing. The NHLR page is the only source for the post-1936 history.

Only the NHLR page is an official record. Build year and the 1969 staffing end come from two hiking-guide sites, not from Forest Service or archive records. A Transylvania Times destination-hike article (1934 build, USFS and CCC) returned HTTP 429 twice, so it is not used. Another guide snippet (theoutdoorsapp) mentions the tower was 'originally in 1934' and 'reconstru...' (cut off). If the tower was rebuilt, the built and restored events need correcting, so check the Forest Service or NRHP records before publishing. The record has no height; the NHLR gives only the cab and base dimensions, so height_m was left out. Access is marked public on the basis of trail access on national forest land; confirm current climbing rules with the Highlands Ranger District.

Two independent sources agree on 1936 and 100 feet. The 2005 PDF text runs in columns, so the quotes are single lines. The standing status comes from the FFLA list, which is undated. No staffing record was found, and no source says whether visitors may climb the tower. The FWS refuge page (fws.gov/refuge/lostwood) was checked by keyword and mentions no tower. The brief had no agency; USFWS was taken from the 2005 brochure. No NHLR or FFLOS detail record turned up in search.

Build year and builder not found in any source reached (WebSearch and the Wikipedia refuge page had no tower entry). Relocation (1992), cost and registration are well sourced. Access is unconfirmed: the museum's visitor page does not mention the tower, so no access key was set. Height 33.5 m is our conversion of the register's 110 ft. Do not confuse with the separate Northern Lights Tower, an 88.5-ft steel sculpture in Rugby that the museum page also describes. LOC HAER photos returned 403, so no new photo was recorded.

The register and the firelookout.org list conflict on whether the steel tower still stands; the register's 'now primarily used as a radio relay station' is the only current-status claim found, and the register's own entry is undated. The register also calls it 'the only fire lookout in North Dakota', but its state page now lists a second one, Rugby Tower (was Salyer Wildlife Refuge Tower, US 1414, added 2020), which was not used in the story. No build year, staffing dates, or public-access information was found, so none is given. The brief's note that NHLR lists lookouts standing when registered is not resolved by these sources. The brief's status 'gone' should be checked by a person before the record changes; no physical check was made.

Identity is the weak link. The West Lookouts list files the 100-foot tower under 'J. CLARK SAYLER WILDLIFE REFUGE (UPPER SOURIS)' with no HQ label. The HQ match rests on the Forest Fire Lookout Association row 'Upper Souris NWR – HQ' at 48.46032, -101.57283 plus the Upper Souris label. Treat as probable, not confirmed. The same list moved a different J. Clark Salyer HQ tower to Rugby in 1992; that is not this tower. Lead, not cited: HAER survey photos on loc.gov (hhh.nd0028, hhh.nd0033) describe a lookout tower at the refuge headquarters, but loc.gov returned 403 to fetch_text. Not found in any page read: reason for construction, staffing, notable fires, current public access, rentals. The FWS visit-location page in the cache has no directions. Brief record had no height; 30.5 m is 100 ft converted. Verification 2026-10-09: the story no longer says the tower was erected 'at the site' or that it 'stands at its headquarters'; the HQ link is stated as unconfirmed. 'And rest' was dropped from the founding sentence (the Wikipedia text says breeding ground only).

Build date is the open question. 1935 (register and West Lookouts, which may share a source) conflicts with the USFWS early-1940s CCC statement quoted on the register and with the 1937 WPA newspaper item quoted on the south page. Needs a primary source (refuge history, USFWS or Nebraska State Historical Society) before the built event is firmed up. Height 18.3 m is our conversion of 60 ft. Nominator is listed as 'Admin' on the register page. A Living New Deal search snippet reportedly says the WPA built 'the fire tower' at the headquarters site; not used because that page returned 403. Access and visit rules not confirmed; the FWS visit page was not read. Read budget exceeded: several reads returned 403 or the wrong page.

Build date unresolved (see resolved_conflicts). The 100-foot figure comes from the 1937 newspaper item and does not name which refuge tower it describes, so no height_m was set; the north page gives 60 ft for its own tower. Primary source to try: the FWS press release 'U.S. Improves Duck Refuge in Nebraska (Crescent Lake Refuge)', June 12, 1937 (fws.gov archive; PDF is 19370612.PDF on the media page, not reached: a guessed URL returned 404). Access not established; the FWS visit page does not mention the towers. Read budget used: 6 page reads and 2 WebSearch calls. Register nominator is 'Admin'.

Only two lookout listings and one forest page turned up; no build, staffing, fire or removal detail in any source read, so the story is under the 120-word floor. Brief access 'unknown' is not recorded because the access schema has no unknown level. Map sites (anyplaceamerica, getamap) give coordinates 42.72333, -101.07028 that differ slightly from the association's; not used as sources.

Brief said status standing; kept, with a status note for the cab loss. The 1944 date comes from NHLR only. A Forest Fire Lookout Association post seen in search (not fetched, so not cited) gives 1973 for the current third tower; check before changing the 1944 date. Elevation: NHLR 2,907 ft (886 m); Forest Service page shows 2,922 with no unit. Height 50 ft is from one news report. No staffing source found, so staffing is omitted. Photos on the NHLR page have no captured URLs; none added.

Build year (1935), CCC origin and registration rest on the NHLR entry; the same text appears on westlookouts.weebly.com, which is not cited separately. The only lookout-era record found is one August 1937 CCC work report, so staffing, end of fire watch, and any notable fire remain unknown. Nothing found says whether the cab survives in its original form. The brief's access 'unknown' is now public via the trail to the observation deck. height_m is converted from 100 ft. wheninyourstate.com returned HTTP 403 and was not used. No NPS or Nebraska Game and Parks history was checked.

The NHLR page narrates refuge-wide CCC/WPA history (canals, fencing) and separately states the tower itself was CCC-built, but gives no specific construction year for the tower. No source here covers staffing history, climbability, or visitor access, so those were left unknown rather than guessed.

The 1937 article is known only through the Forest Lookouts page quoting it; not checked against the newspaper. Year 1937 is inferred from the article date. No removal date or present-day description in any source read. Brief access 'permission' has no supporting source in the pages read, so it is not recorded; please verify before restoring it.

The sources say the Abenaki Tower was never a fire tower, but the Forest Fire Lookout Association list classes it as an observation tower ('Obs Tower'). The editor should decide whether a fire-lookout directory should carry it; the brief's kind 'tower' does not claim fire use. The marker names the builder only as 'residents of Melvin Village'. The Laker article (2018) was read in full on the 2026-10-09 check. It names Tuftonboro resident Lewis McIntire as the winning $400 bidder to construct the tower, and describes a taller rebuild in 1977-78 (Kirk Titus hired to rebuild, Bill Cornell designed it, re-dedicated 22 July 1978). The 1977-78 rebuild is now a 'rebuilt' event and the story says so. The story keeps the marker's builder wording and does not name McIntire; the editor may decide whether the builder line needs the Laker's account. The marker page (HMDB) was read in full: its trailhead location, its 'historical and continuing contributions' wording and its Abenaki Tower Trail Association excerpt are confirmed. The association's own site was not read; it is the likeliest source for upkeep and current climbing rules. Other search snippets say the tower was 'originally constructed in 1924 by local volunteers' and describe it as stone and wood; they were not read, so they are not used. The FFLA row has no NHLR or FFLOS number. Its coordinates match the brief (43.67226, -71.29064). The climbable flag rests on the 2018 visit. About seven page reads were used for this tower, which is over the budget.

The 2022 chapter report and the FFLA New Hampshire list are the only sources read. Both date from 2022 or are undated, so the current condition and access are unknown; the story says so. The brief's events were garbled: '2022 built' is corrected to a relocation and erection, and 'None relocated' contradicted 'Moved from Alabama'. The FFLA list says 'Relocated from AL'; the 2022 report says the seller has not said where the tower came from, so the Alabama origin stays attributed to the list. Two searches found no other source naming the earlier site. A Davana sale-list PDF (DAVANA-LLC-0725.pdf) was read in part for context; the matched lines do not mention Hooksett or Bass Pro. The coordinates match the brief (43.04077, -71.47663). About six page reads and two searches were used for this tower. Fact check 2026-10-09: the story said the 2022 report 'says something different'; it only fails to confirm the Alabama origin, so the wording now says that. The story also said all sources date from 2022; the FFLA New Hampshire list has no date, so the story now says the report dates from 2022 and the list is undated. Both pages were read in full and the quotes were confirmed.

Brief's height_m 121.9 (about 400 ft) is not supported; NHLR's 34 ft tower plus 1979 10 ft addition gives 13.4 m, and that is proposed as the correction. Build date: 1914-15 (Historic Structures), 1915 (NHLR), 1913 (Trailspotting), left as a stated conflict. Agency: NHLR names the NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development; a search snippet pointed to a dncr.nh.gov news release, which returned 403 when fetched, so the newer agency name is unverified and not cited. Final 2023 costs and the actual 2024 reopening are not confirmed beyond the newsletter's expectation and Trailspotting's 2025 'refurbished in 2023' statement. Staffing: NHLR's 2016 visit report says 'Sometimes' staffed, during fire season; no current staffing source found. No specific fires were named in sources read. Left out on purpose: a 1952 death at the lookout cabin in the Forest Lookouts item and a 1957 newspaper mention of a named lookout, since they concern private individuals and are not needed for the tower's history. The Historic Structures page is a third-party history site; its dates are cited as its own claims. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with public trail access and seasonal road-gate hours from Trailspotting; climbing the cab is not stated in any source. Budget note: the Historic Structures page was grepped several times from cache; it counts as one page.

Brief's 2002 registration and 2008 cab replacement check out (NHLR; FFLA 2008 chapter report says a new cab was installed). Brief's record has no built year or height; built 1915 is supported by NHLR, Historic Structures and the 1915-1916 state report quoted on Forest Lookouts. Height conflict: 32 ft (NHLR, Trailspotting) versus roughly 40 ft if the 1970-1980 cab addition is counted (Historic Structures); no height_m set. First-use year 1912 or 1913 is unresolved. The NHLR 2016 visit report and the Trailspotting 2025 hours are the only current-condition sources; the NH state staffing claim is from the 2016 visit. The 1948 hay-fire item is from Forest Lookouts and spells the town Stratford; it is cited as a fire the lookout reported, names of private officials omitted. Town spelling: Farmington (Historic Structures, Trailspotting) with Strafford County (NHLR). Wikipedia was read as a lead; its town and county lines agree but it is not cited. Page budget: six distinct pages read, one WebSearch.

Record elevation_m 848.3 does not match the 3,121-foot summit in the 1954 press reprints (about 951 m). elevation is not a facts key, so it was not changed; please check it. climbable=true is inferred from the register's stairs and the 2024 visitor reports, not from a published visit rule. No rental information was found. The state's closure notice gives no year, so the access note does not name one. No current 2026 status check was done.

Only secondhand sources back the history: an undated NH Family Hikes roadside guide with no citations, and a 2014 hike report. No NHLR entry, FFLA chapter report, state record or newspaper item was found, and the Forest Lookouts Carter page has only a title card. The 1897 date and the Carter family's role should be treated as tentative. Do not confuse with Carter Dome (us-nh-carter-dome, a gone tower at 44.26715, -71.17922), which is a different site. Access: the NH Family Hikes guide says the tower is private property, so the record should not invite visitors to the door. Leads: Jefferson town or historical society files, and Carter family or railroad history, for the owner and build date.

Height after the wooden cab conflicts (41 ft vs about 51 ft implied by the Register). Open days differ by year: the 2019 newspaper gives October 13 and 14; the 2021 blog says one weekend a year. henniker.org returned 403 to fetch, so current open dates are not verified. The 1997 Register date and the 1997 rescue are both sourced. No specific fires were found. No photos added.

The main history comes from Historic Structures, which reproduces a detailed description of the tower and its history. It is a secondary source and its own citations are not visible to us, so treat its dates as strong but not verified against the state record. The Forest Lookouts page has only three dated lines. The 2009 record event should be 'modified' (cab), not 'replaced' (tower); see corrections. Height is unresolved (24 ft vs 34 ft) and is left out of facts. Access: the tower is inside a private preserve and the sources say it is closed to the public, so the record should not invite climbing. Leads: the NH Fire Tower Quest Program PDF from NH Forests & Lands, cited by the Corbin Park Wikipedia article (not fetched; the state site returned 403 for the related history PDF); and the Blue Mountain Forest Association for lease and access terms.

Cab fate conflicts: NHLR says the cab was later removed and Trail Finder says it was removed once out of use, while FFLA says the state burned it around 1985. Stairs: FFLA says burned, Trail Finder says removed to discourage climbing. The story reports both. NH Family Hikes lists a 'North Deer Mountain' in Pittsburg whose stairs were removed; it may be this tower, but I did not use it because the name match is not certain. onlyinyourstate.com returned HTTP 403 and was not used. The rehabilitation status is only as of the 2023 FFLA report; no later news was found. The access level 'restricted' is my reading: the wooden steps were removed to discourage climbing (trail guide), and no source says the tower is formally closed to climbing, so the story no longer says it is. The steps are cited to FFLA and the trail guide, since NHLR does not mention them. No photos added.

Coordinates differ between NHLR (42.81339, -71.65592) and firelookout.org (42.80479, -71.63033), about 2 km apart; not changed. The 2016 renovation completion is not confirmed by any source read. Access: the cabin is closed per a 2021 hiking blog; the story now says visitors can climb to the level below the cabin, and does not encourage climbing. The NH state fire-tower page returned HTTP 403, so state access and staffing rules are from news and blog sources. Staffing as_of is the 2016 visit date. The 2021 height and access notes rest on one hiking blog.

The 1934 date rests on NH Family Hikes alone (AllTrails repeats it, unread). NHDFL pages and PDF returned 403 to fetch_text and WebFetch, and Living New Deal returned 403, so the state record is unchecked. The record's kind 'platform' conflicts with FFLA's 'Open Tower'. FFLA files the site under non-lookout structures. Current stair condition and closure status are not verified.

The record's kind 'tower' is kept, but the sources describe a public park observatory. FFLA lists it as 'Obs Tower', and NH Family Hikes says whether it was ever a fire tower is a matter of debate, so the editor should decide whether it belongs in the fire-lookout set. The 1880 to 1913 history rests on Wikipedia and the Dover page, which agree on the main events. The 1993 date comes only from Wikipedia. Leads: the NRHP nomination for Garrison Hill Park and Tower (NRHP No. 87001413), which Wikipedia cites and which would confirm the 1880s ownership and the 1990 and 1993 dates; and any City of Dover record of fire-tower use, if one exists.

Elevation is unresolved: the Register lists 525 ft (160 m) for the site, while the Weirs Times describes a 1,300-foot summit. The record's 160 m is left unchanged for the editor to check. Register coordinates (43.86, -71.26) differ from firelookout.org (43.87691, -71.29874) by about 3 km; not changed. The Forest Lookouts page for Great Hill has only a header and no body text, so it is not cited. Living New Deal and franklinsites were not read (Living New Deal returned HTTP 403). Access is public per the town's reopening notice; the story does not encourage climbing.

Height: the record's 14.3 m is the original 47-ft tower; the register's 39 ft (11.9 m) is proposed. The 1958 survey's 35 ft overall is unresolved. Elevation: the register's 855 ft conflicts with the 1,884-ft (2025 guide) and 1,907-ft (1966 item) summit figures; the proposed 574.3 m needs a human check. Status: the register (undated) says part-time; the 2025 guide says no longer active. Access: public trails and a locked cab per the 2025 guide; not checked with NH DRED. Staffing as of 2026 unknown. Not verified: any changes after 2025. No photos added.

Built date conflict: 1930 (register and hike guide) versus a May 1939 newspaper item about buying land and erecting a tower at once; the 1939 item may concern a replacement or a new site, which no source confirms. Height conflict: 53 ft (register) versus 80 ft (2016 newspaper); the brief's 24.4 m matches the newspaper, so it is not proposed as an error. Brief event 2002 registration and 2020 removal are confirmed. The 2020 report is by the FFLA New Hampshire chapter and names a state contractor; the brief's 'removed' date is 'early June 2020'. Pack Monadnock's NHLR entry says it replaces the Hyland Hill fire tower 'which is still maintained' (search snippet, not read; not used). No photos added: none with a stated license in the pages read.

Current status and access are unverified after 2010. The NHLR rental link points at nhdfl.org, which did not resolve, and the NH state reservations page returned 403, so rental terms are unconfirmed. Sources 2 and 3 are secondary (a hobbyist site quoting newspapers; a hiking article with no date visible in the cache). The 1937 closure and 2009 vandalism are known only from the Forest Lookouts page. Brief record's access 'unknown' can be set to public for the trail; the cab's visitor status stays open.

The tower's own NHLR page is rich (built year, design, WWII use, administering/cooperating agencies, nomination, and a 2019 field inspection with staffing/condition detail), but outside corroboration is thinner than the 'well-documented' label implied: Wikipedia and the state park site confirm 1932 and public access but add little else, and a promising newspaper piece (Conway Daily Sun, 'Milan Hill's fire tower is 1 of 15 still in use') returned HTTP 429 on every fetch attempt and was never read -- worth another try, it likely has more on current staffing and may confirm or refute a claim (surfaced only in AI-synthesized web-search summaries, not in any page actually read) that the 1932 tower replaced an earlier one on nearby Jodrie Hill. I left that claim out of the story entirely since I couldn't verify it against a primary source. On location: the record's existing lat/lon (from ffla) is corroborated by OpenStreetMap's independently mapped tower node, while the NHLR page's own stated coordinates sit about 1.65 km (roughly a mile) away -- this likely resolves the 'conflicts' entry already in the tower record in ffla's favor, though I'm not proposing a formal correction since the record's location field already uses the better-supported value. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04): the CCC-camp sentence was footnoted to the state park page, which does not mention the CCC at all; moved that citation to Wikipedia, which does state it. Also corrected the story's claim that the NHLR/FFLA coordinates differ by 'a mile and a half' -- the actual gap (1,653 m) is about one mile, not 1.5. Used 2 of 3 allotted WebSearch calls (research); fact-check pass used WebFetch only, no WebSearch.

The 1910 build and Timberland Owners funding come from the NH Family Hikes history page, a secondary source. The NHDFL state PDF returned 403 to both fetch tools. The 1940-1981 steel tower dates and the platform age come only from VFTT forum posts and are flagged unverified in the story. The cab removal date is unknown. The record's kind and status_note are correct; agency is null in the record. Staffing is inferred from 'not in active service' in White Mountain History, which is undated.

Record gaps: no height and no access rule found. Access was left out because no source read gives a visit or climbing rule, so the story asks visitors to check with the state. The FFLA report is titled 'FFLA New Hampshire Chapter Report for 2019' in its text, so the 2019 year is confirmed. The record's 'state replaced the cab' is not in the report; see corrections. The 81.7 m height in the record looks like an error and should be checked before publishing. The fire record is for the mountain station and watchman, not necessarily this structure. Search results mentioned a 27-foot 1924 steel tower and a 1953-54 larger cab; I could not read those pages in the session, so they are not used. One search snippet also said a 2019 date was not found; the FFLA 2019 report does mention cab work, so that snippet was wrong.

The Forest Lookouts Monadnock page also carries a February 13, 1960 lightning story, but it describes Pack Monadnock (Miller State Park), a different tower, so it is excluded here. The NHLR lists Pack Monadnock as a standing tower (US 646). Wikipedia's Halfway House passage concerns a hotel and toll road, not the lookout, and was not used. The 1972 article's own ages for the foundation (45 years) and building (20 years) do not line up neatly with its 1957 rebuild date, so the story does not repeat those ages. The record's 'ground' kind fits a building on a stone base. No photo was added.

Core history (1912 estate tower, 1941 transfer to the state, enclosed cab, 1992 registration) is consistent across the Register, the historic-structures summary and the 2026 state sheet. Open points: whether the cab came in 1941 or after; current height (37 ft in one summary; a Weeks State Park Association search snippet says 56 ft, not fetched so not used); staffing is not stated. The historic-structures page gives 420 acres for the estate in one place and donated 431 acres in another; the story avoids acreage. The NH Division of Forests and Lands history PDF returned HTTP 403, so it was not used.

Most history comes from the Register and a 1929/1947 newspaper excerpt quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the 1947 article is not checked against the original paper. The 2019 chapter report does not name the tower's operator and its staffing line is for the state's towers in general, not Oak Hill, so staffing is left as historical only. Its staffing line also rests on one member's account, as the report says. The 19.8 m height is from OpenStreetMap, not from the Register. The blog spells the road Sharker in its URL and Shaker in its text; the story uses Shaker. Climbing is described in one hiking blog only; no official rule was found, so the story does not say the tower is open to climb. Lead for later: any Concord or Loudon city or town record that confirms the tower's ownership and public access.

The brief's built year 2004 comes from the NHLR Built field, which dates the replacement cab; the tower is 1939 per NHLR's own description and Historic Structures (see corrections). Height: 41 ft (NHLR, Historic Structures) vs 27 ft (NH State Parks history, undated). The park history also says the 1939 cabin no longer exists; that is not a conflict with the 2004 replacement cab, but the document is undated and gives 27 feet, so I treated it as the weaker source. The story no longer says the watchman was on duty when lightning struck in 1960: Historic Structures names the watchman of that time (on the job since 1941) but does not place him at the cab then. The 1960 cab: NHLR says burned and repaired, Historic Structures says destroyed and rebuilt that season; the story reports both. Staffing as_of is 'undated' because the NHLR page has no date. NHLR says staffed on class 3 days and above; Wikipedia says staffed seasonally. Historic Structures states the tower is one of 15 active NH fire towers; not used. No photos added; no on-site check.

The Register and the 1914 and 1930 items are consistent on the first steel tower, the 1971 raise and the 1976 cab. Sources do not agree on the site elevation: the Register says 549 feet, but the park sheet puts the tower on the 908-foot summit of South Mountain. The 1930 house item is a plan from a newspaper, not a confirmed use. The 1938 and 1920 items are from a Portsmouth Herald excerpt quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and not checked against the original paper. The 2016 chapter report's statewide staffing line is not specific to this tower and is not used. The OpenStreetMap way lists the operator as NH Division of Forests and Lands; the Register names NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development, so the story uses the Register. Climbing is supported only by two personal blogs and a park mention of the view; the story says to check with the park. Leads: park or NH Division of Forests and Lands notice about tower access; a 1914 Biennial Report copy for the original build detail. The 1930 notice also says the tree line was replaced by ground wire; the story does not say the Goodrich house was wired.

Current staffing is unconfirmed. The 2025 chapter report says Kearsarge was staffed, but Wikipedia says that name also belongs to a Merrimack County mountain, so the report cannot be tied to this tower. The NHLR entry gives no visit reports. The 28-foot height is read as the tower's height from the register's '28' steel tower' line. The 2025 Press Herald and SectionHiker results were not opened, so 'open to the public' rests on the Forest Service page and Wikipedia. climbable=true follows the observation-site description and the 'fire tower' visit wording; check before publishing.

The 2016 visit reports are volunteer observations on the Register. The Keene Sentinel article has no date in the fetched text. The NH state fire-tower page and a state PDF both returned HTTP 403, so state staffing and access rules rest on news and blog sources. Staffing as_of is the 2025 blog date. The 25-ft 1925 height is used only in design, not as a current height. Register coordinates (43.09236, -72.12881) and firelookout.org (43.09405, -72.13498) differ by under 1 km; not changed. Andorra Forest access rests on blog quotes from a trailhead kiosk; the kiosk sentence about opening trails is truncated in the fetched text and is not quoted. The story does not encourage climbing. The 2025 blog author climbed the tower, which the story now says; access is still listed as restricted because the cab's status is unknown. That classification is an editorial call to confirm.

The NHLR page read for this brief has no 2010 shingle-replacement entry and no 2010 grant entry, so the brief's 2010 'restored' event could not be confirmed. The 2011 report gives 2009 for the grant, which is the basis of the correction. The 1972 height is disputed (55 ft register vs 37 ft Eastern lookouts) and height_m was left out of the facts. Current access terms for the stairs and cab were not found, so access.level is unknown and the story does not encourage climbing given the 2016 landing report. The 2025 report does not say who the private association is. The Town of Moultonborough flyer, the Red Hill Tower Watchman Facebook page and the trail-site snippets were not opened.

Start date disagrees across sources: Forest Lookouts gives a 1910 lookout station; the Weirs Times gives a 30-foot wood tower built 1911 and a 2,702 ft summit. Both are kept and not reconciled. Not used: a web search summary attributed a firelookout.org/lookouts/nh/signal.htm entry (2,673 ft, 37-ft structure, steel, NH Forestry as operator). That URL returned 404 on our fetch and its text was never read, so those details are omitted. The NHDFL forest lookout towers history PDF returned 403 to fetch_text and was not read; a search snippet mentions Timberland Owners funding for seven stations including Signal, but nothing rests on it. Owner, operator and staffing are unknown. A different Signal Mountain in Monroe (Grafton Co.) is a separate peak; a VFTT thread says it has no known lookout history (not cited). The forum visit reports are undated in the pages read and describe climbing. The story gives no route and advises against climbing. Pages read: FFLA NH list, Forest Lookouts page, Weirs article, two VFTT threads (the Millsfield one in part).

Builder is disputed: the register credits the NH Forestry Commission, Willhite credits the CCC with Forest Service funds. Ownership is disputed: the register lists the U.S. Forest Service, Willhite says the site went to NH DPW&H in 1980, and the 2014 chapter report says the Forest acquired the tower in an AT land purchase (date not given). Willhite gives 1973 as last active year and also says staffed to 1980. The access line rests on a 2020 photo caption and a 2016 visit report; check current status before publishing. Record: the 1939 build event was missing and is added; height_m 12.5 matches the 41 ft in sources.

Height: the record's 24.0 m matches no source; the register's 53-ft steel tower (16.2 m) is proposed, though it is not stated whether 53 ft includes the cab. Elevation: register 273 ft summit vs town page 'about 288 feet tall' for the hill; the register figure is kept. Material: register says steel tower with wooden cab; 2026 article says the original was built of wood. Fires: 1997 is in two sources; the 1980s fire is in the 2026 article only, with no year. Staffing end: 1976 (register, 2026 article) vs a 1973 item and a 1977 memorial (15 vs 16 years). Agency: the register lists the Stratham Fire Department; the 2026 article says the Select Board acted on a Public Works recommendation and the town maintains the park and tower; agency left as the register has it. A 2001 Seacoastonline item on an arson charge for the 1997 fire appeared in search results but returned HTTP 403, so it is not used. Not verified: current climbing rules, hours, or whether the observation deck is open in winter. No photos added.

Elevation conflict: the register's 388 ft (118 m) matches the brief's 118.3 m; the crest figures are 605 ft (Derry News) and 604 ft (Derry survey). The story reports the Derry News figure and the register's figure. Agency: the department name the brief used is on the register, so it was not an error; the story names only the Division of Forests & Lands. Access and staffing conflict: the register says unstaffed with no signs; Derry News says a watchman has served since about 1985 and the tower is closed except on the most dangerous fire days, though the top landing is climbable. Check with the Division of Forests & Lands before publishing access wording. The 1935 survey date is an outlier. The Derry News column is undated; its 75th-anniversary remark points to about 2014. Historic Structures gives both a leased 1-acre tract and a 2-acre purchase for the Mears land; the story uses the 2-acre figure from the quote. No photos recorded.

Thin record: two short sources. The Aermotor design and about 60-ft height rest only on the Forest Lookouts entry, which cites Google Earth imagery from February 2020; the entry is not dated otherwise. Private is read as ownership, but the page does not expand it. Two web searches returned map and listing pages (a mytopo ridge page and FFLA list pages) that were not read. No build date, builder, owner or access rules found. Editor may want a reference check (Baird and Haartz field guide, Coos County registry) before publishing.

The brief's 1950 build year is the move date; the register says the tower first stood at Big Hill in 1938. The nj.com article on the 2016 closure returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The 1914 newspaper text is quoted through Eastern US Lookouts, not the original papers. Wikipedia gives the hill as 205 feet tall, while the NHLR and the NJ tower table give the tower site at 179 feet (55 m). No source found on current staffing. The NJ Forest Fire Service remains the register's administrator even though the state DEP closed the access in 2016.

Current public access, climbability, and staffing status (volunteer vs. paid, active vs. seasonal) were not confirmed in this pass; the NJ DEP detection-program page would not render via the text fetcher (JS-only or blocked). The elevation_m (14.3) and height_m (24.0) already in the tower record match the Wikipedia fire-tower table's 47 ft elevation / 80 ft height for this tower, so no correction is needed there.

NJ DEP fire-tower pages (dep.nj.gov/parksandforests/wildfire/fire-towers/ and nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/fire/program/detection.html) returned no text from the cache, so they are not cited. A search snippet attributes a 100 ft height and active service to the DEP page; verify before relying on it. Current public access and observer schedule are unconfirmed; the register page is undated. The WHYY text read does not name the tower or give the year. The Batsto Mansion lookout (US 79 / NJ 3, Batsto Mansion House Station) is a separate register entry and is not covered here. The brief's 2004 registration is confirmed.

Status is unverified. The brief says standing, but I found no source that says the cab survives today, so no status key is written. Wikipedia lists the Batsto Mansion House Station among towers in active service, but that list gives no condition. Cab size and form disagree: 9x9 ft (NHLR manor entry), 10x10 ft (NHLR station entry), about 8 ft square in a newspaper quoted by Forest Lookouts; the newspaper also says 'glass-sided room' where NHLR says 'enclosed wooden cab'. The Rutgers article describes a 90-foot tower at the mansion; I could not reconcile that with the other sources and did not use it. Julia Cramer's service end date is unknown. The access level 'restricted' is my judgment: no source says the cab is open. The brief's kind 'tower' is loose; the lookout is a cab on the mansion roof or tower. Corrections: none proposed, since the brief's standing status is unconfirmed rather than shown wrong. Page reads went over the budget of six (the Batsto Facebook post came back empty and the NJ forum thread was an extra read). No photos added.

Pre-1934 tower chronology is genuinely muddled across sources (1880s platform / 1909 iron tower / 1916 frame tower claims); worth noting as unresolved rather than picking a version. Exact April 1932 fire date not pinned down beyond 'last Friday' before an April 15, 1932 article.

Brief status 'gone' is right for the 1916 wooden lookout. The mountain still has the steel tower covered by us-nj-bearfort, so keep the two records apart. Height (40 vs 50 ft) and successor year (1934 vs 1937) conflict across sources; both are reported. The 1913 watcher entry refers to a tower already on the mountain; sources do not say whether it is the 1909 iron-frame tower. Access not classified because no source says whether the old site is open. Cached text has no image URLs, so no photos recorded; FFLOS and NHLR both caption a 1925 photo of the wooden tower.

Access level 'restricted' is an inference from active agency service; no source states a public visiting rule. No current staffing data was found, so no staffing fact is recorded. The 1966 item is a bid notice, so relocation is unconfirmed. The brief had no build date; 1921 comes from the register and 1922 from the annual report as quoted. The NJ DEP fire-tower page returned no text from the cache and was not used.

Good corroboration across a historical register, a period newspaper quote (Courier-Post, 1940), the Wikipedia tower-list table, and a 2024 news feature confirming the tower is still actively staffed; all of those checked out against their cited sources. One claim did not hold up on cross-check: NHLR's Blue Anchor page says the original Aermotor tower was relocated to Stokes State Forest in 1932 to become 'the Culver tower,' but NHLR's own page for that lookout (Culvers Lookout, US44/NJ1) dates its present 47-ft Aermotor tower to 1933 and never mentions Blue Anchor — so the 'same tower, still standing at Stokes' claim in the earlier draft was an overclaim, now softened and the discrepancy disclosed in the story. Also removed an invented 'winter of 1920-21' detail not supported by the cited annual-report quote. No source found on public climbing access, so access.level was left unchanged rather than guessed.

Staffing as_of is the April 2023 visit report; no newer staffing data found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from active status and the locked cab. The 2025 guide says the No Trespassing sign is not enforced and that climbing most of the way up is possible, so the story reports that rather than calling the tower off-limits. The 1925 clipping's lookout details (season opening, visitor counts) are not used as Budd Lake events because the location conflicts. Brief height 18.0 m matches the register's 60 ft.

History from 1922 to 1997 is well sourced (NHLR plus 1922-1924 press and state reports). Current status rests on NHLR visit reports from 2018 and a 2022 repainting comment, not a 2026 check. No notable fires were found in the sources read, so none are listed. The NJ DEP fire-towers page returned no text when fetched, and a Willhite lookout-history page (willhiteweb.com) appeared in search but was not read. The record's height 18.0 m matches Wikipedia's 60 ft (18 m). The record's access 'unknown' is replaced by public trail access. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's unsupported staffing claims ('Staff came early', 'Staffing has been irregular since') were removed; the 1922-1923 staffing picture is unknown. The 'Newspapers disagreed' wording was corrected (one 1922 newspaper against the state report).

Staffing as_of is the December 2004 visit report; no newer staffing or access data found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from the fence and locked gate. The Old Bridge re-erection rests on an unpublished manuscript as quoted by NJPineBarrens and is marked 'believed'. The brief had no build date; 1924 comes from the register and NJPineBarrens. The register gives 177 ft (54 m) elevation; Wikipedia's list gives 204 ft (62 m); elevation is not used in the story. The NJFFS Facebook post was not readable (login wall), so the 1983 vs 1987 move date is unresolved. No visiting directions were confirmed; the earlier 'directions are signed from the road' note was not supported by the register and was removed (the register's access checklist has an unanswered 'directions signed' item).

Dates conflict: first use 1908 (Wikipedia, NHLR) vs first state tower 1918 with April 1919 start-up (Willhite); present tower 1933 (NHLR) vs CCC tower 1934 (Willhite). Not settled. A Takeahike.us page search result also gives 1933 and an Aermotor attribution; it was not opened and is not cited. Staffing and gate details come from NHLR visitor comments (one dated visit report, August 6, 2018) and from Willhite's 2021 account. Willhite is a personal hiking site. Do not encourage climbing: this is a manned working lookout. Brief height 14 m and Sussex County are consistent with sources; no corrections.

Only the NHLR gives the 1944 build year. A web search snippet (a lookout database, firelookout.org, not reachable: 404) gave 1945 and NJ Mosquito Commission ownership; not opened or cited, so not in the story. Staffing and access are not documented beyond the undated 'put back into service' statement. Route 47 comes only from the 1968 bid notice; the NHLR 'US 567 / NJ 20' entries are registry numbers, not highway routes. Brief record elevation 4.0 m and height 30 m are consistent with sources; no corrections.

The Greystone link is solid across the register, the NHLR and Wikipedia. The build year (circa 1919 versus 1920) and the height (45, 47 or fifty feet) differ across sources; the brief's 13.7 m follows the 45-foot figure. The 'Foundation' photo on the register is undated and has no image URL captured, so no photos entry is recorded. Access to the original site is not described in any source I read; the 119firecontrol.com page had no Edison or Greystone match and the NJ DEP fire-towers page returned no readable text. The brief's record has no errors I could confirm.

Built date and builder are not given by any source read, so no build event is recorded. The only account of the 1954 fire is the register's own description; no newspaper or state record was found. Ralph Colfax and Frank Scardo appear only in the register. Brief's 'removed 1954' matches the register's Removed field. Story says no source describes the site today.

Brief record checked: the 1994 NHLR registration is correct. No corrections needed. Access was 'unknown' and is now 'closed', per the NHLR 2020 visit report. Sources disagree on the 1994 cab restoration: the NHLR description (undated) says it is complete and the NJ FFLA chapter took on the rebuild; the Army article credits the NHLR volunteers and says the cab has since decayed. The newest source is the September 2023 visit report, so current condition and whether the 2020 demolition plan went ahead are unconfirmed. Wikipedia's 380 m elevation differs slightly from NHLR's 378 m; the story does not use either. No new photos recorded (no image URLs read).

Only two sources (NHLR and Wikipedia), and they agree. A firelookout.org listing (Active, 1937) seen in a search snippet could not be fetched (404) and is not cited. The brief's other name 'WDHA-FM (Dover)' is unverified and not used. Search results included the Greystone Park fire department, a different organization; excluded. No staffing, access or notable fire data found. The Edison tower's location and dismantling date are not in the sources.

Thin record: one register entry plus the register's New Jersey list. Two web searches and the NJ DEP fire-tower page (returned empty) found nothing on this site. The 1900 build date rests on the register's Built field alone. Record has no county field; the register says Sussex County. Fact-check 2026-10-10: status changed from 'gone' to 'unknown'. The register's former-site listing is not a removal record and no source says what remains; the story makes no claim either way.

Record's 'built 1942' matches NHLR, but that date is for the original Old Bridge tower; the structure was relocated to the current Jamesburg site in 1963, which the record's events list omits. The nomination's claim of a possible 1924 origin is explicitly unconfirmed. Current access/staffing/rental status could not be confirmed from a quotable primary source within budget; a WebSearch summary suggested climbing is allowed only when Forest Fire Service staff are present, but I could not verify that against an actual page I read, so it is left out of facts/events and the record's 'access: unknown' stands.

The 1922 opening and the registry's 1922 build year agree on the year; the month is unclear. The registry's 95-foot hangar height conflicts with the 1922 press and is not resolved; the sources never name the hangar. The Navy society's door height is for Hangar No. One, which the lookout's hangar may or may not be. The NJ Forest Fire Service Facebook post cited in searches could not be read, so it is not used. No staffing end year is given beyond 'after World War II'. No photo was found with a usable license. Current condition is unverified beyond the registry.

Closure, dismantling and replacement all come from local news (the Lakewood Scoop, 1st Responder News). No NJFFS statement was read, and the Scoop says officials did not give a reason. A search snippet from the NJFFS Division B site says all 21 towers are in active service; that page was not read and is probably out of date. The Jackson tower's opening date is not given in the sources, so recheck before publishing. Corrections above cover the two record errors (status and height_m).
