Disputed: (1) Closure: Zinn's overview says the tower closed 'during the 1970s'; Trehern's account has it staffed in the 1970s and not used for detection by 1981-1987. Story reports both. The 1987 event year is the end of Trehern's tenure, not a single date. (2) Location: register says the former Main Gate; Zinn says the agreement's 'main entrance' and an 'east entrance' figure caption; LANL says East Gate. Probably the same gate under different names, not confirmed. (3) Who ran the 1944-1948 structure: register says jointly AEC and Forest Service; Zinn describes an AEC security tower whose duties the Los Alamos Fire Department handled. (4) Owner: register says 'Administered by Los Alamos County' (checked 2026-10-09). The record's kind 'tower' versus FFLA's 'Security Tower' (non-wildland list) is a possible kind note, not an error. A LA Daily Post item on current maintenance returned HTTP 429 and was not read or cited. Access rated restricted by inference; no visiting rules found. Zinn's caption for the figure is split across columns, so the east-entrance wording is cited from Zinn's own text and the LANL post.

The register's removal year is internally inconsistent: the Removed field says 1975 and the description says 1976; the 1976 newspaper says the department stopped using the chair in 1975. Story says 'removed from the peak in 1976' per the description and flags the field. Height: the newspaper gives a 34-foot pine and the register 35 feet; the record's height_m of 10.4 matches the 34-foot figure, so it was not changed. Built 1958 vs '20 years' in 1976: the newspaper figure is loose. The site's present condition is not described by any source read. The RMEF access project covers Luera Mountains state trust land and does not say whether the easement reaches the lookout site, so no access level is recorded. Two WebSearch calls were used; the register's Luera Peak photo is credited to Dixie Boyle, but no image URL was found, so no photo entry.

Height: the record's height_m 9.1 (about 30 feet) matches the 1934 USFS history's 30-foot figure, but the register and the 2020 report give 31.6 feet (about 9.6 m). Not changed and not set in facts. The record's material steel refers to the tower; the register describes a wooden cab. Forest name is unresolved: the register says Apache, the 2020 report uses both Apache and Gila, and Wikipedia says Gila. The 1924 lookout's name is spelled Bitmore on the source page; the spelling is unverified. Living New Deal (which quotes the NRHP nomination form) returned HTTP 403 and was not read; the npgallery nomination text is not digitized. The 2020 report spells the listing Mangus Mtn. A recommendation sentence in the 2020 report near the Mangas photo was ambiguous about which lookout it covers, so it is not used. Access and current staffing are unknown.

Construction date and original builder remain unknown; the Register says so and no source read dates the tower. The tDAR keyword links the tower to a 2002-2003 survey of Forest Service land withdrawn to Kirtland AFB and DOE in the Manzanita Mountains, but the record gives no build or use date for the tower. The GlobalSecurity Manzano Base page (read, not used) describes a DoD weapons site whose construction began in 1947; no source read ties the lookout to that work, so it is not in the story. The Westlookouts Manzano page gives only a header ('Department of Defense'). Access is recorded as restricted on land-status grounds; no visitor rule was found. Brief's agency entry matches the Register.

Brief status 'gone' is right for the original site; the RIDB 'standing' result appears to refer to the James Ridge tower, which I could not check directly. Height conflicts (62 ft vs 48 ft) are unresolved and reported as such. No staffing or fire history found in two searches and the pages read, so none is in the story. The FFLOS 'Date Registered' and Forest Service 'Built 1935' match the brief.

Build history is well sourced (Register, Forest Lookouts page and 2020 report agree on the 1965 cab and tower). The brief's 'Aermotor' design is corrected: the Aermotor MC-39 was the 1934 tower. Staffing 'when fire danger is high' rests on one hiker's undated blog post, cited as a tag page; no official staffing source found. The blog also says the landing was closed on that visit; the story advises checking before climbing and does not encourage it. Access status not established. Register elevation 8,137 ft (2,480 m); an OpenStreetMap tower node gives 2477 m; not used in the story. Height 16.5 m is the 54-foot tower converted (16.46 m). The 2020 report year comes from its title, 2020 Year-End Report. No photos added.

Tower history (1948 tower, 1924 and 1921 earlier cabs) comes from Forest Lookouts; NHLR confirms the 1948 date and the 30-foot height, and describes the cab as wooden where Forest Lookouts gives no material. The New Mexico Magazine profile carries a page date of Apr. 10, 2024, so staffing is recorded as of that date; Irving's '42 summers' is her own count as reported. The Mogollon Baldy Fire is undated in the sources, so it is not logged as an event. The 1913 fire-detection date comes only from NHLR. Access rules are not stated (access omitted). The Komoot and Facebook pages were not used as sources (the Facebook post repeats NHLR text). Not checked: the NRHP nomination on npgallery and the Wikipedia cabin article's full reference list. Budget limit reached after six page reads and one search.

Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found three sourcing errors, now fixed: (1) the story cited Wikipedia for the claim that the CCC built an original 1936 lookout later rebuilt in 1940, but Wikipedia only says 'completed in 1940' and never mentions 1936 — the 1936/1940 two-stage claim is supported by Living New Deal (now added as source 5) and the USFS page, not Wikipedia, which now cites only the 1940 date alongside NHLR. (2) The New Mexico State Register of Cultural Properties claim was cited to the NPGallery NRHP record, which does not mention the state register at all; that fact is supported by Wikipedia (source 2, which gives the exact date March 4, 1988 and State Register No. 1445) and has been re-cited and split into its own event. (3) The story claimed Monjeau was 'the first lookout entered into the National Historic Lookout Register' outright; NHLR's own page says only that it was 'the first NHLR listing in New Mexico' — corrected to match. Did not find the NRHP nomination PDF text itself (only the NPGallery metadata page), so architectural/material description beyond NHLR's dimensions is thinner than ideal. No source found addressing current (2026) staffing beyond the 2007 volunteer visit report, which found it unstaffed with water damage and a stalled restoration contract; NHLR's current page description separately calls the lookout 'still in active use' as a visitor destination, which is about recreational use rather than fire-watch staffing and does not contradict the 2007 report.

The register and the FFLA 2020 report agree on the 1952 station. The 1934 cupola appears only in the NHLR text. No staffing, fire or rental listing was found; the 2020 report does not mark the lookout for the cabin rental program. Road details come from a travel guide, not a Forest Service page, so the closure dates (Oct 1 to May 15) should be checked before anyone relies on them. drive_up true refers to the summit road, which the guide describes as seasonal and 4x4-only. The record's built 1952 is right for the present station and is left unchanged; no correction filed. Not verified: current condition, and whether the cab is open to visitors.

Staffing start is disputed. The register says first staffed in 1918 by the Whitesides; the Cibola Citizen says newspapers suggest informal lookout work around 1905 to 1910 and that Lucy took the post after David's death in March 1919. The story reports both. The 1920 item names the Manzano National Forest, while the register names the Cibola National Forest. No source describes the lookout's design, what remains at the site, or whether the site is open, so facts.access and facts.design are omitted. The brief's record (gone, tower, coordinates, elevation, 1918 and 1975 dates) matches the register; no corrections proposed. The Cibola Citizen article says it revises a July 2025 feature, and its own date is not stated in the text read.

Register and the 2020 NM chapter report agree on design, 1934 erection, 1984 remodel and no staffing. Open point: the 1934 newspaper item (quoted on Weebly) refers to the lookout in April 1934; the story says a lookout was in use that spring and does not claim an earlier structure. Not verified: current staffing (NHLR staffing line is undated; 2020 report is the latest source read), access route, and whether Negrito is listed for rent. The Weebly page's access text was not read, and the Divide Trail #15 page does not mention this lookout, so no trailhead is given. The record's 1984 note says the remodel cost it National Register eligibility; the 2020 report attributes ineligibility to loss of integrity, which the remodel plausibly caused, but the report does not name the remodel as the cause, so no correction is proposed. Record coordinates and elevation match the Register. No photos added.

Thin: the register page is the only history source found, and the FFLA list supplies the standing status. Nothing found on the lookout after 1960 except its registration in 1999 and the standing listing. Searches for tribal or BIA records returned nothing usable. Archuleta Mesa attracts unreliable online material (some tying it to unrelated claims); none is used. The record's other_names 'Osborn (Arachal)' is confirmed by the FFLA list. The record's material 'wood' (material_from 'design') does not appear in the register text read, so it is not supported here; a human should check it. The register does not explain the name Osborne. Do not confuse it with the Osborne firefinder described in Zinn's Santa Fe history, which is an instrument and not this lookout.

Standing status rests on the undated state index and a 2012 caption; no 2025-26 source found. Access and staffing today are unknown, so no access key. A WebSearch lead (a July 2020 hiker report, about 2.5 miles round trip via NM-53 and Forest Roads 50 and 187) could not be fetched, so it is not used. The register's 14x4 cab figure may be a typo, but the story reports it as stated.

Thin record. The FFLA list is undated and gives no builder, build date, height, design or NHLR number. The only history is a 1963 map description on Pastmaps, a secondary site, not the map itself. The reservation status comes from that 1963 description alone; confirm current land status and access rules before any visit. No photos found. Staffing, fire history and current condition are unknown. Access is left out of facts because no current source gives it. Story now uses the description's wording (reservation lands dominate the survey), hedges the tribal-access point, and drops the NHLR expansion, which the list does not define.

Access not established: no source read says whether the cabin is open to visitors, so no visit or climbing advice is given. NHLR links a 2001 Albuquerque Journal article that returned 404 and was not used. The Taos News article is undated in my copy. Its first fetch returned 429 and a retry succeeded. The staffing as_of is undated because the NHLR description carries no date. No photos added (no image URLs read).

Built year 1929 is consistent across Wikipedia, the NRHP record (significant year) and the Weebly history page. The NRHP listing conflicts: Wikipedia and NPGallery say the tower was listed January 28, 1988, but the 2020 NM chapter report says the 1988 review found the tower not eligible because of the 1965 stairs and that the listed property was the 1925 Observer's Cabin. The brief's 1988 nrhp_listed event is kept with that conflict noted; an editor with the NRHP nomination PDF (npgallery asset 273946c3...) could settle it, but that PDF was not retrievable from the cache. Staffing: only two newspaper-based notices (1957, 1974) found; no current staffing or climbing status found. Access is set to restricted because the only documented route is a 12-mile wilderness trail, not because a closure was found. The Weebly page is a hobbyist site quoting USFS and newspaper sources; treat its details as secondary. Verification pass 2026-10-08: the story's 'steel frame' was corrected to 'steel tower' to match the sources; the 1925 Observer's Cabin wording was confirmed in the 2020 report.

Build-year conflict: Living New Deal guesses a 1933 CCC origin but the NRHP nomination and NHLR both say 1940; the story follows 1940 and flags the disagreement rather than proposing a correction, since no source firmly contradicts the record. The Trinity-detonation anecdote rests solely on ranger Herbert Lee Traylor's own 1983 memoir, relayed by Wikipedia with no independent corroboration found; included but clearly flagged as single-source. Could not fetch the 2016 Ruidoso News NRHP article (fetch tool blocked ruidosonews.com) or an NRHP nomination PDF on npgallery.nps.gov; a human with better access to those could firm up the 1933-vs-1940 question and current staffing status. No corrections proposed to the tower record: name, location, height, agency and built year all match NHLR, Wikipedia and Wikidata.

History is well sourced (register, 2020 report, 1967 newspapers). Present rental and access status is unverified: the 2020 report describes a planned cabin rental program, and two searches found no listing for this lookout. The Weed and Wofford results are other towers and were not used. The brief's access 'public' is unsupported; see corrections.

No source read gives staffing, current condition or public access, so the story says so and gives no visit advice. The 2013 vandalism item has no detail. The CR report caption credits a photo to Dave Lorenz, but no image URL was read, so no photo added. The older NHLR page (Lookout.aspx?id=685) returned 500 and was not used.

No staffing history, fire record or construction detail beyond the 1934 date was found. Two searches turned up only other towers (Mt Withington, Grassy, El Caso). Access level omitted: sources say trail access only, and no closure or permission notice was found. The brief's record matches the sources; no corrections proposed.

The NHLR page gives the build and cab history; the Forest Service trail page gives the access details. Do not confuse this with the Arizona Signal Peak Lookout on the Tonto National Forest, which search results also returned. An FFLA Facebook post titled 'First report! The Signal Peak...' reportedly mentions a call-in during the Skate fire, but the page would not load beyond its title, so no fire claim is made; this is a lead for the editor. Staffing and fire history were not found. height_m 9.1 converts the register's 30-foot height and may not equal the cab-floor height. Not verified: current condition, and whether the tower is closed to climbing.

Two searches returned only other Otero County towers (Bluewater, Weed, Monjeau and similar), which are not used. No NGS datasheet for Silver was found; the station ID would need a lookup. The Forest Lookouts Silver page has no body text beyond its header, so it gives only the agency label. The NM list gives the status, county and coordinates only. The story stays short because no dated or narrative source was reachable.

Build date (1931) comes only from the register. The 1957 item's wording implies an older station, so check Lincoln NF or New Mexico records before relying on it. Removal date not found; the Forest Lookouts 'Removed' heading has no details. No source found on the site today or on public access. The 1959 item reports an announced rename only; the register lists both names. The register's 'Administered by' field reads 'U.s. Forest Service' (casing as printed), which matches the 1959 item; this JSON uses the standard 'U.S.' spelling. The story does not name the agency. Two search results (a tribal fire crew article and Monjeau Lookout) were not used.

Access is marked restricted as an editorial judgement: the register calls it an unstaffed communications site and no current visitor rules were found; the only approach description is a 2016 hike notice. The brief's access 'unknown' and staffing gap are filled from the 2020 report; there is no staffing source after 2020. The brief's height is not in any source read, so none is given. The Zinn history PDF cited in the register (fs.usda.gov fseprd542352.pdf) returned HTTP 404 and was not used. No photos added.

Brief's access value of 'permission' is not supported by the NHLR page or the other pages read, so no access key was written rather than guessing. Brief's agency field repeats the NHLR 'Administered by' value, which is a reservation rather than an agency; BIA is the listed cooperator. Brief's elevation of 2690.5 m matches NHLR's 2,690 m. Single substantive source. A NOAA tree-ring fire dataset titled 'Guiterman fire data from Tohatchi Lookout' turned up in search but was not read and is not used. Fact-check 2026-10-08: added the McKinley County and cooperator evidence the story cites; the BIA advice in the story now rests on the register's cooperator line.

Only the NHLR entry and the FFLA New Mexico list give usable facts; no history, staffing, fire or fate record was found, so the story is thin. Brief record says access 'permission' and that Tohnitsha and Washington Pass share a register number; neither is supported: no fetched page states an access rule, and both sites give US 434 for Tohnitsha and US 435 for Washington Pass. Access left out of facts. Leads not cited (search snippet only, not fetched): a firelookout.org New Mexico table row seems to list International Derrick, 1936 and 82.6 ft; worth fetching to check the 82.6 vs 82.9 ft gap. The Forest Lookouts Weebly page for Tohnitsha holds only navigation text.

Only the NHLR entry and the FFLA New Mexico list give usable facts; no history, staffing, fire or fate record was found, so the story is thin. Brief record says Washington Pass and Tohnitsha share a register number; the sources give US 435 and US 434, so that conflict note looks wrong. Brief access 'permission' is not supported by a fetched page and was left out of facts. Search snippets (not fetched, not cited): a 2024 Navajo guide listing a Washington Pass lookout on the Chuska route, and Narbona Pass name history. A search-returned npgallery PDF was a Washington State (Chelan Butte) nomination and was not used.

No information found on staffing history, notable fires, or public rental/visitation program for Weed Lookout specifically. NRHP nomination PDF (npgallery 87002487) not opened this pass; could add staffing/fire detail if read.

Two sources only. Standing status rests on the FFLA New Mexico list; the register does not state current condition. The register's height figure is 60 feet, converted to 18.3 m for height_m; it may be the tower height rather than cab floor height. Record coordinates (36.867458, -107.06948) sit about 50 m from the FFLA point (36.86785, -107.06985); not treated as an error. Record design and height were null and are now filled from the register. Access is a judgment from the reservation location and the BIA administrator field; no visitor information was found. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 2 page reads (NHLR, FFLA list).

Build date, builder and staffing appear in no source read; NHLR says construction date and use status are unknown. The 1950 fire rests on one passage quoting the Clovis News Journal on a Western Lookouts page; the newspaper original was not checked. NHLR names the New Mexico Forestry Division as administrator while RMEF says the land is state trust land under the State Lands Office; both are sourced and are not treated as a conflict. Record coordinates and elevation (2681.6 m) match NHLR (2,682 m) and the FFLA list. Record access 'unknown' can be replaced with the restricted level above after a human check. No corrections proposed.

One search returned Atole, Wells, Cedar Springs and other Rio Arriba towers, none tied to Wirt; none used. A search snippet linked Atole to Jicarilla Apache land, but that is a different tower and is unverified, so it is not used for Wirt. Land status, build date, and staffing are open; a Carson National Forest or Jicarilla records check would be the next step.

Current status rests on a Forest Service page last updated Feb 19, 2025; the cabin rental opening was not confirmed. The brief's access value was corrected from public to restricted. The MPS nomination (NRHP 64000046) and a recreation.gov listing were not read. No notable fire at this site was found in the sources read.

Built year is unresolved: the register says 1962 and UTV Guide says 1964. The Review-Journal article ('It's lonely at the top for Nevada's last fire lookout') returned HTTP 500 on every fetch attempt, so it is not used; it is likely the best source for staffing history and should be retried. A Facebook post by Eastern Nevada Interagency Fire repeats 1964, but Facebook was not readable, so it is not cited. No fire history or rebuild information was found in readable sources, so the story has no fire section. The access level is omitted because no source says whether visitors may enter the cab. Staffing as_of is undated because UTV Guide shows no publication date. Elevation (2,265 m per register) and coordinates match the brief; the FFLA listing gives longitude -114.46730, a small difference from the register's -114.468050.

The firelookout.org list and the SummitPost plateau guide describe the same McClellan Peak area, but the guide never names the lookout, so tying the plateau's cell towers to the lookout site is an inference. No source describes remains or current access. The 1931 and 1932 items say Virginia range; the 1951 item says Washoe range. Staffing comes from newspaper items, so a gap between named lookouts is not evidence the tower stood empty.

Brief said the lookout was built by the Tahoe NF; the 1942 articles credit the Mono forest and the Grazing Service, so the builder is disputed. The removal date is unknown. The radio sites on the summit come from Wikipedia only. No photos found.

Only one substantive source exists (the NHLR register page, cached locally); the FFLA list just repeats the same register number without added detail. No NRHP nomination, BLM press material, newspaper coverage, or trail/visit guide turned up in three web searches. Two oddities worth a human look: (1) the NHLR page says the lookout is 'administered by' and 'cooperated' with the Bureau of Land Management, yet Sheldon National Wildlife Refuge is normally a US Fish & Wildlife Service property — I found no independent source to confirm or correct this, so left the tower record's agency field as-is rather than guess. (2) FFLA's coordinates (41.83586, -119.62492) sit about 1.7 km from NHLR's (41.850064, -119.63278) despite citing the same register number US 301/NV 2 — already captured in the tower record's own conflicts field; no third source to break the tie, so no correction proposed here.

Source [2] (westlookouts.weebly.com) is an amateur compilation site, apparently drawn from old newspaper clippings; its specific names (Buck Wheeler, Jim Cain, A.K. Bourne, Mrs. T.C. Clifton) and fire dates (1936, 1941) could not be cross-checked against a primary source and should be verified against Nevada newspaper archives if this page gets more scrutiny. The build year (1931 start vs. NHLR's 1932 completion) is not a real conflict - both describe the same winter 1931-32 construction. On fact-checking, the 1964/1970 staffing detail was also not a real cross-source conflict: 'closed for the season' in 1964 (source 2) describes a routine seasonal closure, not an end date, and source 3 (Tahoe Daily Tribune) independently corroborates staffing continuing into the 1970s - the story previously framed this as 'sources disagree,' which overstated it, and has been corrected. Also corrected on fact-check: the NRHP-eligibility-in-1997 claim was mis-cited to sources 1/3, which don't contain it; it is only in source 4 (South Tahoe Now), and has been re-cited there. The source 3 article (Tahoe Daily Tribune) is itself dated December 19, 2001, not current - it names a 'National Trust for Historic Preservation' registry listing, a different, private-nonprofit designation from NRHP eligibility; the story does not currently mention that National Trust listing. 'Last Forest Service lookout built in the state' was also corrected to 'remaining in the state,' since NHLR's source text says 'the last U.S. Forest Service lookout in Nevada' (i.e., the only one left), not that it was the last one constructed. The 2013 relocation-to-White-Hill proposal's outcome is unknown; could not find any later source confirming or denying the move happened, so current physical location/status is uncertain despite the tower record's 'standing' status. A 2001 Las Vegas Sun piece and a 2013 Carson Now piece look relevant but returned paywall/403 errors and were not used.

Core facts agree across NHLR, the NYSFFLA Southern Tier list and the Eastern lookouts site: 1950 Aermotor LS40 erected by the Conservation Department, officially closed 1971, 1973 auction, now on private land and closed to the public. Open items for a human: (1) the observer's cabin date is disputed. The 1941-model cabin is said to date from 1950, but the 1964 survey description quoted by the Eastern site says there was no cabin at the top and that one was added later; the story reports both and does not pick a side. (2) Record coordinates (FFLA 42.04976, -78.01363) and NHLR (42.054757, -78.014137) are 557 m apart, as the record's own conflict note says; no source here settles which point is the tower. (3) The 80 ft figure is overall height; the sources do not give height to the cab floor, so height_m is left unset. (4) The record's agency 'Private Owner' matches NHLR; the Conservation Department built the tower but is not the current administrator. (5) The current landowner is a private individual and is deliberately not named. (6) Visit or access after 2002 is not documented; access is recorded as private/closed on the strength of NHLR and NYSFFLA.

Built 1921, closed 1970 and removed 1977 are well supported. Record height 15.2 m conflicts with 22 ft in most sources; see corrections. Access changed from unknown to public (summit trail on state land). No source describes whether the tower footings survive; the 1942 survey point sat at the centre of the tower base. The 2022 blog says the memorial dates Rice to 1915-1923, which conflicts with the 1922 newspaper.

Unresolved: cost ($300 in the register vs $530 in the group chronology) and height (35 ft vs 40 ft in Wikipedia) disagree; the story reports both and the record keeps the register cost in the event note. The register's elevation (2,500 ft, 762 m) is for the lookout site; mountain heights in other sources differ, but those came from search snippets that were not read, so they are not used. The 2018 visit notes glass not intact; the current condition of the cab and any climbing rules are unverified. Andy Arthur's trail map page returned 403; the Daily Gazette centennial article and the 2003 Azure Mountain News PDF were not read. Brief record's events listed only the 2003 registration; the 1914, 1918, 1978, 2001 and 2002 events were added from sources 1 and 2. A July 5, 2007 register visit report says the tower is currently open for general public use; that is too old to treat as current, so the story does not rely on it.

Built dates agree across the three sources (1887 club tower, 1905 wooden replacement, 1919 first steel tower, 1930 present tower) once the NHLR, state guide and Wikipedia are read together. Wikipedia's section heading dates the club's establishment 1885-1909 but its text says 1887; the story uses 1887. Height differs (47 vs 47 1/2 ft). The reopening year is not stated in the Wikipedia text read, so no restoration year is recorded. The access and staffing evidence is from a 2017 NHLR visit report, so current status should be checked. The state guide is a multi-column PDF; its quotes were taken from single lines. Wikipedia's coordinates (42.06972, -74.57444) differ from the record's (42.045395, -74.594604), which matches NHLR; left unchanged. A later NHLR visit report says the tower is open Friday to Sunday, but it is undated in the text read, so it was not used.

Sources agree on the 1948 build, 1959 closure and 1960 removal (register) and the 'Removed' status (Long Island page). The Long Island page's paragraph that says a tower was 'dismantled and removed in 1960 by a local demolition contractor' sits under the Kings Park and other tower entries, not Bay Shore, so it was not used. The 80-foot figure is the tower height from the Long Island page; no source gives a cab-floor height, so no height_m was recorded. The register calls the site Bayshore, the Long Island page Bay Shore (community Brentwood). The record's coordinates were not checked against a map. Ownership: the Long Island page says DOT property at the time; the register says privately held now. No photos found.

The tower's history is well documented in the NHLR detail page, which the record cites. The planned NHLR history PDF (2966), chapter PDFs (2962, 2963) and beebehill.info all failed (404 or DNS), so their content is not used. Relocation year conflicts: NHLR gives November 1963 for the move to Beebe Hill and Wikipedia gives 1964; a web search summary also mentioned a 1932 versus 1933 Washburn re-erection and a 1988 end-of-season closure with a 1989 official closure, but those came from search snippets and were not read on a fetched page, so they are not in the story. Current status is the main open question: Wikipedia (late 2024, unsafe) versus NYSDEC page (open to the public) and NHLR (restored 2025). Verify on site or with NYSDEC before any climb. Access level is public for hiking the forest; climbability of the tower itself is not established and is left unset. The NHLR notes the tower was Aermotor LS-40 60-foot as first erected, not necessarily its current height.

Build history is consistent across sources only at the level of a 1912 station with a wooden tower and a 1917 steel tower. NHLR lists 1917 as the build year, which the brief also uses; Wikipedia and the Explorer say 1917 replaced a 1912 wooden tower. Closure date conflicts: NHLR says closed 1988; Wikipedia says out of service 1988 and officially closed early 1989; Stream & Steeple agrees with Wikipedia. Ownership conflicts: NHLR says administered by NYSDEC and the Explorer places it in the Hammond Pond Wild Forest, but Stream & Steeple says private land. Trail length conflicts (0.3 vs 0.4 mile). Access is set to public for the site only; no source confirms that climbing the tower is permitted, and the story advises treating it as closed. Stream & Steeple lists Belfry in an ADK Fire Tower Challenge that requires climbing fire tower summits; that is not a state opening. Staffing history rests on the Explorer's 'until 1988' and the 2017 visit report; the Podskoch book and the Landmarks of Moriah post were not reachable. andyarthur.org pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The height is converted from 47 feet. Verification pass 2026-10-08: the story's 'site is open to the public' wording was changed to the tower being accessible, as Stream & Steeple states; the 'no source says climbers' sentence was corrected for the challenge text; 'cab glass broken' was changed to 'not intact' to match the form.

Three independent sources agree on the 1934 CCC build, the 1988 end of fire watch, the early-1989 closure and the September 13, 2021 reopening. The NHLR page gives no build year, so 1934 comes from the DEC release and Wikipedia. The 1935 first-staffing date rests on Wikipedia alone. The DEC release says the tower was open for recreation after the upgrades; access is recorded as public, climbable true, on that basis. Current staffing is not documented after the 2017 NHLR visit (not staffed). An andyarthur.org page gives an early-fall 1934 construction date, but it could not be fetched, so it is not used. The DEC release's sentence on a Forest Service chapter agreement was cut off in the cache and is not used. Height is 59 ft 3 in per Wikipedia (18.06 m). The NHLR visit report predates the 2021 work, so its condition findings are historical. Verification pass 2026-10-08: the story's visitor-rules sentence had no support in the DEC release and was replaced with the DEC's sunrise-to-sunset hours; the 1,960 ft figure is from the NHLR and DEC, and Wikipedia's 1,962 ft is named in the story; 'no one had a key' was corrected to the report's 'we had no key'.

The brief dated the build to 1918. Sources show a wooden lookout in 1911 that the 1918 steel tower replaced, so both are listed. Three different closure years (1988, 1989, 1990) are reported as found; a DEC or NYS Archives record would settle them. NHLR says the tower is closed and fenced; do not encourage climbing. The NYS Archives has 1918 photos of fire observer William C. Noble at Black Mountain (digitalcollections.archives.nysed.gov), seen only in search results and not used. The andyarthur.org pages returned 403 and were not read. No NRHP listing was found. Revised on fact-check 2026-10-08: the 80-ft total is now reported with the caveat that 35 ft plus 39 ft is 74 ft, and the story does not resolve it; 'still stands' is now footnoted to the present-tense Wikipedia text; sentences reworded where they copied source wording.

Brief status_note says the cab is gone (FFLA). Not verified: the NHLR 2007 visit report says there is no roof and does not mention the cab, and the FFLA asterisk footnote was not read, so the cab claim is left out of the story. Wikipedia's Black Rock Forest article also mentions an observation tower on the 1,402-foot Black Rock peak; it is not established that this is the NHLR tower (398 ft elevation), so it is not used. Searches found no construction or Stillman-era records for this tower.

Dates are solid: the 1911 wooden tower and 1917 steel tower (NHLR, brochure, Wikipedia), 1990 closure, 1994 rehabilitation, 1995 NHLR registration, and 2001 NRHP listing. Current status rests on an undated Fire Tower Challenge brochure and a commercial listing, so re-check opening status and the summer steward programme before relying on it. The brochure layout mixes several towers, so only its single-line statements are quoted. The NHLR 2018 visit report notes plans to repaint and redeck in 2018; the outcome was not found. The NRHP nomination PDF is not digitized (NPGallery says so), so no nomination text was used. The Blue Mountain Fire Observation Station Wikipedia entry gives a 1975 observer cabin and 1960s radar remains; not used. No photos were added.

Brief claims not found in any page read, so left out: the Davanna LLC inventory on 25 Aug 2020; the 2023 Delaware County permit-holder role; the Excelsior Towers re-erection and 17 Oct 2024 visibility date; the 4 January 2025 opening day. Not verified: whether the tower can be climbed outside steward days. No photos added.

Core facts (1933 build, private owner Cedar Heights Timber LLC, September 2, 2023 opening, trail details) are confirmed by two or three sources each. Not confirmed: the brief's 2022 restoration details (stairs, roof, painting by August 2022), which the town notice does not support; a correction is proposed above. The Adirondack Almanack and Wikipedia results were seen only as search snippets and are not cited.

Height disagrees: the Long Island list says 60 ft, the January 1932 report says 70 ft, so facts.height_m is omitted. No corrections proposed.

The build year is not given beyond 'after 1932' in the register, so no built event is recorded. Removal year disagrees: the register's south page says 1956 with the steel tower; the Long Island list says 1955 or 56; the register's north page says 1955 for the steel tower. Build dates (1911 wood, 1917 steel) and the 1925 cabin are well supported. Closing year conflicts (1970 vs 1971). Height 15 m comes from Wikipedia, which cites the NYSFFLA searchable list (not read); verify against that list before publishing. Brief's 1924 build and 1970 closure are confirmed. Only one NHLR/FFLOS page was searched for Chapin Hill.

Height is given as 60 feet in both sources; 18.3 m is converted from feet. Build year: NHLR says 1950; the October 1950 Post-Star report says the tower had just shipped and was in temporary storage; the April 1951 Times Record says it was being built. The story reports this rather than choosing; the NHLR 1950 date is kept in events. Height: 80 ft (NHLR and 1950 report) vs 81 ft (1951 paper). Status label: the FFLA New York list shows this site with status 'Private' rather than 'Standing'; NHLR describes it as still standing and in NYSDEC use, so the record's 'standing' is kept, but a human should check the FFLA label. Observer names come from a state roster and a 1951 paper; no residences are given. The private property where the tower was stored in 1950 is not named. Radio users: the roster says 'several agencies'; the story uses NHLR for today's NYSDEC use. No corrections proposed.

The brief's Starr PDF link (nhlr.org/nhlr.org/media/...) returns 404; the working URL is nhlr.org/media/2967/... and is used here. The brief's 2008 relocation is contradicted by the Starr article and the Saratogian and is corrected to 2010. A web search snippet for Wikipedia's Cornell Hill page says summer 2008; that page was not read and is not cited. The brief's 2024 relocation is confirmed by the October 2024 newsletter and the 2024 Adirondack Explorer piece. The exact move date is not given. The newsletter's 'about 30 years ago' refers to the Grangers rescuing the cab from scrap, not the move. The trip report page shows no year, only 'Oct 1', so its date is unverified. Height: 35 ft in four sources, 40 ft in the 1919 Post-Star quote; keep 10.7 m. The trip report's 1973 passage dates an observer's two fires to 'the weekend of November 27th' in a North Creek News-Enterprise item dated November 1, 1973. That date is internally inconsistent, so it was not used. The Explorer photo caption mentions a 1982 photo by Ed Burke; no image URL was retrieved. No source describes the summit today. The access level stays unknown.

The original tower is gone; the brief's status 'gone' is right, but a restoration (described by the register and project as a restoration, with steel sections going up in 2026) is under construction and not open, so access is set to closed and the brief's 'permission' is proposed as a correction. Removal date conflicts inside the register (1980 vs around 1982) and the elevation/height figures disagree across sources; both are left open in the story. The 2023 board-funding line is a single newsletter item; the county's own record was not read. No photos found; a future check of crmfiretower.org after the tower opens should confirm access and any visitor rules. Used 0 WebSearch calls and about 8 page reads.

The brief's 1979 removal date is supported by Wikipedia and the Adirondack Explorer. The brief's 'non-conforming structure' reason does not appear in any source read (Forest Lookouts page, 2022 newsletter, Wikipedia, Explorer), so the story omits it; verify or drop it from the record. Staffing evidence is limited to 1928. Sources disagree on Wild Forest size and summit height (Explorer 3,305 ft; Wikipedia 3,317 ft); neither is used. No fire events were found. No source describes what remains of the tower footings or the 1922 cabin on the summit. The Explorer write-up is a hike account, not an agency page; the access level 'public' rests on the state-maintained route and Forest Preserve setting it describes.

Brief's NRHP 11000253 confirmed by Wikipedia (No. 11000253). The register's 'owned by the State Police' note is undated and superseded by the 2012 handover reported in the Almanack. Permission to climb is not stated outright; climbable true is inferred from the 2025 repair of all 80 steps and the hiking-destination description, so confirm with Grafton Lakes State Park. The register's 2016 and 2017 visit reports are old and not used for current condition. The register's 2018 playscape tower and the Helen Ellett observer anecdotes are not used. The NRHP nomination PDF was not read.

Brief's coordinates conflict (Forest Fire Lookout Association 40.8105, -73.346333 vs the Forest Lookouts list) was not verified in the pages read, so the story does not mention it. The Bill Starr fire tower list (NHLR PDF) was seen only as a search snippet and is not cited.

Brief status 'gone' confirmed. No source describes what remains at the site or whether it is open; no access level recorded. The 1933 appointment year is inferred from the June 22, 1933 article date. A fall 2026 library hike listing mentions a possible walk to the former tower site, but both fetch tools got 403 and it is not used. A Facebook snippet places the hill in Southampton; unverified, not used. Brief elevation (75 m) matches the register. No corrections to the brief.

Staffing, closure and 1940 build are consistent across NHLR, nysffla and Wikipedia. Elevation differs slightly (NHLR 2,108 ft; Wikipedia 2,106 ft); the record's 642.5 m is kept and not put in facts. The NHLR photo credit (Laurie Rankin, 2012) has no image URL, so no photo added. Not verified: the current owner or use of the radio equipment, and whether any recent visit or closure record exists. andyarthur.org returned HTTP 403 in the cache and was not used. The NYSDEC fire-towers page was not read. The Oct. 14, 2025 ribbon cutting is only reported as scheduled; no post-event source was read, so the reopening is not confirmed. Climbing permission is not stated outright, so the visit fields stay with trail details only. Brief's record height of 20.0 m appears to be an error (60 ft = 18.3 m). Solid on the 1909 wooden tower, 1918 steel tower, 1919 blowdown and 1920 rebuild (Register, a state report quoted on Forest Lookouts, and the 2020 NYSFFLA newsletter agree). Closure year is disputed: Register says 1988, Wikipedia says lookout work ended after the 1988 season and official closure was early 1989. The record's note that the tower carried State Police radio equipment for years is not supported by any source read: the Warren County document shows the summit as a county transmitter/receiver site but does not say State Police use the Gore site. The record's note that hikers still visit the site is also unsupported; the Register says the tower is closed to visitors, so the story does not say hikers visit. Wikipedia says the 1918 replacement was made by the Civilian Conservation Corps, which was not founded until 1933, so that claim is not used. The record's height_m 5.5 is the 1909 wooden tower (see corrections). The FLO New York list places the tower at -74.04878, about 3.6 km west of the Register and record coordinates (-74.00397), which match the Register's coordinates; the record coordinates were left as they are. No photos added: the Register's June 26, 2020 photo is credited to Laurie Rankin but its licence is not stated.

Build year: the brief had none. The 1930 date rests on the Middletown Times Herald (Aug 1930) and the 1930 state annual report, both quoted on the Pocatello Mountain page of Forest Lookouts, plus the NHLR's statement that the tower was first erected on Pocotello Mountain. A Facebook group post dated the Pocatello tower 1930 but the page could not be read, so it is not cited. Access 'unknown' in the brief is replaced by 'restricted' from Bob Spear's undated Register history notes (gate and private-land remarks), which may be out of date. The April 2021 newsletter's 'Roosa Gap' paragraph about reopening refers to a different tower and is not applied to Graham.

The build date conflicts: register and Starr say construction ran late 1916 to early 1917 (story uses this), while Wikipedia gives 1917 and reports a plaque saying the original wood tower dates to 1916 and the current steel tower to 1920. The plaque was not read directly, only through Wikipedia. Access and staffing rest on 2017 visit reports and a 2017 Explorer article; no 2026 source was found, so current access and whether a steward is present now need confirming before any visit guidance. height_m 12.2 is converted from the register's 40 ft. Not used: andyarthur.org (both pages returned 403); hadleymtfiretower.org (the committee's site returned no text through fetch_text, so its history was not verified; a search snippet mentioned 1903 to 1915 fires and an Ohmer origin, which are unverified and left out); Facebook and Grokipedia search snippets. The brief has no height. Wikipedia's Shawangunk Ridge article gives the 1919 tower as 47 ft; no other source read gives a height, so the story gives none. Brief build year 1919 confirmed. The start of fire watch is 1909 (NHLR) or 1910 (Friends via Explorer). Staffing records conflict across NHLR visits. Built year and height rest on the Starr list and 1950-51 press clippings, which disagree on dates and height; both are reported in the story. Brief's April 2017 closure and 2022 closure are not supported: earliest closure found is the NHLR visit of January 21, 2018; fenced off by November 2021 per Hike the Hudson Valley. Brief status 'gone' confirmed. Heights disagree across five sources (75 to 80 ft), so no height_m is recorded; the story reports the spread. The brief had no build year; 1925 is added with the 1926 operating-year conflict noted. A separate record, us-ny-kempshall-mountain-at-adirondack-history-museum, already covers the exhibit tower; this story covers the original mountain and points to the museum. Removal date conflicts (1977 vs 1980s) and the mountain's direction from Long Lake conflict; see resolved_conflicts. The 1931 build date is consistent across four sources. The us-ny-mount-morris record merges two towers. The Manhattan Mount Morris watchtower in Harlem (Marcus Garvey Park) has its own record, us-ny-harlem-fire-watchtower. The 2019 restored event and the 'Mount Morris Fire Watchtower, Harlem' other name belong to that tower. The nysffla_projects row for the Harlem tower carries the Franklin County coordinates (44.15976, -74.47517) because it was matched to this record by name; fix the matching as well as this record. The 22-foot (6.7 m) height and 1919 completion are consistent across Wikipedia and Forest Lookouts. Ownership and current condition remain unresolved: a state or town records check, or a recent site report, would settle them. Access is recorded as closed, so do not encourage a climb. No new photos were added.

The 1940 build, 1988 end of service and 1989 closure agree across sources. The record's 'ownership: state' conflicts with the NHLR's statement that the Town of Kent owns the tower, so a correction is proposed. The record's 408.4 m elevation is not supported by the sources read; the 388 m mountain figure is proposed. Staffing and the 'open to the public' status come from undated sources and should be checked before a visit. The Town of Kent guide's 'recently restored' wording is undated. The 2009 NYSAC award and the Kent Wikipedia article's 'tallest remaining fire tower' claim were seen only in search snippets and are not used. No new photos were added.

Current condition and public access are unconfirmed. Wikipedia is the main source and cites no update after its restoration call. The marker page is about the Summit tower restoration; only its 1928 caption is cited. An online hiker post (Hike WNY group) says the stairs were removed and the tower is closed off, but we could not read it, so it is not used. Wikipedia gives 2,142 ft in the infobox and 2,144 ft in the text; elevation is not used. Wikipedia spells the park name Alleghany once; the park itself uses Allegany.

Fact-check 2026-10-09: the towers6 entry for New Boston names no fires and no named observers, which is the basis for the story's statement that none were found. Build year conflict, unresolved: the NYSFFLA list gives 1950 for an 80-foot Aermotor LS40 at New Boston. A Waymarking listing that appeared only in search results says 1914 on Tug Hill; the page body could not be read, so it is not used. Reopening conflict, unresolved: the 2004 annual report says the tower was open after a 2004 grand opening, while the NYSFFLA list says it was restored and reopened in 2016; no source explains the gap. A 2016 Spectrum News item seen only as a search snippet calls the zoo tower the old Lowville tower; DEC and the chapter both say New Boston, so that snippet is treated as a mislabel and was not used. The record's 'moved 1999' is kept. The record's original New Boston entry (us-ny-new-boston) is Lewis County and matches DEC. Current climbing rules at the zoo were not found. Used 2 WebSearch and about 6 page reads plus cached local pages; the 2016 annual report was read earlier for another tower.

The original site and the moved upper section are both covered, because the record's status is relocated. Sources disagree on height (75, about 80, 90 feet) and on the stair date (1945 in a 2019 post quoted by the newsletter, around 1960 in Wikipedia); the record carries no height. The 'shortened to 25 feet' figure comes from a 2018 visit account by Bill Hill, quoted in the newsletter, and is reported as a visitor's claim. No access level is recorded for the original site: the DEC page covers only Lowville, and the newsletter describes a campsite near the old site without stating rules. The sibling record us-ny-number-four-at-lowville-demonstration-forest covers the Lowville tower itself.

Height is disputed (75 ft in a 2018 reader quote and Wikipedia, about 80 ft in 1928 newspapers, 90 ft on the DEC page), so no height_m is set. Stair change conflicts: 1945 per Knauf via the 2023 newsletter, about 1960 per Wikipedia. The Aermotor LX25 model and the 1958 land transfer rest on Wikipedia alone. Date of the upper section's move to Lowville not found, so no relocated event with a year. The DEC page gives no opening hours; access uses the DEC invitation to climb. Andy Arthur's page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Facebook search snippets (Tug Hill Commission, FFLA NYS group) were seen only as search results and are not cited. Reads used: 6 (newsletter PDF, Andy Arthur 403, cached eastern page, cached FFLA NY list, DEC page, Wikipedia); one fallback web search.

Solid on the 1933 derrick tower, its origin in Orangeburg, South Carolina, the 2007 move and the NHLR visit-report details (NHLR, blog and the FFLA list agree). Disagreements left open in the story: removal of the 1942 wartime tower is 2000 in the Register but 2006 in the blog and Wikipedia; the Register says moved in 2007 while the blog says constructed that summer; the Register calls the wartime tower a 40-foot wooden tower and Wikipedia calls it an enclosed tower. Record's events 2019 and 2021 ('restored', graffiti painted out) were not verified: no source in the cache or read for those years, so they are not in the research events. The 2023 newsletter describes vandalism and a planned paint-over; it does not clearly confirm the paint-over was completed, so the event is worded as the visit finding. Record's 2007 'relocated' event was missing its year; 2007 is set from the Register. Climbability is inferred from the NHLR's description of an open overlook with stairs OK in the 2018 visit report; no current staffing source (the Register's staffing answer reads 'No Response'). A search summary named a contractor and a 79-foot replacement tower; this was not verified on any page read and is not used. No photos added: the Register's photo is credited to Homer Staley with no licence stated.

Built year is disputed (register 1917 vs DEC 1927, with the tower at its present location since 1950 per DEC). The 1971 closing year comes only from the register; a search snippet pointed to a 1988 closure at catskillsvisitorcenter.org, but that page returned HTTP 403 and was not used. andyarthur.org (403), catskillcenter.org (404), and a firetower.org page (404) could not be read. Public access is by a 5-6 mile hike (DEC). Vehicle access by permit (CP-3) was a draft-plan proposal that the FFLA opposed in a letter dated December 15, 2016 to NYSDEC. The register's 'Staffed? No' refers to Forest Service staffing; the volunteer weekend presence is from the register text. Fact-check 2026-10-08: 'small' cab and 'hotel' were removed as unsupported; the story now gives the register's 7 by 7 foot cab.

Restoration year rests on the NHLR alone (2003). A WebSearch summary mentioned 2004 and a 2005 Friends group, but no fetched page confirmed them, so they are not used. andyarthur.org returned HTTP 403 and was not used. The brief's elevation of 828.1 m matches the NHLR figure (2,717 ft); Wikipedia gives the summit as 2,786 ft (849 m), so elevation was not added to facts. The NHLR visit report carries no date. Roster quotes were checked against the cached PDF text. Observer names are not used in the story.

Built and first-observer facts rest on two 1940-1941 newspaper items quoted by Forest Lookouts; no later primary source found. The DEC and FFLA list agree the tower is at the fairgrounds. Original-record coordinates (42.36463, -76.26985) are roughly a kilometre from the DEC Blackman Hill Road parking area (42.356657, -76.26149); not checked against the tower footprint. A 1940 elevation (1,800 ft) and 1941 elevation (1,920 ft) differ; elevation is not in the story. No fire events in the sources read.

Heights conflict: 75 feet in the August 1940 Ithaca Journal item, 68 feet in the April 1941 item. No height is recorded in facts for that reason. The early-1980s move has no exact year in the sources read, so the relocated event has no year key. The record's status 'standing' fits: the tower is on display at the fairgrounds. Whether the cab can be entered is unknown. No fires are named in the sources read. No photos added (no image URLs were read). The Forest Lookouts page transcribes Ithaca Journal items, so those quotes are secondhand transcriptions.

The record had no build date, height, staffing or access. Added the 1935 build, 1936 first season, 1988 last season and 1989 closure from the state list, which Wikipedia also cites, so they are not independent. Ownership is not changed: the 2007 report and the state list disagree, and no land record was checked. The 2008 window caption does not name the site, so the window repair is stated as a photo caption. The state list's visit contact details were left out on purpose. No usable photo URLs found, so photos is empty.

Wikipedia and the NYSFFLA entry agree on 1930, the 1971 closure, the 1979 reactivation, the end of 1988 and the early-1989 closure. A Facebook group snippet (not fetched, not cited) gives a 1977 or 1978 reactivation; it conflicts with both and was left out. FFLA lists the tower as standing, but no recent condition report or photo was found, so 'standing' rests on listings and the Wikipedia and NYSFFLA wording that it remains. The owner is not named. The brief's record (standing, no staffing) was consistent with sources; no correction. Used 1 WebSearch and about 3 page reads.

Height disagrees: register 40 ft, attached report 50 ft, 1934 newspaper 'some sixty feet'; record height_m 19.8 (about 65 ft) matches neither the register nor the report, so facts omit height. Opening: report says completed and open 1933; register says 1931-34. Honoree: register says 'a Chairman'; 1934 newspaper says the first president; Wikipedia names George W. Perkins Sr. Predecessor steel tower: report says 1923 and removal at 1930; Wikipedia's 1928 tower, taken down seven years later to make room for the stone tower, appears to be the same predecessor, so the story reports the disagreement on its date. Footings distance: 500 ft (2016 visit report) vs 300 ft (report). Wikipedia (lead only) claims fire use until 1953 and a 1990 family funding pledge; not verified against a primary source. Do not confuse the stone tower with the 1923 steel tower the report titles 'Lost Fire Tower'. No current-hours source found; the observation deck status comes from a 2016 visit report. County is unconfirmed: the record and the Forest Lookouts header say Orange; a historical marker (hmdb.org m=65286, seen in search only) says Rockland; Wikipedia says the mountain lies partly in each, so the story names no county. Record source 'firelookout.org/lookouts/us/ny/' was not read.

Height and early-history dates disagree across sources and are reported as disagreements, not resolved. The roster's own preface calls it an incomplete accounting. Current condition rests on a 2016 NHLR visit report and an undated hiking-guide page; no official DEC source was fetched. A WebSearch summary claimed the tower was closed in 1985 and that it is open except the cab; that claim is not used because no fetched page supports it. A WebSearch summary named a different 1924 observer than the fetched roster does; the story names no observers except Bill Starr, the roster compiler and NHLR registrar, who recalls working there. Roster quotes were checked against the cached PDF text.

Two sources only: the NYSFFLA entry (detailed) and the FFLA state list (name, coordinates, standing). Location conflict: NYSFFLA says about 3 miles southwest of Salamanca, but the listed coordinates 42.08896, -78.86361 are about 9.0 miles (great-circle distance, calculated by hand from the city coordinates in source 3, not a quoted figure) from Salamanca's Wikipedia coordinates. Left unresolved; no correction proposed. Erection year: NYSFFLA says about 1940. Facebook group snippets from search (not fetched, not cited) mention a June 1941 steel delivery and a 1941 erection; unverified and left out. The NYSFFLA entry gives no staffing history, so staffing is omitted. The name 'Venison Hill' comes only from the FFLA list (and FB snippets). Permission is from 'the Nation' as NYSFFLA words it; the nation is not named in the sources read. Used 2 WebSearch and about 3 page reads.

Only four sources, and the Pine Ridge name appears only in the FFLA list. The OpenStreetMap node matches the FFLA coordinates, and the Almanack photo credit names an Altona Flat Rock Fire Tower, but no source ties the three names to one structure. The 1957 tower on the central Flat Rock is not linked to this site. Record kind 'platform' is proposed as 'tower'. Almanack photo credits have no image URLs, so no photos were added.

Restoration year is disputed (1998 per Wikipedia, 2003 per an NHLR photo caption). WebSearch summaries also mentioned 1996 and 1997 from the Adirondack Almanack and Daily Gazette, and 2005 from a Friends blog, but none of those pages could be fetched (Daily Gazette returned 429; pokeomoonshine.org/about returned no readable text), so they are not cited. The steward line on the NHLR page is undated; as_of 2016 reflects the latest NHLR visit report. The brief's 1998 NHLR registration matches the register. Roster quotes were checked against the cached PDF text.

Sources agree closely; one minor discrepancy: NHLR gives the elevation as 2,980 ft (908 m) while Wikipedia gives 2,990 ft (910 m) — the story uses the NHLR figure and cites it there, not andyarthur.org as originally drafted. The tower record's design, height, staffing and access fields are currently blank/unknown even though NHLR and Wikipedia both support specific values (see corrections). Tried catskillcenter.org's Red Hill fire-tower page directly but it 404'd; Wikipedia and a general web search covered the same restoration history, so it wasn't pursued further within the search budget.

The main conflict is whether anything stands today. NYSFFLA's Rock Mt. entry (the 1922 wooden tower built by Fisher) says Removed. The FFLA state and county lists show a standing Windmill Tower at 43.81416, -75.23833, under the name Rock Mountain, which may be the same site or a different structure. CNY Hiking's intro names Rock Mountain (Lewis County) among privately owned towers, but its table has no Rock Mountain row, so it is weak support for 'standing'. Brief record said standing; proposed correction to unknown. The 1922 date is consistent across the newspaper transcription and NYSFFLA. Site identity (Rock Mt. = Rock Mountain) is assumed from name and location, not confirmed. Used 2 WebSearch and about 6 page reads, mostly shared lists, which is over the per-tower page budget because of the conflict. No photos found.

The 2025-2026 renovation status rests on a trail guide (Komoot, last updated February 2026) and an FFLA project list; no town notice was found. The NPGallery NRHP page returned only its title, so the NRHP date comes from Wikipedia alone. The brief's coordinates (42.1039, -75.226733) sit several hundred metres from Wikipedia's tower coordinates (42 06 14 N, 75 13 06 W) and from the Tower Mountain summit (42.10944, -75.22611); not changed, so check the pin. No notable fire was found in these sources. The trail length of 3.9 miles from Komoot is not used. Grokipedia and a video appeared in search results and were not used.

The 35 ft height is the NHLR figure and the only height found; the LS-40 model name is not explained in any source read, so height_m 10.7 is unverified. The NHLR note describing a removed Bald Mountain tower near Old Forge conflicts with the other sources and needs an editor's check. The NHLR claim that the tower is on the National Register is unverified; NPGallery was not read. Andy Arthur pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The 15,000-visitor figure is from Wikipedia alone, and the 'more than 30 observers' figure is from a blog. Adirondack Explorer does not give a date for its article.

The newsletter (April 2026) is the newest source and says the tower is closed; the 2023 blog says open, and the chapter homepage says closed pending inspections. The closing year differs (1971 season vs 1972). The andyarthur.org page returned 403 and the NHLR page was unreachable, so the register entry was not checked. No public-access or staffing statement after 2026 was found. Height 10.7 m comes from the 35-foot figure; the record's 11.0 m is from OSM.

Most of the story rests on one first-hand account in the April 2022 FFLA-NY newsletter. Its staffing and end-of-service statements are the writer's recollection, and the article that named the Elkdale man is lost, so the 1945 end date is approximate. The 1938 build year matches the record. No builder is named by a source; the writer credits the city and the newspaper credits the Water & Light Department. The record's 'north of the city' is kept. The 2022 article's own pictures are not linked. A Facebook group post surfaced in search but was not read. No photo URLs found, so none added.

Standing and poor condition rest on Wikipedia, which is undated and cites the NYSFFLA searchable list that we did not open. The June 2025 NYSFFLA line is a note written to the best of its author's knowledge, so it is cited as a note. Height 11 m is Wikipedia's rounding of 35 ft. Wikipedia says 'Conservation Commission' for a 1933 context; we did not check the agency's name for that year. The two Explorer reports are the only sources on the sale; the later one says the deal failed and the estate is back on the market, and we found no report of a new buyer. Owner of the tower today is unconfirmed. Record changes: height_m null to 11; access unknown to private; no corrections to the existing record. About 4 page reads and 2 WebSearch calls.

The move to the school is disputed: 1978 (NYSFLA list, EverybodyWiki's Wikipedia text) against the early 1970s (Hamilton College, citing a 2005 ASPFTRC webpage that was not read). The EverybodyWiki introduction gives 1932 for building on the mountain, which conflicts with its own history section; the story follows the history. A search summary placed the Mount Irvine to Science Hill move in 1931 (Mount Irvine article, not read), so 1931 is unverified and left out. Assumes the Ellicottville CTE School (Forest Lookouts) and the Ellicottville BOCES school (NYSFLA, EverybodyWiki) are the same site; no source says so outright. No source describes the current condition, public access, or a photo of the reassembled tower. The record has no height; the 18 m figure is for the original Mount Irvine tower and is not applied to the current structure.

Built, dedication and 1971 end of lookout use are consistent across sources. Height conflicts (65 ft in 1923 vs 60 ft in 2023). Ownership and visit rules conflict: the Register says guests of the Preserve only; the resort lists a tower walk for its guests and does not say the public can enter. The 1924 papers spell the keeper's name Osborne; a 1926 article spells it Osborn. The story uses Osborne for 1924 and notes the 1926 spelling. The reservoir location differs between the resort's page and Hudson Valley One (see resolved_conflicts). The 1912 lookout was at this point but may not have been the stone tower. Not verified: the current owner, any restoration, and the stair or deck condition. No photo added (NHLR photo credit has no image URL).

The brief's andyarthur.org page for Snowy returned HTTP 403 and was not readable. Its claims of a 1923 observer's cabin, a 2011 restoration led by Greg George, and the July 2024 fencing being completed are therefore unverified. The 1923 cabin is not in facts or events. The 2011 and 2024 items are corrected above because NHLR, the 2005 FFLA report and the April 2024 newsletter conflict with them. The NRHP nomination PDF is not digitized per NPGallery, so only its record metadata was used. Height is unresolved: NHLR implies about 42 ft, Wikipedia says 45 ft; 12.8 m is used with the conflict recorded. NHLR's photo (courtesy Laurie Rankin, Feb 2018) was not added because no image URL was found. The 2004 FFLA report lists the restored towers in prose and does not state a date for Snowy's restoration.

The historical record (1928 build, 1988 last staffing, 2014-2015 restoration) is consistent across DEC, NHLR, Saratoga PLAN and SummitPost. The current closure of the tower comes from a Saratoga PLAN page that cites DEC; no date for the structural closure was found, so re-check before publishing. The brief's staffing and access fields were unknown; the 2017 NHLR visit reports say unstaffed. Wikipedia says the tower is one of only 23 remaining in the Adirondacks, and Saratoga PLAN says the park has 25 mountains with towers; neither is used. No notable fire was found in these sources.

Only the FFLOS record describes the lookout itself. No build date, staffing or fire history appears in any source read. The '20-foot' figure is used as the tower's size; height_m is omitted because the source does not say it is height. Elevation conflict left open: FFLOS gives the site 1,433 ft (437 m), Black Rock Forest gives the summit 1461 ft, and the 2010 blog also says 1,461 ft. The story flags the difference. Coordinates differ between the FFLOS record (41.39092, -74.02125) and the New York list (41.38968, -74.02397); the brief's coordinates were not changed. Access 'restricted' rests on one 2010 blog post and the forest's own rules were not read; check them before publishing. The Karnig 1966 Black Rock Forest PDF returned no text and was not used.

The Friends history is the main source and is a local-group account that cites Fred Knauf's history; the dates it gives for the observer, the 1918 tower, the 1990 closure, the 2014 management plan and the 2016 reopening agree with NHLR and the Adirondack Explorer. Open point: NHLR's 1909 site date versus the Friends' April 1910 observer date. The NRHP nomination PDF was not read. The Explorer's 6.6-mile round-trip figure from the main trailhead was not used. No photos were added; NHLR credits Bill Starr and David Petrelli for its photos, but their licences were not checked.

Story is built on the register page, the Forest Lookouts page, two NYS chapter documents, a 2006 radio log and the NPS record. Closure start date is not in any source read; the 2023 event year is the report date, not the closure date. The brief's 2017 closure, 2019 cab-window work and 2022 inspection-completed events were not verified in sources read and are left out. The chapter's annual report file is named cr-ny-2023 but its header reads Annual Report 2024; its content covers 2023. Agency correction (DEC to NY State Parks) needs confirming with OPRHP or NY State Parks. The register calls the listing a Federal Register placement; the story says 'historic register' for the June 12, 2006 date and cites the NPS National Register record for the 7/28/2006 publication date. The 2006 radio log's author is not identified. A fresh check of the tower's current status (reopening or inspection result) is advisable before publication.

Seasonal closure: the DEC map says the trail and summit close from the second Tuesday in October through December 20. Our count puts the 2026 start at Tuesday October 13, which is five days after the research date. Confirm with DEC or the Friends before anyone plans a visit. The Friends' homepage banner (closed until December 20, 2025) is stale. The record's 2017 NRHP listing is not confirmed: the Explorer reports only that the state nominated the structure, and the NRHP nomination PDF was not read. The 1882 Colvin tower rests on one source (the Explorer); the Forest Lookouts page and the Register begin in 1912 and do not mention it. Trail length differs: 1.2 miles (DEC) vs one mile (Explorer, Friends). Staffing is from a December 2017 Register visit report only; no current staffing was found. No photos added. The Explorer photo credit (Nancy Ford) is not reusable without permission. Pages read: 8 (including one 403 that failed) plus two web searches; the Explorer and DEC map were read last and carry the access and history claims.

Only two sources could be read. The Friends of Stissing Landmarks site (stissingfiretower.org/history and the home page) rendered no text, and the New Pine Plains Herald article on the stair and landing replacement (completed October 24, year not visible) returned no body text, so neither is cited. The nysffla.org fire tower list returned 404 on the URL tried, and a search showed an alphabetical list at nysffla.org/alphalist.html that was not read. The story stops at the page-read budget. The register and Wikipedia conflict on the build year (1933 vs 1934), the height (86 ft vs 79 ft 6 in), and the end of lookout service (April 1971 vs 1979-1982). Those are unresolved and need the FOSL history page, the Herald article, or the nysffla list to settle. The register's 2017-2018 restoration is described as expected, so current completion is unverified. The story does not state the restored tower's current hours. The brief's events are kept as they stand: '1934 built' is supported by the register's Built field and the opening date, and the Wikipedia date is noted as a conflict.

Brief status 'gone' and coordinates confirmed by the register. The NYSFFLA list spells the name 'Stoney Hill'; the brief and register use 'Stony'. No source describes the site today beyond 'privately held', so access is recorded as private. Search turned up East Hampton land-protection documents for Stony Hill Road parcels and an East Hampton Star piece; they were not fetched or linked to this tower, and are not used. No corrections to the brief.

The DEC notice says the tower is closed; the crawl date of that page is unknown, so confirm with DEC Region 8 before publishing as current. The CNY Hiking and Wikipedia access text is undated. The NHLR credits DEC Region 8 staff with preserving the 1941 cabin, but no current cabin status was verified. The NY Almanack 2026 article (consistently staffed until the 1980s) was seen only in search and grep output and was not used as a citation.

The record's height_m 20.0 is proposed for correction to 18.0 (60 feet). Access is the main open question: the Southern Tier listing (fenced, limited dates) and the DEC listing (stairs climbable, top closed) disagree, and the 2021 and 2026 newsletters show set open days. A human should confirm current access with Allegany State Park before the page goes public. Staffing as a fire lookout ended in 1970; no later staffing is recorded. A 2019 FFLA newsletter (Friends of Allegany State Park climbing days) could not be fetched from the guessed URL (404), so it is not cited. A search snippet mentioned a 66-foot height from a park article; that page was not read and is not used. No fires are named in the sources read. No photos added.

Design model disagrees: the register says LS-47, the 2023 FFLA grant report says LS-40. The brief's 2024 entries (interpretive panels added by Warren County; a roof panel installed before an Aug. 31 lighting event) were not found in any source I read, so they are left out; the roof work's completion is unconfirmed. The register's Administered-by line (NYS DEC) conflicts with the 2021 news report (Warren County owns it); the agency correction is for human review. Post-Star article date is not shown in the text I read, so it is cited only for the trail opening and the 47-foot height. No staffing or climbing status sources were found. Access is public per the 2021 news report, which is five years old; check current status before relying on it. One WebSearch call and eight page reads used on this lookout.

Gone since 1977; no source describes the site today, so the story says so and gives no view or remains. Height conflicts (50 ft per Wikipedia vs one hundred feet in the 1924 newspaper quoted on Forest Lookouts); height_m left out. Wikipedia summit elevation (3,058 ft) differs from figures in other sites; not used. Wikipedia's own references were not checked, so its 1977 account rests on a secondary source; the Forest Lookouts newspaper quotes were read on the cached page. Access not stated by any source read, so facts.access is omitted. Budget: 1 WebSearch, 7 page reads (one more than the 6 allowed, because the 1928 article sat in the Forest Lookouts page and needed a second grep). No photos found.

Unresolved, so left out of facts: height (Wikipedia 60-ft Aermotor vs 69 ft in the 1918 Echo item, quoted by Forest Lookouts); current land owner (FFLOS says privately held, Forest Lookouts says title transfer to Suffolk County was arranged), so access is unset. No source describes public access or what remains on the site. Summit radio facilities come from Wikipedia, undated. Record elevation 98.5 m differs from Wikipedia's 102 m for the hill. No photos fetched.

This record is the original site. The Cathedral Rock tower already has its own story and research file under us-ny-tooley-pond-mountain-at-cathedral-rock; the two overlap on the rebuild. Wikipedia's lead (1919) conflicts with its own history section (1913); the 1913 date follows the Conservation Commission report. The rebuild dates disagree across sources. No fresh photos found.

Dates for the move are the weakest part. The register says late 1990s; Wikipedia says the rebuild began in the 1980s, the cab was finished in 1999 and the tower was dedicated in July 2000; a 1982 newspaper shows erection under way. Wikipedia cites a 2021 Adirondack Mountain Club book and a NYSFFLA list that were not checked. The 1971 removal rests on Wikipedia alone. The 47-foot height is given without a cab-floor figure, so height_m is left out. The record's 'relocated' event had no year; 1982 is the first dated mention, not the move date. The sister record us-ny-tooley-pond-mountain carries an unverified location (44.27104, -74.93038) that these sources do not confirm. Current access is unverified beyond the register's wording. The Adirondack Explorer hike write-up (cite 5) also dates the reassembly to 2000; the story does not give that date.

Dates and height conflict across sources (closure 1971 vs 1975; 47 ft vs 65 ft in a 1917 item). The Catskill Center page is undated, so staffing as_of is the year only. Andy Arthur pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The NHLR photo (Feb 2016, courtesy of Laurie Rankin) has no licence or URL, so no photo was added. The brief's access 'unknown' is now public based on the Catskill Center and marker.

Four sources agree on the 1910 windmill, the 1919 steel tower and the closed private status. Unresolved: the observer cabin date (Wikipedia by 1916 versus the 1917 annual report and a 1924 cabin report quoted by Forest Lookouts) and the summit elevation (NYSFFLA 2296 ft versus Wikipedia 2,293 ft); both are kept in the story and the elevation is not recorded in facts. The 'sold to the landowner' detail comes only from Wikipedia. The 1953 Air Force line is quoted by Forest Lookouts from The Oneonta Star and we did not open that original. Record changes: height_m proposed to 14.3 m; access unknown to private; staffing set to unstaffed from 1972; events added. No current photo or condition report found. About 2 page reads beyond the shared NY index, 1 WebSearch.

Core dates (1934 build, 1989 end of service, village ownership, 2004-05 restoration, 2015 registration) agree across the Register, the FFLA and Wikipedia. Conflicts are recorded in resolved_conflicts. The 1933 newspaper report on Forest Lookouts names a 60-foot steel tower to be completed in September 1933, so the 1934 build year is the consensus, not a certainty. The Register's visit report is dated October 21, 2017 (Laurie Rankin); its 'needs paint' and 'good overall condition' lines come from that visit, so they are nine years old as of 2026. The brief's agency (NYSDEC) is corrected to village ownership. No photo was added: the Register's photo is credited to Laurie Rankin (Oct 2017) and no image URL was retrieved. The brief's andyarthur.org page for the summit (p/216687) was not read.

The end of fire watch conflicts (1971 NHLR vs 1988 Wikipedia), and whether the cab is open to visitors is unconfirmed. Recommend a DEC check before the story is published as safe-to-visit. The brief's elevation (1,013.5 m) is the NHLR tower-site figure, not the summit. The AARCH item is a columnar newspaper PDF, so quotes are short fragments. Facebook group posts about the 1911 wood tower were not used. The Andy Arthur page was not used. No photo added.

Opening date: the record's 3 October 2019 opening is not found in any source read. The August 2019 newsletter says the tower would not open until the NYSDEC put up a fence. Search snippets from catskillcenter.org and catskillsvisitorcenter.org (not read; the visitor-center page returned HTTP 403) mention a fall 2019 opening, a fire-tower steward schedule and a short trail, but these are unverified and not cited. Check them before adding current access or visit details. Height: Florida articles give 85 feet (about 26 m) for the original; OSM gives 24 m for the re-erected tower. Unresolved, so height_m 24 comes from OSM only and is flagged. Build year 1956 rests on one 1969 newspaper item. Location disagrees: the 1969 article puts the tower on US 41 between Venice and the Englewood road, the 1974 notice on State Road 775 about four miles south of Venice; the story gives both. Read: NHLR Tappan page; Times-Reporter 2018 article (live page returned 403, Internet Archive copy used and quoted from); Eastern lookouts Tappan page (1967 clipping and ODNR header); FFLA Ohio 2010 chapter report; FFLA Ohio list. The 1940 item says a secondary tower was to be established, so the built event is a planned date; completion is not confirmed.
