The brief's kind 'ground' is not confirmed: sources say L-4 cab or lookout house and give no height or tower. The 2010 registration date matches the brief. The register's map and 1940 and 1959 photos were not read and no photo URLs were added. The 1931 emergency-station item is a plan, recorded as 'other' rather than built. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with closed per the trailhead page.

Size conflicts between register (12-ft tower) and 1955 report quoted on weebly (14x14 cabin). No source gives a removal date beyond 'gone 1966'; the weebly page says only Removed. Oregon Hikers (undated page, trip reports 2021) describes the gated summit with a satellite relay station; no source describes remains of the cabin. Brief access was unknown; the summit track is gated, so restricted is proposed. Brief kind ground and 2010 registration check out. No photos added.

Removed vs destroyed in 1953 is a wording conflict only. The register's 'about 1 miles south of Fish Lake' has a typo in the source (1 miles); the story says about a mile. Height 20.7 m is the brief's value and matches 68 ft. Access is not described by any source, so no access fact was written; the brief's unknown stands. The Forest Lookouts remnants line is undated. The 1946 staffing is the last staffed reference found; a 1947 social item names the Gentry family at Trinity lookout and was left out as unclear. No photos added.

Height is the main correction: the brief's 22.9 m is the 75-foot planning figure, and three sources give 86 feet. The Register's comments on bullet holes and paint are undated. The NHLR staffing field (no) is undated, so staffing rests mainly on the 2020 visit. The Oregon Lookouts history was read to 1958 and then 1992 (an outhouse move); the 1960s-1980s history is not covered. The Milli Fire date and summit burn come from Cheryl Hill only; a search result for a Sisters-area Nugget article describing a mosaic burn was not read and is not cited. A 1991 Forest Service eligibility report for Deschutes lookouts appears in the Oregon State Library collection but was not read. No photos added: the Forest Fire Lookout Association post and the museum photo credit lack image URLs that were read.

Access: firelookout.com says private property with no public access; the brief's unknown is replaced with private. A web search turned up a real-estate listing (landandfarm.com) saying the historic site of the former Tumalo Butte Lookout is offered for sale and describing a home and lookout tower on it; the fetch was refused (HTTP 403), so it is unverified and not cited. Editor may want to check the parcel before any today line goes beyond private with no public access. Removed vs destroyed in 1981 is a wording conflict. Staffing to 1965 rests on the 1965 weebly entry. Brief kind three_story and 2011 registration check out. No photos added.

No source describes what remains on the summit today. The 1930s two-story cab and the 1948 one-room house conflict or overlap; the editor may want the infobox to say which house is meant. The brief's height_m 4.9 has no source here and is proposed for removal. Wikipedia is used only as a lead and its tower claim is not independently confirmed. The 1948 Bend Bulletin items are quoted via Rex's page, not the newspaper. The brief's kind two_story is kept on the strength of the register. The register's photo captions were not read. Access 'public' rests on Wikipedia's route description alone; check the land status before publishing.

Dates disagree across sources: first set-up 1920 (ORWW) vs 1923 (register); cab is an L-4 cab in 1932 (register, firelookout.com) vs a gable-roofed R-1 type house c.1931 (Forest Lookouts). The 1939 item's 5,942 ft elevation is the outlier; the record's 1,619 m matches the register. Access stays unknown: no source describes access or the site today, so no access or visit fact is written. Do not confuse with the Washington lookout also called Twin Butte (washingtonlookouts.weebly.com); it is a different site and was not used. The record's kind 'ground' was not changed; no source describes the structure's base.

Removal year disputed: 1962 (Forest Lookouts) vs the 1970s (register, firelookout.com). The c.1938 15-foot tower with gable cab (Forest Lookouts) does not match the 14-foot 1930 tower; it may be a rebuild but no source says so. Correction proposed for height_m (3.7 to 4.3) because 3.7 m is the 12-foot early platform. Access and current site condition are not described by any source, so no access or visit fact is written. An unsourced social media post saying the lookout was removed in the 1930s was not used.

Removal is disputed: gone by 1945 (register) vs the 1950s (firelookout.com). A 1944 photo caption places the lookout on the site that year; the caption is not a photo of the tower we can see, so it is cited as a caption only. Agency conflict: Forest Lookouts says Mt Hood National Forest; the register and firelookout.com say ODF. Height is not recorded: firelookout.com gives 20 feet for the tower but does not say whether that runs to the cab floor, so it is kept in design, not height_m. No staffing, fire or access sources were found. The register's photos are credited but carry no licence, so none were added to photos.

Three sources agree the 1938 tower is gone. None gives a removal date, staffing, fires, or what remains at the site, so those are left out. Access is unknown and the Forest Service was not reached. Used 2 WebSearch and 4 page reads.

Coordinates conflict in the brief (FFLA 43.30207, -122.36368 vs west_us_lookouts 43.3053, -122.3466); the story gives none. Wikipedia's Umpqua Hot Springs article gives 43.295035, -122.365873 (not cited), about 0.8 km from the FFLA point. The bare 'Removed' label on the Forest Lookouts page has no date and its meaning is unclear, so the story quotes it only as written. Two WebSearch queries found no separate lookout record; Butler Butte and Red Butte on firelookout.com are other towers and were not used. Access and visit are left out because no source describes the site today.

Brief height_m 1.8 corrected to 18 m. NHLR, Wikipedia and the Oregon site agree on a 1938 CCC build; a 1939 newspaper notice reports completion at 63 ft. Cab size conflicts (6x6 vs 7x7). Wikipedia cites the 1986 NRHP nomination, which was not read. Living New Deal returned HTTP 403 and was not used. No notable fire found. Current status rests on 2018 and 2022 sources; no later check.

The 1949 items name the agency two ways: the July 23 item says Coos Forest Protective association and the July 26 funeral notice says Coos Fire Protective association. The story uses the funeral notice's name for the lookout charge. The 1929 date appears only on firelookout.com; the Forest Lookouts page does not mention it. Mrs. Allen's initials differ across the 1957 and 1958 items (C.B., C.E., C.F.), so the story says only Mrs. Allen. The bare 'Removed' label on the Forest Lookouts page is not used. Two WebSearch queries surfaced no Vaughn Point record beyond a map listing; the offbeatoregon.com AWS article is general history and is not cited. Unread leads: a Bill McCash article in Waterways (Coos County Historical Society, September 2007), and Oregon State Archives record APD/25/224, a June 1942 AWS circular.

Build date is disputed: 1940 (register), 1930s (Firelookout.com), a 1936 panorama captioned View Point Lookout, and a 1931 plan for a 20-foot wood tower. The story says so and does not pick one. The brief's kind 'platform' fits the register's crow's nest wording, so it is unchanged. No source gives the site's condition or access today. Used 2 WebSearch and 3 page reads.

The L-4 build year (1941 in three sources, 1942 in the 1971 notice) and the removal date (1971 in two sites, while the notice says in use until 1969) disagree; the story says so. The NGS listing for QC0925 gives two rows, one with the surface-mark-destroyed code and one with no geodetic control, so the survey-mark remark is the weakest claim here. Oregonlive was blocked (403). No access information found. Used 1 WebSearch and 5 page reads (one failed).

The summit's current condition is undocumented beyond the 2002 fire. The Oregon Hikers page carries a 2021 forum thread titled as saying the lake and peak are unaccessible; it is unverified and was not used as a finding, but the story now mentions it as a reason to check conditions before any visit. The 1964 item is taken from the Forest Lookouts transcription and was not checked against The World. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced by public, based on the wilderness hike listing and no reported closure; the forum title is the only contrary note. The fact-check removed the story's visit advice (a walk into the wilderness) because no source supports the access it implies.

The brief's height_m 4.6 is not supported by any source. The only size given for the 1961 cab is about 15 feet square (Forest Lookouts), which may be the origin of the 4.6 m figure (15 ft is about 4.6 m); it is left out of facts for review. The Everything Mountains page cited in a search snippet returned only an empty directory listing, so its footings claim is not used; the footings and railing are taken from Oregon Hikers. Grokipedia and the cherylhill.net blog were not cited. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with public, based on the National Forest trail. The fact-check rewrote sentences that copied quote wording and added quote evidence for the dates the story gives; no date or fact in the story was found to be wrong.

Built 1967 and BLM-administered are consistent across all four sources. Staffing is the open question: NHLR (undated) says staffed every summer; the May 2022 visitor says no longer staffed; firelookout.com says available for emergencies. No fire history or rental information found in the sources read. The cherylhill.net visitor thinks cameras were installed after the 2022 visit; not verified and left out. The Forest Lookouts page for Wagontire (oregonlookouts.weebly.com) was not read past the county index, so its 1967 entry is unverified. Brief had no height_m; none is in the sources read, so none is recorded.

No source describes what remains at the Waldo Hill site, or whether it is public. The Little Grayback cab is an active fire-detection and camera site with a surveillance sign, so the story gives no visit advice. The NHLR listing for Little Grayback gives a 1971 build date, while the 1980 annual report and the 2020 blog date construction to 1980-81; the story follows the latter, and the NHLR date is worth a check. The 2020 blog is a personal visit report, not an official source. The geocache page cited on the Waldo register page returned no text and was not used. Access fields are omitted for Waldo Hill because they describe the gone site, which no source covers. The county name was removed from the summary because no cited source names it.

Build year of the current structure is disputed (1956 vs 1957) and staffing status is ambiguous (NHLR implies occasional emergency use; FS and Wikipedia say unstaffed/non-functioning). No rental program found for this lookout.

Four sources. Brief's build year 1932 and the NHLR 1996 registration check out; the brief's height (10.7 m) matches the 35-foot tower. Build dates for the stone cabin (1915 vs 1917) and the steel tower (1932 vs 1933 within NHLR) conflict. Staffing end is unresolved across the 1991 report, the Roaming Civic 1940s claim, and the 2024 visit. The Forest Lookouts page for Walker (oregonlookouts.weebly.com) was not read past the county index, so its August 13, 1932 entry is unverified. The Roaming Civic also mentions a garage added in 1934 and a 1996 restoration program; those lines appeared only in search snippets, so they are not cited. The 1942 and 1967 cherylhill.net photo captions have no text, so they are not used. The abandonment date (since the 1940s) is not recorded as an event because no exact year is given.

Kind 'ground' is not stated in any source; the cab is only described as half a mile east of the summit, so kind is left as in the record. The Rex page's 1963 quote on the Walker Point (Western Lane FPA) page names a rebuilt lookout 'Walker Peak Lookout'; see us-or-walker-point-western-lane-fpa. Rex page's 1959 Oregonian and Water Bureau items are quoted second-hand, not read in original.

Record kind 'tower' matches the 1942 tower; the cabin came first. Elevation 3,812 ft agrees across the register and firelookout.com. No source describes remains or access today. The 1940 item is quoted second-hand from The Forest Log via the Rex page. Do not confuse with us-or-walker-point-western-lane-fpa, a separate site in Lane County.

The 1942, 1962 and 1969 dates agree across all three pages. Height, the 1951/1952 replacement year, elevation and the 'Walker Peak Lookout' name conflict; the record's height_m 16.8 is the Rex page's 55-ft figure and is left for editor decision. Today: only the 2014 reactivation item. The Rex page quotes the 1963 and 1951 state annual reports second-hand. Record kind three_story fits the 1963 cab.

Gone: dismantled July 2006 by volunteers; cab stored at the High Desert Museum; the rebuild is planned but unconfirmed. One WebSearch found no current status and only old pages. A 2026 Nugget article on the museum expansion was checked only in part (the first section) and is not cited. Elevation conflict: the brief's 1,230.5 m matches NHLR (4,037 ft); firelookout.com gives 5,697 ft, which is not used. The brief's access 'unknown' is kept out of facts because no source describes access. No new photos found. Reads: NHLR (2), firelookout.com (1), Forest Lookouts (2), firelookout.org list (1); one WebSearch.

Gone site. The current status and site condition are not described by any source read; a WebSearch turned up only old pages and a topo map with no lookout detail. The brief's 12.2 m height matches the 1934 40-foot tower, not the 1963 replacement, so the story says sources differ on the replacement. Gone by 1975 per firetower.org and firelookout.com; Forest Lookouts says discontinued 1975 and dismantled 1976. Story and quotes avoid the names of private people in the 1936 wedding and 1957 snake items, which are left out. Reads: firetower.org (1), firelookout.com (1), Forest Lookouts (1); one WebSearch. Photos: none new in the pages read.

The tower record's existing events list (built 1969 / removed 1969, sourced 'firelookout_com') appears to misread the firelookout.com page: that sentence describes the Logger Butte cupola's 1969 removal, not Warner Mountain's. I've flagged this as a resolved_conflict rather than a correction since it's the events array, not a record field, that needs fixing; recommend a human replace those two events with the 1986 relocation and 1987 build instead. Minor elevation discrepancy between NHLR (5,667 ft) and firelookout.com (5,723 ft) not worth a correction. Did not find a precise end date for seasonal staffing (current vs. historical); firelookout.com's staffing claim is undated. Fact-check 2026-10-04: Recreation.gov's own listing text gives a third elevation, 5,300 ft, for what it's worth (not cited in the story, which only cites the two register-style sources for elevation).

No source gives a removal year or describes current access, so the story says to check with the Oregon Department of Forestry. The 2003 photo captions are the only description of what remains (old foundation and tower leg bases); they are not dated later than 2003. The register (administered by Oregon Department of Forestry) and firelookout.com (Oregon Dept. of Forestry) both name ODF as the agency; Rex's header also lists Mount Hood National Forest > Oregon Department of Forestry, which the story does not repeat. The 1936 bearing (seven miles due west) differs from firelookout.com (8 miles southwest). The brief's height 9.1 m matches the 30-foot tower; the 1951 tower is the second structure. The 1953 Forest Log item is quoted via Rex's page.
Minor date ambiguity: NHLR says built 1931/completed 1932; NRHP record/Wikipedia infobox say built 1932. No rental program; it's a day-use hike within Crater Lake National Park.

Brief record checks out: coordinates, 1,733 m elevation, L-4 design, Douglas County, and the April 22, 2011 FFLOS registration all match the register. The build date conflicts (1933, 1934, 1937) are reported, not resolved. Staffing is thin: a 1962 newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and the Roaming Civic line that it was not actively staffed after the 1960s. The access level closed comes from a July 2024 notice on a 2022 page and may be out of date; a search turned up closure news for the Umpqua but no newer notice for this site, and none was read. The Forest Lookouts page also quotes a 1942 Umpqua archive photo caption, but it has no URL, so it is not listed as a photo. The firelookout.com page was read but is not cited because it adds nothing new.

The story runs about 124 words, just over the 120-word floor, because the three sources give only a location, a 1930s date, an abandoned status and a possible-proposal note; it was not padded. Two WebSearch queries found no West Eagle lookout record; Mount Emily, Hat Point and Red Hill results are other lookouts and were not used. The brief's status 'gone' is not supported; see corrections. The Forest Lookouts page gives little beyond the location.

Gone ground site. Brief record checks out: elevation 6,057 ft (1,846 m) per firetower.org matches the brief's 1,846.2 m, and design L-4 matches. Not in facts: elevation (no schema key). Sources differ on removal versus destruction in 1970. Nothing describes the site today; one WebSearch found only unrelated Ochoco pages and a grazing allotment notice, which is not cited. No photos added. The firelookout.org list line for West Maury was read once during the Wanoga pass and is quoted from that read. Reads: firetower.org (1), firelookout.com (1), Forest Lookouts (1).

Build year and height conflict across sources; the story says so. Cheryl Hill's Oregon list (count as of July 2026) is the newest source found and still lists the tower as standing and unmanned; the 2021 trip report is the newest detailed condition report, so today's condition and access are unconfirmed. Staffing 'unstaffed' rests on that July 2026 list and the 2018 plan (not in the staffed list). The 2021 trip report says the tower was open to climb although the Forest had deemed it unfit; the story advises against climbing, citing the Forest's unfit-for-use finding. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with 'restricted' based on the Forest's recommendation to secure the towers, not on any closure order. Elevation is a conflict, not an error in the brief.

Brief record (L-4 design, 2010 FFLOS registration, gone status) confirmed. Access not stated in any source, so no access level is recorded. Only one staffing item (1936 Forest Lookouts page quote, itself reproducing a column by A.O. Waha). No source describes remains. Two-source conflict on 1950 fate left open. The 2005 site photo is on firetower.org but its image is not described, so no photo record was added.

Brief record (ground kind, gone status, 2010 FFLOS registration) confirmed. The 1930s build date has no exact year, so no built event was recorded. The footings line on the Mount Hood history page sits between the West and East Zigzag passages and does not name a site, so it is reported with that caveat. The Oregon Hikers page is undated (oldid 103138). The firetower.org photo credited to Pat Lynch (circa 1957) is captioned only, so no photo record was added. The AWS abbreviation is not expanded in the source.

Only two detail pages and the FFLA list; no built year, staffing, fire or site-today source found. The sources disagree on removed vs destroyed and give decade-only dates, so no built or removal event is recorded. The brief's note that Westfir shares a register number could not be confirmed: US 1001 appears twice in cached data/sources/fflos.json, both on this record, and I found no second holder. Lead for a future pass: the Willamette lookout thesis on ScholarsBank (scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/items/271eae30-098a-4fb7-b37c-048460d97265) had no text in cache; its PDF may name the Westfir cab.

Brief record (elevation 1,522 m, July 18, 2011 registration, gone status) confirmed. Brief height 15.2 m matches the early 50-foot tower; see corrections. Access is not stated in any source, so no access level is recorded. The 1979 NGS note is the latest description found, so today's condition is unknown. Search results mention 1932 and 1959 photos on a Facebook post, but the post was not read and no image URL was captured, so no photo record was added. The 1959 annual report on the Forest Lookouts page has the typo 'Wheedler', which is avoided in quotes.

Brief height_m 24.4 is contradicted by all sources (10-foot pole tower). Access is unknown: no source found. Forest Lookouts' 1930 article gives 4685 ft for Whetstone Peak / Old Baldy, while the register gives 5,073 ft; not reconciled, and the 4685 figure is not used. Staffing 'unstaffed as of 1958' is inferred from 'short period of abandonment'. No photos added.

Oregon Hikers files the hike under the Mt Hood National Forest; the Forest Service trail page is on the Willamette. The closure notice is dated August 2026 and may be out of date by 2026-10-09; not verified against the closure order. The register links a photo 'Whetstone Mountain Lookout 1958' (Howard Verschoor collection); no image URL was read, so no photo was added. No staffing or lookout-fire information found in the sources read.

The 1989 salvage and the 2011 register entry are well sourced. Unresolved: the first house date (1922 register and firelookout.com vs 1924 Rogue River NF history via Oregon Lookouts); the builder (Forest Service per the register and Oregon Lookouts vs CCC per the 2019 field-trip guide); and the trail length (field-trip guide says half-mile; a Forest Service search snippet says 0.8 miles, not read in full, so not cited). Foundation remains rest on one 2019 guide only; Applegate Siskiyou Alliance Facebook snippets also mention a foundation and an outhouse but were seen only in search results, so they are not cited. The access level 'public' is an inference from the Forest Service trail and a 2019 public field trip; check closures. The Forest Service trail page was read but its cached text has only the heading. Used 1 WebSearch call and 6 page reads. Oregon Lookouts marks the site 'Removed' at the end of its entry; the brief's record matches the sources; no corrections.

Current status rests on a July 2023 visit; no later visit report was found. Elevation differs (4,961 ft on the register; 5,075 ft on Fire Lookout and Cheryl Hill), not carried into the story. Access is rated restricted as a judgment from the gated spur road and state ownership; the brief's access was unknown. No fire history found in these sources. Used 1 WebSearch and 6 page reads.

Building history is contradictory: 1917 construction, 1919 first cabin (register), 1923 replacement, then a 1926 log cabin and 1928 ground house in Forest Lookouts; the story says the history is unclear. Removal is 1967 (Forest Lookouts) or 1970 (register, firelookout.com). Brief height_m 3.0 has no source. Two searches found nothing describing the site today. Forest Lookouts quotes both 4,010 ft (1931) and the register's 4,019 ft. No photos added. The 1931 lightning story in Forest Lookouts is a real event at the lookout, not a fire.

Thin record. The only dated entries are a 1930 crow's nest marked abandoned (firelookout.com) and two 1931 items quoted from the Heppner Gazette-Times on the Forest Lookouts page. No staffing, fire, or current-site information found. Two web searches returned an Idaho lookout with the same name (Kaniksu NF, 1924-1959); it is a different site and was not used. The brief status 'gone' is not what the sources say; see corrections.

Only two short source pages describe the tower. Height is disputed (40 ft FFLOS vs 50 ft firelookout.com). The burning rests on one first-person account (Keith Argow) with no year, so no burned or removed event was entered. The 1952 staffing event rests on a photo caption. No source describes the site today. The oregonlookouts.weebly.com index gave no Wickiup detail. The record's coordinate conflict (west_us_lookouts 46.1056, -123.58624) was not checked.

The record says kind 'ground', but the sources say only 'rag camp' and 'L-4 cab' and never say whether the cab stood on a tower, so the record was not changed. End date conflicts (1952 vs 1953). Today's description comes from a 2013 blog and an undated field guide; no source describes remains. Access is inferred from the hiking guide, not from a land-manager notice. The guide warns that target shooters are abundant along the roads around the trailhead and asks for caution; the story does not mention this. A search also surfaced a different Wildcat Mountain site (WNF, 1934 L-4 cab) which is not this record and was not used.

Register and firelookout.com agree on the 1920s crow's nest, the 1932 90-foot tower and the 1971 end. Staffing and the 1937 storm come from Central Oregonian items quoted on the Oregon lookouts index page for this site; the index page is headed Wildcat Mountain, Ochoco National Forest, 13S-18E-22 and quotes only Central Oregonian items, but it gives no tower number, so tying the items to this tower is an inference from that heading. height_m 27.4 is 90 ft converted. The 1920s crow's nest has no exact year, so no event was entered for it. No source describes the site today; no modern search result matched this site. Coordinates and elevation in the record match the FFLOS page.

Brief record checks out (Linn County, gone, FFLOS US 1002). Oregon lookouts page 2 (wildcat-mountain2.html) describes a different Wildcat Mountain in the Mt. Hood NF (3S-6E-23, 1931 construction) and was excluded. A separate Wildcat Mountain site in the Mt. Hood NF also has its own FFLOS record (MHNF, US 662); it is not this lookout. Elevation is 5,353 ft in the register and firelookout.com, and 5355 in the 1939 newspaper quoted by the Oregon lookouts site. No photo with a usable image URL was retrieved. The register's 1949 photo credit (Mark Swift collection) has no image URL in the text read.

Current condition is the main open question: FireLookout.com (undated) says only the superstructure stands; the SMS project page describes planned reassembly and may be out of date. A search summary mentioned a 2011 completion claim and earlier 1929 and 1931 cabins; I did not read those pages, so they are not used. The Oregon survey PDF (heritagedata load=34737) returned no extractable text. Access and gate claims rest on the SMS page only; check with the Gold Beach Ranger District. Fact-check 2026-10-08: staffing recorded as unknown (register and FireLookout.com disagree); fire-closure events retyped as other; story reworded where it went beyond the sources ("heavy snow", AWS post, "watching for aircraft"); Curry County and US 509, OR 101 evidence added.

Brief record checks out: L-4 design, 7.6 m (25 ft) height, gone status, FFLOS US 1050. The build-year conflict (1933 vs 1940) is the main open question; the story reports both. The Crane Mountain replacement has its own FFLOS record (Crane Mountain Lookout Site, Lake County, US 1014) whose current condition was not checked. No photo with a usable image URL was retrieved. No access information found.

Brief record checks out: 30 ft tower (9.1 m), Douglas FPA, FFLOS US 937, gone. Source 4 is a different Windy Camp (Mt. Hood NF, Hood River County, 'Abandoned 1940s'); it is mentioned in the story only to prevent confusion. The Oregon lookouts page has no removal date for this tower, so 'gone by 1959' rests on the register and firelookout.com. No staffing found in the sources read. No photo with a usable image URL was retrieved.

Brief's height (50 ft, 15.2 m) and BLM agency are consistent with the register; no correction needed. The 1941, 1943 and 1949 newspaper items are quoted through the Oregon Lookouts transcriptions, not the original papers. The 2024 BLM release closes Windy Peak Road but never names the lookout, so the story does not say the closure blocks the site. A two-year closure from November 2024 would run to about November 2026; that end date is not verified. Web search found no current status for the summit.

Brief's elevation (1,433 m) matches the register; the brief lacked design and agency-level detail, which were added. The 1930s build date is a decade only, so no build year is recorded. A user-written geocache listing (GC36BYJ, Sherar Burn) reportedly describes surviving footings and a survey benchmark, but fetch_text returned only its title, so that claim is not used. No staffing or fire sources were found, so none appear in the story. Access is not stated by any source beyond PeakVisor's wilderness placement, so no access key is recorded.

Current staffing is not confirmed: the staffing statement is from the 2011 NHLR registration and firelookout.com, both undated. The access level 'restricted' is an editorial inference from the Forest Service staffing, not a source statement. The record's height_m of 15.2 appears to be the earlier wooden tower. A 2011 blog and a search summary mention a road and staffing visits, but these were not fetched, so they are not used here.

Brief's height_m of 4.3 is wrong for a 65-foot tower; see corrections. Brief's design (L-4) and elevation (1,969 m) are confirmed. Do NOT confuse with the Ochoco National Forest Wolf Mountain in Wheeler County (staffed 107-foot tower, Road 5840 area); those pages were read and excluded. The onX listing does not name the lookout; it describes a Wolf Mountain at 6,480 feet, close to the register's 6,461 feet, so the road and winter-gate details are probable but unconfirmed for this site. The access level 'public' is an inference from National Forest land, not a stated source. Newspaper items are quoted via the Oregon Lookouts transcriptions. No source describes remains at the site.

Dates conflict: register 1941 build versus dated entries 1932-1935. Height conflicts: 30 ft (register), 20 ft (firelookout.com); the record's 5.5 m matches neither. Removal conflicts: removed (register) versus destroyed (firelookout.com), both 1964. Geocache GC5B5BG (about this site) came up in search with a snippet mentioning footings, but the cached page is a stub, so it is not used; check it for what remains. The record's other_names 'Wolf Mountain' also fits two other Oregon lookouts (us-or-wolf-mountain, Wheeler County, standing; us-or-wolf-mountain-2, Lane County), so consider removing it. No source read gives an access level, so none is set.

The Forest Log item (January 1972) is quoted only through the Forest Lookouts page; we did not reach the original. Searches found nothing new about Wolf Point. The 1972 burn is reported without saying which structure burned. No staffing, fire, or current-site information found. The 1950 total covers the lookout and a storage garage.

Built date conflict: 1935 (register, firelookout.com) versus 1932 and 1936 labor entry (Oregon Lookouts page, which quotes Six Twenty-Six). Removal conflict: removed (register, Oregon Lookouts 'Removed') versus destroyed (firelookout.com), both 1966. The 1957 accident item on the Oregon Lookouts page was left out. The Oregon Lookouts page also carries a 1946 Coast and Geodetic Survey station description for the summit (PID RA1137); it does not describe present conditions. No source read describes the site today, and none states whether the point is open to visitors, so no access level is set.

Access is not established: no fetched source names the land owner or says whether the site is open to visitors, so no access key is given. The only firsthand account is the July 2020 PNW SOTA report. Search results describing a 9-mile rough road and a 1.25-mile hike were not fetched and are not used. The 1970 staffed_last year is a placeholder for 'into the 1970s'. A 1915 telephone line and 1924-1925 lookout entries also appear on the Forest Lookouts page and were not used.

The record's height_m 24.4 is the 1929 steel tower (80 ft); the last structure was 20 ft (about 6.1 m). No access level is set: no source read states whether the site is open to the public, so none is recorded. A climbing guide gives road directions and no closure notice was found, which does not establish open access. The 1928 letter in the Oregon Lookouts page places the mountain on the Klamath Indian Reservation; no source read says whether the summit is on tribal land today, so check before any access wording. The timber tower's removal is dated 'after 1974' (PeakBagging.com) against 'used for emergency in 1973' (register); the dates are reported as given. The 2017 photo is the most recent source; no source read describes the site after that. The 1937 truck-trail item and other 1968 entries on the Oregon Lookouts page were left out.

Status is removed: the tower is gone and a camera replaced it, but no source describes the site today beyond that, so access is unknown and the story says so. The brief's height of 15.2 m (50 ft) fits the 1943 tower per FFLOS and FireLookout.com; the 1949 report says the replacement was 3 feet taller than the old 50-foot pole tower, so the 1949 tower may have been about 53 ft. No source states that height directly, so it is not in facts. The brief's '1943 built' is corrected to a 1936 first tower; the 1932/1934 CCC dates are a real conflict. The brief's 2016 removal date is kept as a conflict; two sources say 2015. No photos added (licences not stated). Used 1 WebSearch and 7 page reads (3 grep reads of one cached page), over the per-tower budget, because the record conflicts on dates.

Two sources describe different uses: firelookout.com a 1930s cabin abandoned 1953, the Forest Lookouts page a 1943 Army aircraft-warning observation post and a 1944 tree platform. They may describe one site at different times, but no source links them. Check the county: firelookout.com and the FFLA index say Josephine, the Forest Lookouts county index says Douglas, and the Western Lane FPA credit and township reference may point to Lane County; no source says so. The FFLA coordinates (about 43.8 N) also look well north of Josephine County, which lies near 42 N; check on a county map before the county is published. Check the coordinates against the second list in the record. The 1943 memo says the post was to get new living quarters and a woodshed; the sources do not say whether any cabin stood then.

Dates conflict. Register and firelookout.com say built 1921; Forest Lookouts quotes a station in charge in April 1913, a newly established lookout in May 1925 and a new lookout being erected in August 1926. Removal conflicts: Forest Lookouts says removed in 1970; register and firelookout.com say in ruins by 1993. The record's gone status rests on these entries; no source we read describes the site today. Ray/Roy Cather spelling varies across 1940-41 items. The Linn County Fire Patrol name comes from the Forest Lookouts pages; the register uses Linn FPA. A WebSearch found no independent source for the cabin. Record photo is the register's own; no new photos.

Staffing years come from the personnel tables in the Rogue River history, dated by the nearest year heading above each table; the years are inferred from those headings. A 1944 Medford Mail Tribune item on the Forest Lookouts page gives the same guard and the same date (September 5) as 1924 but a different year; left out as likely an error on the page. The geocaching page for GC34T92 did not load. Present condition is unverified; a recent visit or a Forest Service record would settle it. Fact-check 2026-10-10: removed the earlier 'Forest Service set up' attribution (no cited page names who built the lookout); added the 1922 Alex Schichtl listing and the Crater National Forest naming with the July 1932 rename.

The 1941 build year rests on the register and firelookout.com; no second source confirms it. A web search linked a 1941 structure on the same forest (High Ridge), which may be the source of the date; unverified. The likely dating source is the 2002 Umatilla National Forest fire lookout eligibility study (Oregon digital collections record 275450); the cached page had no matching text, so the study itself is unread. No staffing, fires, or removal date found. Record kind remains unknown.

Only one history sentence was found: the register says the tower was used in the early 1900s and is no longer standing. No build date, staffing, fire or removal date was found in the register, the Weebly lookout index (its Amberson entry reads 'No information'), or two search rounds, which returned only topographic and index pages. The story is short for that reason; a later pass could check Pennsylvania forestry reports or Perry County newspapers. Access and the site today are not described by any source read.

Build and removal dates conflict: register says 1919 and 1975; notices suggest a tower in 1920-21 and a removal sale in May 1976. Brief height 3.7 m is unsupported; notices say 64 ft planned (1920) and 80 ft (1927-1938), so 24.4 m is proposed. All newspaper material comes through one transcription page; the original papers were not read. No source describes the site today; the Mapcarta point labelled Centralia Fire Tower may or may not be this lookout. Access is not stated in any source.

Two sources only; both give 1909 and no longer standing. No removal date was found. A Facebook post by a Casshews page (found as a search snippet, not read; Facebook would not load) says a 'Bald Knob Fire Tower' was 'still in use when this 1972 image was taken', and gives no county, so it may describe a different Bald Knob. If it is this tower, the removal date is later than the sources suggest; worth checking. A search snippet also gives Tussey Knob as an alias for Bald Knob in Centre County; the Anyplace America page returned 403 and was not read. No access or site-today information was found.

Built date conflicts (before 1924 per register; 1925 per Forbes history); story gives both. No staffing or fire records found on the lookout page, the register, or the forest history. Brief height_m 15.2 (50 ft) left out: the only 50-foot mention (1913) is not named to this site. Brief access 'unknown' not upgraded; no source states the tower site's access. A YouTube title seen in search, 'The Fire Tower Logbook on Bald Knob Recorded a Fire That Never Burned' (youtube.com/watch?v=Kb4Yn6rIaUc), could not be read (no description returned), so it is not used; it may concern a different Bald Knob or this one, and is worth checking.

Thin record: one 1908 forestry report, a 1914 post, and the register. Height 10.7 m is the 35-ft viewing point of the 1914 post, not a confirmed tower height. Removal date unknown. No staffing, fires or current-site description found. Neither source gives coordinates, so the brief's lat/lon (40.75257, -77.63389) could not be checked. A search returned a 'Friends of Bald Mountain Preservation Project' page with photos of a tower; it is not clearly this site, so it is not used.

Newspaper items are as transcribed on the lookout page (Wellsboro Agitator and Gazette); the originals were not checked. The 1964 removal date rests on the register alone. Height conflict (47 ft vs 50 ft) is noted in the story. Brief access 'unknown' not upgraded: no source states whether the site is open now. The NGS survey mark (1933 description) may or may not survive; not checked. Brief record (14.3 m, Tioga State Forest, 2008 registration) matches the sources; no corrections.

Four sources, none describing the site today. The storymap web page is script-only, so its text is cited through the ArcGIS item data URL that was read. The record joins the Tark Hill and Bear Springs names on nearly identical coordinates (storymap 41.2628, -75.7062; record 41.2629, -75.7061), but no source says the 1960 replacement is the storymap's Bear Springs tower. Newspaper quotes come from the transcriptions on the Eastern US Lookouts page, not from the original papers. No height or access is recorded for the Tark Hill tower: the storymap's 80 feet, Aermotor maker and State Game Lands 91 location apply to Bear Springs, which no source ties to this site.

Thin record: one register entry and one map-feature page. No removal date, reason, or staffing found. A statewide PA lookout inventory (firelookout.org, last updated 2008) appears in search results as listing a 'Beaver' steel 1949 tower in Snyder County as not standing, but that page would not fetch and is not cited; link to this site is unconfirmed. Brief's coordinates match both sources exactly. Brief's elevation_m 639.5 is consistent with the register's 639 m.

Current status is the main open question. The NHLR spells the forest 'Michael State Forest'; the Forest Lookouts page gives Michaux State Forest, which is used. Access level 'public' is inferred from state ownership (1942 survey) and the road-walk detour, not stated by a source. A 2024 review giving 80 ft and good condition appeared only in a search summary and was not fetched. The DCNR self-guided tour brochure gives 1921 and 60 ft, but its text was too interleaved to quote, so it is not cited. Lookout observers are named in the source; they are not named in the story. Confirm current status with the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry before publication.

Current climbing rules and whether the 1921 tower is open today are unverified; newest source is September 2022. The record's coordinates point to Big Pocono State Park, where the 2017 replacement stands; the 1921 tower is at Grey Towers (Milford), and no source here gives coordinates for it, so the point was not changed. Height: register and Grey Towers say 21 ft, Courier 2017 says 35 ft; height_m 6.4 is converted from 21 ft. The NHLR 2017 entry lists 'Built 1921' for the replacement tower, which looks like a copy error. No notable fire found.

The brief's Aermotor design is supported only for the 1921 predecessor, so the record should not attribute it to the 2017 tower. Predecessor date and height disagree across the NHLR, the Forest Lookouts history, the 1921 newspaper item and the Pike County Courier, and the story reports those disagreements. Re-erection timing disagrees too (NHLR 2018 vs Grey Towers 2019 reassembly and 2021 plan). Access for the 2017 tower is not established: the NHLR entry has no visit information, and no state park or DCNR visit rules were read, so the access and visit keys are left out rather than guessed. Staffing history was not found in these sources. No photos were added because no licensed image URL was confirmed. The NHLR 1921 entry's photo credits were not used. Searches surfaced a Wildfire Today article and a PA Environment Digest piece on the 16-tower replacement program, but those were not read, so they are not cited. Story is about 330 words.

Almost all of the history comes from one compiled page (Eastern US Lookouts), which quotes newspapers and an NGS datasheet; the NGS text was not checked against NGS directly. The DCNR link to this site is unproven: the listing names no tower or date. Do not merge with the Perry County Big Poe Mountain record (a separate 1909 tree tower on the register). No source states current access, so facts.access is omitted. No photos found.

Thin record: two sources give one line each about the tower, and they agree on 1914 and the tree form. The height_m value is the 40-foot platform figure converted to metres. Mapcarta is a gazetteer, used only for location context; it does not place the tower on a particular spot. Do not confuse with the Big Ridge Fire Tower built in 1935 at Lost River State Park, West Virginia, which surfaced in search and is a different structure. The Eastern page's 1928 Tioga district tower on Buck Run Mountain is also a different tower. No photos found.

Built and moved dates rest on two register entries plus a 1939 newspaper. Nothing found describes the site today. The OpenStreetMap node exists at 41.6203514, -77.1369155, close to the record's coordinates, but its tags do not show whether a structure stands. The record's elevation (718.4 m, register) differs from OSM (720 m); not material. Access not stated in any source read, so access is omitted.

Record id and an OSM label say Blue Knob; every source read calls the site Big Knob in Jackson Township, Perry County. The 1921 height conflict is unresolved. Nothing read describes the site today; the 2024 Instagram post is a personal account and is the weakest source. The 2016 plan supports access but says nothing about remains. Agency taken from the 1921 notice (Department of Forestry) rather than the record's Tuscarora State Forest.

Do not merge with us-pa-blue-knob, which is the Big Knob tower in Perry County. The Gazette's highest-point claim is reported as the paper's claim and not repeated as fact. The 1924 Altoona Tribune item about damage and fines concerns the Blue Ridge tower in the Buchanan Forest District, not Blue Knob, and was not used. The brief's Eastern coordinates (40.2886, -78.5614) do not appear in the page text; the register gives N 40.295354, W 78.573906. Access rests on Wikipedia's trail description, not a current site visit. Most history comes from one compiled page that quotes newspapers and an NGS datasheet. No photos found.

No staffing, fire, access or visit information was found, so those keys are omitted. The Eastern page coordinates (41.247, -78.64669) sit close to the register's. A gazetteer (mapcarta.com/22708066, not cited) lists a Boone Mountain Fire Tower in Horton Township with no date or condition; that does not show anything stands. The register's separate Boones Mountain Tower Site (US 215) is a different record and was not used. The county conflict is unresolved beyond the register's Elk County.

The record's design 'Aermotor' describes the original tower; the register gives the current structure as steel (proposed correction, for human review). Unreconciled: the register's 1939 Aermotor date versus the Forest Lookouts' 1939 raising to a height printed as 'eight-six feet' (OCR or typo, unchecked), and whether 1921 steel is the same site. The PA Fire Towers StoryMap and MapSeries pages returned no text (JavaScript only), so the record's pa_storymap 1939 claim is unchecked. The DCNR 16-tower program is given as context; the blog's text we read does not name Boot Jack, and it covers state forestland while Boot Jack is on State Game Lands. No public access or current condition source found, so access is omitted. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 7 fetches (6 distinct pages plus a repeat grep), one over the per-tower budget.

Height: 67 ft in the 1921 notice vs 47 ft in the 1927 article; the register gives no height, and the 14.3 m in the brief matches 47 ft. The 1975 removal date rests on the register alone. The DEP fact sheet is for the reclamation project named after the lookout; it does not say the tower was removed by that project, and its 'currently' means 2014. Access and visit facts were not established, so they are omitted. Newspaper text is as reproduced on the Eastern page; the originals were not checked.

Thin record: one register entry and a map page for the mountain summit. The register gives no coordinates ('No coordinates are available'), but the brief's lat/lon 40.94037, -77.24901 sits about 30 m from TopoQuest's summit point (40.940629, -77.249140); the brief's coordinate source is unknown, so it is not changed. TopoQuest describes a summit, not a tower, so the tower's location is unconfirmed. Register does not say 'Buffalo Township' and nothing found supports it. Statewide PA inventory (firelookout.org) would not fetch. Story sits at the low end of the length range because the evidence is thin.

Brief coordinates (41.82488, -77.41562) are not on the register, which says 'No coordinates are available', and I could not check them, so they are not in the story. Brief kind 'unknown' could read 'tree' per the register. The 40-foot figure is converted to 12.2 m as the height of the observation post, not a verified structure height. The history's 1916 entry gives no source of its own. The per-site easternuslookouts page for Broad Ridge returns 404. Two searches and about four page reads found nothing on staffing, fires or current access, so those are left out.

The record's built 1941 is a relocation date. Relocation year is disputed (1940 vs 1941). No current staffing status or climbing rule was found. The trail listing's operational wording is the only current-status evidence, and it is a hiking site, not an agency.

Unresolved: the register says moved in 1940 and renamed Scalp Level, but a March 1945 item says the tower was still on Brush Mountain and damaged. The Scalp Level site was not located in any source. The brief's coordinates (40.52173, -78.33219) are not from the register, which says no coordinates are available; verify before publishing. Newspaper text is as reproduced on the Eastern page; originals were not checked. Access and visit facts were not found, so they are omitted.

Brief status 'gone' is not supported by any text read; the register only calls the site former. The 1970s move date appears only in the Buck Ridge entry; Staley's Knob gives 1934. The Staley's Knob entry (Adams County) is a separate record worth checking for consistency. The firelookout.org Pennsylvania inventory URL returned 404 in the crawl cache, so no inventory status was used. Buck Ridge (Mifflin County) is a different site.

Two Forest Lookouts pages (buck-ridge.html and the Pennsylvania A-F index) put Buck Ridge in Cumberland County, not Mifflin. The Cumberland register record (US 229) is a Blaw-Knox tower built in 1934; its existing research file says the Staley's Knob entry dates the move to 1934, while the register page says the 1970s. Those two should be reconciled. Brief coordinates (40.69646, -77.70055) are not on the register and could not be checked, because the gazetteer returned 403, so they are not in the story. One search surfaced a standing 'Buck Ridge Tower' summit in Cumberland County (TopoQuest, Mapcarta); I did not verify that it is the Cumberland register record. Brief kind 'unknown' could read 'tree' per the register. No staffing, fire or access source was found.

The record's 1935 build year is unconfirmed. The only source I found for it is an ArcGIS storymap that returned no readable text to fetch_text or WebFetch, plus an unreliable Facebook group snippet, so I left it out of events. The record's 68-foot height comes from the same storymap, while the register says 60 feet. A 2011 Pocono Record article calls it a rare Blaw-Knox, but the site returned 403. The register has a November 2024 photo but no 2024 visit text. Visit notes date to 2017 and 2021.

Brief coordinates (41.01091, -77.05997) match the MountainZone summit coordinates (41.0109138, -77.0599673), but the register lists none, so they locate the summit rather than a verified tower site. No source dates construction: the 1912-13 report only recommends a small tower, and the register's circa 1917 is the only tower-era date, so the story does not link the two. Do not confuse with the Buffalo Mountain in West Virginia (Mingo County, which has a 1961 tower on the Forest Lookouts page buffalo-mountain.html) or the Tennessee Pinnacle tower. Two searches and about four page reads found nothing on staffing, fires or current access.

Height and build history conflict across sources (60, 65, 70 ft for the 1917 tower; 80 ft for the 1938 tower, given by one source only). Climbing access is unconfirmed: no source states whether the tower may be climbed, so access is 'unknown' and the story says not to climb until the Bureau of Forestry confirms. A social-media post (not cited, not verified) dated the first tower to 1921 and said it stopped being used in the 1990s; the story does not use either claim. The staffing as_of is undated because the Lumber Museum page carries no date. No notable fire is documented in the sources reached.

The only history source is one 2019 StateImpact article, which describes a new Chestnut Ridge tower used by the Moshannon Forest District. The OSM point (41.1632, -78.3559) is about 2 km from OSM's 'The Knobs Fire Tower' (41.1487, -78.3354). The article calls the Knobs a 98-year-old tower no longer in use and describes an older tower near the new one without naming it. Check whether the record point is the new tower or the old one before trusting the location. Pennsylvania's best-known Chestnut Ridge tower (Pondfield, Fayette County) is a different structure and was not used. No access, status or staffing record beyond 2019 was found.

Thin record: three short pages, no photo, and the register gives no coordinates. The brief's coordinates (39.8162, -77.46999) sit near the pinnacle of the Chimney Rocks formation (39.81897, -77.47108 in the Hemlock State Explorer page), but no source ties the lookout to that spot, so check before using them. Do not merge with the separate Chimney Rocks Tower Site (Perry County), US 242 / PA 71.

Thin record: two pages, no build date, no structure description, no current-site source. The staffing item rests on the 1908-09 report quoted by Forest Lookouts, not on the register. A separate Franklin County Chimney Rocks (firetower.org US 241) and Blair County's Chimney Rocks Park are different places and were not used.

Current status rests on one 2024 blog post. No access rules, climbing guidance, staffing status, or notable fires were found. The Eastern US Lookouts page for this site has no readable content, so it is not cited. Facebook posts repeat the register wording but could not be opened, so they are not cited.

Height 18.3 m in the brief matches the Gazette's 60-foot figure, which describes the old Chickaree tower; the Clymer entry gives no height of its own. Status 'gone' rests on the register's 'removed in 1978'. The Chickaree record (Cambria County) is a separate site and may need its own pass if it is not already queued.

Built date rests on 1924 newspaper items quoted by the Forest Lookouts page; the newspapers themselves were not checked. The page's May and August 1927 items look like dating problems or a later project: the August 1927 item repeats the August 1924 steel-delivery wording word for word. Removal date and fate beyond the register's foundation-blocks note were not found in one web search. Record design and height_m were null; the 30-foot figure comes from the 1924 newspaper and sits in facts.design, not height_m, because it may be overall height. The trail-guide page is a paid listing; only its public summary was read, and it does not mention the lookout. Staffing names were not found.

Core history (1921 tower, 1985 tornado, 1987 replacement) agrees across four sources. Current access and climbing rules were not found. The 2018 replacement in the brief has no source. The brief's 30.5 m is 100 ft; the NHLR gives 93 ft. The Express article date (April 20, 2024) is printed in the article text. No new photos were checked.

Build history is well sourced by the NHLR and a long run of newspaper items on the Weebly page, which has nothing after 1959. Current condition and access are unverified; the registry entries date from 2008 and 2009. The NHLR page has a photo credited to Ron Stafford, but no image URL was captured, so none is listed. The brief's 1932 build year is a registry convention; the proposed correction adds the 1925 original.

Built year (1913), use (about 1917) and fate agree across both sources. The county does not: the brief's Lycoming (matching the register, coordinates 41.40735, -76.85541 not found in any source), Franklin (Forest Lookouts heading), and Fulton (a January 1923 Harrisburg Telegraph item names Fulton County, and both items mention McConnellsburg). Get a third source (county history or topographic name records) before changing the record's county or coordinates. No photo, staffing or fire data in these sources.

The build year is disputed (1934 register vs 1935 newspaper). The brief's coordinates (39.72843, -77.99167) are essentially the same point as the Cannonball map pin in a Virtual Globetrotting page (mytopo link 39.7283, -77.99160), so they may mark the concrete microwave tower, not the 1934 fire tower; verify before using them. The Cannonball description comes from a visit made by special permission, and the page gives no visit date. Do not encourage visits: the concrete tower is on private property.

Identity and design are consistent across four sources. The build date (1895 or 1896) and builder (Battlefield Commission or War Department) are disputed and the story says so. OSM gives height 18 m; the NPS 60-foot figure is 18.3 m, and the fact uses 18.3. Proposed name correction is for review only. The Stone Sentinels and Gettysburg Daily pages are undated or dated 2008; no current condition or hours source was found.

Single source: the OSM node tags and description. Two web searches found no page naming a Curry Run lookout. Grep of the cached PA storymap, Wikipedia lookout list, FFLA, FFLOS, GNIS and NHLR pages found no mention. Check the DCNR tower map and the local forest office for ownership, build date and status. Access is recorded as restricted (OSM: 'not accessible by public'); the story tells visitors not to climb it. Coordinates are 40.9509, -78.7490.

The record already holds the 2000 Pete Carron photo; no new photos were added. Source 5 is a hobbyist survey page, not an official source. Its NGS notes say photographs were not submitted, while the page says they were, so check NGS datasheet LY2684 before relying on the 'destroyed' status. The statewide list has two Dancing Ridge rows: a bald site used circa 1917 and this steel tower. The bald row may refer to this site or to Dancing Ridge Tower Site I (US 262); this was not resolved. The register and the Snow Hill entry disagree on whether 1935 was construction or the move. Staffing, fires, access and visitor rules are not in any source read.

Location is not established: the register gives no coordinates, and the record point is an approximate GNIS gap match. A Mount Minsi lookout page (https://willhiteweb.com/appalachian_trail/fire_lookouts/mount_minsi/del_water_forest_046.htm) describes a 1921 steel tower of 47 feet on Mount Minsi with footings still on the summit. Its height differs from this record's 60 feet, so it is probably a different tower. It is not used in the story; please check whether the two are the same. Removal date and any description of the site today were not found. Record agency 'August 1921:' is a parse error; the proposed correction is in corrections. The 1934 article quotes 'Forest Leaves' indirectly through the Forest Lookouts page and was not read at source.

Status conflict is real and unresolved from these two sources alone: StoryMap implies a current tower (replaced 2018), the lookout register says "Removed" with no date. The StoryMap's own text is internally inconsistent, calling the tower both '60 foot' and '80 feet' in the same sentence. Newspaper elevation figures also vary by 10 feet (1,921 vs 1,931 ft) between 1949 and 1948 clippings -- likely OCR/reporting noise, not a real change. A primary PA DCNR or Bureau of Forestry record, if available, would help settle current status.

Only two sources, and they agree on the 1934 build and 1975 removal. Neither gives height, builder, staffing or fires. The code M-M is not expanded in either source; the project's designs file has a McClintic-Marshall entry for Pennsylvania steel towers, but no source ties this tower to that maker, so the story does not name one. The regional Pennsylvania listing has a Dry Meadow row with only the county, so it is not cited. No photo was found. The corrections entry proposes kind 'tower' from the register's wording.

Build year and first site are disputed: register says 1930s near Reynoldsburg as Elliot Tower; storymap says 1930; former-sites register says 1931 at the Elliott Tower site (Jefferson County), moved 1985. The move rests on the former-sites register alone. No dated source confirms current condition. Access is inferred from private airstrip ownership (City-Data); no visiting information found. The record's built 1930 (from the storymap) is left unchanged, so a human should reconcile it with the 1931 event. The register's 'near Reynoldsburg' is unexplained; a Reynoldsville in Jefferson County would fit the former-sites register, but nothing checked confirms that.

No exact removal year found; 'before 1989' is the register's bound, so no removal event is recorded. The only description of what remains is one survey-mark page from a single 2008 visit. Wikipedia gives the summit as 2,693 ft (821 m) while the register gives the site as 2,678 ft (816 m); these are probably summit versus site figures, not a conflict about the tower, and the record keeps 816 m. The survey page's 1959 date is in the mark's name only and is not used. Visitor access was not established.

The record's map point (41.46429, -77.06481, marked approximate) comes from a GNIS name match to 'Elk Knob', not from any lookout source; the register says no coordinates are available. Treat the point as unverified, or remove it, before publishing. The record's elevation is blank and no source gives one. The register ('bald tower') and the regional listing ('unimproved bald top observation point') disagree on whether anything was built, so the kind should stay unknown until a source settles it. No photo was found.

Only two sources cover the tower's history: the register (build year, removal year 1981, registration date) and the Forest Lookouts page (1930 construction, 1939 observer). The 80-foot height is the planned height reported in 1930; no source gives the height of the finished tower, so facts.height_m is the planned figure. The removal year rests on the register alone. No source describes the site today or its public access, so access is omitted and the story says so. The Mapcarta point is an OpenStreetMap-based map entry with no status and is not evidence that anything stands there. The brief's coordinates and elevation (751 m) match the register. Forest Lookouts' 1930 article spells the village 'Elistie'; the story uses the register's spelling. No photos with URLs and licences were found. No fire history found; topic left out.

Generic name; the OSM node gives no builder, date or height. TopoQuest's Christman Fire Tower (historical) is at N40.916478 W75.681301, about 12 km southwest of this node, so it is probably a different site (not verified). The cached FFLOS register page for christmans-tower-site (firetower.org) says a steel Aermotor tower was built in 1921, moved in 1925 and renamed Mauch Chunk, with no coordinates; not used in the story. Do not confuse with NHLR's Mauch Chunk tower (US 1265, Weiser State Forest, 1936, 40.873685 -75.699445), which is a different structure. Status 'standing' is unverified. Two searches found nothing about this node.

Only the NHLR page yielded verifiable content within budget; the eastern_us_lookouts cached page for Cook Forest is a thin stub (nav index only, no body text) and the PA StoryMap/Wikidata/OSM sources already in the tower record were not independently re-verified. The 'design: Aermotor' and height_m=24.4 fields in the tower record come from pa_storymap and were not confirmed here; NHLR's stated 87.5 ft tower height conflicts with the record's 24.4 m (80 ft), flagged as a correction. Current staffing/operational status beyond 1977 is unknown from available sources.

Thin. The register and the Pennsylvania A-F list agree on 1917 and a tree post about 35 ft up. No source gives staffing, fires, fate beyond 'no longer standing', access or the present-day state. Searches for a Centre County source found nothing; the firelookout.org Pennsylvania inventory returned 404 on fetch, so it is unchecked. The record's coordinates are an approximate GNIS name match and are not verified for this tower. Clinton County First Mountain is a separate 1911 wood tower and must not be merged.

Two sources. The register gives the 1922 build by AFPA and the 1929 removal; only the register gives the 1929 date, and the Forest Lookouts page does not mention removal. The brief carries coordinates (40.8556, -75.7458) that no source read gives; the register says 'No coordinates are available', so check before using the map pin. The brief's agency and 42-foot height are kept. The 'Flag Staff Park' landmark comes from the Forest Leaves note only. A different tower in the same area, the Mauch Chunk Fire Tower on Bear Mountain (built by CCC crews in 1936 per its NHLR record), is a separate register entry and was not used. No photos with URLs and licences were found. No staffing or fire history in any source read; topic left out.

Thin. Two sources agree on a 1910 wooden tower of about 35 ft and on the Pike County location. Neither gives coordinates, staffing, fires, fate beyond 'no longer standing', or access. A search returned a firelookout.org inventory row that mentions Flat Ridge, but that page returned 404 on fetch, so nothing from it is used. The record's coordinates are an approximate GNIS name match and are not verified for this tower.

The 1916 tower is described two ways (steel Aermotor in the register, 20-foot wood in Forest Lookouts), so facts.height_m uses the 60-foot Aermotor from 1920 and the correction is proposed, not applied. Brief height 24.4 m matches the 80 ft figure; the 85 ft figure disagrees. The FCC entry comes from City-Data, a copy of FCC data; check FCC ULS call sign KDX454 before relying on it. No source describes the site now. Access left out: no source gives it.

The brief's record holds up: gone, registered September 16, 2008, elevation 605 m. The 1990 removal date comes from the register alone, and no source describes the site today or whether it is public, so facts.access and visit are left out. Brief height_m 61.0 is not supported by any source and is corrected to 27.4 m (about 90 ft, 1968 survey description); the 1919 plan of sixty feet is noted as a conflict. The 1949 bear-hunter story is not a fire and is included only as a notable event. Used about 6 page reads and 1 search.

Thinnest of the three. The register entry is the only source for the 1922 build, the 1987 removal and the 2008 registration; the Forest Lookouts page for Goodwin Knob has only a county header, so it is not cited. Staffing, design, agency and access are left out because no source gives them. 'Built on a building' is the register's wording; no source read says what the building was. PeakVisor gives the height of the knob, not of the tower, and the story says so. The brief's elevation_m is absent from the record and no value is proposed. A Mindat page for the knob was blocked (HTTP 403) and is not used. Used about 7 page reads and 2 searches, slightly over the per-tower read budget, to test for a second source that did not turn up.

The register's wooden tower is not clearly identified. Rambles (1994) describes four 50-ft wooden towers erected by Clarence Schock and removed in 1954, but it does not call them fire lookouts; the register's tower may be one of them, unconfirmed. The concrete tower (66 ft, built 1954) is called an observation tower by the sources and is still standing; it is not a lookout. The record's status 'gone' is right for the wooden tower only, so the status note explains the standing tower. The 1994 and 2019 sources are the only current descriptions read; no current park page was checked. Do not encourage climbing; the story only notes the public trail and the tower as a destination.

Build year and height conflict and no third source was found. Register: built 1942, 100-foot steel tower. Story map: built 1979 by Aermotor, 80 feet. The record has built 1942 and height_m 24.4 (80 ft), so the record follows the register for the year and the story map for the height; a human should decide. Current use is disputed: the register says staffed in fire season, while a 2019 visitor guide calls the tower abandoned. The staffing entry rests on the register alone and the guide may be out of date. The register names the Bureau of Forestry, while the park is a DCNR state park; the Bureau is a DCNR division, so this is not treated as an error. Web search found no history of the tower beyond the Wikipedia mountain article and the 2019 guide. The register's builder-plate photo credit is Mark Haughwout; no image URL was captured, so no photo was added.

Record fields for design, height, elevation, agency and registration all match the NHLR, so no corrections are proposed. Build date is unresolved: NHLR says 1921 and 60 ft, a 1922 visitor account says eighty feet, and a hiking guide says the 1930s. Staffing is not verified; the guide's still in use claim is unconfirmed. Climbability is not verified, so the access note says so. No official land-manager page was read. No photos added because credits and licences were not checked. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the earlier story said the PA 305 park entrance is the start of the loop and that getting there is on foot; the guide puts the loop trailhead near the Visitor Center and the routes read are hikes, and the story now says that. The 1922 account's date and the survey station wording are now in evidence.

Two sources, both read. The NGS survey text is only seen as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not on the NGS site. The agency value (Allegheny National Forest) comes from Forest Lookouts only and is not confirmed elsewhere; the 1926 description names the state department instead. Removal date is approximate (circa 1990). No staffing or fire record was found in the sources read, so the story omits staffing. A WebSearch found a 2007 Bradford Era column listing seven Elk State Forest towers built 1920-1925 without Hanley; it does not settle the date and is not cited.

The newspaper items are quoted on Forest Lookouts and were not checked against the original papers. The register gives no coordinates; the record's coordinates come from the Forest Lookouts map and were not verified. The 1962 staffing line is a dry-spell measure, not a standing crew. A WebSearch turned up nothing about the tower itself. The Irem Temple Country Club founding year (1921 per a search snippet) is not used; the listing says 1922.

Record build year 1945 is contradicted by 1921 (onX) and an April 1922 watchman report; correction proposed. Record design (Aermotor), height (26.2 m) and standing status have no source among the pages read, so they are left out of facts. Record agency (Clear Creek State Forest) is not named in the pages read; the 1922 report names only the Department of Forestry. Current condition, access and visit details are unknown. The 1994 end of fire watch rests on one onX trail-app note. A search result mentioned a campsite called Fire Tower on Clear Creek's Callen Run tract; not verified as this tower and not used.

Unresolved and needs a browser read before publishing. (1) The Pennsylvania storymap (storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/ed47c97ebe7246868ce8ef3e7139a0b4) would not load through fetch_text (27 characters, JavaScript-only). Dates for the move differ by about a year between the 1937 newspaper item and FFLOS. The Holmes Hill site has no coordinates in any source read; the stored point matches Sprout Point, so treat the record location as suspect. Newspaper items are quoted on Forest Lookouts and were not checked against originals. WebSearch found nothing on Holmes Hurst or the 1985 removal. No source describes either site today.

Build history rests on a 1933 to 1939 run of newspaper items, the NHLR entry, and the FFLA history. The Weebly page has nothing after 1939, so staffing and fate after that are unverified. A trail-app listing reportedly says the public cannot climb the tower; that page returned HTTP 403 and is not cited. The NHLR photos (cab interior, cabin) have no image URLs captured, so none are listed. The brief's record matches the NHLR (1935 built, 2012 registered, 24.4 m).

Thin record: two sources, both one line of substance (built 1916, still used circa 1917, no longer standing). No staffing, fire or access information in either source, so the story leaves those out. The brief gives coordinates 40.9836, -77.2729, but the FFLOS page says 'No coordinates are available'; we could not verify the brief's coordinates and did not change them. height_m is left null: the 35-foot figure from the Forest Lookouts page is for the observation post, not a verified tower height.

County conflict left open: the register and the Forest Lookouts heading say Luzerne County, while the April 1923 clipping places a fire near Shellton, Schuylkill County. The story says so and does not pick one. The 1923 clipping names a boy who died; the story and record leave the name out. The brief's record has no build year and no staffing; the register supplies 1921 and the Forest Lookouts page supplies 1937. Brief elevation 610.8 m matches the register's 611 m. No access information in either source, so access is left out. The 1937 staffing is one newspaper item, not a run of staffing records.

Built year 1923 in the record matches the completion reports; no correction. Height 18.3 m matches the 60-foot figure, which may be overall height rather than height to the cab floor. Record elevation 708 m (about 2,323 ft) differs from the 2,360 ft given in the 1922 and 1926 reports (about 719 m); not changed, for an editor to check. Wikipedia is undated, so the closed status and weather station rest on it alone. Record status standing is consistent with the 1972 article and Wikipedia, but no dated 2025-26 source was found. No entry for this tower in the cached NHLR or FFLOS pages.

Thin record: the FFLOS register page is the only Jones-specific source. Two web searches and the cached FFLOS Pennsylvania index turned up no other Union County tower source. No build date, staffing, fires or site description found. Source 2 is a general statewide remark, not about this tower. Checked 2026-10-10: the story no longer glosses 'bald tower' (the register does not define the term), and the statewide remark is paraphrased rather than quoted.

The register is the only Kahill-specific source; its 1922 build and 1946 removal are unconfirmed elsewhere. Source 2 (June 2021 post) dates Blaw-Knox towers in general to 1922-23, but the post is about Little Flat, so it is context only and is not evidence for Kahill. Coordinates N 41.591742, W -76.601338 match the brief, and the brief's elevation_m (701.6) matches the register's feet value. Two web searches found no other Bradford County source and nothing describing the site today; the site's public status is unknown.

Current status is the main gap: the newest source is the 2017 report, and the 2015 bid is quoted secondhand from a bid site via Forest Lookouts. The bid's award and the work itself are not verified. The NHLR still lists the site with no status field. Spelling varies: Keffers, Keffer's, Keffer. The 2017 report sentence is quoted only in part. No photo added; no height in facts (no source found).

History is well sourced from 1933-1952 newspaper items reproduced on Forest Lookouts; the removal date (1987) comes only from the register. Today's condition comes from one user-written hiking guide (MyHikes), dated November 04, 2023 and updated January 02, 2024; it does not say when its author visited, and it is the only source for the footings and the building by the lot. The guide calls the building a fire tower house; the 1933 item's stone caretaker's cabin may be the same building, which the story says is unconfirmed. The MyHikes guide mentions the hunting warning but the text we read was cut off before the rest of it. The brief's height 24.4 m is 80 feet and matches the press, not the 85-foot NGS figure. Access 'restricted' reflects the seasonal gate; no source says whether pedestrians can walk the road when gated. The brief's 'other_names': ['K'] looks like a stray letter from the Forest Lookouts heading 'K ELLOGG MOUNTAIN' and is not a real alternate name; we did not change the brief.

Brief's 1921 build date, 18.3 m height and Clearfield/Moshannon location are supported by NHLR and GantNews. Status conflict is the main open point: NHLR (undated) says active in fire season, while WPSU and Allegheny Front (May 2019) say no longer in use; the story follows 2019. No access source found, so no access key is recorded and the brief's access 'unknown' stands. No fire history found in the sources read. The NHLR photo credit (Ron Stafford) has no image URL, so no photo is added. A 2026 check of the current condition would need a source newer than 2019.

Sources disagree on height (80 ft in 1935, 82 ft in the TribLive article). The TribLive article carries no date in the copy read, so the 1984 deed and the restoration are undated; the restoration has no event entry for that reason. Park naming differs between sources. The Daily American 2015 article returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Check whether the tower is still padlocked and whether DCNR still runs climbs.

Two thin sources, both transcribed histories; no source describes the site today and access is unknown, so no access facts are recorded. Brief height 24.4 m agrees with the 80-foot figure in the 1939 report. The 1939 and 1949 articles are quoted second-hand on the weebly page. A 2025 Tioga State Forest map sheet uses the quadrangle name Lee Fire Tower but shows no structure, so it was not used. The brief agency value was a quote fragment and is proposed for correction.

Main correction: height_m 18.3 to 16.8 (1972 item says 55 ft). The 1922 Wilkes-Barre item quoted on the lookout site places the Little Flat tower at Little Flat, Blossburg, which does not match Centre County; not used, probably a different site or a mistake. The story no longer says the tower was in fire-season use in 1972 (the item shows only that someone was working on it), and no longer says mountain bikers use the forest roads. No photos added because credits and licences were not checked.

Thin record. Only source is OSM node 5718680680. Two searches (Lehigh Mountain, South Mountain, Lehigh County) found no lookout by this name. History of the 1922 steel tower is well supported by two 1922-24 newspaper notices, but both come through one Forest Lookouts page. The Loop page's 78-foot figure is unsourced. Only web source is the OSM node. Two searches and the cached NHLR and FFLOS PA indexes found no page for this tower, so no build year, builder, height, staffing or access. The record's status 'standing' is unverified. A local GNIS file (data/sources/peaks_gnis.json, not cited) has a named summit 'Lost Mountain' about 30 m from the node. Next: Pennsylvania DCNR Rothrock district records or local newspaper archives.

Thin record: the FFLOS register page is the only Low Knob-specific source. Two web searches, including one for a 1908 Pennsylvania forestry report, found no Low Knob-specific source; the 1908 lookout-station text they surfaced is from Maine and is not used. A TopoQuest Low Knob summit in Pike County (about 1,991 ft) is not clearly this tower site, so it is not used. The High Knob fire tower nearby is a different, still-active structure on Delaware State Forest land; not used. The register gives no coordinates, so the brief's point cannot be checked.
