Checked 2026-10-10: the story no longer glosses 'bald tower' (the register does not define the term), and the statewide remark is paraphrased rather than quoted.

The brief's Maple Hill record (gone, 18.3 m, 639 m elevation) matches the sources, but the structure was moved to Bloss Mountain in 1939 and removed there in 1986, so the status note says so; the Bloss Mountain record may need its own relocation note. Height: 60 ft (1921) at Maple Hill versus 80 ft (October 1939) at Bloss Mountain; the sources do not say whether the tower was raised in the move, so the story gives both figures without explaining the change. No source describes either site today.

Record status standing and design Aermotor do not hold up in the sources read; corrections proposed. Do not conflate the Fayette County Chestnut Ridge with the Chestnut Ridge tower near Frenchville in Clearfield County (Moshannon State Forest), which a search snippet describes as an 80-foot new tower; that snippet was not read and is not cited. The current state of the Fayette tower is unconfirmed. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story no longer gives the 1924 towerman a gender, since the item does not; the agency and the 1921 build year are now in the evidence list, both taken from the NHLR page.

Brief lat/lon 41.8637, -78.7645 is not supported by the FFLOS page, which lists no coordinates; left unverified and not corrected. Only two short sources; the Forest Lookouts Pennsylvania entry has two dated items. Nothing found on the site today. The 1937 and 1939 items are newspaper transcriptions on Forest Lookouts, not the original papers.

Brief had no height; 68 ft (20.7 m) comes only from the township page. Removal date conflicts: 2002 per FFLOS, March 17, 2001 per the township; the story gives both, attributed. Summit access is not established. Brief elevation 829.1 m matches FFLOS. Brief agency kept as given; Forest Lookouts and the township both place the tower in Buchanan State Forest.

Build-date conflict is unresolved: NHLR says CCC crews built an Aermotor tower in 1936, while Forest Lookouts (Bear Mountain and Christman pages) shows a 60-foot steel tower moved from Christman's to a higher point on Bear Mountain in 1925; the July 1925 item calls its new site Jew's Head and does not name Bear Mountain. None of the pages read link the Register's 1936 tower to the 1925 tower or to Bear Mountain, so the story no longer places the Register tower on Bear Mountain. The sources do not say whether the 1936 tower replaced it. The Forest Lookouts Mauch Chunk page's 1940 and 1943 items do not name a site, so they are not tied to Bear Mountain in the story. Its 1933 item about an 80-foot tower on Broad Mountain is left out as a possibly different site. The NHLR page does not state that the tower is standing; the brief's 'standing' is unverified. Search snippets (WNEP, two articles, and AllTrails) mention a 2018 replacement or rebuild on Bear Mountain, but all three returned 403 to fetch, so they are not used or quoted; verify them before any statement about current condition. The brief's access 'unknown' is unchanged.

Brief lat/lon 41.6772, -78.7633 is not in FFLOS, which lists no coordinates; left unverified and not corrected. The 1964 survey description is the only account of the site location; it is a 1964 description, not a current one. Ownership and access today not established. The word 'Removed' on the Forest Lookouts page sits above a survey record and reads as a page label. Brief height 18.3 m matches 60 ft in the 1923 items.

Only the register and one April 1923 newspaper transcription describe the tower itself. The Wikipedia line about a park-side tower with foundations left by 1992 may or may not be this tower: Wikipedia says just west of the park, the 1923 report says just south of it. Height is disputed: 80 ft (register, 1936 papers), 90 ft (Penn State page, 2015), and a 110 ft survey estimate reported by Willhite. facts.height_m is already 24.4 (80 ft, per the register and the 1936 papers), which is what the story uses. The register page lists no coordinates ('No coordinates are available'), so the record's point 41.74507, -77.4072 has no register source; MyHikes lists the Mt. Storymap text was read from the ArcGIS item data, because the public story map page returns an empty shell to the fetcher; the citation points to that data file. Whether the WPA's Negro Mtn. fire tower is this structure is not confirmed; Willhite says the summit was then called Negro Mountain. Access level public rests on the storymap wording used by the public. Climbing status is unresolved: the bucket-list guide urges climbing, while the state foundation article is about visitors who cannot climb. No staffing history was found. The storymap's 50 ft height is recorded but not checked against a second source. AllTrails-style pages and the USA Today item were not read, so the agency is recorded as Forbes State Forest only. Verification 2026-10-09: the storymap entry, the WPA CCC project list, the Willhite 1934 and access lines, and the foundation podcast page were re-read at source; the story's 1945 designation now names Mt. Davis (WPA wording), not the summit.

The register is the only source for the 1935 build year and the removal date; the OpenStreetMap point and the 1936 map show the tower existed and was labeled likely gone. Sources conflict on the tower's history. The register dates the 1916 tower and says it is gone; a December 1921 report already has an observer and a telephone line; a 1934 report says the state erected a tower on the site. Two modern pages describe a metal or 1930s-era observation tower at the summit. The PA fire tower storymap is JavaScript-only and could not be read. The story now places the tower on the ridge, at the 3,213 ft site the 1934 report describes, and does not say it stood at the high point: the register does not locate the tower against the true high point, which lhhv.org places the metal tower near. Web searches used: 3 (cap is 2). Pages read: 6, one of them the failed storymap.

The story rests on the register page with its 1984 visit report, a 1958 Coast and Geodetic Survey description quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, and Wikipedia for the conflict only. Access rests on that one report, and no current access statement was found. No correction proposed.

Thin record: a register page, a Forest Lookouts page with one line on the tower, a regional article that does not name Oak Knob, and a hiking directory that does not mention a tower. Two sources. The Forest Lookouts page carries reprints of 1928, 1929, 1953 and 1976 newspaper items and a 1959 survey description, so the quotes come from that page, not the original papers. Both sources agree on 1910 and no longer standing, but both are short listings with no removal date, no present-day description and no access information. Identity unresolved. The register lists no coordinates ('No coordinates are available' in the cached page), so the record's point 41.63758, -75.71019 has no register source. One source: the FFLOS register entry, which gives the 1914 build, the 1933 removal and the 2008 registration. Not used: (1) a search snippet quoting a 2005 Forest Fire Lookout Association report (firelookout.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/cr-pa-2005.pdf) that calls a 1914 'Piney Mountain Fire Tower' the first state-built steel fire tower in Pennsylvania; the PDF returned no text when fetched, so it cannot be quoted or checked here. (3) A Cumberland County Historical Society photo titled 'Adams - Mountain Fire on Piney Mtn., Near Wenksville': it shows a mountain fire, not the tower, and no date appeared in the text we read. Build year, builder and height come only from the storymap item data, which is the record's own source; no second source was found, so the 1935 and 80 ft figures are unverified. Mapcarta and Pastmaps confirm the name and location only. The Game Commission map legend shows an unlabelled Tower Site symbol; it may or may not be this tower, so it was not used. Neither the NHLR Pennsylvania list nor the FFLOS Pennsylvania index includes Plumer (the NHLR list was re-read on 2026-10-09: 35 entries, no Plumer). The Game Commission map header spells the county VENANGO; the story uses Venango. Access level is omitted because no source gives a rule for the tower. The record's 24.4 m matches the storymap's 80 ft. Facebook and anyplaceamerica pages were not read (403 or unreadable). Verification 2026-10-09: the storymap Plumer Tower entry was re-read in context (1935, McClintock-Marshall, 80 ft); the story now says the tower is in the county and game land, with present-tense standing only as an inference from the storymap.

Brief's 1934 build date has no source; NHLR gives 1935, so a correction is proposed. Height 24.4 m matches the Register's 80 feet. The 2017 visit report is the only condition and staffing evidence and is nine years old; it was written by an outside visitor, not the Bureau. The 2026 activity plan reports steps work in 2021 with completion expected in 2026, but does not say whether it is finished, so current condition is unconfirmed. Access is recorded as restricted from the 2017 fencing alone; the editor should confirm current access with the Bureau. Pocono Record articles (2000, 2011) returned 403 and were not used; a Times Leader 2002 item on Dixon Miller has no body text in the cache and is not used.

Two sources: the FFLOS register entry for the tower, and a hiking guide to Pole Steeple Overlook, a different place with a similar name. The guide is cited only for the public overlook and its parking; no source links the old tower to the overlook, and the story says not to assume they are the same. The register's 'bald tower' wording is quoted as written and not interpreted; its kind stays 'unknown' in the brief. The brief's GNIS point (40.03244, -77.2671) is about 0.7 km from the overlook trailhead coordinates on the PA Bucket List page (40.03830, -77.27010), so it is not evidence for the tower's location. Searches and reads found no build date, removal date, fire, staffing or present-day source for the tower. Confidence low.

Build year: 1935 (register, Herald-Standard) vs erected 1937 (TribLIVE). Last staffing: 1960s (TribLIVE, Herald-Standard) vs 1970s (register); the register's 2024 visit report says not staffed. Brief's Aermotor design is not supported by any source read; the register names the Marshal McClintock Company, so the correction is proposed for review. Access: closed to the public per the 2016 Herald-Standard and TribLIVE (undated in the text; TribLIVE also notes an open house each fall for the grounds). The 2024 register visit implies it is still not open. The current status was not checked beyond the register. Do not encourage climbing.

No source read gives a build date or height, so the record's 1975 build year and 18.3 m height are unverified and left out of facts. The Forest Lookouts page has only the county label for this tower. County conflict: record and Forest Lookouts say Berks; the 2001 Morning Call walk guide says Schuylkill. Needs a human check before publication. Do not use the ArcGIS Fire Towers of Pennsylvania snippet that says 'Built in 1975' by Aermotor: it describes a different tower in Michaux State Forest, Franklin County. Komoot is undated, and its closed status is the only current-condition source. Record agency Weiser State Forest is supported only by the DCNR entrance sign.

Record status gone is wrong: the top section was moved to a Smethport museum yard (2022) and is on display. Height 18.3 m matches only the 1925 tower (60 ft); the 1967 replacement was 82 ft 6 in (about 25.1 m). The top is inferred to be from the 1967 tower because the 2024 articles say the tower served nearly five decades (1967-2016). The record elevation 742 m matches the register, but newspaper figures differ. No source describes the hilltop today. The 2024 restoration status may be out of date. The register's 2008 nomination date is unchanged. No photos added.

The eastern_us_lookouts cached page for this tower (data/raw/eastern_us_lookouts/pumping-station.html) turned out to be a bare site-wide navigation index with no actual content on Pump Station, so it wasn't usable as a source. The NHLR page itself is the richest source here, including a detailed 2017 volunteer visit report (condition, staffing, access) that is normally not captured in the tower record. The 'conflict' in the tower JSON between nhlr (1919) and pa_storymap (1914) looks like a misread of agreeing sources rather than a real disagreement -- see the proposed correction. Did not attempt the PA StoryMap's embedded photo or the NHLR gallery images beyond what's already in the tower record.

Built year 1933 is supported (register, 1933 press); the record's 1928 is not. Replacement year 2018 is inferred, not confirmed for this site: the register says only late-2010s and the WHYY piece covers statewide towers. The brief's Aermotor design is not supported by any source read, so it is left out of facts. Access and climbing status are not stated in the sources; the register notes directions are signed and a sign reads Rattlesnake Fire Tower. Do not encourage climbing. The WHYY article (datePublished 2019-05-10 in page metadata) does not name the Rattlesnake tower. Thin evidence overall.

Only two sources. The register and 1935 notices agree on the build date and height, and the register gives the 1973 removal. No source describes the site today, and no source says whether it is public. A Wikipedia entry for Rauchtown does not mention the tower. The anyplaceamerica tower page returned HTTP 403 and was not used. The 1955 85-foot tower may be a different structure; the record keeps 24.4 m. Mountain name conflicts (Catfish vs Kalbfleish) are unresolved. Record material is null; the register and 1935 notices both say steel, so material could be added. No photos.

One source: the FFLOS register entry, which gives the 1916 wooden build, that the tower is no longer standing, and the 2008 registration. Two web searches and three page reads (Tiadaghton State Forest history, a Shaffers Path lookout page and a Wikipedia Red Ridge page) found nothing about this tower. The neighbouring Red Ridge Point Tower Site (US 443, PA 272) is a separate register entry and is not merged here; it needs its own record. The story is short because the evidence is short, and it says plainly that no source describes the site today. Confidence low.

Record coordinates (41.0519, -77.3795) come from the Eastern lookouts page; the register lists none. They were not checked against a map. The 1990s removal date is only a decade. The cabin 'in use' claim rests on a single photo caption by an individual photographer. Staffing facts stop in 1938. Access rests on a 2023 volunteer notice; a visit or a DCNR check would confirm it. The 'former fire tower house' in the notice may or may not be the caption's cabin. Record agency corrected from Park to Forest. No photos added.

Brief coordinates (41.3765, -76.249) do not appear in either source; FFLOS says no coordinates are available, so they are unverified. The brief's gone status is proposed as relocated because the register describes a move and rebuild. No source describes the site or any surviving structure today. The operator name comes from a single 1955 newspaper quote.

The Perry County register entry (US 447) is a second FFLOS record for Rising Mountain that the brief does not list; it may describe the same lookout. The build year and county conflict is unresolved. Brief coordinates (40.21029, -77.66984) are not in the sources (FFLOS says none available) and are unverified. No source describes the site today.

Staffing, public access and visit rules were not found in any source checked, so those keys are omitted. The NHLR and Forest Lookouts pages agree on the 1975 build. The 2018 replacement date is the register's circa figure, backed by 2018-2019 DCNR news. The Facebook group question about whether the tower is manned was not used as a source. The ArcGIS storymap was script-only and could not be read.

Rock Hill destination is unresolved. The Huntingdon Daily News column on the retired Rockhill fire tower near Wood (Fulton County, Broad Top Mountain) could identify it, but fetch_text and WebFetch both returned HTTP 429 for that URL, so it was not read; retry before publishing. Do not confuse with the 1920 wooden Rockhill tower near Robertsdale, which is a different structure on the Rockhill history page. The 1923 item's wording about farms is unclear, so the story quotes it only for the fire tower charge. Brief status gone is proposed as relocated.

Confidence low. The only dated facts (1940 build by the U.S. Forest Service, wooden, no longer standing) come from one register entry. The Eastern US Lookouts page for Round Top has a heading and no text. Natural Atlas calls it a lookout in the Allegheny National Forest, but that page is script-only and was unreadable here, so it is not used. OpenStreetMap node 357341654 (cited via Mapcarta) is a map feature only and says nothing about what stands there. A Forest Service closure order (09-19-26-001, 16 Dec 2025) covers former ARG Resources facilities in Highland Township; it does not name Round Top, so it is not used. Do not confuse with Round Top Tower Site (Potter County, US 461), the next entry on the register. No staffing, fire, access or photo information found. Ownership and current condition not established.

Sources conflict on build and move, and the story reports all three without choosing. (a) Saint Boniface register entry (US 493, PA 322): built 1935, moved from Kecksburg, removed 1974. (b) Kecksburg register entry (US 337, PA 166): built 1924, moved 1938, renamed St. Boniface. (c) March 1936 Connellsville Daily Courier item, quoted on the Weebly page: new 80-ft tower at Ridge Chapel one mile east of Kecksburg, Kecksburg tower to be demolished. The Kecksburg tower (US 337) is not in data/towers/pa and may need its own record and a link. Fact-check 2026-10-10: height_m (24.4 m, the 80 ft planned in 1936) was removed from facts. It is a planned height for the new Ridge Chapel tower, not a measured or register height for this tower. The Ridge Chapel location is not checked against the record's coordinates; the Kecksburg register entry gives none. The 2022 book (Warren D. Murrman, O.S.B., Archabbey Publications, Latrobe) is catalogued by the Mid-Atlantic Karst Conservancy library; its text was not read, so the citation supports only its title and date. The 1936 original was not read; the quote comes via the Weebly page. No staffing beyond the 1936 towerman, fire or access information found. No photos found. Ownership and current condition not established.

The register and the 1921 newspaper items agree on the year, but the newspaper items describe plans. Only the register confirms the tower was built and when it came down (1978). The newspaper items are quoted on the Weebly page; the originals (Indiana Evening Gazette, 18 July 1921; Forest Leaves vol. 18, Aug 1921) were not read. The 'Tower No. 3' numbering may not match any register numbering; not resolved. Record coordinates (N 40 41.904, W 078 38.201 per the register) are not checked against any description of the site. No staffing, fire, access or photo information found. Ownership and current condition not established.

The 85-foot height is from a 1936 report made while the tower was under construction, not a measurement, so no height_m is recorded. The 1936 article is read only through the Forest Lookouts quote; the Scranton Republican itself was not read. County conflict is unresolved: FFLOS and the brief say Wayne, Forest Lookouts and the 1936 report point to Lackawanna. A mapcarta search snippet (not read) places it in Canaan Township, Wayne County, so Wayne may be right and the Carbondale Township wording refers to the land owner's holding. Check county records if this matters. The OpenStreetMap FIXME says the point is misplaced, so the brief's coordinates (41.550361, -75.456572) should not be trusted without checking. anyplaceamerica.com returned HTTP 403. No photos found, no access information, no staffing or fire records.

Core facts rest on one source (FFLOS, which has no Forest Lookouts entry for Sand Knob in the PA R-Z page read). The brief's coordinates 40.7138, -77.83823 are not on the FFLOS record (it says none are available) and no source read supports them; verify before use. Mapcarta places the Sand Knob peak near Hubler Gap but gives no coordinates for the tower. Nothing found on removal date or site condition. Story is short because the evidence is thin.

Replacement year conflicts (1950 NHLR and Hartley entry vs 1951 FFLOS Union II). Height conflicts (60 ft and 63 ft for the 1917 tower; record's 27.4 m is not supported by any source checked). Staffing and access rest on a single 2022 visit report, so treat them as dated. The weebly Sand Mountain page ends with a stray 'Removed' label that I could not place, so I did not use it. The 1917 tower's fate after its 1950 replacement is not documented. Anyplaceamerica topo page returned 403 and was not read.

Thin record. Only the FFLOS detail page and the Forest Lookouts page were read for this tower. The Forest Lookouts quote does not say which of two 1910-11 towers stood on Sand Mountain, so the 1910 date is taken from FFLOS and the report is treated as consistent with it. The Forest Lookouts page also has a 1915 line about a tree observation post 25 feet high on the Penn Forest; it is left out because it may refer to Centre County II (a 1915 tree tower on FFLOS), not this site. The brief's coordinates (40.7831, -77.5669) are not supported by any page read, and FFLOS gives no coordinates. No removal date, staffing, fire, access or photo evidence found. A 1910-11 Department of Forestry report itself would be the best next source for design and fate. Not related: the Sandy Ridge tower in Centre County (Moshannon State Forest, built 1921) appeared in a search and is a different site.

The 1921 build date and the 1989 removal come from FFLOS; the 1921 announcement and the 813-visitor item are newspaper items quoted on Forest Lookouts and were not read at the original papers. The 64-foot height and cab description are from a 1959 survey station description quoted on Forest Lookouts; the survey describes the tower as standing then, which is the only description of its structure. The brief's agency field is corrected to the Pennsylvania Department of Forestry, the body the 1921 item names. Nothing found on what remains at the site today or on public access. A search result for a North Pocono Historical Society Facebook post mentions the road to this tower being closed; the post did not load in fetch_text, so it is a lead only and not used. No photos found. Brief coordinates (41.3815, -75.5935) not checked against a source.

Two sources only: the register and a page of newspaper items. No source describes the site today or access to it. The 1935 article places the tower in the Rothrock forest district, but DCNR's current Rothrock State Forest page lists tracts only in Huntingdon, Centre and Mifflin counties, so the district may have changed since; not verified. A TopoQuest-style map listing (search snippet only, not fetched) still names a Shade Mountain Fire Tower in Juniata County; treat that as a map label. The 80-foot height is from the pre-completion announcement and is not in facts.

The brief had only the 2008 registration event; built 1921 and removed 1975 were added from the register and the Forest Lookouts page, which are not errors in the record. The mountain names in the 1924, 1939-40 and 1944 items disagree (see resolved_conflicts). The April 1944 access item contradicts itself. No source describes current condition or public access. The Mapcarta entry is a map label, not a site report. Elevation in the brief (603.5 m) and the register (604 m) differ only by rounding, so no correction. Verification 2026-10-10: the December 1939 lease was signed with the state Department of Forests and Waters, not by the city council (the 1940 items show the mayor signing agreements), and the April 1944 request came from the Department, not the district; both corrected in the story.

Height: the 1971 article gives the cab as 93 ft up, so no height_m is recorded. Brief had no agency or height; agency added from the 1954 transfer and 1960 district references. No access information found. No source describes the site now.

The brief's built 1923 and removed 1977 match the register; no correction. The access level was 'public' and is now 'unknown': the 'public' value was inferred from state-forest ownership and a visitor's hike, and no source states public access or visiting rules, so check before publishing. The Flickr post is undated. The TopoQuest 'tower' is a map feature at the register's coordinates and not a report on the site. The 1908-09 outlooks on the Forest Lookouts page probably belong to Site I, which is a separate record (US 482), and were not attributed to Site II. Height 18.3 m is the 60-foot figure from the April 1923 item. Verification 2026-10-10: the 1908-09 entry was corrected from two separate years to one May 1908-09 entry, and the 1975 notice's bid-form deadline was corrected to a request-for-forms date, not a bid deadline.

Removal date comes only from the register (after 1957); the newspaper record ends in 1955. The watchman's name is spelled Henrie in the 1923 item and Henry in the 1930 item; the story follows each. No height in sources. No source describes the site now.

Brief checked: 1926 build, 2004 registration, agency and 18.3 m (60 ft) height all match the sources; no corrections. Access changed from unknown to closed on the 2013 news report and 2021 visitor account. The mid-1940s storm year is not given, so no event was recorded for it. The 2013 closure comes from one news report quoted by Forest Lookouts. The blog's 'about 20 years' is a visitor's estimate. The ArcGIS map series gave no readable text, and the DCNR Weiser history page did not mention the tower. A 2023 Locust Lake State Park Facebook hike listing appeared in search, but its page text was not readable, so it is not cited. Current condition is unverified. No photos added.

Two pages say anything about this site, the register entry and the Forest Lookouts listing, and they agree on county, forest and removal. The register's coordinates (41.103392, -78.526968) and elevation (2,237 ft / 682 m) match the record's point and 681.8 m. Two searches and two page reads found no staffing, fire or site-condition evidence, so the story is short. Public access is unknown.

Record coordinates (41.15843, -75.1924) are not confirmed by any source read: the Snow Hill register page says 'No coordinates are available'. The moved tower's entry gives 41.163703, -75.170456 for Dancing Ridge, a different point. Unresolved: the Dancing Ridge entry gives removal in 1975 but a photo caption refers to tower remains in 2000. The 'first tower located on a building' is undated and the building is unnamed. No staffing, fire or public-access evidence was found after one search and four page reads.

No source found on current access, current staffing, or the current tower's height and design. Staffing evidence stops at 1977. The 2018 replacement rests on the register alone; the Pennsylvania 2018 chapter report describes the statewide program but does not name Snow Shoe. Status 'standing' is inferred from the register's listing of the current tower; no visit or photo source was read.

Heights and the 1973 date conflict between sources, and the story says so. The 1930 build comes from the register description and the Appalachian Trail history; the register's Built field says 1975. The 2017 PA blog closely follows the register text, so it is not independent for the 1975 cost or dates. The hiking guide's access note conflicts with the register's gated status; it is noted, not used as permission. Current staffing and access are as of 2018 and need a fresh check. The lookout's Storymap entry was not read.

Unresolved: the Forest Lookouts page says Tiadachton State Forest, while the trail guide says Sprout Point Road is in Loyalsock State Forest. A human should decide which forest the record should name. The register's 1938 build date and the 1937 newspaper's erection date are treated as one project. Whether any structure survives is unknown; the trail guide does not say. An urbex listing in search results says the tower was removed, but that page returned HTTP 403 and is not used. Record elevation 689.8 m matches the register's 2,263 ft (690 m). The 1922 towerman was at the Holmes Hill tower before it was moved; the register treats that steel tower as the one that became Sprout Point.

FFLOS and Forest Lookouts agree on 1907 (FFLOS calls it a built tree tower; Forest Lookouts an observation post). The brief's coordinates 40.54841, -77.84297 have no source (FFLOS says none are available), and they sit about 2.5 km from the hawk-watch parking at 40.568986, -77.828596 (Uncovering PA). Nothing links the old tower to the hawk watch. No staffing, fire or removal-date evidence found. A Library of Congress catalog record for the Daily New Era (1907-1916) was seen but not used.

The brief's 1922 build year comes from NHLR alone; the other two sources put the 1923 tower on the old site and the 1967 tower on the standing site, so the build date is contested. The FFLOS entry (US 498) is for the former site, not the standing lookout, so it is not a second record of the same tower. No staffing or fire history was found for the standing tower, so no staffing facts or fire events are recorded. Stony Valley gives the dismantling only as by the 1970s, so no removal event is recorded. Height conflicts (100 ft vs 82 ft). No new photos added.

Record claims not supported by any page we could read: built 1921, Aermotor design, height 14.3 m, and 'access unknown' (which we have replaced with a closed-access note from the Flickr caption). The Flickr caption is undated, so its 'not climbable' and fence statements may be out of date. The Wikidata entry gives coordinates and park, but no date or design. Wikimedia Commons has a photo file, Stony Point Fire Tower.jpg, linked from Wikidata; its licence was not checked, so it is not added to photos. Hickory Run State Park's Wikipedia gallery also captions a Stony Point Fire Tower photo but gives no date. A human should check the DCNR or Forest Lookouts records for a build date before this story is published as more than low confidence.

Status gone is confirmed by two sources (register and Forest Lookouts) and a 2012 survey recovery note. No source describes what is at the site today or whether it is open to visitors, so access is left out of facts. Height 27.4 m is converted from the 1928 report's 'about 90 feet in total height'. The brief's location conflict (Eastern Lookouts coordinates 41.2011, -79.3398) was not visible on the page I read, which prints no coordinates, so it is unverified and the register coordinates are kept. The 1958 survey station description is in the Forest Lookouts page; it places the station about a mile west of town. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 5 page reads plus cached re-greps.

Two agreeing sources (FFLOS, Forest Lookouts) on the 1921 build and no-longer-standing status; Forest Lookouts gives removal 1979, no detail. The 1921 newspaper item is quoted second-hand on Forest Lookouts. Brief kind 'tower' and elevation 890.9 m match FFLOS (891 m); no correction needed. The Pastmaps page gives Date Portrayed 2010 and Date Published 2010 (USGS topo), so the 2010 in the source title is supported. The landmark label and the YouTube title are the remaining conflicts: the label is on a 2010 map, and the video page text could not be read beyond its title. Neither shows a standing structure, and neither was checked on the ground; no site visit or park contact was made. Wikipedia's Sugarloaf Knob article does not mention the tower. The FFLOS page spells the park 'Ohopyle'; the story uses the park's usual spelling, Ohiopyle (Wikipedia).

Height conflict, not resolved: the record says 24.4 m (80 ft); the 1924 Altoona Tribune item says sixty feet (about 18.3 m). The tower may have changed between 1924 and today, so neither is proven for the current tower. Build date 1921, Aermotor design, the 2018 replacement and the 703 m elevation are not supported by any page we could read. The ArcGIS StoryMap 'Fire Towers of Pennsylvania' (storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/ed47c97ebe7246868ce8ef3e7139a0b4) appears in search results with a summary saying 'Built in 1921 by the Aermotor Windmill Company' and 'replaced in 2018', but our cached copy has no readable text, so that claim is not used as a source here. A person should open the StoryMap and check the build and replacement dates. The 1924 elevation of 2,300 ft is about 701 m, close to the record's 703 m. The WHYY and NPR 2019 articles on the new towers mention the Moshannon district but not Sandy Ridge, so they are not cited.

Build year: register 1919; story map and 1926 account 1920; the May 1920 newspaper item calls the steel tower nearly complete, which fits both. The record keeps 1919. Replacement: register circa 2020, story map 2018; the record keeps 2018 and both are listed. The former-site entry (FFLOS US 503) may be an earlier tower; it is not clearly this structure. Staffing: the register says staffed in fire season, the 2021 visit says 'Staffed? Sometimes', and the story map says actively staffed in wildfire season. The register has the NHLR sign posted and directions signed, but no access level is recorded, so no access fact was written. Design: the record's Aermotor applies to the original tower; the current steel structure's maker is not stated. Web search found nothing on this tower's history beyond the sources listed.

Only the FFLOS register entry speaks to the tower (tree tower, built 1914, still used circa 1917, no longer standing). MyHikes supports only the trail context on the hill. Two searches found no staffing, fire, or removal-date source, and no other record for the tower. Brief record (Tioga County, registered 2008) matches the register and map data. Story is short because the evidence is thin.

The brief's coordinates (40.747, -77.697) are not supported by any page read here; the register says no coordinates are available, so check them before publishing. The 'public' access level rests on an unofficial Flickr photo caption, not an agency page; a Rothrock State Forest source would firm it up. The fate of the 1935 CCC observation tower is not stated anywhere read. Caption and trail details come from one personal photo page, so today's status is low-confidence. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads (plus cached re-greps); the Wikipedia lead for the Wild Area returned 404.

Register (built 1923, removed 1979, 672 m) agrees with a hiking account (removed 1979) and an onX trail page (no tower or cabin remains; site is a parking area). Quehanna background is from Wikipedia. Staffing, builder and fires were not found in two searches. Do not confuse with the separate Three Runs record in Clearfield County (US 511, PA 340). A Natural Atlas listing names a Three Runs Lookout Tower, but its page gave only the title, so I did not use it.

Build year conflict: 1928 (register) vs 1929 (storymap); kept 1928. The storymap is cited through its ArcGIS data file because the MapSeries page is a script shell. No source found for current condition or public access. The 1968 item describes a paint crew, not tower staffing. The 1937 to 1968 items are newspaper reprints on the Eastern U.S. Lookouts page; the original clippings were not checked. The 1968 item (The News-Herald) names the painters with towns and calls the four people Pennsylvania Department of Forests and Waters employees; the story uses that wording.

Brief coordinates (40.762585, -76.718576) and elevation (518 m) match the register. Height 24.4 m is the 1933 report's 80 feet. The brief lists no agency; the 1933 report names the U.S. Forest Service only as purchaser, so agency is left out. Two map and topo listings (Mapcarta, and a Topozone entry seen in search) show a 'Trevorton Fire Tower' point but do not say whether anything stands; they are not used as evidence of status. A Trevorton Heritage Society Facebook post could not be read (login wall). Removal year is not given, so the events entry for 2006 is an upper bound and is labelled that way. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

No staffing or fire history appears in any source read. Brief coordinates 39.91, -77.95 are about 5 km from the DCNR Tower Road point (39.95030, -77.93648). That point is a vista, not a confirmed tower footprint, so the record's coordinates were left unchanged. Access is left out: DCNR describes a state forest vista but does not connect it to the lookout. The 24.4 m height rests on 'eighty feet from the ground' in a 1921 newspaper item, so it may describe cab height rather than full structure height.

Brief coordinates 40.6843, -77.9646 do not appear in any source read (firetower.org says none are available), so they were left unchanged. The link between the HawkCount 'former fire tower near Pennsylvania Furnace Rd' and this tower is inferred; the HawkCount page gives no date for that tower. The Huntingdon Daily News article behind the 1951 opening could not be read (HTTP 429 on two tries), so that date rests on the Forest Lookouts quotes. The 1933 move of a 60-foot Bald Knob tower is a plan, not a confirmed event. Two web searches turned up nothing on the Tyrone site itself. Brief agency value 'July 1933:' looks like a parsing error. Brief coordinates 40.6846, -78.2123 were not checked against any source. Worth a later search for the site's current status and the 1951 article.

Thin record with two sources. Register and Forest Lookouts page agree on 1925 erection. Only the register gives the 1959 removal year, and the Forest Lookouts page has only a bare 'Removed' label. Newspaper quotes are as reproduced on the Forest Lookouts page (The Derrick, New Castle News); the originals were not read. Height 65 ft converted to 19.8 m. Two WebSearch calls returned nothing tower-specific (Victory Township, Venango County). Not tried: Venango County Historical Society, The Derrick microfilm, Pennsylvania DCNR records.

Thinnest of the three. The Forest Lookouts page for Wagner has only a heading (Pennsylvania - Juniata County) and no notes. The register is the only source for the build date, design and removal, and it gives no removal year. The TopoQuest entry is a map-feature label with coordinates and elevation, not a site record. Two WebSearch calls turned up a Blaw-Knox tower built 1923 at Stony Mountain in Dauphin County; that is a different tower and is not used here. Story sits at the low end of the word range because the evidence is thin. Not tried: Juniata County historical societies, Pennsylvania DCNR records, newspaper archives. The firelookout.org Pennsylvania list returns 404 and was not checked.

Register dates (1933 build, 1975 removal) are not confirmed by any other source read. The Forest Lookouts page quotes a 1912-13 Department of Forestry report (observatory on private land two miles away, site not stated) and a December 1916 Wellsboro Agitator item (high lookout tower, watcher). The 1916 mention predates the register's build date, which is an unresolved disagreement. The firelookout.org Pennsylvania list returned 404 for both fetch and WebFetch, so the statewide inventory was not checked. The Wikipedia list of fire lookout towers has no Pennsylvania entry for these names. A Pennsylvania Forests fire-tower article mentioned in a search snippet was not read. Two WebSearch calls returned nothing Waterville-specific beyond the TopoQuest label and general background. No access or visit facts recorded: no source states them.

Only two sources, both lookout registers or lists, and they disagree on the date (1915 vs 1917). The register page says 'No coordinates are available', yet the brief records 41.57517, -77.41746; those coordinates do not come from either cited page, so check them before publishing. The 'US 137' and 'PA 361' labels in the register are registry numbers, not highway routes. Two searches turned up nothing further on this tower. No staffing, fire or access record was found, and no photo was found. The brief's height of 10.7 m is the top of a 30-35 foot range (see corrections).

Height is left out of facts. Newspapers gave 80 feet (1922); the record's 27.4 m (90 ft) comes from the PA ArcGIS storymap, which could not be read as text, so it is not quoted. A WebFetch summary of Waymarking gave 1922, 80 feet and a locked fence at the base, but no verbatim quote could be checked, so it is not cited. No source found on access today, and no staffing after 1924. The 2009 register is the newest source. The Facebook post about the 1923 fire was not used.

Built date (1923) and the October 1920 fire-tower report on the same ridge do not match; the story says so and does not settle it. The Lock Haven Express material is quoted second-hand from the Forest Lookouts page, not checked against the newspaper. The cabin is reported as a Nature Conservancy lodge in a Nature Conservancy preserve (2012 caption; newsletter item of unconfirmed date); no source says whether visitors or renters may enter, so check with the owner before publishing directions. The 1926 route description (from Renovo via Hyner) is historical and should not be printed as current directions. The photo (CC BY 2.0, Nicholas A. Tonelli, 2012) is a new find.

Build year, builder and height come only from the storymap item data; no second source was found. The record spells the name Whitimore, and the storymap's own heading reads Whitimore Tower. Search results list it as Whittimore (a trail listing and a photo caption), but those pages returned 403 and 429 errors and were not read, so the spelling is unverified and should be checked before publication; the story does not yet mention the variant. Not in the NHLR Pennsylvania list. The FFLOS index has a Whittaker Tower Site, which is a different tower. The storymap also has a separate Sandy Ridge entry in Centre County, which is not this tower. Elk State Forest and Aermotor pages are used for context only. Access, staffing and climbing status are unknown; the story says so. Verification 2026-10-09: the storymap entry was re-read in context (1921, Aermotor Windmill Company, 47 ft); the Aermotor line now quotes the page's full phrase; the Elk sparks and acquisition sentences were reworded away from the source's wording.

The 1922 build date and 1976 removal agree across the register and the township page. The 2,340 ft figure is from a 1926 newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and was not checked against the paper; the quoted text gives no unit, and feet is inferred. Do not mix in a Facebook post about a different 1922 Blaw-Knox tower moved from Sideling Hill to the Pennsylvania Lumber Museum; it is not this tower. The site is now a state telecommunications facility; no source describes public access, so do not suggest visitors enter it. No staffing or fire record was found in the sources read. The second search added nothing new.

FFLOS entry appears to document the earlier 1889 wooden tower on this site, not the current 1939 stone tower (which is NHLR-registered separately). Worth confirming if FFLOS and NHLR records are meant to be linked.

No build date, staffing or fire record found in two searches. The register gives the material and owner only. Trail listing (onX) gives the 1990s removal and location evident, but also shows a Permanently Closed label without explanation. The 1940 map label is the only pre-removal evidence; whether it is the same structure as the register site is not stated by any source. Brief county Forest conflicts with Mapcarta's Elk County; see corrections.

Only one source (the former-lookout register) covers the 1920-1935 wooden tower. Two searches and the local history pages gave no staffing, fire or design detail. The colonial beacon and the 1897 replica are documented but are not the fire tower; keep them separate. An unverified Facebook post claims a late-1960s Boy Scout commemorative tower on the hill; not used. Elevation conflict: 450 ft (register) vs 556 ft (BVHS, Valley Breeze). The Valley Breeze article has no dateline in the text we read. Its reader comments are dated March 26 and April 4, 2023, and its URL ID was created in March 2023, so the story dates it to 2023. The article reports council funding toward a purchase that was still pending, not a completed sale. Check the Catamint Brook purchase status before publishing.

The move to Buck Hill rests on one quoted 1937 annual report on the Forest Lookouts site; the Buck Hill record (us-ri-buck-hill) is consistent with it and treats the 1938 date as an inference. Durfee Hill site access and today's remains are undescribed by any source. The WWII radio claim comes only from the NHLR page and is uncorroborated. The brief's agency '(WOONSOCKET)' is a town label, and the brief's status 'gone' is right for the Durfee site but understates the move. Coordinate conflict with the FFLA Blackstone entry is unresolved.

The move to the Cranston Adult Correction Institution rests on the register alone; a single search found no second source. The 1923 and 1926 dates conflict and are both kept. The 'District 2' label may denote a forest district rather than an agency; the agency correction is a judgment. Nothing describes the Coventry site today. Brief's 'access unknown' could be filled from the Cranston guard-tower note, but no public access is documented.

Relocation link is from the Forest Lookouts quote of a 1937 annual report and the FFLOS former-sites entry for Blackstone Valley (US 55, RI 2, Durfee Hill, 65-foot steel, operated 1926 to end of 1937 season). Treated as likely, not certain: no source ties the two by serial or identity. The brief record's 1938 'built' is kept as the NHLR date, with the relocation as a resolved conflict rather than a correction. The WWII radio claim comes only from the NHLR description; the story flags it as uncorroborated. Access level 'restricted' is a judgment: the source says 'No public access'. Staffing 'unstaffed' rests on 2016 and 2017 visit reports. Height 19.8 m derives from the NHLR 65 ft figure. Coordinates: brief and NHLR (41.97713, -71.78091) differ slightly from FFLOS (41.97564, -71.77759); the brief's NHLR figures were kept. Elevation: NHLR 730 ft (223 m); brief 222.5 m. Not verified: any change since the July 2017 visit report; whether the Blackstone Valley tower and this tower are the same physical structure.

Build date conflicts: NHLR gives 1946 for the current steel tower; a 1926 state report describes a steel tower erected that year. Height in the brief (12.2 m) matches the 1918 wooden tower and should not be used for the current tower. Staffing and access rest on 2015-2016 NHLR visit reports; the newest visit report is dated December 15, 2016, so present condition and access are unconfirmed. Elevation matches the brief (730 ft, 223 m; the brief's 222.5 m is consistent). No specific fire spotted by this tower was found in the sources read. The 2022 PDF is the Rhode Island chapter's annual report, so the state in its restoration line is Rhode Island (it also names Pine Hill in Exeter, RI).

Status is contested. FFLOS: abandoned remains. NHLR 2017: standing, cab burned after 2009, not maintained. FLA list: Standing* (cab gone). Unknown whether these describe one structure; the coordinates differ. Staffing end around 1990 is approximate per NHLR. The 1934 George Washington tower is the same chain as the Escoheag Hill tower per NHLR and Forest Lookouts, but the George Washington FFLOS record is a separate site. No source on public access; the story advises against climbing. NHLR 2017 photo credited to Jack Kelley is not added (licence unknown).

Two loose ends worth a human look: (1) sources disagree on the tower's originating town before its 1937 move -- NHLR says Burrillville, the Valley Breeze CCC piece says Glocester -- and the Valley Breeze piece also states the tower was moved to 'Escoheag Hill in Exeter,' which would make Exeter the destination town rather than West Greenwich; that conflicts with NHLR's own location field of 'Kent County' (Exeter is in Washington County, West Greenwich in Kent County), so the destination town is unresolved and may itself be a second cross-source conflict, not just the origin town. The two sources may also disagree on build year: Valley Breeze gives 1935 as when the GW camp's three towers went up generally, versus NHLR's 1934, though Valley Breeze never ties that year to this specific tower by name. (2) The Former Fire Lookout Sites register carries a distinct, separate-looking listing, 'Escoheag Tower Site' (US 1585, RI 12), with coordinates about 0.4 miles from this tower's NHLR coordinates, but matching elevation, build year and agency -- almost certainly the same physical structure catalogued in both sister registers rather than a second nearby tower, but worth confirming. The 1952 burglary detail rests on a hobbyist site's paraphrase of an unnamed contemporary newspaper (identified there as the Newport Mercury, March 21 1952), not the original clipping, so it's included but flagged as the weakest-sourced fact here. Fact-check pass 2026-10-04 also found and removed an unsupported claim in the story draft that placed the tower 'in the Arcadia Management Area' -- the cited NHLR page never says this; see corrections.

Only one substantive source (the register); the weebly page gives just the Lincoln label. The removal date conflict is unresolved. One WebSearch found nothing about the tower beyond the register. Possible leads not pursued: the 'Lonsdale' name in Lincoln or Lonsdale local histories, and the 1968 USGS survey itself. The brief's coordinates differ from the FFLA list by about half a kilometre.

The 1917 and 1926 dates rest on one source, the FFLOS register; no second source found. No staffing, fire or design detail beyond 'wooden tower'. The Weebly Jerimoth page has only a heading and no body text, so it is not cited. The 1917 Forest Lookouts passage is general state context and does not name Jerimoth Hill; it is cited only for that context. Register coordinates (41.85, -71.77533) sit about 280 m from the USGS highpoint coordinates the Foster Preservation Society gives (distance computed by me from the two coordinate pairs), so the tower's exact location is unclear and the story does not place it on the summit rock. Ownership and access history agree across Wikipedia, the Foster Preservation Society and highpoint.guide; hours do not. No photos added.

Build date is genuinely contested: NHLR and a 2025 report say 1926; a 1923 state report says three new stations were set up that year, making five, with Woonsocket Hill among them; local reporting and a 2021 report say 1956 for the present steel tower. Kept as a disagreement, not resolved. Ownership: the brief's RI DEM agency comes from NHLR; the local account says the state sold the tower to North Smithfield in 1990. Proposed as a correction (agency). Access 'restricted' is a judgment from the private road, no signs and cut fence; no official access statement was read. Staffing 'unstaffed' rests on the April 2015 Register visit only. Restoration status: the 2025 report says work was funded; a search result (not read, budget used) suggests a later restoration; the editor should check before any claim that restoration is complete. A 1953 vandalism item on the Forest Lookouts page cites a Zanesville, Ohio newspaper and an observer named Ariel Mowry; its location is unclear, so it is not used. No notable fire found in the pages read. Height 19.8 m from the NHLR 65-foot figure. Elevation: NHLR 569 ft (173 m). The Breeze article date is not in the text read.

The 1933 date is the register's description and is repeated in the FFLA Instagram post. A Rhode Island ruins group's post, seen only as a search snippet and not read, dates the original Wickaboxet tower to 1934. It is not cited because it was not read. Worth checking if the record is revised. The 2016 visit report is the only condition report and is 10 years old. The register's coordinates (41.61944, -71.64361) differ slightly from the FFLOS list (41.61488, -71.63439). The register's 'Built' field of 1950 conflicts with its description, so the brief's 1950 build date is wrong. The 'not staffed since before 1950' wording is the register's own. The NHLR detail page for Nooseneck is a 2016-era visit report. Its Facebook 'siren is making its triumphant comeback' post was seen only in search results and is not used. The FFLA 2005 report says the restoration grant went to the owners; the work it paid for is not named anywhere in the sources read. NHLR detail page at www.nhlr.org Lookout.aspx?id=672 returned HTTP 500 and was not read.

Only OpenStreetMap (volunteer map, way 384208227) names this tower. It is not on the FFLA Rhode Island list or the FFLOS former-sites list for Rhode Island (12 former sites, none named Park Police). The record's 'standing' status is not supported by any source read, so it is corrected to unknown. It is unclear whether this is a lookout at all; the name points to the Park Police, but no source says what the structure was. Worth a check against Newport or RI Park Police history, or a site visit, before the record is kept as a lookout. Build date, builder, staffing, access and condition all unknown. Brenton Point's own park history does not mention a tower.

Brief's restored 2022 was narrowed to reconnected power, which is what the FFLA 2022 report names for Pine Hill. The report describes general restoration work across the state, not a restoration of this tower. The brief's height 15.2 m is the 1917 wooden tower's height and is corrected to the current 65-foot steel tower. Staffing status 'unstaffed' rests on the register's Staffed? field alone. The 2016 visit is the only condition report. No source read states current public access, and the search results for an Arcadia or RI DEM access page did not mention the tower. Two search results for Pine Hill (a directory listing for an address on Gardiner Rd, and a mapcarta entry) were not read and are not used.

Construction start (October 1934), first operation (1937) and removal (1963) come from the Forest Lookouts newspaper clippings and the register. The clippings give the start of construction, not its finish. Height conflict (60 ft stairway in 1934, 65 ft in the register) is recorded, not resolved. The agency value 'Sub' looks like a parse of a district label; the correction is proposed from the 1950 notice, which is the only source naming the state division. The Tiverton relocation and the 1964 date are linked by inference, not by a source that says so. No source describes the Portsmouth site now. Coordinates differ between the register (41.5865, -71.25367) and the FFLA list (41.58401, -71.25457), about 290 m apart by my calculation from those two pairs; the story does not place the site precisely. A Facebook group post titled North Brayton Road Fire Tower appeared in search results but could not be fetched and is not used. No photos added.

Brief correction: '2022 destroyed' changed to burned (see corrections). Brief's 1968 build kept, but NHLR's description (1986) and the 1926 and 1954-55 references show the history is tangled; the story says so. Fire date: FFLA July 6 vs NHLR July 7; record uses July 6. The Westerly Sun text has no year on its 'Nov. 4' vote; 2025 is inferred from the federal shutdown reference and its sequence after the February 2025 BRVCA item. Unresolved: whether the old tower will be restored (Westerly Sun; council letter) or replaced (BRVCA). Facebook and CitizenPortal search snippets were not used as evidence. NHLR photos are not in the fetched text, so none added. Status after November 2025 is unverified. Access from the Westerly Sun: a fenced municipal radio site; no public visiting information found.

Only the register and one newspaper notice give Tiverton-specific facts. The 2005 demolition date comes from one source and is given as approximate. The link between the 1963 relocation notice and the Tiverton tower is inferred from the Quaker Hill register and the dates, not stated by a source. A Facebook group post titled North Brayton Road Fire Tower appeared in search results but could not be fetched; its snippet mentions a demolition for school tennis courts, which is unverified and not used. The Tiverton Historical Society page had no tower mention. No photos added; the existing FFLOS photo is already in the record.

Two sources agree on the 1935 build. Staffing, notable fires and any later condition work are not in the sources read. Providence Water pages at provwater.com and the Providence Journal Scituate article (2026-09-30) returned HTTP 403 and may hold more history. The register's 'active ever since' wording is general. Brief access 'unknown' is now resolved to permission-only by the NHLR text. No corrections to the brief.

Unresolved: (1) move year: FFLOS says moved to Escoheag in 1938, NHLR says moved 1937 and rebuilt 1938; story reports both. (2) Height: FFLOS '65 ft' for the original tower vs NHLR '80ft' for the Escoheag structure it traces to the same 1934 build; not reconciled. (3) Brief record status 'gone' is right for the original George Washington site only; the structure stands at Escoheag Hill, so the record is not wrong but a visitor could misread it. No correction proposed. (4) The 1952 break-in is at Escoheag Hill, not at the original site; its only source is a Forest Lookouts page quoting the Newport Mercury, not the clipping itself. (5) FFLOS registers a separate 'Escoheag Tower Site' (US 1585, RI 12) about half a kilometre from the NHLR coordinates; it lists abandoned remains on site while NHLR lists a standing structure. Likely the same structure catalogued twice, not confirmed. (6) Not read: the Valley Breeze CCC article used in the existing us-ri-escoheag-hill story (it places the first tower in Glocester as the 'George Washington Memorial Fire Tower'); this run stayed within its page-read budget, so the Burrillville-vs-Glocester dispute is left to that story. (7) No staffing history for the original tower in any source read, so none is stated.

Unresolved: (1) build date: FFLOS says first operated 1926; the Forest Lookouts page quotes a 1934 federal work-project line. The same 1934 line also appears on other RI Forest Lookouts pages, so it may be a generic programme note rather than a record specific to this tower; not confirmed. (2) Status: FFLOS says the tower is used as a guard tower at the Cranston Adult Correction Institution, but the Forest Fire Lookout Association list has a separate 'Cranston ACI' entry marked gone. It is not clear whether they are the same structure, so whether a tower stands there today is open. A human should check the ACI site before the status is set. (3) A social-media post (Greater Rhode Island Ruins, Facebook) says the tower was erected in Wickaboxet State Forest in 1934; not used because it is not a citable page. Wikipedia gives the state forest's founding as 1932 and no source links the tower to the forest. (4) Record status 'gone' matches the Wickaboxet Hill entry; no correction proposed. (5) No staffing or fire history found. The access note is deliberately omitted: the tower's current location is a correctional facility and no source describes access.

Build year conflict left open: the register's Built field says 1930, its description says late 1930s, and no other source read settles it. Current condition is unconfirmed; the only evidence is the 2013 register entry and one Facebook post whose visible text gives no date and may not refer to this tower. That post mentions the poster's grandparents in connection with the tower but is cut off, so no operator is confirmed. The sale and move were in the late 1990s (register) or 199?? (Forest Lookouts), so no event year was assigned. The owner is a private individual named in the register; the story does not name them. Height 80 ft (24.4 m) is the tower height; the register's 207 ft (63 m) is ground elevation and matches the record's elevation_m. The register does not give coordinates for the new site, and it is unclear whether the record's point is the original Appleton site or the moved tower, so the point was not changed.

Only two sources on this tower: the NHLR register entry and one Eastern US Lookouts page. Two web searches found nothing about it. Built near 1936 is approximate. Current condition, access and staffing are unverified; the standing status rests on the register wording and its October 2013 photographs. Worth asking the SC Forestry Commission.

Ownership and agency conflict, not resolved: the record says state ownership, the register says a private owner, and the Eastern US Lookouts page lists the SC Forestry Commission. The register also mentions an original Forestry Commission sign and Forestry Commission repeater equipment. Circa 1936 and Bethlehem Steel are the register's own tentative wording. Two web searches found no newspaper or Forestry Commission record of this tower.

The 1936 paper lists three towers (Reynolds station, Barnwell near the Charleston highway, and Dunbarton) but does not name the register's tower, so linking it is an inference. Register and SC Picture coordinates differ by about 40 m; the record keeps the NHLR point. Post and Courier statewide articles returned HTTP 429 and were not read. The 1938-39 CCC detail is quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page from a 1939 state report; I did not read that report directly.

Built year 1938 agrees across the register and Forest Lookouts. The record's county (Sumter) is the current location; the register gives the original site as Marlboro County, so the record is not wrong but both counties are relevant. Sale date is 'late 1990s' (register) and 199?? (Forest Lookouts), so no event year was assigned for the move. Condition after the 2013 registration is unknown. The owner is a private individual; the story does not name them. Height 100 ft (30.5 m) is the tower height; the register's 248 ft (76 m) is ground elevation.

The build date is only 'the 1930s' (NHLR), so no build year is recorded. The moved structure is the Witherbee lookout (data/towers/sc/us-sc-witherbee.json, verified): this record may duplicate it. A human should decide whether Bethera stays a separate relocation entry or is linked to Witherbee. The Witherbee record uses 1930 as a placeholder build year; this record does not. The FFLOS footers remark and the Firefighter Nation article are both undated. facts.status already reads 'relocated', so the gone-to-relocated change is already in facts; corrections[0].current ('gone') is stale and a human should review and clear that entry.

Design, original owner and 1938 build are well supported. The McIntosh purchase year conflicts across sources (late 1990s vs 199?? vs early 2000s) and is left open. The Register's 100 ft height versus the magazine's unassigned 110 ft towers is also unresolved. No staffing names, notable fires, or public-access statement were found. The magazine copy we read is dated June 2018. The 2013 registration date is from the Register.

The NHLR detail page is the main source. The FWS visitor guide gives island access and describes a 16-foot observation tower near the public dock, far shorter than the 110-foot lookout. Wikipedia is used only for the boat-access and ferry claims, which are not checked against the ferry operator. The Forest Lookouts page has only a header and no narrative. No staffing or fire history was found. No source says whether the public may climb the tower, so no access level is recorded. The NHLR's construction-by-Bureau-of-Biological-Survey claim versus the 1936 transfer is unresolved and needs a 1930s refuge history. The NHLR photo credit (Sarah Dawsey) has no image URL in the cache, so no photo is recorded.

Build date, CCC erection and the 100-to-40 ft reconstruction come from the Register and Forest Lookouts. The McIntosh purchase year conflicts (late 1990s vs 199?? vs early 2000s). A trail-guide search result (thedirtymule.com, Sumter National Forest Cassatt Fire Tower Ridge Circuit) returned 403 to fetch_text. A WebFetch summary, not a verbatim quote, says the page places the tower's old foundation in Sumter National Forest near Camden and that the tower's own build and move dates are not given. That is unverified and not used in the story; it needs a human check, since the original site may still hold a foundation. No staffing names or notable fires found.

No source gives a build year, a height or a site description. The Forest Lookouts site files the 1946-47 report entry under Davidson; a web search found no other source tying the Davidson name to that tower, so the link is unconfirmed. The removal date is unknown. The FFLOS elevation of 85 ft is the site elevation, not a tower height, and is not recorded as a fact.

Build date, height and the 1995 move are supported by both the Register and Forest Lookouts. The current location rests on the Register's 'yet to be moved' statement and a June 2018 magazine feature that describes a visit about fifteen years earlier, so treat it as inferred. No staffing names or notable fires were found. The Register's coordinates place the record in Richland County, and the current site may differ from the coordinates in the brief. The magazine's '2003' auction note is general and not used.

Build date is circa 1933 per the register and 1933 per the Facebook post, so it is treated as solid. Staffing, notable fires and any recent condition report were not found; the Forest Lookouts page has only the 2005 sale. The register's 'Bamburg' is read as a typo for Bamberg. The Facebook post comes from the Butterfield Plantation page, so its statements are the owner's account. The status 'standing' in the record is consistent with the post's account of the tower being erected at Butterfield, so it is not changed. Used 1 WebSearch and about 5 page reads.

Status is the main open question. NHLR registered Elko in 2026 with a photo and no description of present condition. The Eastern U.S. Lookouts list marks it Removed with no date. No build date was found. The SCFC closure date applies to the whole tower system, not to Elko specifically. This is not the Barnwell lookout (us-sc-barnwell), which is a different tower. The standing-to-removed correction is dropped: the register does not say whether anything stands, so the status stays open.

Thinnest of the three records. No build date, staffing, fire or tower-height information in any source read. The FFLOS 'Elevation 98 ft (30 m)' is ground elevation of the site, not tower height, so it is not used as a height. The removal date is not given anywhere; the commission-wide closure (1 Oct 1993) is recorded only as context, not as this tower's removal date. The OpenStreetMap node (357111601) still carries the name 'Foreston Lookout Tower' with tower type 'observation', which may be a map carry-over and is not evidence of a standing structure. Two web searches and about six page reads were used. The story is kept short (about 150 words) rather than padded. A future pass could check Clarendon County or Manning newspapers for the tower's history.

Only the register, the SCFC history page and Wikipedia were readable. WLTX and Post and Courier articles on the tower returned 403 and 429 and were not used; they would likely add access and staffing detail. Access and staffing are left out because no readable source states them. The Wikipedia article cites the register, so its 1936 date is not independent. A search snippet from an SCFC 'important fires' page mentions a different 'Gaston Fire' (a wildfire elsewhere, not linked to this tower); the page was not read and it should not be tied to the tower without a source.

NHLR gives only the 1930s for construction, so no built event is recorded. Staffing status none rests on the Forest Service statement that the tower is no longer in use and on NHLR standby status; the as_of date is the research date, and the staffing end (1993) is the last documented date. The county conflict is unresolved. No climbing information was found in the sources read, so visit.climbable is omitted. Hillmap and the OpenStreetMap node were checked but add no history. No new photos.

One substantive source (NHLR). The Forest Lookouts page has only a header (Charleston County; spelled 'Cape Romaine Wildlife Refuge' there, 'Cape Romain' in NHLR; the story uses NHLR's spelling). The record's status 'standing' is contradicted by NHLR (abandoned, legs collapsed June 2014), so a correction is proposed for human review. Height 60 ft converted to 18.3 m (structure height, not cab). No source gives access, staffing, or condition since 2014, so no access or visit facts are recorded. One web search for removal or collapse news found nothing relevant. The record's June 2014 downed-tower photo was not re-read. No new photos added.

Build year (1938, CCC and WPA) and registration date (July 27, 2006) are from the NHLR entry alone. The brief's status 'standing' is not confirmed by any source read; the NHLR entry does not state current condition, so facts.status is omitted. No staffing or fire history was found, so no staffing facts or fire events are recorded. Tower-specific access and climbing rules were not found; the access level 'public' reflects the open university forest with trail rules, not a statement about the tower. The Clemson World items concern the Lake Issaqueena recreation area, not the tower, and are used as context only. The 'other' event for 1934 is the WPA land program, not a tower event. The brief's coordinates match the NHLR coordinates. No new photos.

Key Bridge (1912, rebuilt 2007) is a separate bridge; the tower stood one to two miles away per the 1935 plan. Do not map the tower to the bridge. Removal date unknown; the register says only 'removed' and the Forest Lookouts page has a 'Removed' heading without a date. Staffing evidence is one 1936 item (Norman Cook). County conflict: Edgefield (Forest Lookouts) vs McCormick (register and marker). Coordinates in the record are about half a kilometre from the bridge marker coordinates, which conflicts with the 1935 distance; a human should check the point. No photo with a clear licence found. A 2007 Augusta Chronicle snippet on CCC towers in Sumter National Forest was seen in search only and not used.

Thin record. One substantive source (NHLR). The Forest Lookouts Leeds page has only a header (Chester County, Sumter National Forest, satellite view). Two web searches for current status or staffing found nothing. The record's status 'standing' is not supported by any source read, so facts omit status; a human should check whether the tower still stands, perhaps through the Forest Service Enoree Ranger District. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m (structure height). Elevation in the record (200.3 m) matches NHLR. Story uses 'about 1936' for the build year. No photos added; the record already holds the NHLR image (us959_leeds.jpg).

Only the register and the SCFC history page were usable; no build year, operator or fire history for this tower turned up in two searches. The register's 'one of the original ~140' figure is not the same as a later SCFC social post that says 'more than 130'; that post was not fetched and is not cited. The register calls the tower in poor condition as of 2013; no newer condition report was found. Height 80 ft converted to 24.4 m, matching the record.

Thin record. Only the register page supports any tower-specific fact: location, elevation, registration, nominator and administrator. No build date, design, staffing, fire history or condition was found in the sources read. The register names the Forestry Commission as administrator, yet the Commission closed its fire tower system in 1993; the sources do not explain the link, so the story says so. The record's 'standing' is not confirmed by any source read, so facts.status is 'unknown' and no correction is proposed. The Forest Lookouts page for this tower returned a 404. Searches used: 3 WebSearch calls for this tower, one over the 2-call budget, because the first results did not identify a build date. About 4 page reads. Verification pass: the SCFC history page was searched for Lesslie, York, Ballenger and the tower name and has no mention of this tower; the story now says so, and no longer says the landowner is the contact (the register names only the administrator).

Two accounts disagree on Joe Price's years at the tower: 30 (May 1972 item, which also gives Trula 25) versus 35 (1992 obituary). Neither gives a start date; the story says so. The 1972 and obituary texts are as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not read from The Index-Journal itself. An Augusta Chronicle 2007 article (CCC-built towers in Sumter National Forest) returned HTTP 403 and is not used. HikingWNC is a hiking guide, cited for access only; its upper-deck line may be dated. Thin sourcing: only the register and the SCFC history page were readable. Two dates conflict and are unresolved: the register puts the 1990 private sale 'after the abandonment' of the state system, but SCFC says it closed the system on 1 October 1993. Unread sources: a Facebook group post by Ted Brown says the tower was built in 1938/1939 (fetch returned title only, so not used); a Waymarking page calls it the summit of the county's highest point (fetch returned title only, not used). Do not confuse this with the Little Mountain in Newberry County, which has a Wikipedia article. Height 75 ft converted to 22.9 m from the register.

Brief lacked design and height; added from NHLR (54 ft = 16.5 m). Brief elevation 645.3 m matches NHLR 645 m. OpenStreetMap node 357111624 tags ele=658, not used. Build date is unresolved: NHLR says around 1935, but a February 1941 newspaper item, as reprinted by Forest Lookouts, announces plans for a tower on Long Nose mountain west of Walhalla. The story gives both; this may be a replacement or a different site. Current use is undated (NHLR). No source read documents public access or current condition. Search results for Long Mountain (a Facebook reel and a blog) were not read as page text and are not used. No photos. Confidence is low because the only substantive source is the register.

Register and one 2020 blog visit are the only sources read. Height converted from the register's 54 ft. Register says the Forest Service used the tower until the 1980s; no exact year, so no staffing event was recorded. Access and climbing status are unconfirmed; no Forest Service page was checked for closure notices. The brief's standing status rests on the 2020 blog and the register. The OpenStreetMap node (height 16.5) agrees but is not cited. Story does not encourage climbing.

Builder and date disagree: the Register gives 1940 and the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service; the Town's RFQ gives the 1930s and the U.S. Biological Survey. Both are cited, not resolved. Staffing end date is unknown ('until recent years'). Access is unknown: no source read says whether the public may visit or climb. Record coordinates match the Register's; elevation 7.6 m matches 25 ft. Unfetched search snippets (a Village Museum Facebook post, a Town picture PDF with no text layer) suggest c. 1935 and Forestry Commission use into the early 1980s; not used in the story. Worth a human look: the FFLA report's '$14,000 matching' phrase is broken across lines and was not used.

Ownership is described as the garden (NHLR says Moore Farms Botanical Garden, LLC). Visit rules come from Wikipedia and the garden's booking prompt; no source says the tower can be climbed, so none is claimed. No photo credits were recorded because no image URLs were captured.

Thin record: one substantive page (a Forest Lookouts entry that is mostly a navigation list, with a callout of two 1973-80 notes and an undated Removed label) plus an OpenStreetMap point. No build date, height, design, fires or current site description found. A second OSM node (367805749) repeats the name with a USGS Geonames tag and was not used.
