No build year, height or site description is in the sources. The Forest Lookouts Ridgeland page (cited by the record) describes a 100-foot steel tower erected near Ridgeland in November 1931 and marks it removed; it may be the Ridgeland entry or this tower, and the story does not decide. The 2026 notice is an emergency-services site project and does not say a tower stands there. The alias removal is proposed in corrections for human review, not applied.

Built date, design and Forest Service use are well supported by the Register and 1935-36 newspapers as quoted on the Forest Lookouts site. Open points: (1) the Forest Lookouts site gives the tower's location about 2 km from the Register's coordinates (34.10012, -82.35429 vs 34.08306, -82.36278); the record keeps the Register point, which was not checked on a map. (2) Elevation differs: the Register gives 824 ft, the marker gives 832 ft for the mountain, and the Forest Service page says an 800-foot mound. (3) The Forest Service trail page's Hurricane Helene closure note sits under a 'Current Conditions' heading, and the page's last-updated date is April 22, 2026; access today should be confirmed before any visit. (4) The access level 'closed' is inferred from the 2020 visit notes, not from a current agency notice. Visit report and fence observations are from one 2020 volunteer visit.

Two real sources for the tower: the FFLOS register (1) and the Forest Lookouts page (2). The 1931-32 details are quoted there from period newspapers and the state commission report, not read in the originals. Owner count differs between the state report (five) and The Columbia Record (six); both are in the story. Brief kind is 'unknown'; sources call it a steel lookout tower, so 'tower' looks right. No staffing, fire or access information in sources read, so those are left out. The SCFC closure date (3) is system-wide and is not presented as this tower's removal date. Registry numbers US 921, SC 7. Two WebSearch queries were used.

Thin record: the FFLOS register (1) gives the build date, height, location and removal, and the Forest Lookouts South Carolina index (2) gives only the county and refuge. The 1940s and 1960s dates are the register's own approximations. Registry number US 917, SC 3. Horsehead Lookout (NHLR) is a similar 60-foot steel tower on the Intracoastal Waterway but a different site; it was seen only in a search snippet and is not used. A Fish and Wildlife Service photo titled 'Fire tower' (fws.gov/media/fire-tower) is not labelled with a tower name and was not used. No staffing, fire or access information found, so those are left out. Two WebSearch queries were used.

Brief said built 1936; NHLR gives circa 1936-1938, so the event year is the low end of that range. 'Possibly a Bethlehem Steel model' is NHLR's own hedge. The 1993 abandonment is one NHLR statement, backed by the statewide SCFC closure date; the staffing 'unstaffed as of 1993' is inferred from those two, not from a staffing record. No access or visit data was found, so the access and visit keys are omitted. The eastern lookouts page and the hillmap and OpenStreetMap pages add only name, county and agency, so they are not cited. Used 3 web searches, one over the 2-search budget. No fire history, newspaper coverage or NRHP listing was found.

The sale is undated in the sources: 'late 1990s' per the register and '199??' per Forest Lookouts. It is left out of events until a year can be sourced. The record's agency field holds the owner's name, so a correction is proposed for a human to apply. The 40-foot height is the current structure; the register does not give the year of the reconstruction. No staffing names or fires beyond the 1936 towerman notice were found. Used 1 WebSearch and about 4 page reads.

Thin record: one register page with a 2020 visit report, one Forest Service history page that does not name this tower, and one hiking guide for access. No staffing, fire or repair sources were found, and the story says so. The record's material 'steel' is not stated in the sources read (the register gives an Aermotor LS-40 with a metal cab), so it is not repeated in facts. The 100-foot figure is the register's tower height and is taken as height_m 30.5. The access level 'closed' rests on the 2020 visit and the hiking guide; the current agency status is unknown. The Forest Lookouts page for Tip Top was checked and adds only the county and forest names.

Only one page is about this tower: the NHLR detail page, read in full. Everything tower-specific rests on it. Wikipedia's Ulmer town article has no tower mention. Read for context: the SCFC pictures page and history page, and the NHLR Leesville entry. Not read: the anyplaceamerica topo page and the rootsandrecall Ulmer page. Three search calls ran (one general query, two Ulmer-specific), one over the per-tower budget. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. 'Built circa 1935' is the register's own estimate. The agency field holds the administrator the register names, a person, not an agency. No corrections proposed. Access is unknown: no source gives visiting rules. The photo credit 'Michael T. Finch, Jr.' on the NHLR page was not added as a photo because no license is shown.

The NHLR detail page was read in full and gives the tower facts. The tie to the Forestry Commission rests on the NHLR administrator line; no source reads that Varnville was one of the Commission's lookouts in service, so the story treats it as likely, not certain. The 140-tower figure comes from the Leesville entry, not from this page. Date reading: 'built circa 1936' is the register's estimate. Height 100 ft converted to 30.5 m. Access unknown. The SCFC history page was not separately read (it did not add anything tower-specific). A WebSearch hit for an FCC tower registration at Varnville (2007) was not used because it is not shown to be this tower. No corrections proposed.

Thinnest of the three. The NHLR page gives name, route, county, coordinates, elevation, registration date, nominator and a photo credit, but no build date, type, agency, owner or condition text. The 76 ft figure is the page's elevation, not tower height, so height_m is omitted. The brief marks status 'standing' and kind 'unknown'; the page does not state condition, so status is left out of facts and the story does not claim it is standing. Two WebSearch calls and reads of the NHLR SC list, the FFLA SC list (no matches), and the Pineville SC Picture Project page (a different tower) found nothing more. The Post and Courier article on SC towers does not mention Vert. Next steps for an editor: ask the nominator Dan Curry about the tower (photo license unknown, so no photo was added), or check whether the Forest Fire Lookout Association profile fills in later. Access unknown.

Build and replacement years are the fiscal-year report windows (FY 1940-41 and FY 1957-58), recorded as 1940 and 1957; the exact months are not in the sources. The history comes through Forest Lookouts' transcriptions of the commission's annual reports, not the originals. Status and access are unconfirmed. A social-media post in search results describes the site as overgrown, but its page could not be read, so it is not cited. Mildred Zeigler's dates are not given.

Brief record checks out: built 1936 and registered October 2, 2012 match NHLR. Left out of the story: a StoryMaps search result (storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/c7196e87d7af47e2a90c4eb79831e87e) says the tower was first built at Fort Jackson and moved to the park in 1940. Fetch returned only the page title, and a WebSearch on the claim found nothing confirming it, so it needs a human check; it conflicts with NHLR's 1936 build at this site. The Friends of Sesqui post is undated in our copy and is the only source on climbing safety; its comment thread (not used) mentions the tower being dismantled, which is unverified. Access level restricted is our inference. No fire history found. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the Register's 1936 build date is a year before the 1937 land purchase in Wikipedia, so the story now says the two are not reconciled. The story also uses the agency's full name and footnotes the park-celebration sentence, which had none.

Register (NHLR) and one HikingWNC listing only; no Forest Service or Forest Lookouts page for this tower was found in the cache (easternuslookouts.weebly.com/whitmire.html returns 404). 'Standing' and the closed upper deck rest on the undated HikingWNC listing, so a current check is worth doing before publication. Staffed-last year is a decade placeholder (1980). OSM node 357098866 (ele 145, tower:type observation) was read but not cited; it differs slightly from the register's 147 m.

Only two sources, and neither gives a current condition. The Former Fire Lookout Sites register has no entry for this tower (firetower.org/lookouts/us/sc/winyah-bay-lookout/ returns 404). Two searches turned up no news or photo report after 2017. 'Standing' is the brief's record; the register's 'presently inactive' is the only support, and status_note says so. The 1938 modified year covers 1938-39 work. The Forest Lookouts page cites a 1939 state report that was not read directly. Recommend a recent photo or local source before publication.

Register, the Former Fire Lookout Sites Bethera entry, and an undated news story cover the history. Current status rests only on the undated news story ('still standing'). The 2024 NEPA page covers two administrative buildings and does not name the tower. Built year 1930 is a decade placeholder for the 1930s. OSM node 357111662 (ele 15) was read but not cited. A current photo or ranger-district check would firm up status before publication.

Only one visit report (September 2020) appears on the Register page, so current condition is unknown. Access is set to restricted from HikingWNC plus the 2020 report; no official closure notice was found. HikingWNC is a hiking site, not an agency. The Index-Journal text is available only as quoted by Forest Lookouts. No photos added.

Brief's facts hold up: 1965 build, 22 ft (6.7 m), standing. The 1964 authorization and the 1965 contract come from a newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not from the newspapers themselves. Staffing is unknown; a search turned up no staffing or fire history. Tower-specific access is not stated: the SummitPost guide covers the surrounding game production area only, so no access level is recorded. The NHLR says the land is managed by the state fish and game department, while the brief lists the agency as the state forestry department; both are recorded. Used 2 web searches, within budget. No photos were added. Two photo credits exist on the NHLR and Rex's pages (Ron Kemnow; Dave Masters), but no image URLs were captured, so none are listed.

The 1939 steel tower and L-4 cab are supported by at least two sources (register and firelookout.com) and the Forest Service. The 1910 first tower rests on the Forest Service page alone; a 1915 newspaper item shows a lookout station by then. Access 'public' is an inference from the register's road note and the Forest Service description of recreationist use; the Forest Service page is undated and nothing says whether the cab may be climbed. Height 9.1 m converts the 30-ft figure.

Rapid City Journal rename article returned HTTP 429 on this pass; not used. Height_m 11.0 and precise elevation carried from the existing record, not independently re-confirmed by a new source this round.

Elevation conflicts: register 5,175 ft (the record's value), firelookout.com 5,335 ft, 1939 newspaper 5,400 ft. Removal: register says appropriations ended and removal circa 1961; firelookout.com lists a lookout through 1963. Newspaper quotes are as transcribed on Forest Lookouts; the originals were not read. Caption on the register photo matches the foundations. A geocache listing and a summit-blog reference were not used (the geocache page returned no text). No new photos.

Brief elevation 1937.3 m matches the register's 6,356 ft. The 30-foot height comes from the firelookout page's '30' wooden tower' entry and is an inference that it is tower height, as with the Cicero Peak tower. No source read describes what remains on the summit now; the SummitPost 'Fire Tower Ruins' heading is not backed by its text. Staffing evidence is thin: no lookout names were found for Castle Peak.

Brief height 9.1 m matches the 30-foot tower in the firelookout and Forest Lookouts pages. The register's Removed field shows 1980 but the register text does not give the month. No source read says where the tower is now (Rapid City attraction, Custer buyer, or elsewhere), and none describes the summit remains; the SummitPost guide only describes the road and views. The 1967 fires come from a Rapid City Journal item quoted on Forest Lookouts, and the 1990 Cicero Peak Fire on Wikipedia is near the mountain, not tied to the lookout, so it is left out. The firelookout page gives June Johnston Stenson for 1964-1972 and the register gives June Johnston; this is probably one person and the story says only June Johnston.

Sparse record. The 1929 item is quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the Deadwood paper itself was not opened, so whether the tower went up in 1929 is open. The 1940s date is decade-only and comes from a Peakery highlight line; no year is given. Fact-check 2026-10-10: added the 1940s wording to the evidence quote, the SDPB publication date (June 23, 2020) and the Crow Peak name to the evidence list, and a 1940s event. A search surfaced a Black Hills fire-tower page and a 2020 SDPB list; only the SDPB list was read. No access rules or present-day site description were found.

Brochure PDF text extraction was garbled/reflowed in places (OCR-like layout artifacts); only the clearly legible fragments were used. Could not independently verify current rental/visitation status beyond 'public' access level from the existing record.

Two register claims (CCC build in 1941, cabin burned in the late 1990s) conflict with other sources and are reported as disputed. Current staffing comes from an undated Forest Service page. The Aermotor attribution rests on firelookout.com alone. Access 'public' follows the Forest Service page, which describes visitor climbs in the staffed season; drive-up is not described.

The brief height 4.3 m is most likely the 14-foot cab dimension, not a tower height; no total height is in the sources, so the height is omitted and a correction proposed. The register's Removed field gives 1975 but no source describes the removal. The base is described as stone (firelookout, Forest Lookouts) or concrete (blog, onX); the photo credits on the firelookout page (National Archives, USFS) have no image URLs in the text we read, so no photos are added. The 1942-1963 lookout names are from the firelookout page only.

The record's height (32.6 m) and elevation (929.6 m) match the sources: 107 ft and 3,050 ft. The 1936 date comes from one source (Forest Lookouts); firelookout.com gives no date. A 1936 CCC or WPA observation tower is described in the camp history (cite 5), but the sources do not say it is the fire lookout, so no event is recorded for it. Access for the tower itself is not stated anywhere we read; the refuge-wide foot-traffic statement (cite 6) should not be read as permission to climb. firelookout.com credits photos to Scott Schroeder; no photo URL or licence was found, so no photos are added. A person may want to check with the refuge whether the tower is open to the public.

Built year (1955 vs 1954) and county (Custer vs Pennington) disagree across sources; story reports both. Two searches found no description of the site today and no access information, so access stays unknown. Newspaper items were read as quoted on westlookouts.weebly.com, not from the original papers. The 35-foot height comes from firelookout.com alone.

Only two pages describe the site in detail. The 1942 newspaper item reaches us through Forest Lookouts, which quotes The Daily Republic; the Daily Republic itself was not read. Firelookout.com's 'Co-op' label is unexplained and was not used. The Wikipedia article titled Medicine Butte is about a Wyoming butte, not this one, and was not used. No source gives the date the cabin came down or the summit's condition now. Brief's status (gone), kind (ground) and agency (State) are supported; no correction proposed.

Brief coordinates (43.94637, -104.009381) differ from the Moon row on the firelookout.org South Dakota list (43.91341, -104.00147). Not changed, because I could not check which is right. Staff names on firelookout.com (1941-1966) belong to the standing Summit Ridge tower, so they are left out. A Forest Service PDF (fs.usda.gov/media/62905) came up in search but is about Cement Ridge, so it is not used. No source read describes the meadow today or whether it can be reached. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

Build year of the current stone tower is disputed between 1939 (NHLR, Parkwolf) and 1940-41 (FFLA); a 1939 newspaper excerpt describing a log tower adds ambiguity. Height given in the brief (15.2 m) likely refers to the tower structure; elevation sources consistently give the peak as 6,023 ft, slightly different from the brief's 6,003 ft NHLR figure -- flagged as a minor discrepancy, not corrected since NHLR is the brief's own source.

The 1966 destruction date rests on firelookout.com alone. Height and cabin descriptions conflict between the register and firelookout.com; story follows the register and the 1932 newspaper. Two searches found no description of the site today and no access information. Newspaper items were read as quoted on westlookouts.weebly.com.

Built year is disputed (1940, 1941, 1943); story leads with the register's 1943. The 20-foot height is from firelookout.com alone. The SummitPost caption is a 2013 user photo caption; its 'ill-fated' wording is not explained, so the story quotes it without repeating a cause. Two searches found no description of the site today and no access information.

No source describes the site today, so no access fact is recorded. Removal year conflicts (register 1970s vs lookout page 1960s). County and coordinates conflict: the register gives Fall River County and 43.500252, -103.901869 (the record matches), while the South Dakota list gives Custer County and 43.45999, -103.90388. Staffing evidence is a single 1962 item, quoted from the Rapid City Journal on a lookout page; the original newspaper was not checked.

Build date, builder, agency and staffing are unknown; two web searches found nothing on them. The directory and Wikipedia disagree on elevation and county name. Access level 'permission' follows from the reservation location; no visiting rules were found in the sources. The 1890 event is local context, not the tower's history, and the Wikipedia text cites Jack Utter's book, which was not read. Corrections: county is proposed for review only.

Strongest sources are the NPS Wind Cave assessment (npshistory.com PDF) for construction, use and 1998 access change, and the NPS trail page for current climbing rules. The 1954 newspaper quoted on westlookouts calls the Rankin Ridge watcher a State Park lookout, which does not fit the national park; the story avoids naming that person. No rental or staffing information after 1998 was found; access is recorded as closed to climbing, with the trail open. The NHLR CL100 design label and the NPS 'Standard Steel Lookout Tower' proposal are not in conflict, but only the register gives the CL100 name.

The 1936 build date comes from the marker alone. The height is disputed (100 ft listing vs 108 ft in three sources); a correction to 32.9 m is proposed for review. The CCC camp dates conflict (marker 1925 to 1939 vs brochure 1935 to 1939). A 2025 federal solicitation for fire tower rehabilitation appeared in search results, but its page is behind a Cloudflare check and was not read, so it is not used; it may bear on current condition. Current access is unconfirmed; the marker's daylight-hours statement may be out of date. The tower is not tied to the headquarters building. Another Sand Lake tower (NWR 2) is listed as gone in the FFLA state list and is not this lookout.

The 1966 versus 1975 steel-tower date is the main open question; a Black Hills National Forest history or a Forest Service lookout inventory would settle it. Current access rests on one hiking blog of unknown date plus a SummitPost route description; no Forest Service page for this tower was found, and the Black Hills NF page checked says five towers remain in service without naming them. No rental listing found. The brief's height_m (16.2) was left out of facts because sources conflict.

Gone status is supported by three sources (firelookout.com, the FFLA list, and SDPB's 2020 guide, which lists it as a former site). The 1939 description is the only account of the tower itself and comes via Forest Lookouts, which quotes the Rapid City Journal; the newspaper was not read. The brief's height_m 9.1 equals 30 feet, but the 1939 text does not say whether that is to the cab floor, so height_m was not written to facts. Brief's coordinates differ from the firelookout.com sources key by roughly 70 m; no correction proposed. No source gives a date for removal or describes the hilltop now, and no access information was found; access was left out.

Thin evidence: the Forest Lookouts page has only a header, and firelookout.com has a location block and no history. No build, staffing, fire or removal record was found, so none is written. The brief's access 'permission' and its note 'Ask the tribe before visiting' do not appear on any page read, so no access facts were written; the reservation boundary (Wikipedia) supports only that the site lies inside it, not who owns the land. The brief's status 'gone' rests on the FFLA list alone. Confirm the status and access with a human reviewer or the tribe before publishing.

Build-date conflict across four sources (1935/1939/1939-40/1942) could not be fully resolved within the research budget; flagged in both story and corrections. Worth a closer look at NRHP/npgallery nomination documents if available, which might clarify construction vs completion dates.

Strong record: NHLR, firelookout.com, a long newspaper transcript page and the FFLA list agree on the core story. Open points: the removal year of the upper floors (1973 vs 1978 vs 1970s) and the 1949 vs 1950 build year are reported as ranges. The 1978 removal date and the 1970s date in the 2011 book are from the sources as printed. The travel-site wording about the road is a blog claim, so the story keeps it as a note. The record's height_m 4.3 is unsupported and is proposed for removal. The 1950s-1960s named lookouts are from firelookout.com and the newspaper; names are historical, not verified against Forest Service records.

Removal year conflicts: the register and summit guide say the 1950s; a June 1963 newspaper item (quoted on a lookout page, original not checked) still lists the station, so the record's 1950 is flagged in corrections. The access fact rests on the summit guide, which describes a road to the summit and says nothing about gates or closures; the summit is now a radio site, so check before a visit. Staffing names come from two lookout pages (firelookout.com and westlookouts), not from the original newspapers. Record elevation 1621.5 m matches the register's 1,622 m.

Built 1935 (brochure and marker agree on the CCC work). Height of 110 ft above ground and 133 steps come from the brochure only; height_m 33.5 is the brochure's figure converted, and 'above ground' is taken as the structure height. 'Steel' rests on one listing (westlookouts). Current condition not verified. Search results said the Waubay tower is a steel tower built by the CCC; only the listed sources were used. The Sand Lake marker also says the Waubay tower is open to the public during daylight hours, but the story uses the refuge's own page.

Thin record. No build date, height or design found in any readable source. Route 296 location comes from a one-paragraph blog post and is approximate. The Tennessee Landforms table lists the tower at 1697 ft and status 'standing'; the 2014 list is the only dated status record. The blog post's address gives a December 20, 2015 date, but the post describes no status, so it is not used as one. A Facebook group thread turned up in search (snippet says '40-foot fire tower built in 19..') but the page could not be read, so it is not used. Access and climbing rules are unknown; the story tells visitors to check first.

Build year is only the decade ('built in the 1940s', Register); no event year was assigned for construction. Access is unknown: no source says whether the public may visit or climb, and the 2006 visit report mentions a climbing sign and broken cab glass, so the story advises against climbing. Record coordinates and elevation (619 m) match the Register. The Eastern US lookouts page gives little beyond county and district. Search snippets (a CCC Camp P-62 Facebook post saying the camp built several area towers) were not fetched and are not used; they do not name Altamont. Worth a human look: whether the Register's 2006 visit still reflects current condition, and whether the Division of Forestry allows visitors.

Elevation disagrees: the Register gives 1,026 ft (313 m) and the Tennessee Landforms table gives 1,020 ft; the record's 312.7 m matches the Register. The story reports both. The Register's 11/26/22 site visit has no findings on the page read. Staffing, access and any current fire-watch use are not documented in the sources read. The record's other_names value 'A' is proposed for removal in corrections. The LS-40 stairway point comes from a general Aermotor history, not from this tower's record, and the story says so. Record coordinates match the Register.

No build date, construction, staffing or fate found. Two web searches returned nothing on this tower. The only status record is the Tennessee Landforms row; the Forest Lookouts Antioch entry is a heading with no text. The record's elevation of 131.1 m matches the 430 ft listing. No register page exists for Avondale on nhlr.org or firetower.org (checked cached TN listings for both; it isn't there), no NRHP nomination, no newspaper hit, and no mention in a general East Tennessee fire-tower news piece that was checked. Height (60 vs 100 ft) and county (Hawkins vs Sullivan) conflict across sources; editor should decide height_m and county. Whether a state 80-foot tower was erected on this ridge in 1955 is unresolved. One web search used for this tower.

Identity conflict to check before publishing. The brief lists Lobelville as an other name, but the Register page does not use that name. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from state ownership and the nomination's account of staff use; no visiting rules were found. Staffing as_of uses the 2021 nomination. The brief record had no height; 60 ft (18.3 m) comes from the nomination. No build date, builder, reason for siting, staffing, fires or public access rule appears in any source we could read. Build date, design type and elevation conflict between the register and the NRHP nomination; both kept in the story. Low confidence. No build date, builder, design or staffing was found for the Sharp's Ridge fire tower in two searches and several page reads. Three sources, two of them listing only. Build date and builder not found after two searches. Two sources only, and the county encyclopedia is secondary. No build date, design, use or staffing found; a second search and a guessed encyclopedia URL (404) gave nothing. The sources do not show these are the same tower or what the three miles is measured from, so the story does not link them. The record's status_note matches the FFLA asterisk footnote; no correction proposed. No build date, height, staffing, fire history, cab-removal date or access found. A YouTube video titled 'Horton Fire Lookout Tower Jasper County TX' appeared in search results but was not read. Confidence low.

Build date not found in the three sources read, so there is no built event. Record: the register describes the tower as it now stands downtown, so its design details apply to the moved structure; the 1958 NGS description (reproduced on the Central US page) describes the original site 1.5 miles west-northwest of Jefferson. NGS gives 'overall height of about 100 feet', used for height_m 30.5; it is not a cab-floor height. The 1957 newspaper item is quoted on the Central US page, not read from the newspaper. The register's 2003 move date is the only source for the relocation; the lookout list supports the move but not the year. Access is private: owned by Etex Wireless and used as a cell tower. Two web searches and about five page reads were used, and the Jeffersonian Institute and Jefferson tourism pages gave no tower detail. Worth checking: the Texas Forest Service history of the Jefferson tower, and whether Etex has agreed to the restoration offered.

Register (firetower.org) and FFLA list disagree on the location and status of the standing tower; no build date found. Distance of about 3.4 km is computed from the listed coordinates. The 1957 quote is from a Marshall News Messenger item reproduced on the centraluslookouts page; the newspaper itself was not read. Searches for a Jimplecute article on a tower move found nothing. Related record us-tx-jefferson (Loc 1) says relocated while FFLA says gone and the register says standing downtown; that record needs a separate pass.

Thin record. Readable sources were the Forest Lookouts Karnack page (header only, no history), the FFLA Texas list (status and coordinates) and an undated Texas travel page (general context). Not reached: Texas Forest Service pages and NHLR or FFLOS pages for this site. A library catalog page describes the book Fire in the Piney Woods (Texas lookout towers, the forest service, and the Civilian Conservation Corps) as a lead, but its text was not read; the Duke University Press abstract returned HTTP 403. The FFLA list shows two Karnack entries: Loc 1 gone, Loc 2 standing. The sources do not say whether these are two towers or two sites for one tower. The record's 95 m elevation comes from OpenStreetMap; it was not verified here and is not in the story. Access is unknown and no access fact was added. Fact check 2026-10-09: the travel page says the towers came before airplanes but ties the word long to the earlier tree-climbing sentence, so the story drops long from the tower claim.

Record name is Kirby Forest; the Forest Lookouts page calls it Hyatt. The only current status is the FFLA list (standing). The Find a Grave memorial (1940-1980) was added by a contributor in February 2026; its citation names Hyatt Cemetery but does not say which record gives the dates. If 1980 is the end of the tower, the FFLA listing is wrong. The Tyler County entry is dated January 1, 1941 but does not name Hyatt, so it is not evidence of the build date. No reliable build date found; the 1943 newspaper item shows only that the tower was in use by then. No access information found, so no access or visit facts are recorded. Two WebSearches used. A site visit or landowner check would settle both status and access.

Tower is on the E.O. Siecke State Forest, renamed in 1951; the record's name Kirbyville is the historic one. Record height 24.4 m matches the 80 ft given in 1926 and by TFS. A 1948 newspaper said the tower would be raised to 120 ft; no later source confirms it, and the TFS release still says 80 ft. The 1927 count (175 fires, fall 1927 season) and the TFS count (135 in the first year in use) appear to cover different periods. The 1926 and 1927 newspaper items were read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. No current photo or condition report found; standing status rests on the FFLA list and TFS saying the tower still exists. Public climbing is not permitted per TFS.

Two November 1960 reports name different mountains: Latch Mountain (Joe Schuler's place) and Chamberlain Mountain (O.V. Schuler land). They may be one tower or two; the 1966 report calls the tower the Latch tower. Unresolved record conflict on location: FFLA gives 32.69691, -95.08512, and the second coordinate set in the record is 32.6968, -95.06911, about 1.5 km east. Not checked against a map or a source that gives coordinates, so no location correction is proposed. The Facebook post is undated and is the only present-tense mention found; it is a community group post, not an official record, and only its preview text was readable. No photo or visit found. The county correction (Upshire to Upshur) is typographic and should be easy to confirm.

No source read gives a build year, height or design. The marker is the only source that dates the tower, and it gives the in-use years 1955 to 1969 only. The Forest Lookouts page is nearly empty apart from the name, county and agency. A Waymarking NGS benchmark page (BL2173, title mentions 'LIBERTY HILL LOT 1966') came up in search, but the cached page held only its title, so it is not used. The hmdb marker has 2020 photos by James Hulse; not recorded because no license is stated. Access is unknown: no source says whether the tower may be climbed. NHLR and FFLOS register pages were not checked. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 5 page reads.

Generic name ('lookout tower') and no town, county, state or owner on the map. The OSM tag is observation, not fire lookout, so this may not belong in the lookout set. The brief's Texas placement and coordinates (33.03 N, 97.08 W) are not confirmed by any page read; the OSM page names no state, so the story no longer says the outline is in Texas. A WebSearch hit for a 150-ft Grapevine Main Observation Tower in downtown Grapevine was a search snippet only, not read in full; it does not appear to be this record, but that is not verified. Used 2 WebSearch calls; page reads: OSM way (twice), FFLA list, NHLR list. Suggested check: the OSM way's location on the map, or a county record, before keeping it in the set.

NHLR (decommissioned 1970) and Texas Escapes (functioned into the 1980s) disagree on when the tower stopped operating; noted in the story rather than resolved. The on-site historical marker (hmdb.org #31698) returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, so its exact inscription is not cited here. Texas Escapes is a general-interest history site, not a primary source, so the Wesley Love / WPA narrative rests on that one article; a Texas Historical Commission marker file or a Jacksonville Daily Progress archive piece would strengthen it. A draft citation to 'Forest Fire Lookout Association (firelookout.org)' claiming its Texas lookouts list records this tower as standing has been removed: the cached source is actually the Former Fire Lookout Sites register (firetower.org, a sister site of NHLR, not FFLA), it catalogs decommissioned/removed lookouts, and its one Texas entry is Jefferson Lookout Site, not Love's Lookout. The source neither supports the claim nor matches the cited publisher, so both the footnote and the sentence were dropped.

Build year and height come from the NGS datasheet quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the datasheet's own PID and page were not fetched. The Forest Lookouts page gives no coordinates, so it is not confirmed that its tower is the Loc 2 site on the Forest Fire Lookout Association list; the brief's Loc 2 identity is kept but unverified. The CCC camp link is inferred from the 1933 date and the camp's general work only; no source ties the camp to this tower's construction. Access is unknown. Used 1 WebSearch call and about 3 page reads plus the shared Texas index and FFLA list.

Only tower record is the Forest Fire Lookout Association one-line listing (standing, Newton County, coordinates). No build date, height, design, staffing, fires or access found in the sources read. The Texas Escapes narrative also gives the 1834 land grant as 1934; its quoted marker says 1834, and the story does not use the grant year. Lead: the Cavallerano book Fire in the Piney Woods (muse.jhu.edu/book/137054) is described as covering every Texas fire lookout tower; not accessed, and it may hold the build record. Worth asking the Texas Forest Service or Texas Historical Commission. Used 2 WebSearch calls; page reads: FFLA list, HMDB marker, NHLR list, FFLA p=784 (table not in text), Wikipedia, Texas Escapes. Verification 2026-10-09: story now says 'unincorporated community' (Wikipedia wording) instead of 'small community', and drops 'named for the community', which no source gives.

Thin record: three sources and no build date, design or history. The community history (1843 church, 1847 furnace) is context, not tower history. Record height and elevation come from OpenStreetMap (lattice tower tag, 151 m) and were not used because no readable historical page supports them. Access and landowner are unknown. A Texas Forest Service history or a newspaper search for Lake O' the Pines or Marion County could add a build date.

Height 6.0 comes from the OSM height tag, which prints as '6' with no unit; metres assumed. The brief's status 'standing' is not supported: OSM maps the object, not its condition, so it is corrected to unknown. The name suggests a Martin Luther King Jr. link, but no source says so. The latest edit note mentions downtown walking paths; the city is not named. The OSM page names no state, and the brief's Texas placement is not confirmed by any page read, so the story no longer says the outline is in Texas; the story also drops a speculative line about whom the name honors. Used 2 WebSearch calls: one for a Waco 'MLK Lookout' (no record found), one for Waco's Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park (event pages only; a snippet gave a 300 MLK Blvd address, not verified). Page reads: OSM way (twice), FFLA list, NHLR list. A city parks record would settle whether this is a fire lookout at all.

The 1936 date comes from a June 1936 newspaper item saying the tower had been erected; no later construction record was read. The 1936 item calls the agency the Texas Forestry Service, a branch of A. and M. College; the Forest Lookouts page and the FFLA list use Texas Forest Service. Standing rests on the FFLA list only. A texasescapes.com article says some East Texas towers can still be found near Mount Enterprise; it is undated and general, so it is not used. No access source found. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 3 page reads plus the shared FFLA and Texas index pages.

Thin record. The FFLA list is the only tower-specific source and gives no build date, builder, design, staffing or access. Bowman's East Texas lookout page is about Lufkin and other East Texas towers, not Neches, and must not be used to date this one. The story now calls it a web page, not a column. The 2025 Cavallerano book is the best lead; only its MUSE publisher summary was read. An undated 2011 'Texas lookout towers' list in the crawl cache has a 'neches' entry (TFS-style number TX095) with garbled coordinates; its source URL could not be recovered, so it is not cited. Record is consistent: standing, Anderson County, matching coordinates.

Only the Forest Lookouts transcription page (newspaper clippings 1937-1966) and the FFLA Texas list were read. The 1937 and 1954 items are transcriptions; the original newspapers were not checked. The 1937 articles call the agency the Texas Forestry Service; the page header uses Texas Forest Service. A Facebook group post seen only in a search snippet, an aboutus.com page (elevation 137 ft, HTTP 429) and an NHLR entry (connection reset, guessed URL 404) were not read. Access level could not be determined, so facts.access is omitted. Check the NHLR/FFLOS for a register entry and current condition.

Only the NHLR page describes the tower itself, and it hedges with 'believed'. No build date, builder, staffing, fire or access record was found in NHLR, TSHA, firelookout.org, or the Forest Lookouts regional page (which shows only the name). NHLR says 'Texas A&M Fire Service' for the repeater, probably meaning Forest Service; the story quotes it as the Register's wording. height_m is 70 ft converted. Brief coordinates match firelookout.org. Access is left out because no read source states it; brief 'unknown' stands. Not checked: Texas A&M Forest Service records or local newspapers. Confidence medium because registry and standing agree across sources, but history is thin. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'Sawmills came first' overstated the TSHA entry (which gives 1850 as the earliest date; a church and school followed by 1854-55), so it now gives the 1850 date; the Register footnote was removed from the advice sentence; the farm-road and registry-number evidence was added.

Almost no tower-specific history exists in the sources read. The Forest Lookouts page gives only a status note, and the FFLA list gives a status and coordinates. No build date, builder, height, staffing, fires or access were found. Two searches and five page reads were used. The NHLR Texas list (five registered towers: Chandler, Love's, Pine Mills, Spring, Woodville) does not include this tower. Next step: local Henderson County newspaper archives or a Texas Forest Service history for the tower's build date and use. The brief's agency field held the status note; see corrections.

Read: the Forest Lookouts page (1928 Alto Herald and Forest Worker items, 1942 NGS station description), the FFLA Texas list, the HMDB CCC marker, the Pine Cliff Resort page (commercial; used only for the State Highway 7 access, the tower's place in the recreation area and the 'last standing' phrase), the USFS Ratcliff Lake page and the Recreation.gov listing (no tower mention). Two searches and five reads used. Not found: staffing, notable fires, whether the tower may be climbed, current owner of the tower itself. The HMDB marker says CCC workers built fire towers without naming this one. Check the Bird Mountain tower (Anderson County, listed Tower Gone) for its own story. The brief's 27.4 m height is supported by the 1928 reports; the 1942 survey gives about 100 ft.

Status conflict. The FFLA Texas list says standing; I saw no date on that list. Our crawl data for the Forest Lookouts record reads gone/dismantled, but I found no sentence on the Salem page or the Texas list that says so, so the 'gone' reading is unsourced. The only page text read is the 1965 bid notice to remove the old tower and erect an 80-foot replacement four miles NE of New Salem. It does not confirm completion. The record's height_m 24.4 comes from that 80-foot figure and is unverified as built. The FFLA coordinates were not checked against the notice's New Salem location. Build date of the older tower unknown. Not read: the original Cherokeean notice (Portal to Texas History may hold it) and any Texas A&M Forest Service records. Ask Texas A&M Forest Service or Rusk County about current status before publishing any visit guidance.

Agency conflict. The Forest Lookouts Texas list credits the Texas Forest Service. The 1952 SFASU photo record (creator United States Forest Service) places the site in Davy Crockett National Forest. Unresolved; a Davy Crockett National Forest office or Texas A&M Forest Service history record could settle it. No build date, design, height, staffing or access found. The FFLA status list shows no date that I saw. TopoQuest gives an elevation of 341 ft (not used in the story). The 1953 Grand Prairie Daily News item was read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not in the newspaper itself. No photo added: the SFASU page text read has no image URL.

Very thin record. Smith Ferry is not registered in the cached National Historic Lookout Register or FFLOS listings for Texas, and no construction date, design, height, staffing, or fate (standing/removed/burned) beyond the FFLA list's bare 'Standing' turned up in two web searches plus the cached regional lookout lists. The Texas Escapes citation is general East Texas context (phase-out to aerial patrol), not Smith-Ferry-specific; flagged as such in the story. Worth a follow-up with Texas A&M Forest Service records or Tyler County historical sources if a human researcher has more time/budget.

Only FFLA gives tower-specific information, and it gives no build date, builder, design, staffing or access. The Community Impact article (published May 6, 2026, per its dateline) gives office context only and does not mention a lookout tower (checked, no match for 'tower'). The story gives the groundbreaking as April 29 and does not say construction is still under way, which the article does not establish. The FFLA Bastrop entry (gone) is a different site and is mentioned only to prevent confusion. Cavallerano's 2025 book has a 'Lost Pines' appendix that may cover Bastrop County; it was not read. Record is consistent: standing, Bastrop County, matching coordinates.

No newspaper, NRHP, or forest-history coverage found specific to this tower; it is recent (built 2023, NHLR-registered Jan 2026) so that may simply not exist yet. The NHLR nominator, Alfred Francis Gessel, shares a surname with a contact address once suspected on the Timber Lane Utility District site, raising a guess that he may be a district official involved in bringing the tower to the park — but this was never sourced (the district-facilities page carries no contact names or emails) and has been dropped from the story entirely rather than left as insinuation. Climbability and drive-up access are unconfirmed; the park's own page references a 'Fire Tower Flyer' that was not reachable in this research. One correction applied: the NHLR elevation figure (113 ft / 34 m) is not labeled by the register as site elevation vs. structure height, so the story no longer asserts which it is. The district-facilities source was dropped (it supported neither the Fire Tower Flyer mention, which is on the parks-and-trails page, nor the contact-name claim, which isn't on the site at all); the FFLA citation is renumbered [^3] accordingly.

Thin record. Only county, agency, FFLA standing status and coordinates were found. Searches surfaced only unrelated Shelby County fire news. Best lead: Cavallerano's Fire in the Piney Woods. The Project MUSE summary was read; the full text was not, and may need institutional access. Texas A&M Forest Service history pages (tfsweb.tamu.edu) returned HTTP 403 to fetch_text, so were not read. The FFLA list shows no date that I saw. The story is intentionally short (about 125 words).

Build date is known only as 'the 1930s' (NHLR); events[0] uses 1930 as a placeholder for the decade, and the story says 'in the 1930s'. NHLR and firelookout.org name the agency Texas Forest Service; the Pine Mills entry names Texas A&M Forest Service. The sources do not reconcile these. The Tyler County Heritage Society has a 'Fire Tower' artifact (index dated January 1, 1941); only a preview was readable and it does not name this tower, so it is not used. No access or visit information found, so access is omitted. Brief coordinates differ from firelookout.org by about 0.0003 degrees, immaterial. Brief status and registration year agree with sources. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the Register footnote was removed from the advice sentence; the company name is given as in the Register ('Emsco Oil Derrick Co.'); the Santa Claus wording is now quoted in full and the Register's administrator line is quoted.

Only one detailed source: a 1948 Salt Lake Telegram account quoted on the Forest Lookouts site. No build or removal date found. The brief's 'gone' is not supported; the FFLOS list says Abandoned. Do not confuse with the Walker Bank Building lookout (1939 to about 1948), which is a different site.

Early history conflicts: the fire year is 1957 in Willhite and about 1963 in the register, and no source gives a firm build date for the first lookout. Willhite is a personal site; the NPS overlook page is official and was last updated August 15, 2026 per its footer. A 1976 theft is recorded on the westlookouts page and on Willhite. It names a private individual and does not bear on the lookout's history, so it is left out. No staffing data was found. The record's status 'gone' and elevation are consistent with the sources, so no corrections are proposed. One web search used.

The brief's record said gone; two newer sources say standing, so the status is corrected. The fire-lookout role is thin: only the 1927 lookout station label, a recalled weather use, and no fire-season staffing records were found. The 2026 lightning death comes from the Tribune and is in one sentence; an editor may want to review that wording. The elevation sources disagree.

Two small date conflicts in the sources, both noted in the story rather than resolved: last staffed year (NHLR: 1968; Deseret News: 1969) and the restoration year before the 2008 closure (NHLR: 1986; Deseret News: early-1980s renovation, reopened 1987). Nothing in hand to adjudicate either. The record itself checks out against all sources on name, location, build year (1937) and status. The tower is now a staffed-by-volunteers interpretive/tour site rather than an active detection post, which the current record's staffing/access/visit fields didn't yet reflect. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found a third, previously unflagged conflict: NHLR gives elevation as 8,819 ft, but Wikipedia, Wikidata and willhiteweb all give 8,834 ft; now flagged in the story and as a correction above rather than resolved. Also corrected three footnote misattributions in the original story/JSON draft: the '360 square miles' view figure and the above-ground-living-quarters uniqueness claim were cited partly to NHLR, which does not state either; and the NRHP listing date/reference number was cited partly to NHLR, which gives only the 1978 nomination, not the 1980 listing date or reference number. Willhiteweb separately gives a 1935 build year, at odds with the 1937 given by NHLR, Wikipedia, Wikidata and Deseret News; left unflagged since the story never cites willhiteweb for the build year and the other four sources agree. Also fixed a pronoun error: the story referred to the current volunteer tour guide as 'him', but the cited Deseret News source names her as Clare Boerigter ('her third season').

Height disagrees: 16 stories (Intermountain Histories, Clio) vs 15 (Former Fire Lookout Sites register, Forest Lookouts); the story reports both. Core dates 1939 start and about 1948 end agree across the register and Intermountain. Record status 'gone' fits; the building itself stands. The KDLY radio tower is dated only to 'the 1940s' by Clio, so it appears in the story but not in events. The roof's current state rests on a photo caption dated about 2015 and Clio; not checked against a newer source. Access is inferred from private ownership; no source addresses roof access. The record's 'U.S.Forest Service' agency is shared with the Salt Lake City Water Department. No source gives the date the alidade table was removed.

The only history found is a 1914 item quoted secondhand on Forest Lookouts; the Ogden Examiner original was not read. No build date, design or end date was found. The brief's status 'gone' is not what the Association says ('Abandoned'), so it is proposed as unknown. The Forest Service page confirms a public trail to the peak but says nothing about lookout remains. Elevation and coordinates are not used. Worth checking Uinta NF archives or the Ogden Examiner for construction and closure dates. The Association's rule that sites move to the lookout lists applies to its Unknown/Undocumented Sites list, which does not include Wolf Creek Peak, so that rule is not used.

Build year and registration are from the register. Removal is only shown as 'Removed' (Forest Lookouts) and 'Tower Gone' (Association list); neither gives a date or cause. One WebSearch found nothing more, and the register has no removal field. Next check: Jefferson National Forest or Forest Service records. The Alleghany Brushy Mountain (US 923, VA 9) is a separate tower and was not used. The brief's status 'gone' matches the sources. The name's origin (Allen Field) is not in any source read, so the story does not explain it.

Thin record. Brief's height_m 24.4 matches the 80-foot figure in two sources. No build date, staffing or access level is given by any source, so none is recorded. The FFLOS list gives status only. The Weebly entry is a short notes block.

The 1965 survey station one mile southwest of Amelia gives the same 125-foot height and four-legged steel frame as the register, so the story treats it as probably the same tower; this is an inference, not a stated link. The survey page's road directions are not repeated because they may be out of date. No source read gives staffing, use history or current access. The register's footings photo is a caption only; its date and licence are unknown, so no photo is listed. Amelia's Denaro tower (also in Amelia County, on the Association list) is a different site and was not used. The brief's 'Virginia Department of Forestry' agency matches the register.

The move to Purgatory Mountain rests on the register sentence alone. The Purgatory Mountain register page is not in the cache (a guessed URL returned 404) and was not read, so the story reports only the Association's 'Tower Gone' entry for Purgatory. Whether any part of the frame stands there is unverified. A WebSearch snippet from willhiteweb.com gave 1955-1958 and a 60-foot tower with a 14 by 14 foot cab for the move; the page was not read, so it is not used. Access is inferred from Wikipedia's 'The summit is open' and should be confirmed with the Jefferson or George Washington National Forest. The record's 'gone' status is proposed as 'moved' in corrections for human review.

Two conflicts are unresolved: height (100 ft in Weebly vs about 125 ft in the 1942 survey) and fate (2015 scrap auction listing vs standing in 2019 and 2023). The 1933 entry is an under-construction report, not a completion date, and the Weebly page presents it as the same tower without proving it. Access is restricted by fence and signage, and the visit report judges the steps too poor in shape to be regularly climbed, so the story does not encourage a visit. No photo added: the Register's photos carry no licence statement in the text. Brief's 30.5 m height is kept, as it matches the 100-foot figure.

The brief had no height. The 35-foot figure is the Register's, converted to 10.7 m. No source states that the public may drive or walk to the tower, so the record gives no access level; the public trails listed are the preserve's, not the tower's. The latest condition record is the May 2018 visit report. The Register has a photo path (nhlr.org /images/Lookout_Photos/US907_Bald_Knob/Scholetzky1.jpg) but no licence is stated, so no photo is added.

Two sources: the FFLOS register (1) and the Forest Lookouts Virginia page (2). Height conflict (50 ft plan in 1932 vs 60 ft register) is shown in the story. Elevation 3,607 ft (1,099 m) and registry US 1725, VA 27 from the register. The NGS entry on the Forest Lookouts page is a 1957 description and does not say the tower is standing now. A Facebook group snippet from a search result says a Molpus Timberlands easement allows visits to the tower site; the fetched page showed only its title, so it is not used and access is unverified. Do not confuse with Bald Mountain Lookout Site (Nelson County), US 1715, a separate record. No staffing, fire or access information found. Two WebSearch queries were used.

Brief record matches FFLOS on coordinates, 1955 build, USFS administration and circa 2000-2002 removal; no correction needed. Gap: no source describes what remains on the summit or whether the site is open. The CCC account is read from a third-party transcription credited to 'Bob Cat - CCC Company 1368'; the April 1940 year comes from the entry heading, so the original newsletter would settle it. A search for the 1955 construction turned up nothing new. The Washington State Bald Mountain pages in search results are a different site and were ignored.

The Nelson record's Built field and description disagree (early 1960s vs late 1930s), and the 1957 survey note supports an earlier date; the editor may want the original FFLOS build year. FFLOS US 1725 (Augusta County, same coordinates) is a separate record for the same peak; consider merging or cross-linking. Access is unverified: a Facebook group post in search results says the land around Bald Mountain is owned by Molpus Timberlands and visitation to the tower site is allowed, but the page was login-walled and only one line was readable, so it is not used. Nelson's Cottages result is about Rondaxe Mountain in New York and was ignored. Brief record: no build year was recorded, and the agency matches the Nelson record.

The brief's record matches FFLOS on coordinates, 1936 build, 1978 removal and VDOF administration; the brief's access of unknown is replaced by FFLOS's private-property statement. Only one detailed source (FFLOS), so confidence is medium. The 114-step figure is FFLOS's report of local memory and is attributed as such. A Dickenson Star article on the tower by the county historical society sits behind a subscription wall and was not used. The easternuslookouts Bartlick page has only a heading for this site. No staffing or fire history was found, so none is recorded.

Two substantive sources: the NHLR entry and a 1929 newspaper item quoted on Forest Lookouts (the newspaper itself was not opened). Build year is unresolved: 1933 (register, 60 ft) against October 1929 (62 ft); the story says so and the record's height_m 18.9 follows the 62-foot figure. Record agency 'Arthur Stiltner' is the register's 'Administered by' line, a person rather than an agency; a human should decide the agency field. Nothing found on staffing, fires, present ownership or condition. A web search snippet said the Virginia Department of Forestry once ran the tower and it is now private, with standing recorded as of March 26, 2008; no page I could open states this, so it is not in the story or facts.

No build date in any page read. Height conflict unresolved: the register and the Forest Lookouts header say 80 ft (record height_m 24.4); the 1964 survey description says 100 ft. Ownership change date not found. The Forest Lookouts page also gives driving directions to the tower through a gate and along a private road; they are deliberately left out of the story, which says the tower is private. Do not confuse with Apple Orchard Mountain (Bedford County, listed gone). No staffing or fire history found. Present condition not verified. The Bedford city history page that a search returned covers fire departments, not this tower, and was not used.

Only one period source: the 1963 Coast and Geodetic Survey station description, reproduced on the Forest Lookouts page. No construction date, builder, staffing, or fire history found in that page, the FFLOS Virginia list, SummitPost, or two WebSearch queries (neither returned a history). The NHLR and FFLOS caches hold no page for this tower. 100 ft is converted to 30.5 m. Access is private per SummitPost; the 1963 gate-and-trail directions on the Forest Lookouts page are deliberately left out. Next checks if wanted: Virginia Department of Forestry records, Russell and Buchanan county newspapers, and an NHLR listing check.

Gone status is confirmed by the Forest Fire Lookout Association county list. The 1941 CCC build year and the 20' cab rest on the register alone; '20' live-in cab' could mean the cab or the tower, so no height is recorded. Scenic Drives USA dates the picnic area to the 1930s, which is a different structure and is not used for the tower date. FSR 206 (Scenic Drives) and FS 206 (register) are treated as the same road; the story now says so. The register's footer description has no date. The register's account of footers is the only source for what remains. No staffing, fire, or design records found in these sources. Visit advice: no tower to climb; the picnic area is the only visit point described.

Standing is confirmed by firelookout.org. The 1958 report and 1964 NGS note are quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, which credits the 1958 piece to the Kingsport News; the original article was not checked. The NGS station is BIG KNOB, VA/SCOTT. The 1964 note also measures the station mark from the tower's legs (10.3 ft from the southeast leg, 4.8 ft from the northeast leg), so the mark sits on this tower's site; the note still gives no construction date. The 1930/1933 date is on the survey mark (a standard disk set in bedrock), not the tower, and nothing in the sources dates the tower from it. Do not use the 1964 access description (locked gate, 3.25-mile trail) for visits; it is historic and the tower is private. High Knob (Wise/Scott counties) is a different tower. No design, height, or build date in any source read.
