The name 'Sussex Courthouse' is unexplained by any source read; a search returned Sussex County courthouse history, but nothing linking a lookout to it. Two search queries found no build, owner, height, staffing or fire record.

Only the FFLA listing (standing, Lee County) and TopoQuest (Lee County, 2,519 ft, named Hunter Lookout Tower) confirm the tower. Wikipedia names the gap, not the tower. The DHR and DOF pages give statewide context only and do not name this tower. Two web searches found no build date, builder, design, staffing, ownership or access record. The FFLA name and the topo name differ; the record name was kept. Confidence low.

Height conflict: the 1933 Daily Press item (quoted on the Forest Lookouts page) says 120 feet; the 1942 NGS station description and the Register say about or exactly 100 feet. facts uses 30.5 m (100 ft). Owner conflict: the 1933 and 1942 sources name Chesapeake (Pulp and Paper Co., then Corporation); the Register names David Nice. No source read dates the change or explains the name change. facts.access level 'private' is inferred from the Register's private-owner line; no source describes public access or climbing. One WebSearch on the tower, Chesapeake and David Nice found nothing that ties them to this tower. The Register description is undated, so current condition is not verified. The Forest Lookouts page also gives a 1942 NGS designation (PID GV4691), which is not in the story.

The 1950 Kingsport Times-News item was read only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the original newspaper was not checked. The register's 1938 cabin is described in its own text, so the 1938 event is sourced. Two web searches found no further history and no description of the site today. The brief's height 9.1 m matches the 30-foot tower. The earlier cabin's date is a register claim with no second source.

The county disagreement is unresolved and should be checked against a county map before publishing. A 1951 Appalachian Trail Histories photo caption (https://www.appalachiantrailhistory.org/items/show/1156) mentions a view 'from the Jones Knob lookout, possibly from the fire tower that used to stand there'; its timing is unclear against the 1973 removal and it is marked 'All rights reserved', so it is not used as a photo or fact. No staffing or fire record found in the sources read. Access not described.

Only the FFLA listing (standing, Buchanan County) and RoadOnMap (a place-name site naming Keen Mountain Fire Tower, 2,710 ft) name the tower. Two other map sites (anyplaceamerica, getamap) returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The Wikipedia page is about the community, not the tower. The story no longer says the page omits a tower, since that negative cannot be quoted. An article on the Keen Mountain coal camp was read and does not mention a tower. Two web searches found no build date, builder, design, staffing, ownership or access record. Confidence low.

Build year not found. The CCC is named by a 2014 blog and the 1991 state survey gives only a statewide CCC total (88 lookout towers through 1941), not a date for this site. The rebuild date, PATC role and Fort Valley Ranch help come from that one blog; the PATC newsletter it cites was not read. FFLA Standing* footnote confirms the cab is gone. Record county is Page / Shenandoah; a hiker notes crossing the Page-Shenandoah border near the trailhead, so the record may be right. No closure notice, staffing or fire history found. Hiking guides disagree on the structure, as the story says.

Two sources only, and the NHLR page carries nearly all the history. The 2014 county survey is quoted by NHLR, not read directly. Height converted from 80 ft to metres. Access, staffing and current condition are not documented, so no access key is given. The 2014 survey says the first tower went up 'shortly after' 1933, which fits the 1935 build date; no conflict found. The 1933 event is a warden post, not a tower, hence event type other. Two WebSearch-equivalent searches and four page reads were used.

Ownership conflict: the Register (undated page, registered 2015) says the Virginia Department of Forestry still owns it; the 2015 chapter report lists it as private with land for sale. Not resolved by any source read. The 2013 item is a real-estate advertisement quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; its asking price is left out. No build date, builder, staffing or fire history in any source read; one WebSearch found nothing more. height_m 24.4 converts the Register's 80 ft. facts.access level 'private' reflects the ownership label only; no access rules are given. Not verified: current ownership, whether the tower has been moved or removed since 2015, or whether the land has sold.

Thin record: one register entry and one association list. No date for the Rhudy move, no staff or fire history, no description of the Campbell County site today, no photos. The Rhudy record's 'built about 1934 at the Long Mountain site' rests only on the register. The register's 1972 removal year is a lower bound ('after 1972'). Two searches for this lookout yielded nothing usable beyond the two cited pages.

Original Long Mountain history rests on the FFLOS register alone. The Rhudy move and the Rhudy standing claim rest on the FFLA lists only; no Rhudy-specific page was found in two searches. The FFLA lists place the Rhudy entry under Relocated / Replica Lookouts, so the list does not say whether the structure was moved or replicated. The register describes a 1972 conversion and removal, with no mention of moving, so the relocation is unconfirmed. Access, staffing and current condition are unknown. No photos found.

Build year and builder rest on one register entry that conflicts with the CCC's dates; no second source found. The CCC Company 2359 article from The Central Virginian turned up in search but returned 404 on fetch, so it is not cited. The Louisa County 1995 survey was checked and does not mention the tower. Access is inferred from the 2019 visit report, not a current source. The NHLR page lists the Virginia Department of Forestry as both administrator and cooperator, which confirms the record's agency. The Register's claim that this is the only such tower in Virginia is not repeated because it is unverified. A Facebook post placing the tower off West Main St was not used. Height converted from 100 ft. Consider adding a built event as an editor's call; the record had none.

Coordinates: the Register says they are unlisted at the owner's request, yet the record's lat/lon matches the FFLA Virginia list and the Wikidata point. Keep coordinates out of public copy and ask a human to decide whether the record should keep them. No build year is given (only 'the 1930s'), so no built event was added. The 2015 report and the Register spell the county Lunenberg; Wikidata and the FFLA list use Lunenburg (see corrections). One WebSearch found no builder or owner history, so the Aermotor claim rests on the Register alone. The FFLA 'Tower Standing' entry is the only status source; not verified on the ground. Height 33.5 m converts the Register's 110 ft.

Built date is only the spring-1938 announcement; no completion report found. Location descriptions conflict (see resolved_conflicts) and the record coordinates were not tested against them. The 2002 'good condition' note is about the survey mark, not the tower; do not read it as a condition assessment. No staffing history or access information found. The 1942 description is from a Coast and Geodetic Survey station description quoted in the NGS datasheet. Do not confuse with the Matthews State Forest lookout (Grayson County, ex-Morris Knob tower), which appeared in a search snippet only and was not read. Two web searches used.

Built year is only 'early 1930s' in the county text; the 1930 event year is a placeholder. The 1990 staffed_last year is also a placeholder for 'until the 1990s'. No notable fires are named in any source read. Access level is omitted because no source we read supports one (the brief says unknown). Post-2021 condition is unverified: a Henrico Citizen article on the January 2024 marker was found in search but could not be read (newsbreak fetch refused; the henricocitizen tag page gave only a teaser), so it is worth checking. A Henrico County Facebook post (search snippet only, not read) says the tower has stood since 1933 and could be used if read. The brief's 37.5065, -77.2691 coordinate was not read on the Forest Lookouts page and is only referred to from the brief. Designer spelling differs: county uses Aeromotor, Forest Lookouts and the brief use Aermotor.

Thin record. The only sources are two FFLA lists that give name, county, coordinates and a standing status. Searches found no NHLR or FFLOS page for Melfa and no history, staffing or access information. The standing status comes only from the FFLA lists, so confirm it on the ground or with the owner before publishing it as current. Nothing in the record was changed.

No build date, builder, owner or staffing dates were found; the story says so. Searches returned hike guides, a Facebook post and a YouTube result. A YouTube result says the US Forest Service once maintained a tower here; that is unverified and not used. The record county 'Washington' is only one of the two counties HawkCount says the site straddles. The Register's 'no longer manned' has no date, so no staffing key is given. East Coast Hiker's note that climbing partway is possible is deliberately not used, since the tower's climbing status is not documented. Height converted from 100 ft. Two WebSearch-equivalent searches and about six page reads were used.

Identity is the main open question. By coordinates, the register's Mill Mountain site (38.08 N, 79.49 W) and its White Rock site on Mill Mountain (37.84 N, 79.69 W, Rich Hole Wilderness) are far apart, but the Forest Lookouts list treats them as one name. A Forest Service or Bath County history source on the Mill Mountain tower location would settle it. No staffing, fire or access data found. The Forest Service trail belongs to the White Rock site, not confirmed for the register's Mill Mountain site. A Roanoke Mill Mountain observation tower also exists (search snippet only, not read); it is a different structure and should not be confused with this record.

Built date disagrees: 1940 construction and 1941 completion (Willhite, Wikidata) against 1942 construction (Forest Lookouts). Status: FFLA and Forest Lookouts say gone or removed, while Willhite photographed a remaining base and Wikidata says ruinous; status_note records the base. No design, height, staffing or fire source was found. Coordinates match Wikidata to within a few metres. A Shenandoah NPS Facebook post (search snippet only, not read) gives the same 1940 and 1941 dates and mentions a remaining platform; it is not cited.

The 1938 build, design and cost rest on NHLR plus two 1938 newspaper items quoted by Forest Lookouts. Staffing and the fire history rest on NHLR alone; no source read names a fire the tower spotted or staffing after the 1980s. The Rappahannock Record article is paywalled, so only its lead was read. The book by Anthony-Tolbert was not read and may fill the gaps. The seasonal staffing value describes the historical pattern, not current staffing. The brief record checks out (height 30.5 m, elevation 38.7 m from 127 ft, the 1938 and 2026 events), so no corrections. No new photos: NHLR credits a photo to Susan Anthony-Tolbert but gives no image URL. The April 1938 clipping spells the chairman's name 'Wolbur' and the June item spells it 'Wilbur'. Not verified: current condition beyond the Forest Fire Lookout Association standing listing.

Thin record. Only the register and the forestry page were read. The register is the sole source that the tower stands at the forest office; the forestry page does not mention the tower (checked: no tower, lookout, or move wording on that page). Build date, builder and move date are not in any source read, so no relocated event is recorded (events need a year). The forestry page says the forest is operated by VDOF and lists the office, but gives no visiting rules for the tower, so no access level is recorded. The phone number is on the forestry page only, for reserving facilities; the register does not give it, so the story cites it to the forestry page alone and asks readers to call ahead about the tower. The Forest Fire Lookout Association Virginia lists give the Matthews entry as standing and the original Morris Knob site as gone; those lists were not quoted here, so the 'standing' status rests on the register's present-tense description. Original site record us-va-morris-knob is marked relocated, which fits. Editor could confirm the tower's condition and visitor access by phoning the forest office. No corrections proposed.

Two sources only. The county conflict (Bath per register, Highland per Forest Lookouts and its Virginia index) and the height conflict (40 ft register vs about 50 ft in a 1941 survey note) are both reported in the story. No removal date appears in any source, so no removed event is recorded. No source describes the site today. Two web searches; a Facebook group post claims removal and 'highest point in Bath County' but is not used. The brief's Bath County is supported by the register, so it is not corrected.

The brief's '1961 built' is the NHLR erection date at Partlow; the tower stood at Prince William Forest Park from early in WWII (FFLOS build year 1942). FFLOS calls the earlier tower wooden while NHLR calls it an Aermotor; unresolved. The newest source is the NHLR visit report of August 9, 2019; no later condition or staffing data was found. The site has security cameras and cell antennas, so the story does not suggest approaching the base. Record elevation 126.8 m matches NHLR 416 ft (127 m). Staffing dates are unknown.

History is documented through 1964 by newspaper clippings quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; nothing later was found. Height comes from a 1938 newspaper (35 ft = 10.7 m) and is not in the record. Staffing after 1964, current condition and current access are unknown. The 1939 'staffed_first' entry is a planned observer, not a confirmed staffing. Not in the NHLR or FFLOS Virginia listings in the local crawl. Two web searches used.

The Suffolk move rests on one interview account quoted in the register description. The state list shows a standing Dismal Swamp tower in Suffolk, but no source links it to Pender, so the story does not say they are the same. The 30.5 m height comes from the 1933 plan for a 100-foot tower, not a measured figure. The agency text 'now Fifty West Fairfax' is copied as the register gives it; the organization was not identified. No source found for the site today. Research went about two reads over the per-tower budget while checking the Suffolk claim.

Thin record. Status comes from the FFLA list and its asterisk legend. The only history is the NHLR Crafton Gate entry, which mentions Phenix in passing and gives no date. The Phenix town history page and the Wikipedia article for Phenix do not mention the lookout. The 564 ft elevation is from a topographic map site and was not written into elevation_m. Access and ownership are unknown, so the story says to treat the tower as off limits until the owner confirms otherwise.

The register withholds coordinates at the owner's request, but our record carries lat/lon 37.43541, -78.80471 from the FFLA index. Please decide whether to keep them public. The owner is named in the news report; the story does not name him and omits the register's contact email. The register's nominator (Ricky Butler) and the news report's former forester (Rick Butler) may be the same person; the story does not link them. A 2020 blog says about a dozen towers remain in Virginia while WTVR says about 50; no count is used. Visits are by appointment only; the register names Krissy Reynolds as the contact, so the story sends readers to her and does not name the owner or print the contact email.

The register (1996) says the tower was still operational; the current state list says gone. Two web searches found no removal date, cause or site description. The October 1933 item is a proposal to share the cost, not proof of completion, so the 1933 build date rests on the register alone. The 1933 article spells the partner county 'Greenville'; Virginia's county is Greensville, and the story does not name it. Height 30.5 m is the register's 100-foot figure. No photos added.

Two registry sources and one 1953 newspaper item quoted by Forest Lookouts; the newspaper itself was not read. No source read covers fires the tower spotted, staffing after 1953, or current access. NHLR prints the build year as l937 with a lowercase L; recorded as 1937. The brief coordinates (37.18222, -77.2) are the NHLR figures; the Forest Fire Lookout Association list places the tower about 1 km west, at 37.18149, -77.21294. The record keeps NHLR's coordinates. The brief record checks out (elevation 44.8 m matches 147 ft); its status 'standing' stands with the NHLR inactive note added. Encyclopedia Virginia's essay on CCC work in Prince George County was checked and does not mention this tower, so it is not cited. No new photos. Not verified: current condition beyond the standing listing.

The Partlow tower is a separate register record (US 1163, VA 29, NHLR) that holds the standing status and visit report; consider linking the two records. The visitor-center claim rests on one register caption credited to the nominator; the NPS contact page does not mention a visitor center, so the story attributes it to the register. The 1961 Free-Lance Star item is read only as quoted on Forest Lookouts, not the original newspaper. The brief's events match the register, so no corrections. The NHLR visit report is from 2019; any change since then is not known.

Do not confuse with the Red Oak Knob fire tower in West Virginia's Monongahela National Forest, which is a different structure. Only the register and one 2020 blog post are cited, so confidence is low. The register gives no builder and no build year finer than the 1930s. No staffing dates, watcher names or fires were found. The cupola-style description comes from the register. The 2020 blog repeats the register's description word for word, so it is not independent support for the history.The record's kind 'ground' matches the state index. A MountainZone listing gives the mountain summit as 1,404 ft (428 m); the story uses the register's 1,399 ft (426 m) for the lookout.

The brief's source list includes the Friends of Shenandoah Mountain History of High Knob Fire Tower page; that page is about a different tower, so it is not cited here. A Friends article 'What Ever Happened to Reddish Knob Tower?' is linked from the FFLOS listing. Search snippets describe a 1972 Forest Service proposal that would have removed all towers except Elliott Knob and Reddish Knob, and a $400 dismantling by local men. The page text was not retrieved, so neither claim is in the story; it should be fetched and checked, since the 1972 exemption would conflict with the 1975 removal. Build date: the sources give only 'the 1920s'. Access is public per the Friends page and Wikipedia; the Forest Service listing was not checked. No source describes the foundations today.

The register gives two conflicting accounts of the tower's fate (converted to a communications tower with the cab and stairs removed, or removed and replaced by a non-original Century Link tower). No source we found settles it. No source gives a build date, builder, or staffing. The microwave license record (Radyn copy, KJH27 path 5) shows a 107.6 ft lattice tower at SAND MTN but shows no date, so it does not show whether that tower is the same one. The register's photo caption 'Foundation to which stairs were mounted' is undated. Elevation: register 3,687 ft; the Roanoker article says 3,721 ft (not used). Brief's status 'gone' and agency kept; access was unknown in the brief and is now set to restricted.

The Upper Henrico to Short Pump identification is inferred from name and place. The Gillies Creek standing claim rests on the association list alone, with no date or mover. A 2009 Waymarking post (WM6Q0E) says the Goochland exhibit tower may be the Short Pump tower or a Hanover tower and that the Short Pump tower's location is unknown; fetch_text cannot read that page because its content sits inside a form tag, so it is not cited and a human could check it by hand. A Facebook group post asks whether a Short Pump tower went to Gillies Creek; it is a question and was not read as evidence. The association list also has a Goochland entry named Field Day of the Past (Relocated Negrofoot) marked Tower Gone; the story does not use it because it names no Short Pump link. Consider a call to Henrico County. No photos found.

Only the register and the FFLA list cover this site; two web searches found nothing else about Simmons Mountain or a lumber company removal. The register's Built field reads 1960s with no exact year, so no built event is recorded. Access and current condition are unknown and the story says so. The register's nominator is not named in the story. The removal event has no year because the register's Removed field reads 1980s only; a map view of years standing will not show a removal year for this site.

Thin record. NHLR is the only detailed source; Forest Lookouts gives only a county and an agency heading, and the Forest Fire Lookout Association list confirms the tower is standing. No construction date appears in any source read. The brief record elevation (456.6 m) matches NHLR's 1,498 ft. A Lake News article on Smith Mountain fire tower history (lakemagazine.life) turned up in search but the site returned HTTP 429 on two tries, so it was not read or cited. A Facebook group post and a YouTube video also describe the tower but could not be read. Do not confuse with the Alabama Smith Mountain lookout (us-al-smith-mountain) or the separate Bedford lookout in Virginia (us-va-bedford). The agency conflict is not resolved by any source. Not verified: whether the radio equipment is still mounted, and who now has access. No new photos.

Original site: FFLA says Tower Gone. Jones describes a CCC camp foundation a short way up the road, not tower footings; no source describes tower remains at the old site. The current tower and its access are covered by us-va-sounding-knob-moved. Access changed over time: fenced in 2017 per Jones, gated but open daylight since November 2020 per the register. Build year 1934 vs 1935 is unresolved in the sources; the story reports both. No new photos added.

The record name 'moved from its original spot' is not supported by the cited sources, which describe dismantling and reinstallation on Jack Mountain. The coordinates differ: the record's tower point (38.395783, -79.563883) and the separate FFLA 'Sounding Knob' point (38.34636, -79.59001) are about 6 km apart by my estimate. No source explains that gap, so it needs checking. A Highland County Chamber of Commerce directory lists 'Sounding Knob Fire Tower (Firetower LLC)', which suggests a business operator. I saw only a search snippet, so ownership and access may have changed since 2021. Elevation 1214 m is kept from the brief, not re-checked. Staffing 'until the 1960s' is a decade only, so no event year is given. Read budget: five distinct pages and two searches, close to the cap.

The 1963 clearing and the 1964-1965 start of operation are a sequence, not a conflict. The brief's built date (1941) is not in the source; the register says before 1941. The 2005 sale is taken from the WSET report and is not named in the story to protect the private landowner. No source describes the lookout tower's design, staffing, or fires. The register's 1954 description is the only account of the tower itself.

No construction year found in any source read; the register and the Forest Lookouts page are silent. The 1942-1948 staffing items are transcriptions of Smithfield Times pieces on the Forest Lookouts site; the original newspaper pages were not checked. The record's agency 'State' and ownership 'state' are not confirmed by any source read. The register's poor-condition note is undated. The 100 ft height is from the 1948 notice and is overall height, so it was not entered as cab-floor height. Two WebSearch queries found no Virginia Department of Forestry or construction record.

Two searches and about six page reads turned up no build date, designer, staffing record or fire history. The Long Lines page is a hobbyist site, so treat its wording as a lead. The Amherst County memo at https://www.countyofamherst.com/egov/documents/1238777346_488494.pdf appeared in search as a memo about American Tower's use of the 'Old Fire Tower' and repairs to its wooden enclosure. fetch_text found no text layer in it, so it needs a manual read; it may hold the build date and ownership of the cab. The Amherst County survey PDF (DHR, 2009-10) has no mention of a fire tower. Facebook group posts say the tower is no longer used for fire lookout; they are not cited. The brief's access 'unknown' is recorded here as restricted, based on the register's description of a commercial communications site; please confirm.

Two web searches found no removal date. The Willhite page is the only source for the ground structure and the 2024 visit; its photo captions are quoted only as captions. The 1934 items are funding, not a confirmed completion date. The 1948 in the FFLOS id is a registry number, not a build year, and is not used. Height 18.3 m converts the 1957 description of about 60 feet. The 1934 Forest Service observations are from the Willhite page. No photos added; the 2025 photo credit on the Willhite page has no license stated.

The 1938 build year and the dismantling rest on one register description; no second source was found. Two web searches found no staffing, fire history or removal date. Not used: the easternuslookouts.weebly.com page titled Walker Mountain, which is for Union, Windham County, a different site; and Big Walker Lookout near Wytheville (37.04575, -81.22835), a separate standing tower that the Virginia list records.

Only the FFLOS register page and the FFLA Virginia list were read. The WebSearch call for this tower was refused because the shared WebSearch budget for the run was already used up, so no search was run, and websearch.py was not used to get around the limit. The Hawthorne tower rests on one association list entry; no date, mover, owner, or access was found. The register describes a conversion to communications use and does not mention a move, while the association marks the site as Tower Gone. What, if anything, remains at the White Oak Mountain site is unknown. A separate record, us-va-white-oak-tower-site-at-hawthorne, covers the same move and has an overlapping story; the two should be reconciled by an editor. Fact-check 2026-10-09 re-read the register page and the FFLA Virginia list: the register's 'Removed after 1975' field and the Hawthorne entry under Relocated / Replica Lookouts are confirmed, and the story now cites the first sentence. Re-run search for the Hawthorne tower (Montgomery County) and for a White Oak Mountain communications site before publishing.

The White Oak half rests on the FFLOS register, which the association list agrees with on removal (the list marks the White Oak Mountain site as Tower Gone). The Hawthorne half rests on one FFLA list entry, which gives coordinates and a county but no date or mover, and sits under the Relocated / Replica Lookouts heading, so the list does not say whether the tower was moved or replicated. Two searches turned up no Hawthorne-specific page. The register describes a conversion and removal with no mention of moving. Access, staffing and current condition are unknown. No photos found.

No build year, staffing, fire history or removal date was found; two web searches turned up nothing on this tower. The Forest Lookouts page is the only source that says Removed, and the register description is a single sentence. The Forest Fire Lookout Association Virginia index flags Rich Hole as a possible duplicate ('same as White Rock?') and lists a separate Mill Mountain tower (Bath / Rockbridge, 38.07240, -79.49338, Gone); check whether these are one site. The same index also places FFLOS US 1706 beside a White Rock in Lee County and Harlan (KY); the Bath coordinates match the register, so the Bath entry is used.

No staffing history, fire-watch dates, or height figure was found in the sources read, so facts.height_m and staffing are omitted. The register's purpose (fire spotting plus recreation) and the county library's (tourism) differ in emphasis. A travel blog (thecommontraveler.net) says it was built to help rangers spot fires; it was not read and is not cited. The brief's elevation 557.8 m matches the register's 558 m. The brief's kind 'tower' matches 'Obs Tower' on firelookout.org. The Facebook and YouTube posts that surfaced in search were skipped as sources.

Elevation differs: NHLR gives 3,304 ft (1,007 m), which the record and story use; Wikipedia gives 3315 ft for the same peak. Not reconciled. Build history: the NHLR detail page gives no build year. Forest Lookouts, quoting a 1921 state report, has a tower and telephone line on Westmore Mountain that year, and a new steel tower built by the New England Forest Emergency fund in work dated 1938-40. Whether the standing tower is the 1938-40 steel tower, or whether the 1921 tower was replaced, is not stated in any source read. The NorthWoods Stewardship Center page cited by the 2013 and 2024 chapter reports returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The Ranger's Cabin (2013 report), the summit cabin (2002 and 2016 reports, 2025 roof) may be the same building; sources read do not say. 2016 condition conflict: the NHLR visit report of August 21, 2016 describes cab graffiti, bullet holes and a portion of the roof blown off, while the chapter's October 2016 hike found the tower and summit cabin in good shape. Roof: the 2008, 2010 and 2012 chapter reports call for repair or replacement; the 2022 report says replaced 'last year', read as 2021, which is an inference. Agency: Wikipedia says the forest is managed by Vermont DFPR; the 2022 chapter report calls the tower state-owned. The tower's own managing agency is not named in the sources read. Access: signed route from the 2016 NHLR visit report and the 2025 report are the newest; no current closure, staffing or booking notice was read. Staffing: the NHLR visit report has a Staffed? question; not used as a fact. Budget: four fetch_text page reads (NHLR, Forest Lookouts, the 2025 chapter report, Wikipedia) plus one blocked NorthWoods page; two WebSearch calls; the other chapter reports were read from the local cache with pdftotext -layout. No new photos added; the record photo is from the NHLR (Jack Kelley, all rights reserved).

Steel tower date is unresolved: the state record says a steel tower from Gilson Mountain went up in spring 1956, while the NRHP nomination says a private organization built the present tower in 1966. A geocaching page also says 1966 but is not used. Brief corrections: height (12.2 m is the 1932 wooden tower; 48 ft now) and the 2019 event, which no source read supports. Access: the park is a state park, but no climbing rules or closure notice were found, so the access level is a judgment. The 2025 closure dates appeared only in search snippets and are not used. The NRHP title is taken from the nomination header. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

Record height_m 21.0 (from OpenStreetMap) does not match the 45 ft 9 in height the January 1939 paper gave for the planned replacement. Left out of facts and corrections for a human to settle. FFLA marks the cab as gone, but the GMC 1984 account does not mention a cab, so that is unresolved. Summit land owner and climbing safety were not checked; access is set to public only from trail guides. Newspaper quotes come from the Eastern U.S. Lookouts transcriptions, not the originals. The Kinsley initials differ between sources.

Current tower's build date, builder, height and condition are unknown. The 1922 steel tower on Bolton Mountain may or may not be the same site: the Forest Lookouts entry ends with Removed, and the Chronicle describes the surviving tower as wooden. A 1921 newspaper quote gives the mountain as 3,600 with no unit, which does not match 3,150 ft; left unresolved. The OSM ele tag of 3200 is proposed for correction to metres. Guides disagree on how many Vermont towers still stand (14 in one, about twenty in the Chronicle). Ask Bolton Valley Resort whether the tower is open to climb before any visit.

Brief's 2007 'concrete steps repaired, no cab or tower work' event is not included. It appears only in a search snippet from cr-vt-2007.pdf (firelookout.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/cr-vt-2007.pdf), which was not read, so it is unverified here; worth a fetch and a quote. The 2025 MyChamplainValley closure notice is posted May 2, 2025, so the closure is now dated and used in the story. The register's 'open to the public' line is undated. Burke 54 ft matches brief height_m 16.5. Brief elevation_m 981.5 matches the register's 3,220 ft (981 m). Brief access 'unknown' is now public per the register. Conflicts: first tower year 1922 camp / 1923 tower (WillhiteWeb, 1923 newspaper) / 1927 pole tower (register, firelookout.com); the story gives 1923 for the first tower and notes the 1927 cab. Morris Ewell: 1928 (WillhiteWeb, 1928 newspaper) vs 1929 (firelookout.com). The Quartz tower is the moved Churchill tower; it was burned in October 1997, so no structure stands at either site. The Churchill site has no described current condition beyond a 'Churchill Footings' photo caption on WillhiteWeb. No access information found for the Churchill site, so no access key was written. The NGS designation 'Churchill Lookout Tower' is a survey mark name only. Record status 'gone' and elevation 1465 m match the register. Quartz Mountain site is itself gone (not a new lookout record). No new photos with usable URLs and licences were found.

Design conflict: register and Forest Lookouts say 12'x12' frame cab (1930); firelookout.com says gable-roofed L-4 cab. Blasting date conflict: WillhiteWeb ties rock blasting to the 1930 build; Forest Lookouts quotes a June 1932 Six Twenty-Six item about rock being shot away. Removal: register says removed 1967; others say destroyed or burned 1967. Record height_m 3.7 is not used as a tower or cab-floor height: the only height found is a 1950 NGS description of a building 12 feet tall, which does not say it was the lookout; left in facts out of caution, editor to decide. Road access reopened 2020 per a trip report; no official closure notice found. No photos with usable URL and licence were added.

Brief record checks out: coordinates, 1,724 m elevation, Lewis County and the March 17, 2011 registration match the register. The build year (1925, 1926 or 1928) and the fate (burned 1956 or dismantled) conflict across sources, and the story reports both. Only one source (the register) describes the 1982 finds and the archaeological report. The Forest Service trail page calls the site Cispus Point, while the register and most others use Cispus Mountain; the story keeps Cispus Mountain. The SummitPost road note dates from 2016 and is marked as such. Photo credits on the Forest Lookouts and firelookout pages have no URLs, so no photos are listed.

Thin record: four web pages and the FFLA list. No source read names the builder, gives the reason for the site, dates staffing, dates the removal, or states a current access rule, so access is left out of facts and the story says none was found. The record's access stays unknown. Willhite's captions (1932 cab, 1936 views, 2018 site photo) and the Weebly page do not state a licence, so no new photos are added. The Weebly page has a bare 'Removed' line near the entry; its meaning is unclear, so it is not used. Worth checking with the Gifford Pinchot National Forest for current access or any closure.

Brief lists kind 'ground'; sources give only an L-4 cab and do not say whether it stood on a tower, so the record's kind is unverified. Two searches found no staffing or fire records, so none are included. Access 'public' is inferred from a hiking description with an undated bridge note.

Jefferson County site only. Do not merge with the Clearwater lookout in Garfield County (Umatilla NF, 82-foot steel tower that firelookout.com describes as available for emergencies) or with the Clearwater South emergency site near the 705 ft benchmark, which Willhite describes separately. Willhite's trip report is undated, so the footings and permit details are as of an unknown visit. The 1942-44 Air Warning Service station 'Baker 4-4' listed on the Forest Lookouts page is not in the story because the sources do not say it stood on this lookout site. The register's 'Removed' field and the brief's 'removed' event are the same year as 'destroyed'; the record uses 'destroyed'.

Height is genuinely disputed across three sources (90 ft Umatilla NF inventory, 94 ft Kresek, 82 ft firelookout.com) and I left height_m out rather than pick one. The 'built 1938' field in the current tower record looks like an error against the CCC narrative that NHLR itself tells (1933 tower / 1935 cabin) - see the proposed correction. A same-named 'Clearwater Lookout Site' in the FFLOS register (firetower.org) is a different, unrelated former lookout near the Olympic Peninsula (~-124.3, 47.6) and was not used here. Distance from Pomeroy is also given two ways (15 mi per firelookout.com, 25 mi per the rental listing) - left out of the story as not load-bearing. Fact-check correction (2026-10-04): the draft had attributed firelookout.com's 82 ft figure to 'the Fire Lookout Museum' - that credit line is actually for the 1997 photo on that page, not the height, so the story and this file no longer carry that attribution. Also removed an unsupported claim that the tower is closed to 'climbing' (no cited source says this; the OSM node carries access=no but no climbing tag), and lightly reworded one sentence in the story that paraphrased willhiteweb.com too closely.

Core dates agree across four sources: 1946 cabin, 1954 cab, 1968 or late-1968/1969 tower, last staffed 1998, toppled 2007. Coordinates and elevations differ, and the tower-leg damage differs. The 'today' paragraph says no source found; the Willhite photo caption 'Towers on the summit' is undated and does not say the lookout remains. The washingtonlookouts.weebly.com page was not used for citations, and no WebSearch was used.

Brief's record (tower kind, 1,153.7 m, Stevens County, coordinates, 2012 FFLOS registration) matches the Register; no correction needed. Two searches found no fire records, so none are included. Access 'public' is inferred from a 2023 route description on National Forest land; the page describes no closure. The Forest Lookouts newspaper items are quoted from the Colville Examiner through that index, not from the newspaper itself.

No staffing or fire records found; one search returned nothing site-specific, so none are included. The 1930 built-event year is a decade placeholder (sources say 1930s). Willhite's photos, including 2016 views, are the only view of the site today. Brief's 'ground' kind fits the concrete foundation but no source states it. Forest name is the Register's and was not checked against a current Forest Service source.

Current use is disputed and not resolved: the register text (undated, also on firelookout.com) says staffed most summers; the Willhite page (undated text, photo captions 1934 and 2016) says it appears recently abandoned; TrailChick (visited May 2019) does not say. Check with the Colville Tribes before publishing either claim. The $80/yr permit comes from a TrailChick page updated March 2026; verify with the Tribes. A search summary claimed the Colville Tribes staff the tower periodically, citing a photo entry; no page read confirmed it, so it is left out. Access note in facts is permission per the record. Record fields height_m and status are unchanged (45 ft tower height is not converted because the register does not say whether it runs to the cab floor).

Built date 1935 agrees across the register, Willhite and Wikipedia; removal in 1968 agrees across the register, FireLookout.com and Wikipedia. The 1964 closure notice names Coldwater Creek, not Coldwater Peak, and the page files it under this lookout without saying they are the same; the story flags that. The record's access is unknown; sources describe a public hiking route, so access is set to public. Staffing rests on one 1937 item. No source describes footings or other remains on the summit today. Summit elevation (5,722 ft, Wikipedia) and lookout-site elevation (5,727 ft, register) differ slightly; both are measurements of nearby points.

Build year is disputed (1931 or earlier, 1932, 1933, and a 1934 ground house in a structural inventory). The record's design R-6 is only one of the readings. The record's height_m 4.3 is not supported by any source read, so it is left out of facts. The 1931 newspaper item gives the Halls' origins differently from WillhiteWeb (Iowa and North Dakota reversed); not used in the story. The 1943 Harold Deery entry is a photo caption, so treat it as weak. Access: no source describes the trail's current condition or the summit's remains; the WillhiteWeb trip report may be old. Map and photo links on firetower.org were not read (images).

The brief matches FFLOS on build year, coordinates and registration (April 3, 2020, nominated by Tammy McLeod). The brief's conflict note ('They share a register number') was not checked. WillhiteWeb disputes the elevation (6,718 ft). Search snippets from FFLOS and FireLookout.com Sunset Park pages say a 1948 Sunset Park lookout replaced Colonnades; those pages were not fetched, so nothing here cites them. That lookout may deserve its own record. The page gives only the decade (the 1950s) for the lightning account, so no destroyed event is recorded. Reads: 5 pages, 2 searches.

Brief listed access as unknown; no closure notice or official access statement was found in the sources read, and WillhiteWeb gives distance and gravel-road access only (it does not call the trail open). Sources disagree on the drowning year (1931 vs 1933) and on the spelling Colquhoun vs Calquehoun; the story uses Colquhoun. The blog is a personal history blog, used for the 1931 date, the 1932 naming approval and the 1943 end date (which WillhiteWeb also gives). The blog's suggestion that the CCC built the lookout is speculation and is not used. The firelookout.org WA list row (Ground, Gone, FFLOS US 796) matches the brief but is not cited. No photos added.

The brief's status note (tower still stands, cab gone) and its 4.9 m height describe a pole tower that the NHLR and WillhiteWeb say is gone; corrected. The FFLA Washington list page the brief cites (firelookout.org/lookouts/us/wa/) was not read, so the source of the brief's wording is unchecked. The staffing history comes from newspaper items reprinted by WillhiteWeb (1915, 1919) and FireLookout.com's personnel list (1923, 1929); the 1919 item is written in the future tense, so the story says 'set to run' it. The Slagle brothers are undated, so no events entry was made for them. The 1960s burning and 1970s decommissioning are not pinned to exact years, so no event was made for them either. The weebly page's 1913 and 1915 newspaper items were not used. No photos added. Current access into the cabin is not confirmed. Confidence is medium: the cabin's facts agree across sources, but the pole-tower dates conflict.

Thin record. The 1931 build date agrees across all four pages. The end of the tower is undated; the register says removed, FireLookout.com and Willhite say destroyed, and the lookout history site lists it as removed. No staffing or fire history appears in any page read, so no staffing facts are recorded. Access as public is an inference from Forest Service land and an unobstructed road and hike described by Willhite, not a stated status. Willhite's photo captions on the page are undated, so the footings sighting has no date.

Rich record from four pages, two of them agreeing closely. Sources disagree on how the tower ended in 1968 (removed per the register, destroyed per FireLookout.com and Willhite); the story says so. A 1930 item quoted on the weebly page announces a planned lookout cabin on Cooper Mountain that fits neither the 1927 cabin nor the 1932 replacement exactly; it is left out of the story as unresolved. Do not confuse with Copper Mountain (North Cascades, Whatcom County), a different lookout. Access as public is inferred from a drive-up route in one 2020 account; no source mentions a gate or closure. The brief's county 'Okanogan/Chelan' matches the register.

The Spokesman-Review and Republic News-Miner passages reach us through WillhiteWeb and a Weebly transcription; the newspapers themselves were not read. Staffing names come from one source (Fire Lookout). The hike write-up is from June 2024, so today's condition is two years old. The Former Fire Lookout Sites registration date was not visible on the cached page and is not used. The 1950s removed-versus-destroyed question is unresolved.
Build-year conflict (1932 vs 1934) resolved by reporting both with their likely explanation, per brief's own flagged conflict.

Height 42 ft converted to 12.8 m. Brief elevation matches NHLR; other sources differ by about 30 to 35 ft. Current status is from TrailChick (updated March 2024) and firelookout.com ('as of last report', undated). Ramblr (2019) and geocache pages were not read. The stair removal is undated. Access is drawn from WTA and TrailChick; the story does not encourage climbing. No corrections to the brief.

Only the Forest Lookouts page cites the 1937 newspaper, and only through WillhiteWeb's quote of the Wenatchee Daily World; the paper itself was not read. The 2001 account is one quote by Irene Potter (dated 2001 on WillhiteWeb), repeated in the register; the story keeps the source's 'appeared' hedge. The gate's current status is not stated, so access is marked restricted. The SummitPost photo has no licence noted and no photo is added. Summit lookout mention rests on the photo caption.

Access: the WTA closure notice is dated 7.30.26 and the cached page may be out of date. Check the current closure before anyone advises a visit. Two approaches are described: the Forest Service's Cougar Ridge Trail behind gated Forest Road 5700, and WillhiteWeb's route from Maverick Saddle up the Mad River Trail. The footing caption is undated. The record's height_m 4.3 appears to be the 14-foot building width, so a correction is proposed rather than applied. WTA lists its hike as Cougar Mountain (#1415), while the Forest Service calls the Cougar Ridge Trail #1418 and says it ends at Tyee Ridge Trail #1415, so the WTA closure may not cover the Cougar Ridge route; the story now names the WTA hike.

Brief access was unknown; Willhite describes a hike from Council Lake Campground on National Forest land, so access is set to public. Fate dates conflict (1950s vs 1960s) and the story reports both. No source describes what remains on the summit; Willhite has 2018 drone photos that were not viewed as images. Brief record otherwise matches sources (elevation, status, agency).

Brief names the site Cowan Point; Willhite and the Washington Lookouts page use Cowan Peak, so both names are given. Storm-versus-fire account of the 1947 tower conflicts across sources and is reported as a conflict. Glover's 1959 death is included as staffing history and kept brief. Willhite's route page gives no visit date, so the footings are not dated.

Brief access was unknown; Willhite gives a legal route needing a Longview-St Helens permit, so access is set to permission. The 1942 AWS origin is disputed by Willhite. The 2012 footing report is secondhand and Willhite did not find footings in 2017; neither source dates a current visit. Brief record (elevation, county, status, agency) matches the sources.

firelookout.com and FFLOS share much wording, so they are not fully independent. The 1950 vs 1955 date is unresolved. No access level is recorded because no source states whether the summit is open to the public. A trailgroove.com search snippet (not read) calls Snyder the last occupant in 1952, which conflicts with the 1955 date; not verified and not used. A whatcomtalk.com 2024 article did not name Crater Mountain in the text read, so its volcano-monitoring reference is not used. Brief status 'gone' is correct.

Access is recorded as restricted because of the locked gate and the no-longer-allowed north route, not a posted closure; the 2023 trip report notes a lack of signage forbidding entry. The only current-condition evidence is the January 2023 trip report and an undated WillhiteWeb caption, so the summit's present state may have changed. Brief status 'gone' and agency are correct; no corrections.

Coordinates conflict: the record and FFLOS give 48.9039, -117.18418, while the west_us_lookouts record gives 48.89131, -117.20052, roughly 1.8 km away. That source was not read, so the record is unchanged and the story gives no coordinates. The 1929 build date is consistent across three sources. The access level 'public' rests on the wilderness hike described by WillhiteWeb; no closure was found.

Existence is disputed. FFLOS and firelookout.com give an NPS cab built 1934 and gone in the 1970s, but Willhite's 2016 visit (no footings found; he doubts it existed) is a direct challenge, and he ties the details to Crystal Peak (see us-wa-crystal-peak). Agency NPS and the in-park location are from the register and Forest Lookouts; Willhite disputes the location. Record elevation_m 2013.2 matches the 6,605 ft figure that Willhite calls a 1945 map value; no correction proposed because the register itself gives that figure. The access level 'restricted' (seasonal) rests on Willhite's summer gondola route, not on the ski-area setting; no source states the resort's access policy, so an editor may want to change it. Used 1 WebSearch, 5 page reads, and 1 grep read of the Forest Lookouts page. Staffing and fire history are absent from every source read.

Record built year 1930 is not in any source: the FFLOS Built field reads 1930's and Willhite gives 1934 (see corrections). The end date conflicts: the register and firelookout.com say abandoned in the 1950s; the NPS history and Willhite say removed in the 1960s or 1970s. The 1974 dynamite account is one 2018 correspondent's recollection printed on Willhite's page; the road crew member is not named in the story. Fires and staffing: none in sources read. Access 'public' rests on national park status and the Willhite hike description. Firelookout.com calls the site Crystal Lake and Willhite also uses Crystal Point; the story names both. Used 5 page reads (2 of them grep reads: NPS and weebly), 1 WebSearch, and the firelookout.org list as already cached from the Crystal Mountain research.

Tower year conflicts: register and firelookout.com 1935, Willhite 1934 (his page also dates panorama photos to 1934). Removal versus destruction in 1966 is reported both ways. The 1924 forestry report quoted on Willhite's and Forest Lookouts' pages does not name Darland Mountain in the quoted text, so it is left out. A 1955 photo caption naming lookout Barbara Vanderlaan is left out because the year is not clearly tied to it. Staffing names come from 1950s and 1960s newspaper items as Willhite and Forest Lookouts quote them; I did not check the originals. Access 'public' rests on Willhite's drive-up description; he places the summit where National Forest, state forest and Yakama Nation land meet, so an editor should check whether any part is tribal land. The record's kind 'tower' and elevation 2127.8 m match the register's 2,128 m. Used 4 page reads (1 grep read of the Forest Lookouts page), 1 WebSearch.

The brief records the site as gone, but the barn still stands and the Washington list marks it Abandoned; the correction is proposed. Whether a platform survives is disputed: SummitPost and Discover Darrington say it was removed or covered in the 1940s, TrailChick (visited 2018) describes one. The public access level is inferred from directions and SummitPost's note on the interior. The 1916 barn date is the only firm construction date for the building.

Build (1934) and end (1968) agree across sources; the wording of the end varies (removed or destroyed). Staffing: Lumsden (1944, 16 years in total, last season 1965 per Willhite) is in the register and Willhite. The Fire Lookout Association lists Aaron Jurgens for 1933, a year before the 1934 cab, and Marianna Kearney for 1964, with no context; both are kept as flagged events and the story says so. The 'Powderhorn/Davis Peak' alias in the record comes from a Willhite page that describes a different lookout near Woodland; see corrections. What remains on site is described only by SummitPost, a climbing site, and no Forest Service record was read. Access: trailhead directions only; no closure notice was read. Used 1 WebSearch and 5 page reads. The register and Willhite spell the place Rosyln; the story uses Roslyn.

Staffing as_of is the last year named in our reading (1966). The 1944-1969 history rests mostly on Willhite Web; the register and firelookout.com supply the 1946 date, the 1964 replacement and the abrupt 1969 removal. Access level 'permission' is inferred from Willhite Web's note on permits, not an agency statement. No photos added (licences not checked). Distance, cabin size, replacement location and elevation disagree across sources and are reported as such.

Height 12.2 m is the 40-foot 1954 tower; the 1942 cabin is about 25 feet per a 1953 USGS note quoted by Willhite Web but is not recorded in facts. Staffing as_of is the last year named in our reading (1957). Access level 'permission' is taken from Willhite Web's note on the private timberlands permit; no agency statement was read. The summit's current status is described only by Willhite Web's 2020 visit.

Identity: the WA list's Clallam County Blue Mountain entry (Olympic National Park, 28N-5W-1) is taken to be this site; its 1959 item names Deer Park and the lookout station. Today's condition rests only on 2004 photo captions; no source read gives current access, so the brief's access value (unknown) stays unfilled. The NPS article is a coastal-defense history that describes Deer Park's fire lookout as used for Aircraft Warning Service. The 1959 quote is from a newspaper item as reprinted on the WA list, not from the paper itself. No photos added.

The brief matches the register on coordinates, elevation and registration (November 11, 2012, nominated by Ray Kresek). The brief's FireLookout.com URL was malformed; the page was read at http://www.firelookout.com/wa/defiancepoint.html. Two searches found no description of the site today, so access is unknown and no visit facts are recorded. No corrections to the brief. Reads: 3 pages, 2 searches.

Sources disagree on the structure before 1947: the register says an 80-foot pole tower in 1929, while Weebly says a small tower of native materials with no date. The DNR tower's dates differ slightly (register 1965; Weebly 1964-66; WillhiteWeb gives 1965 for the cab). The museum's name also differs: the register says Forks Museum, the WillhiteWeb heading says Forks Timber Museum; the story uses both. The brief's status 'relocated' fits the cab only, since the tower was removed in 1985. No source names lookouts or gives staffing years, so no facts.staffing is recorded. No source describes the mountain site today, and the display's current status and hours are not verified. Access is left out for the same reason. Reads: 2 WebSearch-equivalent queries (websearch.py) and 6 page reads, one of them a guessed Forks URL that returned 404.

Reads: register, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts page (two passes on the cached page), FFA Washington list, WillhiteWeb Forks page, museum exhibits page; one WebSearch. A WebSearch hit on WillhiteWeb's Deming page (sumas_mountain_271) was not read and is not used. Record check: the Forks record's county (Clallam), coordinates and standing status match the FFA list. The register's Date Registered value did not appear in the cached text, so the March 26, 2012 date in the us-wa-deming record is unverified. The record has no year for the relocation; the story adds 1985 for the cab move. Height is left out: the 75-foot and 40-foot figures belong to different towers, and the source tower for the cab is disputed. Access 'public' rests on the museum display page; the museum invites visits, but no hours or climbing rules were found. Story is about the lookout, so the original Deming site is covered only as the place the tower came from.

No access level is set: no source states whether the summit is open to visitors today. Height is left out of facts because the sources disagree. The namesake's death is in the story as background, not as a site event. The brief lists the agency as U.S. Forest Service; sources name Olympic National Forest. Staffing as_of is the last year named in our reading (1956). No photos added.

Fate of the steel tower is contested, and the story says so. The first tower is dated only to the 1930s in every source, so no 'built' event with a year is recorded. Staffing rests on one line in Willhite's stories page (summer 1975). Willhite's 2013 photos are the only description of the site today, and it is a second-hand account. Used 1 WebSearch and 5 page reads (FFLOS, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts, Willhite, and the firelookout.org index).

Build year conflicts: NHLR says 1933; NPS inventory form, Seattle Times and firelookout.com say 1932 (the NRHP record also keys 1932 as its significant year). Distance to the site conflicts across three sources. Elevation differs (NHLR 5,982 ft; Seattle Times 6,102 ft; the NPS form's elevation is garbled in the OCR). The Seattle Times profile is undated in the copy read, so the staffing as_of is undated. No source states whether the cabin is open to visitors, so access level 'restricted' is an inference from its active NPS-staffed status. Structure and elevation are disputed: the story reports the tower description and Willhite's ground-cabin description side by side. Willhite's site identification is his own inference from a 1942 list and Metsker maps, and it came after the April 2020 FFLOS registration. The brief's kind 'tower' is kept, but the Willhite page calls the remains a ground cabin, so an editor may want to change it. The 2020 visit is the only description of the site today. Used 1 WebSearch and 6 page reads (FFLOS, firelookout.com, Forest Lookouts, Willhite site page, the Willhite Cascade Creek page, and the firelookout.org index).

History is consistent across sources (1933 cab, 1968 abandonment, gone). No source read describes what remains on the summit today, so the story says so. Access is marked public because the WTA lists permits for a hiking loop; no Forest Service page was read. The brief's kind 'ground' matches FFLOS ('L-5 cab on rocks') and the firelookout.org index. Used 1 WebSearch and 6 page reads, including the firelookout.org index.

All four sources are hobby or register pages with no primary Forest Service or DNR record reached; firetower.org and FireLookout.com share the same description text. Staffing names rest on one source (WillhiteWeb). The register's 1956 photo caption looks like an error and is treated as one. Height_m is the final 40 ft height; the original tower was 84 ft. Access is coded restricted from the gated-road description; the brief said unknown. No photos added because none of the pages gave direct image URLs.

Patrol tower 'still stands' is undated on Willhite; the register dates it only to the 1980s. The access level 'restricted' is inferred from the year-round gate and the 1990s closure; no source states the legal status. The patrol tower's loss is second-hand (Forest Fire Lookout Association via TrailChick). Willhite's page is undated and says it stood. No source gives a build date for the patrol tower. The 1934 summit lookout is a separate FFLA record (Diamond Peak, US 1493, WA 393); it is mentioned in the story as context, not as an event of this record. Distances: Willhite puts the patrol tower 3/4 mile from the summit; TrailChick puts the summit footings half a mile from the patrol site. Record elevation 1316.7 m matches 4,320 ft. Brief kind 'ground' is not stated in any source; the sources describe only a cab, so the record may be right but is unverified. The 1930 and 1952 dates appear on all four pages, but the register and FireLookout.com share wording, so they are not independent. The Culp anecdote is undated. No staffing record was found in any of the four sources, so staffing is left out. The 1961 newspaper item is known only through Washington Lookouts; the newspaper itself was not checked. The road and site account is about 2014 at the latest, so current conditions are unknown. Build year (1961 item vs 1962) and removal wording (removed vs destroyed) both conflict across sources. Sources disagree on whether the 1933 L-4 cab was built, so the story reports both. The 1975 burn date is taken from the planned June 1975 removal and the R.I.P. dates on FireLookout.com; no source states the burn date outright. Only five sources. No staffing names appear in any source read, so the story says nothing about staffing. The 1964 fate differs by source (removed, destroyed, burned), and the story reports all three. Unresolved: the end of the Aircraft Warning Service use. The history rests on three sources that agree on 1935 and gone-by-1952, and on the register and Weebly panorama dates.
