Elevation conflicts: register 2,459 ft (750 m) vs Willhite 'Elevation: 1,172 feet'; township conflicts: Weebly 28N-11E-30 vs Willhite 'T23N, R11E'. Record location and elevation not changed; a human should check. A search summary claimed concrete foundations remain at Maloney Ridge; not verified on a fetched page, so left out. Weebly lists a 1939 Air Warning Service Post No. 42 telephone report under the Galena heading; not tied to this site in the story.

Thin record: three short pages, with no year finer than the 1930s, and no independent record found (one search added nothing). Willhite says DNR records show the site, while the register lists the U.S. Forest Service as administrator; the story does not resolve which agency held it. The brief's coordinates (48.50709, -120.48816) and elevation (2711.8 m) match the register (N 48.507090, W 120.488160; 2,712 m), so no corrections. Access 'public' rests on Willhite's route description in a wilderness area; check current wilderness rules before publishing. Read budget: six fetches, two of which were lookout lists that added nothing.

The register, FireLookout.com and Willhite agree on 1942, the 1957 100-foot tower and the 1971 abandonment. The 1952 tower appears only in the register and FireLookout.com. The site is on military land, so the story points to permission rather than a visit; the 'permission' level is my reading of Willhite's advice. A search turned up no other source for the lookout, and the results about other Fort Lewis towers were not used. Read budget: three fetches plus the Fort Lewis list page and one search.

Sources are hobby and history sites; no official Forest Service record was read. Access 'public' is inferred from national forest land and a hiking route, not from a closure notice, so treat it as unverified. The AWS end year conflicts within the Washington lookouts page (see resolved_conflicts). No removal year is given anywhere. Willhite's route notes are undated, so the cabin remains may be old. The firetower.org photos are credited to the National Archives, but no direct image URLs were captured, so no photos are listed.

Brief agency (National Park Service) confirmed. Construction date disputed: the 1930s cabin is cited secondhand from a cabin inventory; the 1942 AWS cabin is the one described in the AWS papers. Fire-lookout use rests on one WillhiteWeb statement and one photo caption. Remains come from undated photo captions and an undated visit. Access 'public' is a judgement: park land, no closure described. No new photo URLs captured.

Only Willhite's 2021 visit describes the site today: footings, steps near the lookout site, and a wood-bearing footing. The sources give only the 1960s for removal, with no year. The Kaniksu/Colville National Forests label on firelookout.com may be historical, since Willhite calls the land private timber company property. The 'private' access level rests on Willhite's description; no owner or permission rule was found. The brief's 'Gibralter Rock' spelling appears on firelookout.com; the record keeps 'Gibraltar Rock'. No photos listed because no direct image URLs were captured.

Built and abandonment dates agree across all four sources. Nothing read describes the site today, so the story says so and records no access level. The 1942 relief comes from an account Willhite relays from a book, not from a Forest Service record. Height 12.2 m is converted from the 40-foot tower in the register; it is not a surveyed figure. The firetower.org photos are credited to the National Archives, but no direct image URLs were captured, so no photos are listed. The agency is taken from the national forest named in the register, since the administering line was not visible in the text read.

Built about 1934 and removed 1960 agree across firetower, nwhiker, Seattle Times and firelookout.com. Road status conflicts (Seattle Times passable vs WillhiteWeb washouts) and neither page was dated in the cache. Elevation differs by source (5,450 ft nwhiker top of Glacier View; 5,464 ft firelookout.com; 5,507 ft nwhiker Glacier View Point); the brief's 1665.4 m matches 5,464 ft. The 1942-43 activation rests on one hobbyist site and the Seattle Filter Center is not explained by any fetched source. No source describes remains on site. firetower.org photo captions credit the National Archives Pacific Northwest Region; no new photos added.

Brief record checked and correct (status gone, 2012 registration, elevation 5,416 ft). The brief had no 'built' event; 1934 added from all four sources. Four of the five sources are hobby or register sites that share one underlying record; no Forest Service or NRHP primary record was checked, so the 1960s end date rests on those sites. The 1939 Gleason Mountain Fire is a different event: the federal Lessons Learned page (lessons.wildfire.gov) lists it in Idaho on the Kaniksu NF and no source ties it to this lookout, so it is left out of the story. No staffing records found. No source describes the site today or public access. Budget: 1 WebSearch, 5 page reads.

Built 1930 (firetower, firelookout) agrees with WillhiteWeb's 1930s. Elevation 7,487 ft matches the brief's 2282 m. Spelling differs: Yakima on the registry and Weebly pages, Yakama Nation on WillhiteWeb; the brief's agency field keeps the registry wording. The 1940 abandonment rests on WillhiteWeb's second-hand account of a 1946 USGS party; not verified against the USGS report. Permit requirement comes from WillhiteWeb only; firetower gives no access detail beyond the reservation name. No staffing or fire records found. Fetched a WTA 'High Still Air' lookout feature PDF (wta.org); its cached text did not mention Goat Butte. Needs a second source for current site condition before any visit guidance is firmed up.

Brief record checked and correct (status gone, 2020 registration, elevation 4,115 ft). The brief had the 1934 build right; 1956 abandonment added. Not to be confused with the Goat Mountain lookouts in King, Okanogan or California. The WillhiteWeb site visit is undated, so the footings claim is 'reported' and not dated. The WTA listing corroborates the trail and that the lookout is long gone. No primary Forest Service record checked. Access is public on the sources read; the route is unmaintained. Budget: 1 WebSearch, 5 page reads.

Record height_m 27.0 is not supported by any page read. The register and firelookout.com give a '15' timber' tower, which may mean tower height or cab size, so no height was written. Forest name: the register says Okanogan National Forest; the current name was not confirmed in a page read. Staffing status is undated (WTA). Lightning Bill spelling varies: WTA uses 'Lightning Bill'; OutdoorsNW writes 'Lighting Bill'. A 2023 Cascadia Daily News item (search snippet only, not read) reportedly says the lookout has been back in use since 2021; not used. Page reads for this lookout: five.

This record is the Kittitas County site near Easton and Teanaway. It is a different structure from the Goat Peak Lookout in Okanogan County (Methow Valley), which is standing, staffed and NHLR-registered as US 357, and whose pages I did not use. The brief's conflict note says the two records share a register number, but the numbers I read differ: this record is FFLOS US 1365, WA 265. The shared element is the name. The current status of the moved cab rests on a 2017 hike report and is not verified since. No source names a current owner. The 4,981 ft summit and the 5,100 ft site figure are both reported and not reconciled. Staffing: only one known lookout (1933) appears, so no facts.staffing is recorded. Reads: 2 websearch.py queries and 6 page reads, one of them a 404 for a guessed Teanaway URL, plus one re-read of the cached WTA page to check a sentence about trees.

The brief's 'relocated' event has no year; 1969 is from four sources. The story is about the moved cab; the original site is us-wa-goat-peak-2. The replacement-date conflict (1956 WTA vs about 1960 register and firelookout.com) and the WTA-only L-4 interim cab are unresolved. A different Goat Peak lookout, an NHLR entry in the Methow River valley dated 1923 that appeared in search results, was not used and should not be merged with this one. The geocaching page for this lookout returned only its title, so it was not used. No public access was found.

Built 1933 (firetower, firelookout, WillhiteWeb) agrees. Removal: firetower and firelookout say gone by the 1960s; WillhiteWeb says probably 1966 after use in 1963; treated as consistent. Elevation: brief 1902 m matches firelookout 6240 ft; WillhiteWeb gives lookout site 6,201 ft and ridge highpoint 6240+. Brief access 'unknown' is answered by WillhiteWeb (public trail, no permit mentioned). The 1963 staffing rests on a newspaper item quoted by washingtonlookouts.weebly.com; the 1963 use is also in WillhiteWeb. Search snippets for Mountaineers and trailchick mention scattered artifacts at the site, but those pages did not yield fetchable text, so not used. No source describes remains beyond the Old lookout parts caption; a site-condition check would firm up today's section. Story says the site is a dead end off the loop, which WillhiteWeb states.

This is the Grays Harbor site (us-wa-gobbler-knob). It is not the Mount Rainier Gobblers Knob (us-wa-gobblers-knob), which already has its own story and research; the names are near-identical, so keep them apart. The last staffed year is disputed (1963 per Willhite, 1964 per a newspaper item quoted on the weebly list; that item says the site was to be manned, not that it was). The weebly page is a statewide list and only its Gobbler Knob entry was used. Willhite's visit date is not given. Willhite's photo captions (1958 to 1972) are not used because they do not say what stands on the site. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with permission, per Willhite.

Exact year staffing ended within the 1980s is not pinned down by sources (firelookout.com only says 'into the 1980's'); treat the 1980 staffed_last event as approximate. Brief's height_m (omitted in facts) and elevation (1623.4m / 5325ft per brief) vs. Wikipedia's 5,485 ft (1,672m) elevation figure disagree slightly; not resolved here, flagging for editor.

Thin record: one dated event (1941 crow's nest); the abandonment has no date. The Pastmaps description of the 1964 USGS map mentions a Lookout Tower and a Radio Tower atop Chewelah Mtn, not on Goddards Peak; do not conflate them. Agency: firelookout.com and the record say Colville National Forest; Pastmaps places the peak where the Kaniksu and Colville boundaries meet, so agency is not a true conflict. Willhite gives a 5,548 ft lookout elevation and no hiking distance. Nothing on staffing or fires. No source describes the summit today. Corrections: status gone to abandoned; kind platform to crowsnest.

The brief's R-6 design is documented in NHLR for the 1963 wooden tower; I found no source that gives the cab type of the 1986 steel tower, so the facts field describes the predecessor's cab. Same-name Gold Mountain in Kitsap County (leslieromer.com; firetower.org Gold Mountain Lookout Site, 1947 and 1965 towers) is a different site and must not be merged. Staffing and permit details come from TrailChick (visited 2019; page updated March 2024); confirm the current permit and staffing with the Colville Tribes before publishing access advice. The firelookout.org Washington listing was not verified for this tower. Blog-level sources were used only for access and staffing.

Brief record checked: status gone, 2012 registration, agency and elevation correct. The brief had no 'built' event; 1948 tower added with the 1947 date noted. Build date and tower type conflict across sources and the annual report was checked only second-hand through two sites, not against the primary report. Staffing and most history come from one hobby site (WillhiteWeb), with 2023 site observations. Do not confuse with the Gold Mountain in Ferry County (NHLR US 1526, standing) or the Gold Mountain in Stevens County. Access: the summit road crosses the restricted Bremerton Watershed; the story gives no route. Budget: 1 WebSearch, 5 page reads.

The brief's coordinates from firelookout.com (48.22834, -120.18119) do not appear in the page text that was fetched, so they are not cited. The register gives 48.223987, -120.191486. Willhite's summit placement is his inference ('appears to have been placed'), and the story says so. The access level 'public' is inferred from National Forest land and Willhite's road description, not stated outright; the editor may prefer to drop it. Willhite's separate panoramic-site page (gold_ridge_panoramic/images_338.htm) was not read.

Willhite's page is titled 'Goodie Ridge'; the register, firelookout.com and the NPS use 'Goode Ridge', and the record uses Goode. Willhite had not visited the site, so his page describes records, not the site. The NPS page is about the trail. It says the lookout was removed years ago and that most of what remains of the building is scattered glass among the rocks, which the story now reports. The NPS page contains the spelling 'decommisioned', which is quoted as written. The brief's record has no corrections. No staffing information was found in the sources read, so staffing is omitted. The Alpine Guide and NWHikers pages from the search were not read.

The brief's height_m of 2.4 is wrong for a 100-ft tower; corrected to 30.5. The elevation disagreement (541 ft NHLR vs 480 ft TrailChick and a blog) is unresolved. No source explains why or by whom the tower was built, and the outcome of the 2002 sale is unknown. Access depends on JBLM Training Area 4 schedules and a Range Control permit, which I did not verify with the base. The substack post is undated and was used only for access and elevation.

Brief record checked: agency, 2012 registration and gone status all match the sources; nothing to correct. Three sources agree on the 1938 build and 1950s removal. The only description of the site today is one undated WillhiteWeb visit account, and no staffing or fire history was found, so the story has no staffing section. The 1950 event year is a placeholder for the decade. Access is marked public because the sources give directions and describe no closure; this is an inference, not a stated status.

Brief record is accurate (elevation 2245.2 m matches 7,366 ft; FFLOS registration date confirmed). Staffing not found in any source read, so no staffing fact. Searches also return an Idaho Granite Mountain and a Snoqualmie Granite Mountain lookout; neither is used. Sources: 2025 WTA trip report is the newest; WillhiteWeb visit was spring 2020. No source describes remains at the summit today.

Access upgraded from 'unknown' to 'public' based on USFS statement that visitors are welcome inside during the day when staffed/open; no camping or potable water at the site. Build-year conflict (1955 vs 1956 for the current tower) resolved by reporting both. Fact-check 2026-10-04: two footnotes in the story misattributed claims that are sourced to [1] (Snoqualmie Fire Lookouts Association) to [2]/[3]/[4] instead -- the 'early-2020s renovation' claim and the 'no camping on the deck' claim both trace only to the SFLA page, not to NHLR or firelookout.com; footnotes corrected.

Brief record checked: agency, gone status and 2012 registration match the sources; nothing to correct. The 1928 and 1934 structures are consistent across three sources. The 1922-1931 names come from newspaper items quoted on a secondary page, not from the newspapers directly. The 10-ft figure is the pole height as stated in the sources; height_m 3.0 is that figure converted. No removal date is in the sources, so no removed event is recorded. Today's condition rests on one undated WillhiteWeb visit.

Brief record checked: agency, gone status and 2012 registration match the sources; nothing to correct. The brief's height_m 30.5 is the original 100 ft; the sources say the tower was cut to 50 or 70 ft in 1958, so the current height is not recorded in the facts. Access is marked permission from 2016 sources only; check current rules before publishing. The WillhiteWeb page has photos that are not recorded here because no image URLs were confirmed.

Read the four source pages (one page re-read with a different grep, so 5 reads of distinct pages plus one repeat) and ran 1 web search. The 'today' section rests on WillhiteWeb alone; its photo captions are dated 2015 and the page is otherwise undated. Access is marked public from a hiking description, not an agency notice; a Forest Service trail listing would confirm it. The brief's elevation_m 1112.2 was not checked against a fetched page; a 1953 article calls the knoll a '4500-foot peak'. Not used in the story.

Dates disagree: register 1926 cabin and 1938 tower versus a 1932 newspaper station. Two names appear: Roy Mackay (struck by lightning, 1931) and Lawrence McKay (completed a station on Grassy Top, 1932). WillhiteWeb does not call Mackay a lookout. The story keeps the names separate and does not say they are one person. Brief elevation 1893.7 m matches the register's 6,213 ft. WillhiteWeb page is undated in the cache. No source gives a visit date for the ruins.

Covers the 1934-1985 mountain site and the move to Colville; the museum record us-wa-graves-mountain-at-colville-museum shares most of these sources. Height (72 vs 75 ft) and museum access are disputed across sources and reported as such. No staffing end date or notable fires were found. Lookout names from the 1955-1959 personnel lists are left out, as in the museum record. The NHLR register's Stevens County Park and Museum and the Keller Historical Museum may be the same site; the sources do not confirm it. Not read: Visit Northeast Washington social posts that the sibling record mentions. Museum season is from a regional event listing, not the museum's own site.

The NHLR lookout page gives coordinates and an elevation of 5,901 ft for the original mountain site (the former-site record gives 5,947 ft); the museum coordinates in the record are kept and no elevation is set. The former-site record (US 1449, WA 349, registered 2012) belongs to the sibling record us-wa-graves-mountain and is not merged here. The 1955-56 lookout names on WillhiteWeb are omitted for privacy; the 1944 couple is described without names. Search snippets from Visit Northeast Washington (Facebook, Instagram) say visitors can climb the stairs; those pages were not readable, so climbing is not stated. The WillhiteWeb sidebar (elevation 2,793 ft, Pend Oreille County) looks like another page's template and is not used. No photo URLs were added.

Read the four source pages, two of them with extra greps, so about 6 reads counting repeats, and ran 1 web search. The brief's kind 'two_story' describes the last structure only; the 1945 L-4 cab's end is not dated in any source, so it was not changed. Current-site status rests on WillhiteWeb's undated access note; nothing read describes the summit today. Summit and site elevations differ (WillhiteWeb gives a 3,799 ft summit) and are not used in the story. A Pacific Northwest activation report from 2021 mentions DNR ownership of the summit, but it was only a search snippet and is not cited.

Read the four source pages, two of them more than once, so about 6 reads counting repeats, and ran 1 web search. Today's condition rests on WillhiteWeb's visit notes, which are undated; its access section lists the gated permit road. The first structure is disputed between FFLOS and WillhiteWeb, and the story says so. The brief's elevation_m 701 matches FFLOS but not WillhiteWeb (2,964 ft). No corrections proposed; the brief's kind 'tower' fits the 1960 structure.

Brief lists NRHP added date as implied by 1988-numbered reference (88000117); Wikipedia infobox gives exact date Feb 22, 1988, which resolves the record. Access is wilderness hike-in, not drive-up; no mileage figure verified beyond a secondary fan site's '17 miles east of Darrington' claim, which was not cited as fact in the story.

Brief design L-4 is right for the 1942 tower. height_m is 25.6 (the 84-ft timber tower, per FFLOS); the earlier 15.2 value was the 50-ft wooden tower and has been corrected. Many dates conflict across sources (1928/1929, 1931/1933, AWS 1942/1943, 1962 cause, 1971 fate); all are reported in the story. Staffing names come only from WillhiteWeb, a hobby site; they are sourced but single-sourced. Access: the Wikipedia forest-road claim is the only access source; no DNR page was read. Brief's 2012 FFLOS registration verified.

Thin record. Only the Former Fire Lookout Sites register, firelookout.com and the FFLA Washington list were found. The register and firelookout.com agree on a 1930s tower that is gone, but neither gives a year, a design, staffing, fire history, the date or manner of removal, or access. Story is about 120 words and says so by omission: no sentences about missing evidence. Searches returned other Green Mountains (Snohomish, Kitsap, Stevens, Olympic); none used. The Columbia Gorge News article on Gifford Pinchot historic buildings returned HTTP 429 twice and may be worth retrying. Record check: lat/lon, elevation and status match the register; no corrections proposed. Access is still unknown in the record. No photos added.

Build date unresolved: 1938 in three sources, 1934 newspaper references to a finished or finishing tower. Staffing and fate rest on one register and two lookout-history sites. Access level 'public' is inferred from route descriptions with no closure noted; verify with Colville NF before publishing. Do not confuse with the Green Mountain Lookout near Darrington in Snohomish County (us-wa-green-mountain), a separate standing lookout. The brief's status 'gone' and kind 'tower' are supported.

Build date unresolved: 1938 in the register and firelookout.com, July 1934 panoramas of the cab on WillhiteWeb. Fate and today's state rest on one personal site (2019 visit) plus two register entries. Lead not used: WillhiteWeb links an interview with Gene Sargent, a lookout in summer 1948 at age 16, who mentions hiking to the Three Corner Rock lookout; the page does not clearly state his station, so no staffing claim is made. A replica-cab photo caption on the WillhiteWeb page has no date or place and is not used. The record's agency and county match the sources.

Thin record. Every construction and fate claim traces to the Kresek Inventory (cited by WillhiteWeb) or to pages that repeat it. The 1935 panoramas show a 20-foot tower that may be an earlier structure; no source says whether it was replaced in 1938. The sources were read in full; no staffing, fire or current-site description exists in them. The brief's record (L-4, gone, FFLOS 2012, elevation 1736.1 m) checks out, so no corrections. Access left out: no source gives a level. A WebSearch for the site turned up no new pages.

The 1939 staffing and 1942 move rest on Willhite Web alone, quoting newspapers and 1942 AWS documents we could not check directly. The Boyce item's date is inferred from the sentence that precedes it on the page. The Dennie Ahl tower is a separate record and is cited only for its 1971 destruction; we did not establish that it is the house moved in 1942. Used one WebSearch and five page reads.

Read: firelookout.com, TrailChick, WillhiteWeb and the firelookout.org list (plus a weebly index page that only lists Colville Indian Reservation). Not read: the Moses Mountain page, SummitPost, HistoryLink. The brief's height_m (2.1) and 1938 removal event are corrected. The Moses Mountain origin is a claim all three sites repeat as 'may have come from', so it is kept hedged. No staffing, fire-watch or rental information was found. The access level 'permission' comes from the record and is not stated by any source read; the reservation-land location is sourced. Whether the 2021 Summit Trail fire damaged the tower is unknown. The road description mixes an undated WillhiteWeb visit (its page mentions 2016 washouts) and a 2019 TrailChick visit.

The status Removed on the Forest Lookouts index is one undated word, and the FFLA list says Abandoned; neither gives a removal date. The record's gone status rests on Removed. Do not confuse with Grouse Mountain in Idaho (idaholookouts.weebly.com, Kaniksu NF 59N-1E-1), a different lookout. Access: Willhite's hiking note describes the route in 2023; no source says whether the summit is open to the public, so no access level is recorded. The record's kind platform is corrected to crowsnest. No photos recorded.

Story sources: the story says 'About 7,000 pounds' from the Oregonian via Washington Lookouts; the 7,000 figure is also on WillhiteWeb as '7000 pounds'. The Washington Lookouts page has an 1927 Statesman Journal item, which the story treats as a report of belief, not confirmation that the cabin burned. No source gives a removal year. WillhiteWeb gives elevation as '3,8564 feet' (typo) and the register says 3,910 ft; the register figure is used. The brief's kind 'ground' is not checked by any source: sources describe a cabin and a garage at the summit but never say whether it stood on a tower, so the story says 'cabin' and avoids 'tower'. No staffing found. Access level omitted: no source states one. The 2017 photo captions are quoted but not interpreted. Brief record is consistent with sources except the build date (no build event was in the brief's record). Lat/lon in brief matches the register.

Strongest of the three: several independent accounts (register, FLA listing, WillhiteWeb with Annual Report and newspaper quotes, Forks Forum 2020) agree on the 1948 tower and the 1969 removal. Height 22.9 m is converted from 75 ft. The brief's kind 'tower' and agency match the sources. Staffing rows come from WillhiteWeb recollections and a 1964 newspaper item, not a Forest Service roster, so the story presents them as named lookouts in the sources rather than a full staffing history. The 2020 repeater line is one newspaper item; no later confirmation was read. The brief's record is correct; no corrections. The 2017/2018 drone photo captions are not used as evidence.

Four short pages, several of them repeating one another; no photos, NRHP record or current visit report found. The staffing item rests on one July 1938 Goldendale Sentinel quote reprinted on Rex's page. Height 20.7 m converts the 68-ft 1937 tower, not the 1935 tower. The 1938 employer wording follows the source ('who is employing him'). No source describes the site today.

Four pages, two of them short. The 1931 newspaper item names a private individual; the story and this record leave the name and age out. Firelookout.com credits its photos to the Dave Bula collection and the Fire Lookout Museum, and the FFLOS page has a Photos section; neither was fetched and no licence is known, so no photo is listed. No source describes the summit today or says whether it is open to the public. The 1933 'new' tower may or may not be the 1930 one. The access route WillhiteWeb describes (Sullivan Creek Road trailhead) is not stated as current and is left out of the story.

Six sources; the Forest Service page is the only official one. Early dates conflict (1924 cab per Firelookout.com vs 1929 elsewhere). Staffing is only implied by the abandonment date. The 1938 'L-4 cab' is the Firelookout.com reading only. The 1929 newspaper items name a planned tower that no source says was built. Photos seen but not captured: FFLOS shows 1929 panoramas credited to the National Archives Pacific Northwest Region and a photo from the Ron Kemnow collection; no direct URLs were captured, so none is listed. The cab's current condition is not described anywhere; the phone-line remnant is on Trail 109.

Two records describe this lookout: us-wa-hamma-hamma-g-s (this one; kind unknown, county unset) and us-wa-hamma-hamma-gs (kind ground, Mason; its status conflict is from firelookout.com). Recommend merging, keeping the Mason county and ground kind. The lookout function rests mainly on WillhiteWeb, a fan site that cites 2019 National Archives documents, and on the FFLA list classing it as Ground. The Forest Service page does not mention an observation room. The FS page says the building was nominated to the NRHP; no listing record was found, so the story says so. WillhiteWeb's quote marks are garbled in the cached text, so quotes there were taken without them. No fire history found. Search snippets from recreation.gov and Revisit WA say the cabin was completed in 1937 and rents year-round; those pages were not read, so they are not cited. The story advises booking or asking the Forest Service rather than visiting unannounced.

The site is a combined guard station and lookout cabin, not a tower; the record's kind 'ground' fits the vocabulary. Standing status and the rental are supported by WillhiteWeb (undated) and Campflare. No staffing history and no fire history were found in the pages read, so staffing is left out. The NRHP nomination rests on Campflare alone and no listing was confirmed. The WillhiteWeb page gives elevation as 600 feet (about 183 m), which the record lacks (elevation_m is null). The cached firelookout.com Washington page is only 590 characters and has no Hamma Hamma line, so it does not settle the FFLA conflict. A search summary mentioned fire spotting use and a July 2025 fire in the drainage; neither was verified on a page and neither is in the story. Campflare's trail length (quarter-mile) conflicts with a search snippet (1.5 miles), so the trail length is left out.

Removal verb disputed (removed vs destroyed), decade given by three sources (Forest Lookouts gives none). Staffing names come from 1940 and 1946 newspaper reports quoted by Forest Lookouts and WillhiteWeb; those reports are the only staffing evidence. Footings and display captions are undated. Access notes are from WillhiteWeb as of 2023; closure status should be checked with the Colville National Forest.

Brief said the tower was 60 ft; two sources say 50 ft and the 2008 chapter report says 60 ft. The story says 50 ft and flags the dispute. Brief's access 'unknown' is now 'private' based on the 2008 report; no current owner or access policy was found in any source read. The remains description comes from an undated visitor page; no source from the last few years was read, so the present state of the site is unconfirmed. Elevation differs between sources (see resolved_conflicts).

Three short pages agree on 1937, the platform tower and camp, and the 1940s abandonment. No source describes the site now, its access or any staffing or fires, so those are left out. Elevation (5,921 ft / 1,805 m) is in the story but has no facts key in the schema. Brief access 'unknown' kept unset. A Forest Service Harvey Creek Subwatershed Restoration summary (projects/50972) names the Harvey Creek and Paupac Creek roads but does not mention the lookout, so it is not cited. WillhiteWeb says it would add more after a visit; the cached version has no visit report.

The history (1927 build, 1933 abandonment, gone by 1966) is consistent across four sources. Remains today are not described by any source; the newest first-hand report is TrailChick's July 2017 trip, and no 2020s photo of the summit was read. The Goat Ridge replacement is a separate lookout, with a 1933 L-4 cab that TrailChick says was removed after 1963; it may deserve its own record. The 1956 newspaper's 8,000-foot figure is an approximation, not used.

Dates conflict: Forest Lookouts gives AWS deactivation October 16, 1943; the register and firelookout.com give abandonment in 1946. No source explains the gap, so the story states both. The AWS 'Yoke 2-5' cabin is assumed to be the same 1942 cabin the register describes; no source says so outright. Agency: the record's DNR is supported by the register. No access, visit or remains source was found; the 2023 peak-bagging report at stevensong.com describes the mountain by logging roads and a bushwhack and does not mention lookout remains, so it was not used. No new photos found.

Location conflict: register coordinates 47.809462, -121.751159 vs Forest Fire Lookout Association list 47.82333, -121.67731, about 5.7 km apart; the record's conflict note 'They share a register number' is correct (both cite US 1961). Only two detailed sources (register and firelookout.com) plus a short weebly index and the FFLA list; the 1932 build and 1968 end agree across them. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found the original story had miscited and conflated two of its numbers. (1) The 'five miles northwest of Yelm' location sentence was footnoted to the register (firetower.org), which actually says only 'Olympia, Thurston County' and never mentions Yelm; the Yelm distance comes from firelookout.com instead, so the footnote has been corrected to cite that source. (2) The steel tower's '118 ft' figure, footnoted as the IslandWood rebuilder's figure for the *same 1968 tower* the register puts at 112 ft, is actually that source's figure for the *rebuilt* Canopy Tower as it stands today at IslandWood -- and that source gives two different figures for that rebuilt height (125 ft and 118 ft) in two different places on its own page. The rebuilder's page gives no height at all for the original Fort Lewis tower, and separately dates its construction to 1966, not 1968 (a discrepancy the original story missed entirely). The story and this record have been corrected to state these distinctions rather than conflating them. Also fixed: the rebuilding firm was called 'Sahale Snowkites & Climbing' in the original story and source list -- that name does not appear anywhere on the cited page, which identifies the firm as 'Sahale LLC' (operating as Seattle Bridge Builders LLC); corrected throughout. Location is uncertain per WillhiteWeb, which uses the eastern point of Slide Peak for now. The record's coordinates (47.91393, -120.26551) match the FFLOS listing; they may not be that point, so consider marking the pin approximate. Access is set to public because the route is National Forest roads and a fire trail; no closure was found, but this was not confirmed on the ground. No staffing source found.

Built date (1932) and abandonment (1940s) agree across three sources, and a 1932 newspaper quote corroborates the build. The 1935 fire comes from WillhiteWeb and a newspaper quote on the weebly page. The current condition rests on undated WillhiteWeb photo captions, so the story says what those show and not when they were taken. No staffing history was found. The 'patrol point' use is attributed by WillhiteWeb to Kresek and is undated, so it is not in the event list. Access is set to restricted because of the gates; no closure order was found. The 'ground building' in the photo caption is not identified as the tent cabin, and the story does not say it is.

Gone status and 1946 and 1968 dates agree across sources. Remains, the 2023 visit and the routes rest on Willhite alone. The restricted access level is inferred from the 'gated road' wording; no source states public status. The 1947 airlift is second-hand through Willhite and Washington Lookouts.

Build date conflict: 1933 CCC camp (Willhite) vs 1935 (three sources and the 1935 panoramas). Status is corrected from gone to moved; the 2021 description and photos come from Willhite Web alone. The brief's access 'unknown' is answered as private for the cabin; the ridge is National Forest ground with no reported structure. Relocation distance differs (4.5 vs 5 miles). Rex's page lists only 1935 and Removed, with no other detail. No NHLR or NRHP entry was seen for this site in the pages read.

Construction date conflict: 1942 (three sources) vs 1939 tower of 60 ft (Rex's page quoting a 1939 WFFA report). Height 50 ft vs 60 ft. Removal: removed (FFLOS, Willhite) vs destroyed (firelookout.com). The permit price is from a 2016 visit report; current permit terms were not found. Access is set to permission for the tree farm. No source describes the site beyond the late-1990s harvest, the cables, and the 2000-2001 photos. The brief's status 'gone' is confirmed.

Brief kind 'ground' matches the Forest Fire Lookout Association list (type Ground), so no correction. Sources describe only an L-5 cab, so the tower question stays open. No staffing or fire history appears in the sources read, so none is given. Access level is left out because no source states whether the road or summit is public. Remains rest on a 2022 blog and Willhite's captions.

Dates agree across all sources (about 1937, destroyed or removed 1958). Only the removal wording differs. Present-day remains come from Willhite Web's photo captions (2026 for the stovepipe); the patrol tower site and phone line are mentioned but not in the story's remains list. Access is restricted by seasonal gates on FR 050, not closed. The summit has a USGS benchmark placed in 1992 and sits in Maitlen Creek RNA; neither is in the story. Height_m 3.0 reads the 10-ft pole as tower height.

Do not confuse with the Gifford Pinchot 'Soda Spring Campground' page (Cowlitz Valley, Forest Road 4510.052), which is a different place and was not used. No construction year is given; 1934 is only the earliest dated record, so it appears only as the earliest dated record. No staffing or fire history appears in the sources read. Access level is left out because no source says whether the knob is public. Footings rest on a 2009 trip report and Willhite's photos.

Sources conflict on height (80 vs 90 ft), origin (built in place vs moved from Neah Lookout) and fate wording; the story reports each. The 1964 item is a planned June season, not proof of who staffed it. No fire history found in these sources. Willhite's 2017 photo captions are the only description of what remains; no recent visit report found. Access is taken from Willhite's note that the land is Makah tribal land.

Built 1959 and the 2013 burn agree across sources. Ownership conflicts (BIA and Yakama Reservation vs a private timber owner per Willhite); the story says so and tells visitors to heed the no-trespass note. Register lists a removal year of 2013 alongside the burn; the story uses the burn, not a separate removal event. No staffing history found. Willhite's 'from the air' remark is the only description of what remains today.

Built-year conflict resolved: 1917 cupola was replaced by the 1933 L-4 now standing; brief record's 1917 'built' event should probably be relabeled or a 1933 'rebuilt/replaced' event added. Did not verify current staffing status beyond what NHLR/firelookout.com state.

The brief's height_m of 41.0 is a unit error: the source gives 41 feet, so the correction proposes 12.5 m. Staffing is the open question: the register, Willhite and firelookout.com say not staffed since around 2010, while the Forest Service campground page says staffed in summer; that page is undated. Elevation differs (register 5,944 ft, Willhite 5,961 ft). The 1925 lightning death is in two newspaper reports quoted by washingtonlookouts.weebly.com, which disagree on the date and spelling. The NHLR's 'Staffed? No' and visitor comment are undated. A WebSearch snippet about a 2025 rental listing was not confirmed and is not used. The brief's status and access were not verified beyond these sources. Willhite's 1909 cabin placement is 'about half a mile southeast' per firelookout.com, so the 1909 event note is attributed to that source. Fact-check 2026-10-08: 'four lookouts' is now footnoted to the register's 'fourth lookout to occupy the site'; 'rough road' and 'advises' were narrowed to Willhite's 'rocky' road and 'probably needed' wording.

Thin record: three sources, all on the 1934 cab and the 1952 abandonment. No staffing, fire or removal history found, and no current site description. Willhite's page says 'More to come after a visit', so a visit report may appear later. The brief's access 'unknown' is kept because no source states whether the public can reach the site. Willhite's 1934 and 1938 photo captions were not added as photos (no image URLs read).

Build, abandonment and status agree across the FFLOS register, firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb. No source names staff, fires or a current condition. Brief record needed no corrections. Only one web search beyond the briefed pages; it found no new sources.

Build date is unsettled (1915, 1924 or 1925 across sources), and the 1929 lookout name differs. The 1929 fire item names Huckleberry Mountain, not this lookout, so the link is inferred. No source describes the site today. Brief kind 'ground' fits a cabin; no correction proposed.

Build (1956), replacement of Simpson and 1976 removal agree across sources. Staffing names come from WillhiteWeb alone. The brief kind 'two_story' is not stated in any source; they describe a cab on a 10-foot concrete block base. Editor should check that kind field. Brief record otherwise matches.

Brief checked: the 2012 registration, elevation and coordinates agree with the register. height_m 12.5 is the 1952 41-foot tower converted from feet; it is not a metric figure any source gives. The 1972 fate is disputed (removed vs destroyed, possibly burned). Bob Baldwin's 1951 service appears on three lookout-history pages; the Forest Lookouts page marks it as a personal conversation. WillhiteWeb's 1964 paragraph names Smith Point where the Forest Lookouts quotation of the Longview Daily News names South Point; the story follows South Point. The summit's current state rests on a 2023 trip report and a WillhiteWeb page of unknown date. No Forest Service page read describes the summit radio site. Trail 123 page last updated August 5, 2025.

Brief checked: the 2012 registration and 4,247 ft elevation agree with the register. height_m 6.1 is the 20-foot tower converted; no source gives a metric height. The construction year is disputed three ways (1935, 1936 photo caption, 1938), and the story reports all three. The brief's design field (L-4) is incomplete and is corrected. Status is proposed as ruins because footings and a foundation are reported on the summit. No staffing or fire history appears in the sources read, so none is recorded. Breezy Point (Trail 30A), a separate patrol point with a fire finder base, is not covered here.

The brief lists access as permission, but no source read states an access rule, so access is left out. Willhite gives drive-up directions only. No source describes the site after the 2015 fire. The brief has no height, and none is in the sources. The Wellpinit direction conflicts between cite 3 and cite 5 and is left out of the story.

The brief's height of 12.2 m matches the 40-foot tower of 1955 to 1968. The register's first tower was 83 feet (about 25 m), so the story gives both. The brief's access 'unknown' is left as is; the trip report describes state land with a gate that is often open. Willhite's 1962 replacement sentence is internally inconsistent, so the story says the timing is unclear.

The brief status 'gone' is not supported by any source; proposed 'abandoned' (see corrections). Both sources give the same 1930s build, 1940 abandonment and 1980s date, but the second relies on a Kresek inventory point the author has not visited, so the two may not be independent. No current observation exists. Willhite's page also mentions a 1941 Metsker map ranger station in the valley below; it is not tied to the lookout in the sources, so it is left out. Brief kind 'platform' left unchanged (crow's nest).

Dates agree across the register, FireLookout.com and WillhiteWeb for the 1935 build and the 1966 abandonment. WillhiteWeb's Leavenworth newspaper item places B. D. March at the site in 1933, before the cab; the story calls the site a camp then, as WillhiteWeb does. The 1934 panoramas also predate the cab, consistent with that camp history. The 2020 trip report is a single hiker's account and is cited only for the route. The most recent visit described is WillhiteWeb's October 2021 trip. The brief's 1935 build and 2020 registration both checked out. Access level 'public' is inferred from forest roads and a published trailhead; no closure was found.

Only four sources were read. None gives a removal date beyond gone by 1956, and the Forest Lookouts page says only Removed. The national forest is disputed three ways, and the story says so. The 1934 telephone line year comes from a February 1934 item that gives January 15 as the completion date. No staffing or fire information was found, so none is recorded. The public access level rests on WillhiteWeb's route description and on no closure being named in the sources read; it is not confirmed by a Forest Service page. The brief's other_names entry (Stahl Mountain) is supported by WillhiteWeb and Forest Lookouts.

No source describes the site today or says whether it is reachable, so access is omitted. The 1950 event years are decade placeholders. The 1933 newspaper spells the name Staley; the brief and most sources use Stahley. No new photos found. Brief status gone and FFLOS registration date are confirmed; no corrections proposed.

Brief record is largely right: relocated status, coordinates and elevation match Firelookout.com and Firelookout.org. Not verified in pages read: the FFLOS registration date (June 20, 2012) and the 'U.S. Forest Service' agency label; the agency fact here uses the national-forest name instead. Today's condition of the Camp Waskowitz tower rests on the Firelookout.org index; no recent photo or camp access rule was read. Budget: 1 WebSearch and about 8 page reads, slightly over the per-tower limit because the 1974 move has conflicting sources.

The tower's current condition at Camp Waskowitz rests on an undated Forest Lookouts line that it is used for educational purposes; no recent visit or photo was found. Highline's own pages were not fetched. The access level 'restricted' is inferred from the school-program operation, not from a stated visitor policy. The 1942 entry is recorded as Aircraft Warning Service activation; the sources do not say how many people staffed the site. Wikipedia is used as a lead for the camp; its statements were not checked against the sources it cites.

The brief's design R-6 is confirmed for the 1956 tower; the design field now also gives the 1928 cabin. The 1928 vs 1930 build date and the burned vs torn-down fate are unresolved across sources. The Oregon Hikers page is a hiking guide rather than a historical source, so its fate claim is reported as its own view. No new photos found. Brief status gone and FFLOS date confirmed.

Could not fetch the 2010 Wenatchee World burglary article (HTTP 429, cached twice already); it would add a concrete incident if a human can retrieve it. Record's 'built 1947' is confirmed; the 1925 'camp' predecessor is new context not in the tower record's events list.

Brief kind is ground: there is no tower, only a cab (later a site with rock features). The 1930 newspaper spells the peak Stilleto. The forest name conflict (Chelan vs Wenatchee) is unresolved in the sources. The Will Hite photo caption says 2025 but the page gives no text date. No new photos found. Brief status gone and FFLOS date confirmed; no corrections proposed.

Thin record: the 1938 build date rests on the Kresek Inventory, which Willhite and the two other sites repeat, so the three sources are not fully independent. No removal date, staffing or fire history is in any source. The FFLOS page names Ray Kresek as nominator (seen in search snippet only); not quoted. Willhite's Burn disk is not stated to be on the lookout footprint, so the story does not place it precisely. Access listed as private because of the 'Private Property, permission needed' line; no source says a closure order exists. Brief status 'gone' confirmed. No source describes what remains on the summit now; the guide has a photo labelled 2018 with no description, so nothing is said about remains. Access is marked public from the hiking guide, which mentions no closure; no Forest Service statement was read. Staffing dates come from newspapers quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and from firelookout.com. A second-hand, undated anecdote about Richardson on the guide page is not used. The 1930 fire and L-4 timeline needs a primary check (Wenatchee newspaper or Forest Service report) before publication.

The tower record also carries an FFLA-sourced relocation event claiming Stranger Mountain was moved to 'Crystal Ridge' (linked to id us-id-stranger-mountain-at-crystal-ridge, in Idaho). Neither NHLR nor FFLOS mention Crystal Ridge; both describe only the single 2008 move to the Colville fairgrounds. This looks like an FFLA data error (possibly a different lookout sharing the 'Stranger Mountain' name) and is worth a human look before publishing the Crystal Ridge link on this page.

Sources disagree on what moved. The 2008 chapter report says the cab; Kresek's account (NHLR) says the whole cab and catwalk came off a 40-ft tower with the legs reset on piers; the lookout sites register says the tower. The register's chronology puts the 1983 cab on a 42-ft tower, so the 40 vs 42 ft conflict is unresolved. The record's relocated event has no year; sources give 2008. The move reason also differs: a Homeland Security facility (NHLR crane caption) vs electronics interests (2008 report). Current condition is not established. The only condition note on the register is an undated visit report by Rod Fosback, written after the 2004 visit; it says the structure is still very sound but describes vandalism. It does not say where the structure was, so the story does not place it at the fairgrounds. Visitor access was not found, so no access facts are given. Two search summaries claimed a 1959 original tower and other details that are not on any page read; not used. Mountain site story is us-wa-stranger-mountain.

Removal wording and dates conflict (removed versus destroyed; 1950s versus a 1967 end on a trailhead sign). The story does not pick one. The 1964 entry is a notice that lookouts would be closed, not a record that closure happened. The weebly page also lists an activation from August 31, 1942 to July 1, 1943 under the Seattle Filter Center, with no detail, and it is left out of the story. Brief said Strawberry Lookout Site with elevation 1665.4 m; register gives 1,665 m. Access is set to public from the Mountaineers and Hite route notes. No photo URLs were captured.

Core facts (1936 build, L-4 cab, staffed into 1938, abandoned, standing) agree across four sources. Access level 'permission' rests on the Colville tribal-land permit note, which appears on TrailChick's Strawberry and Whitestone Ridge pages, not on a Strawberry-specific rule; verify with the Colville Confederated Tribes before relying on it. Record elevation 1786.4 m is close to TrailChick's 5,863 ft (about 1,787 m); left unchanged. A 1934 newspaper item quoted on washingtonlookouts.weebly.com/strawberry-mountain1.html refers to a 'Strawberry Mountain' listed under the Colville National Forest (39N-30E-33), a different site, so it was not used. The 1938 abandonment year is an approximation: sources say the tower was abandoned after staffing into 1938.

Several search results describe a different Strawberry Mountain lookout (a 54-foot derrick tower built 1936 near 48.45 N, 118.94 W) and a Skamania County Strawberry Mountain. Neither is used. The brief has no height; 12.2 m comes from the register's 40-foot pole tower. The access level is left out because the trip report gives trail directions and mentions no closure but cites no official rule. The 'Two footings' captions in the trip report carry no date. The brief's access 'unknown' is unchanged.

The brief record had no built or fate events; added from the sources. Open conflicts: build year 1937 vs 1940; height 53 ft vs 70 ft (1957 survey estimate); destroyed vs removed in 1967; Willhite's footings statement vs his 1981 note. The 1968 vandalism item mentions a lookout station after the 1967 loss; the source does not explain it. No source confirms current public access to the lookout spot itself. The Substack post is a blog; check against Clallam County Parks before relying on the park description. No photo URLs captured.

Record matches NHLR on elevation, registration date (July 1, 1995) and the NRHP number. The record's 1933 build year is kept as NHLR's figure; Willhite and firelookout.com say 1932 at Lion Rock, which is noted in the story and the resolved conflicts. Staffing (every summer) comes from undated NHLR, firelookout.com and Willhite pages; no 2025-2026 staffing source was read. A Wenatchee World search snippet says the lookout is staffed annually, but that article returned HTTP 429 and was not read. The 2025 Lower Sugarloaf fire threat is from firelookout.com only. The NRHP entry was read as the NPGallery summary page; the full nomination was not read. Access is public: a gated spur road with a short walk, per WTA and Willhite. No climbing advice is given.

Status corrected from standing to abandoned (last used 1970s; upper stairs removed), proposed for human review; facts.status set to match. Height disagrees: 20 ft in the register and Fire Lookout; 22 ft on the Washington lookouts site; TrailChick gives 20 ft in its history text and 22 ft in its data box, so height_m is left unset. The lookouts history site also quotes a 1933 newspaper item about a named individual's illness while stationed here; deliberately left out. Laurence Davies is named only as known 1959 personnel from Fire Lookout. The last-used date is given only as the 1970s, so no exact staffed_last year was entered. Access is marked restricted based on the gated road and removed stairs. Coordinates and 1959 build year match the record; elevation 1976 m matches the register's 1,976 m.

Name conflict: the register says Sulphur Point; Forest Lookouts and WillhiteWeb say Sulphur Butte. We treat them as one site on the strength of the matching September 11, 1935 panorama date and 2,262-foot elevation; the Forest Lookouts page itself lists the site as Sulphur Butte (point). The sources never expand the acronym AWS, so the story leaves it unexpanded and drops 'wartime', which the sources do not use. 'Burned timbers' is a 2014 photo caption, with no fire date, so no fire event is recorded. The most recent account is the 2014 visit. The 'public' access level is inferred from Forest Service land and the absence of any closure notice. The brief's 1935 build and 2020 registration checked out; the brief's 'tower' kind is supported.

Thin record: no staffing, fire or NRHP history in any source. The built event year in the brief (1930) is a decade placeholder; see corrections. Willhite's photo captions for 'Remaining anchor' are undated; the story does not date them. Access is described as rough roads and a walk, with no closure or permit noted, but no source states the access level, so no access level is recorded. Willhite's '2017' captions sit on other site photos; the anchor captions carry no date. Brief's Summit GS other name is unverified. No photo URLs captured.

Three sources. The Register and firelookout.com repeat the same text, so the core dates rest on one register entry plus Willhite. Staffing names, the 1937 and 1963 newspaper items and the footings caption come only from Willhite, a hobbyist site; no Forest Service record was found. The brief's access 'unknown' is changed to public, inferred from the described route and the national forest setting; no closure rules were found. Brief fields for status, county, elevation, agency and the 2012 FFLOS registration check out against the Register. A second Willhite page on the nearby Dark Cabin came up in search and was not read.

Thin on dates. The Register says the L-4 tower replaced the camp in 1934; Willhite says the house was built in 1930 and cites a 1930 newspaper that describes a station being built. Both are reported in the story and neither is resolved here. Staffing after 1955 is not documented, so the staffing as-of is the 1960s removal. The 'Hand railing is still there' caption is undated and does not name a structure, so no remains claim is made. Access 'public' is inferred from the described road and trail; the brief's 'unknown' is replaced. Willhite's undated claim that a young observer named William Boyer was the youngest lookout in the country is left out as unverified. A WebSearch for a Forest Service history found nothing usable.

Three sources agree on the 1948 build and the 1973 end, but disagree on the Colonnade's distance and the register's 'removed' against the others' 'destroyed'. The 1930 'frame lookout station' is quoted on a hobbyist page and is not placed with certainty at this site; it is reported as unresolved. The only staffing record is the 1930 Chehalis item quoted on the Weebly page. The Mount Rainier National Park lookout history page could not be read (HTTP 503), so no park source is cited. A search snippet mentioned an early-1970s date from Visit Rainier and a 1973 dismantling from a Seattle Times table; neither was read, so neither is used. The brief's record checks out against the Register: county, agency, elevation and the 2012 registration.

Build year conflict (1932/1933/1934) across three sources, flagged rather than resolved. Brief's own record used 1934; that matches firelookout.com but not NHLR or Wikipedia/NRHP, worth a corrections note if the editor wants to standardize.

Build date is contested: 1932 in the register, firelookout.com and SummitPost, but Willhite's 1934 photo survey shows no structure and he guesses about 1937. The 2012 FFLOS registration date from the brief was confirmed on the register page (May 22, 2012). Destruction is dated only to the 1950s; events use 1950 as a decade placeholder. The Mountaineers trip report carries no date in the text read. Access is set to public because the summit is reached on foot in the wilderness; no closure was found. No new photos were added: the willhite page has captions but no image URLs were read. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the 2014 photo caption does not name the lookout and sits among Evergreen Mountain Lookout captions, so the story hedges it. The balloon-bomb attribution rests on the FFLOS and WillhiteWeb account (same text); a web search found no second source and the broader balloon-bomb histories were not read. Only three pages describe this tower in the sources read, and none describes the site today. Registration date November 23, 2012 on the FFLOS page matches the brief. The AllTrails route page returned HTTP 403, and NHLR had no page at the guessed URL, so neither was used. Two web searches surfaced only route listings and an unrelated fire page, none about the lookout site, so nothing from them is cited. The Willhite AWS document names the station in the Chelan National Forest while FFLOS lists Okanogan National Forest today; the story does not use either name for the agency. The 1936 article is by the Brewster Herald and the 1973 item is from the Herald-Reporter, both as quoted by Willhite. No source says what served the emergency-lookout role after the 1967 removal.

Brief status 'gone' and tower type are supported. Public access is inferred from a national-forest road and a described one-mile walk with no closure in the sources; confirm with the Gifford Pinchot ranger district before publishing. The build date has no year in the sources, so the only dated item is the 1935 photographs (event 'other'). No staffing or fire history appears in these sources, so none is written. Willhite's 2019 visit is the only observation of the site today.

Dates agree across sources: D-6 cupola 1929, L-4 cab 1949, cab remodel 1989, NHLR registration 2015. The brief's height_m 3.0 is the concrete base, not the tower; see corrections. Frank Hohenadel's start year is unclear ('194?'). No rental or closure information found. Do not confuse with the Oregon Table Rock Lookout on the NHLR (/lookouts/us/or/).

Four pages agree on the 1944 build and 1957 abandonment; the removal date is not given anywhere read. The register's 2020 registration date matches the brief. The 1944 annual report is quoted second-hand through the weebly page. The DNR page is a general state forest page; it shows two unrelated recreation alerts and does not mention the lookout, so public access is inferred from the forest's public trail use and no closure was found. Whether the AWS 14 x 32 cabin and the live-in tower are one structure is not stated. No photo URLs were read, so none were added; the firefinder photo credited to Willhite has no URL here. Two web searches added the DNR page and no source on the site today. Fact-check 2026-10-09: 'mostly gone' is now 'little view left', following Willhite's wording; the word 'nearby' was dropped from the DNR-cut sentence; Willhite does not say where the half-mile walk starts.

Core facts (1932 build, about 1962 abandonment, 40-foot timber L-4 tower) agree across three pages; the removal year and height disagree. Core facts (camp 1930, cab 1933, removed or destroyed 1966, lookout gone) agree across the main pages. Build year 1932 (nwhiker.com) is the outlier. Build/staffing date ranges genuinely conflict between NHLR and the NRHP nomination (via Wikipedia); kept both in the story rather than resolving. Current record's 'built 1931' and 'abandoned 1942' event years fall within these ranges and are not contradicted, so no correction filed.

Removal is only dated to the 1950s, so there is no removal event and the cabin's destruction a few years after 1926 has no year. Construction (1945) and the 83-foot height agree across four sources. Removal versus destruction is the only disagreement. Record location (48.52702, -117.452515) and the 1959 build year match NHLR, so no corrections. The record's 2005 and 2009 restoration events, and the 2009 date for lightning protection and the rental program, could not be traced in the sources read. TrailChick's note that the catwalk was open in 2018 is not a standing permission, and the story does not encourage climbing. Rental status is unconfirmed: the 2017 chapter report gives plans, Will Hite gives 2007 preparation, and no current listing was found. Four sites, all volunteer or hobbyist pages; no Forest Service document was read. The removal-versus-destruction wording is unresolved. A SnoWest forum result in search says the cab 'burned in 1975', but that thread returned no readable text, so it is not cited. Access is inferred from Willhite's 2020-era text; check the current road status before publishing the access level. No staffing or fire history was found, so none is written. Footings and foundations were checked on all four pages (full text of the Willhite page; keyword searches of the other three); none is mentioned, so the story states that as a negative finding. Three sources. The FFLOS and FireLookout.com lists are in close agreement; Willhite's long history is a single hobbyist's compilation of newspaper clips, which we did not check against the originals. Lookout names differ in 1932-1935 across sources (Harold Kester, H.B. Kester, Albert Kester), so no staffing list is written beyond the lines quoted. Check for a current Forest Service road status on Road 7404 before publishing the access level.

Sources disagree on height: the register and Willhite say 60 ft, the 1933 Republic News-Miner says about 70 ft, and the record's height_m 21.3 follows the newspaper. The story gives both and does not settle it. Sources disagree on how the tower ended: the register says removed, firelookout.com says destroyed, and Willhite says removed or destroyed; all give 1952. The record's built year of 1933 is supported. The Willhite page header reads 'Togo Mountain Lookout 1939' while its text says 1933; the header was not explained. The record's coordinates differ from west_us_lookouts (48.93434, -118.36724); the register's coordinates match the record, and the other set was not checked. No current source on condition or public access was found. Willhite's photos ('Lookout footings', 'Lookout used for firewood...') have no credit or licence, so none are proposed. The 2009 PDF is a compilation of chapter reports; the Togo entry sits in the Eastern Washington section.

The NHLR registration date (April 13, 2022) was supplied in the queue brief but I did not independently re-verify the exact date text on the live NHLR page beyond the description text captured; treating source 1 and 3 as the same underlying page. No source gave a precise current rental/booking status, so I avoided claiming one; described it only as occasionally volunteer-staffed per NHLR and Wikipedia's 'visitor contact point' language. 2026-10-04 fact-check: the 'seven lookouts once stood' detail was previously cited to sources 1/2 (NHLR/Wikipedia), which don't contain it; it's actually from source 4 (TrailChick) and has been re-cited there. The windstorm/deadmen, visitor-contact-point, and Landmark District sentences were cited to source 3 (the NHLR duplicate), which doesn't contain those details; re-cited to source 2 (Wikipedia), which does.

The four sources agree on the 1934 build, the 1947 abandonment and the site being gone. The brief's agency 'U.S. Forest' matches the register's text, which reads 'Administered by U.S. Forest'; it looks cut short. Confirm the full agency name before changing it; no correction is proposed here. Willhite's 'Use as a Lookout' heading is about the approach, not the lookout's use. Weebly's index lists the site as 'Removed' and says 'A ground house was built', which we did not use because it conflicts with the cab description; the story uses the cab wording. Access is from Willhite's directions; no current road status was checked.

Build year, height, staffing and NHLR registration agree across four or more sources. The record's access level 'permission' is not stated by any page I read; check with the reservation before publishing that level. No notable fires or design history turned up in the sources reached, so the story is short. A Cheryl Hill search result for a Tower Mountain was an Oregon lookout (92-foot Aermotor tower, 1935) and was excluded.

Heights disagree across all four sources; the brief's 45.7 m (150 ft) matches none, see corrections. Removal versus destruction is worded differently but not contradicted. Staffing comes from one source (WillhiteWeb) that repeats the year 1965. Access and the site today rest on WillhiteWeb's undated text and captions, which mention 2015; no source from 2026 was found. One web search returned nothing on this lookout.

Camp (1930), L-4 cab (1937, one 1938 dissent) and removal by 1968 agree across the sources. The record's kind 'ground' is not contradicted, but no source says whether the L-4 cab stood on a tower. The current condition rests on WillhiteWeb's 2015 photo captions. The 1961 Daily Chronicle item is quoted second-hand by WillhiteWeb and Forest Lookouts; the original was not read.

Brief's design L-4 describes only the 1933 cab (corrected). Brief's built 1966 is the current tower; the site's lookout dates to 1933 (corrected). Brief's 2005 'restored' is overstated: the chapter report says local management and some maintenance (corrected). Ownership is unresolved across sources: NHLR lists WDNR as administrator with private owners; firelookout.com says state then private; TrailChick says privately owned as of March 2026. Story reports the conflict rather than picking one. The washingtonlookouts.weebly.com and willhiteweb.com pages were not read beyond their indexes. Not read: the 2014-2021 staffing reports for this tower; none were needed.

Build year, L-6 cab and 1971 ruins agree across three pages. Height disagrees (99 ft versus a 1952 USGS 108.8 ft quoted by WillhiteWeb). The tower's fate and the date of its removal or collapse are not documented. Site access and the footings come from WillhiteWeb's undated text and captions. The EWU archive holds the refuge's 1939-40 narrative reports, which may record construction; they were not read. One web search gave no further tower detail.

Dates (1966 built, gone by 1975) agree across three sources. A search hit for an NPS PDF on a Twin Sisters Peak lookout was not used; it does not match this Ferry County site. Brief's firelookout URL was http; the https version was fetched. Cabin dimensions conflict slightly: NHLR says 14x14 ft, Recreation.gov's current listing says 16x16 ft -- could reflect a later rebuild/remodel or simple inconsistency; reported both without resolving. Height_m omitted: no source gave a tower/cab height figure (it's a low groundhouse, brief gave no height_m either). Access level recorded as 'public' via paid rental, but note the 2013 report on lightning-protection non-compliance and the active 2026 wildfire closure -- actual availability fluctuates and should be checked against current Recreation.gov status before publishing anything time-sensitive. Fact-check 2026-10-04: elevation also conflicts across sources -- NHLR itself states 6,511 ft, while firelookout.com and Recreation.gov both state 6,654 ft. Brief access 'unknown' is now public (Monument trail) with the Weyerhaeuser permit caveat from Willhite. The 1960 event year is a placeholder for an undated 1960s removal; treat it as decade-only. The 1942-44 post was an Aircraft Warning Service spotting post, not a fire lookout, and no fires are described at this site in the sources read. The 1964 item is a May announcement; no source confirms closure. Read 6 pages and ran 1 websearch.

The brief's conflict 'they share a register number' did not reproduce in these sources: the FFLOS detail page and the firelookout.org list both give US 1429, WA 329 for Vie only, and I did not find the second record. The coordinate correction is proposed, not applied. Read 4 pages, ran 1 websearch, and read the firelookout.org list for the coordinate check.

Brief access 'unknown' is now public (Forest road, trailhead with parking). The 1915 item is kept as a separate event because the sources do not link it to the 1933 tower. Coordinates in the record match the register and the firelookout.org list; the West US Lookouts pair was not read. Willhite's 2019 photo captions are the only description of the site today. Read 4 pages and ran 1 websearch.

The record's status 'gone' is not supported by any page read. They say the crow's nest was abandoned in the 1920s and do not say it was removed or destroyed, so confirm before changing it. Record coordinates match firelookout.org's list. A USFS photo labeled Wapaloosie Mountain Lookout sits in the Crossroads Archive collection (public domain), but its image URL was not found, so no photo is added. No staffing, fire or access information in any source read. Four short pages, so the record is thin.

Thin evidence: no source gives the cab's size, height, builder or the exact year it was abandoned beyond 'the 1950s'. Willhite's page places the War Creek station in Chelan National Forest in one sentence, while firelookout.com and the record say Okanogan NF; not resolved, the story uses Okanogan. Willhite's photo captions are dated 1934, before the 1940 build; not explained by any source read. The Aircraft Warning Service is written as 'AWS' on the pages read; the story describes it without spelling it out. The 2020 visit date is inferred from the page's references to 2020 conditions. The 1936 build and 1952 removal agree across all three sources. The 40 ft versus 52 ft height gap is unresolved (the register's 40 ft pole tower against Willhite's 1938 roof-height photographs at 52 ft); the story says so and no height_m is given. Willhite's 'Remaining relic' photo has a second caption line, 'Maybe a metal jug', which is a guess; no source confirms the object. Current record's design L-4 belongs to the 1933 first lookout; the 1963 tower is a 14x14 DNR cab. Height (20 vs 42 ft) and distance between sites conflict across sources. Access is restricted; the story says do not climb.

The brief's record for this id mixes in NHLR US 552, the standing 1963 DNR tower already covered by us-wa-watch-mountain: its registers, the 2004 event, coordinates and elevation are that tower's values, so corrections are proposed above. Sources agree on the 1956 build and the 1968 removal, except FireLookout.com's 'Destroyed 1968' (story notes the difference). Elevation differs: the register gives 2,710 ft (826 m, which the record uses) while Willhite's header gives 2,680 feet; not resolved and not used in the story. Access is marked restricted because of the gate; no source says whether walkers may pass it, and the story does not encourage passing it. Ownership is listed as DNR by the register, while Willhite describes the south side of the ridge as private land and the north as Olympic National Forest; the lookout's own parcel is not confirmed.

Build sequence unresolved across four accounts (see resolved_conflicts), so confidence is low. The R-6 label appears only on WashingtonLookouts, which cites a structural inventory; a search summary claimed R-6 dates from 1953, which was not verified by a fetched page, so do not repeat that claim without checking. Built year 1964 and the Spokane Mountain replacement agree across the register and firelookout.com. Built date 1934 agrees across four sources; the end date is only the 1950s and the sources disagree on removed versus destroyed. Elevation: the record's 738.5 m matches the register's 2,423 ft (739 m), but Willhite gives 2,040 ft, which we did not use. Location: the record's point is the register's own coordinates. The 1942-43 activation appears only on the washingtonlookouts list. No photo URLs were available in the pages read, so no photos were added. No correction proposed.

Built 1925 and the 1955 L-4 replacement agree across all three sources. Elevation conflicts (see corrections and resolved_conflicts). Height disagrees: the record's 3.7 m (12 ft) matches Willhite and washingtonlookouts, but the register and firelookout.com give 15 ft. Height is left out of facts until someone checks. Willhite's 1912 map note is the only reference before 1923; it is reported, not resolved. No staffing source was found in the pages read. The register lists the Forest Service as administrator; no access rule is stated in the pages read. The record's coordinates match the register's coordinates. No correction proposed.

Elevation 2,687 ft (819 m) matches the record. The 1940 build date and the 1950s abandonment agree across the register, washingtonlookouts (attributed to Kresek) and Willhite. The two spelling corrections are for human review. No photo URLs were available, so none were added.

No source read dates the removal, so there is no removed event; SummitPost says the DNR destroyed it without a year. No photos added: the FFLOS photos are credited to the Ron Kemnow collection but no image URL was found.

Build year is disputed: 1919 (register), 1922 (firelookout.com and register photo caption), 1923 (completion report); the story says so. The 1935 build, the training use, the 1942-43 AWS activation and the 1955 removal are each supported by at least two sources, though three of the four lookout pages draw on the same register data. Only one source describes the lookout itself in any detail (the Register's one-line description, repeated on firelookout.com). The 1985 built year and the staffing and permit facts agree across sources. Early dates conflict: 1934-35 for the CCC cab and wooden tower (register, 1960 inspection report, 1935 newspaper item) versus 1938 (Firelookout.com, TrailChick photo caption). This record duplicates us-wa-whitmore-mountain (verified, with register number US 1565, WA 92); the story follows this record's subject, the 1934 L-4 cab. Access is reservation land: visitors need a use pass, and SummitPost warns that access for non-tribal members can change. The story does not encourage climbing.

The tower, its 1941 date and its 83-foot height rest on the register and firelookout.com, which both appear to draw on the Kresek inventory that Willhite questions. The AWS cabin (activated September 2, 1942, 14x32 feet, on private land) is documented in Forest Lookouts and Willhite's AWS page, and is the best-supported built feature. The story does not give a removal date, since none appears in the sources. Used 6 page reads (including the Wikipedia AWS definition and the Willhite AWS station list) and 1 WebSearch.

Not a fire lookout. The record sits in the fire-lookout set but describes a city birdwatching tower; suggest hiding it. The City of Auburn park page returned an empty page from our cache, so the tower's current condition and rules are unverified; the record's status 'standing' is unchecked.

Two consistent sources agree on all key dates; did not pull firelookout.com or NRHP PDF since NHLR and Wikipedia already agree closely. Access note on snow/ice-axe conditions worth flagging to editor for a seasonal access warning on the listing. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story's September 15, 1994 NHLR date was cited only to Wikipedia, which does not state it; corrected the citation to also point to the NHLR listing itself, which does.

Sources disagree on the national forest: firelookout.com says Colville, while the Forest Lookouts page and the record say Kaniksu, so agency is left out of facts. Brief status gone is supported. Access was unknown in the brief; sources say a permit is needed. The Vail Tree Farm name comes from WillhiteWeb only. The register's administrator field was not captured by the crawl, so agency rests on FireLookout.com's private timber company line. No source describes remains on the summit.

Brief record matches the sources (gone, Forest Service, 2012 registration). Status gone and the 1962 storm end are consistent across the register and the 1952 and 1962 Longview items. Four sources agree on the 1935 build and the 1940s abandonment, but none gives an exact abandonment year or a removal date, and no staffing or fire history was found. Thin record. The 1984 AHI record (HI22302) says 'Demolished?: No' and is the only state record; it is a survey-date record, not a current status.
