Very thin record. The Forest Lookouts page for this tower contains only a title and the county, so the story is short (about 110 words) because the sources hold almost nothing; it is not padded. Build date, design, staffing, owner and removal date are all absent from the sources read. Two web searches under both spellings returned nothing about this tower; results were about Fifield and Timm's Hill, which are different towers. OSM node 353894286 (45.9707826, -90.0812704, elevation 511 m) is within about 5 m of the FFLA point; the node is not verified against the structure. Page reads: about 4. Web searches: 2.

Only two lists document this tower; no build date, owner, history or access source. Neither the DNR article nor the WJFW piece names Shelton, so it is unknown whether it was one of the DNR's 72 towers. Do not add access or condition claims without a new source.

The Michigan origin rests on the FFLA entry alone; no Michigan source was reached (the michiganfiretower.com homepage has no Silver Lake match). The 2019 post says the tower came down in the Upper Peninsula but names no Silver Lake site, so it is unconfirmed whether that is the same Silver Lake; left open. Relocation year, builder, build date and design are not found. The county list's 48.08286 is treated as a typo. Access and visit facts come from a 2019 post and may be out of date; confirm with the Neustadter Nature Center before a visit. Two web searches used.

Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap name this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. The list has no NHLR or FFLOS entry for it. Two search rounds and reads found nothing about Siren itself. The Wisconsin Historical Society record HI234018 is the Grantsburg tower on State Highway 70 in Burnett County, not this one, and was not used. An FAA antenna registry snippet listed other towers in Siren; those were not verified on a readable page and are not used. The 2015 AP report does not name Siren, so its status under the statewide decision is unknown. Budget: 2 WebSearch, about 6 page reads. The story can be expanded if a Wisconsin Historical Society record or a Burnett County history is found.

Build year (1933) and design are corroborated by two sources: NHLR and the 1934 survey text quoted on Central US Lookouts. No staffing, fire, or access sources found; the access and rental questions are open. The 75-foot (1931) and 64-foot (1934) figures are treated as different towers, which is an inference. Search snippets gave TopoQuest 1,115 ft and Wikipedia summit 1,096 ft, but neither page was read, so they are not used. The Komoot and Devil's Nose results describe a different South Bluff in Sauk County and were ignored. A USDA Forest Service PDF named in a search snippet returned 404 and was not used. The Wisconsin Historical Society record HI55878 is the Babcock Ranger Station, not the tower, and was not used.

The tower's build date, builder, height, owner and access are not in any source read. The memorial page spells the name 'Springsted' once; the Forest Lookouts and firelookout.org lists use 'Springstead'. The National Register nomination covers the Springstead cabin complex and does not mention the tower. The memorial page's dates for Pripps's service are absent. No WHS tower record was found. The DNR closure in 2015 is statewide; the sources do not say whether this tower was included.

Unresolved date conflict: the register says built September 1939, but a December 1934 newspaper item says the Squirrel Hill tower was unused. Either the date is wrong or an earlier tower stood on the hill; the sources checked do not say which. Needs the Wisconsin Historical Society inventory or DNR records. No staffing, fire, or access sources found. Search results for Squirrel Hill mostly returned the Winter Park pavilion and tubing hill, not the tower, and were not used. A USDA Forest Service PDF named in a search snippet returned 404 and was not used. Elevation: the register gives 1,730 ft for the site, Wikipedia 1,735 ft for the hill.

Historic detail comes from one page (Forest Lookouts, Stang) that quotes Chippewa Herald-Telegram items; the newspapers themselves were not read. The 1938 watchman item names Sampson, not Stang, so the story does not attribute it to this tower. Place names conflict (1941 says Pine Lake, 1996 says the town of Sampson); both are kept. No build date, design, removal date or site description was found. Two web searches returned nothing specific to this tower; the WXPR 2015 article is statewide context and does not name Stang, so the story does not link the removal to that decision. The brief's record matches the sources (Chippewa County, WI DNR, gone); no corrections. Coordinates from the FFLA list (45.28490, -91.47189) and OSM node 353894103 (45.2849621, -91.4715496, elevation 372 m) agree within about 30 m; not checked against a map. Web searches: 2. Page reads: about 5.

Thin record. Tower evidence is directory level only: the FFLA county list (Tower Gone), a Forest Lookouts page with the county and no other text, and OSM tags. The WHS record is a 1937 Stiles Ranger Station on the east side of W Stiles Tower Rd, listed as demolished; it does not mention a tower. It is the only local clue and the story says the link is not established. A 1971 Oconto County Reporter item about the community of Stiles appeared in a search snippet; it was not read, and the snippet did not mention a tower. The Mountain Fire Lookout (a different Oconto County tower, standing) came up repeatedly in search and is not used. OSM node 353894115 (44.8305473, -88.0737144, elevation 218 m) is about 20 m from the FFLA point; the node is not verified against the structure. Web searches: 2. Page reads: about 5.

Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap name this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. Two WebSearch rounds found no page that mentions a Swayne tower. The name may be local or a variant spelling; the name matches in both the list and OpenStreetMap. Other Sawyer County towers (West Fork, Connors Lake, Clam Lake, Pipestone) appeared in search snippets and in the Wisconsin Historical Society index pages but were not read as records, so they are not used here. A Forest Service PDF about Chequamegon-Nicolet 1930s towers was offered in a search result but returned 404 on fetch. The 2015 AP report does not name Swayne, so its status under the statewide decision is unknown. Budget: 2 WebSearch, about 6 page reads.

Build year not confirmed: the 1926 Milwaukee Sentinel item says work would start soon, and no completion date appears in the sources read. The Forest Lookouts page is headed 'Thunder Mtn (Lake)' and quotes a 1927 notice about a 'Thunder Lake fire tower'; the FFLA list also has a separate Oneida County 'Thunder Lake' tower marked Gone, so the notice may concern another tower. The 'highest point in Wisconsin' phrase is the 1926 newspaper's claim and was not tested. Geocaching GC3991Z was premium-only in the cache. Brief access 'unknown' updated to private. No design, height, staffing or fire history found. Used 2 WebSearch calls and about 8 page reads, over the per-tower read budget, because the NHLR page is thin and the history rests on one forest-lookout compilation.

Only the two FFLA lists have anything on this tower, and they agree. Two web searches found no other Timberland tower record. The Wikipedia page for the Timberland community came back as raw wikitext and is not cited; no source ties the tower to the community name. Coordinates are the association's and were not checked against a map. The story is short because the evidence is thin; a Burnett County or Wisconsin DNR source would be needed to add history.

Four sources plus the Register. The 1932 item is the earliest date found; the Forest Lookouts page files it under Clark County but does not say the Twin Mounds entry is this tower, so treat 1932 as a 'by' date. The WJFW and Door County Pulse articles are statewide; neither names Twin Mound. Door County Pulse gives no year, so 2015 rests on WJFW and the Register. Nothing readable says whether the tower is open to visitors, has been sold, or has been rented since 2015; JSONline and AnyPlaceAmerica returned HTTP 403, and a Facebook group snippet about a retired tower in the Clark County Forest was unreadable and not used. The OpenStreetMap node gives 399 m against the Register's 398 m, which is not material and was not used. No photos added. Brief record: county, agency and registration agree with NHLR; the brief lists no built date, so one is added; no corrections. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the Door County Pulse page shows only a 'Department of Natural Resources' line beneath the article, not a credit, so the story no longer calls the notice reposted or credited to the DNR; the DNR decision and new-owner wording are kept as the article states them.

Thin record: no build date, builder, height or staffing in any source read. The two Pastmaps items are commercial descriptions of USGS sheets, not the maps themselves; the 1940-labelled page says published 1961, so the 1940 date may be the survey date rather than the print date. The brief's agency '46N' is a land-survey code, so it is proposed for removal. Searches (2) turned up a TopoQuest entry giving 1820 ft MSL, which was not read. No photos found.

Thin record. NHLR is the only detailed source, and it gives design, administrator, the October 1936 build, and the August 2017 registration. The statewide list confirms standing. No staffing, fire, access or rental information was found. Unresolved lead, not used: a Wisconsin Historical Society Facebook post, readable only as a search snippet, describes a 1932 Aeromotor tower moved by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1935 with a cabin built in 1936; the snippet does not name Villas, so it is not used and should not be assumed to be this tower. Current ownership after the state's 2015 decision is unknown; NHLR still lists the DNR, which may be out of date, and the Register does not say whether Villas was one of the 72 towers. Access is unknown. The brief's record matches NHLR; no corrections. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the NHLR coordinates (N 45.236839, W 089.307953) and the OpenStreetMap node (45.2368463, -89.3079481) agree, so the 506 m node is the same point; the 13 m elevation gap is unexplained, and the story says so. The story's 2015 wording now dates the decommissioning (WJFW) rather than a Wisconsin decision, since the Door County Pulse article is undated. No photos added.

Only the Forest Fire Lookout Association list and OpenStreetMap describe this tower; neither gives a build date, builder, height, staffing or access. The list name is Washburn (Bayview); the OpenStreetMap name is Washburn Lookout Tower, and its coordinates match the list. What Bayview refers to is unexplained in the sources read. Two WebSearch rounds found only directory entries and records for other towers (Iron River, Bayfield, Long Mile). The Wisconsin Historical Society record HI24653 is Iron River, not this tower. A Forest Service PDF named Longmile as a surviving Bayfield County tower; it is not established that this is the Bayview site, so it is not used. The Washburn city page was read but its county line did not match the grep and is not used. Budget: 2 WebSearch, about 6 page reads.

Sources agree on 1936 and 100 feet. The Forest Lookouts page spells the forest 'Chequamegan'; the brief copied that spelling, so confirm the forest's correct name before publishing. No staffing, fire or access information was found in the pages read. An OpenStreetMap node (353893853, ele 455, tower:type observation) was checked and could support elevation if needed, but it is not cited. Search results listed Wisconsin Historical Society photo assets for the tower and a tower cabin; they were not opened, so no photos are listed.

Relocation date, mover and destination are not in the sources read, so no relocation event is recorded and the Marathon County entry is not mapped (the FFLA row gives no coordinates). The 1932 build year is inferred from 'already completed' in a May 13, 1932 item and reads as by that date. A WI Historical Society Facebook post surfaced in search describing a 1932 Aeromotor tower moved by the CCC in 1935; the page returned a login wall, so it is not cited. If it can be read and clearly concerns the Wilson tower, it would give the move date and should be added. The Post-Crescent quote is taken from the lookout page; the newspaper itself was not read.

Only one page describes the tower itself (a 2006 sale line); no build year, builder, staffing or buyer found. Height 92 ft is converted to 28.0 m, matching the brief. The 2016 article's list of five Sawyer towers does not name a Winter tower, but it places the Swayne tower between Radisson and Winter, so the story does not link the two. Do not confuse with the WI Historical Society record HI24669, which is the West Fork Lookout Tower (1936, Round Lake, Sawyer County) and is a different tower. No photos found. The 2016 article's Winter Station firefighter says other towers have been dismantled, including one east of the Village of Winter; the article does not name it, so the remark is not tied to this site.

Brief's county (Columbia) follows the Register; Central US Lookouts and the FFLOS list say Adams. Build date 1958 is right per the Register, but a lookout structure dates from 1934. The 2015 statewide decommissioning is dated by NHLR and WJFW; the Door County Pulse piece gives no year. No fire, staffing-roster or photo sources found. Access upgraded from unknown to restricted on the Register's private-land note. A Wisconsin Public Radio article was read for context but is not cited. WebSearch used twice.

Build date (Nov 1939), design (79-ft Stacy) and registration come from the NHLR page alone. No owner, access or fire sources found. A geocaching listing (GC30CBZ) in search results describes a 100-ft Aermotor built by the CCC; its page returned no readable text, so it is not cited and the Register's figure is used. OpenStreetMap node 353893837 gives 572 m elevation against the Register's 575 m; not material. The Register's 'staffed intermittently' wording is cited, not expanded. WebSearch used twice.

Brief's 1940 build date is wrong: NHLR says the date is unknown and likely after 1940, so the correction was applied to the story and events. Worcester is not named in the statewide decommissioning sources, and no staffing, fire or access sources were found; the story says so. The Central US Lookouts Phillips page has only a header and a county line, no tower text. The FFLOS and NHLR agree on Price County, standing status and the 100-ft height. WebSearch used twice.

Build date and height rest on the register alone; no second source for the 1939 date was found. Staffing, access, and rental are not covered by any source checked. The 1977 item is quoted on Central US Lookouts; its newspaper name is printed as Wausaw on that page, so the paper is not named in the story. A 1940 Wisconsin Historical Society photo of a Tomahawk forest protection headquarters came up in search, but it does not mention the lookout, so it was not used. A USDA Forest Service PDF named in a search snippet returned 404 and was not used.

Build date conflict left open: e-WV says a fire tower was erected at Watoga in 1926 (unnamed); the Pocahontas Times says the CCC built the Ann Bailey lookout in the 1930s. The construction material and the naming rest on one local article. Not used: grokipedia.com (unvetted encyclopedia copy claiming 1935 and CCC Company 1525), eathealthy365.com (claims a 1970s restoration; no primary source), and a WPA state files PDF on archive.org (text did not extract; its naming passage was seen only in a search snippet). A guessed westlookouts.weebly.com page returned 404. Whether the tower can be climbed is unknown; call the park before any visit. The West Virginia Outside post says WVDNR publishes no length for the Ann Bailey route, but the official trails page lists the Ann Bailey Trail at 3 miles; the story uses the official page. Two web searches used.

Dates: the Forest Service and two Wikipedia pages give 1922 for the state's tower; the tourism guide gives about 1916 for the first tower and 1922 elsewhere, so the 1916 figure is left as a disagreement. Access: the Forest Service and the tourism guide differ on season, and Wikipedia differs from the Forest Service on the walkway; all three are reported. Names: Wikipedia's Olson page says 'Ernst B. Olson' and the Backbone Mountain page says 'Ernest B. Olson'; the story does not name him. Photo credit: the register page header credits the 1935 photo to the National Archives while the photo caption credits the U.S. Forest Service; the record uses the Forest Service credit and was not changed. Location: an OpenStreetMap node named 'Olson Lookout Tower' (node 356527482, 39.1068, -79.6034, in the cached overpass extract) sits roughly 150 m east of the record point at 39.10668, -79.601629 by my calculation. That node is the Olson structure, not the removed tower, so the record point may be better placed on the Olson Tower; the editor should decide. The original 1922 tower's remains are not described in any source read.

Sources conflict on the build date (Register: early 1930s; Forest Lookouts: a 1923 53-foot Blaw-Knox tower and a February 1930 'new steel fire tower') and on height (47 vs 53 feet). The story says so and does not pick one. Unresolved: whether the 1923 structure is the tower standing today. Current condition is unknown: the 2021 article says a contractor was to start repairs that summer, and the HawkinsRails page is undated and says the summit tower was abandoned; neither is a current report. The Register's visit and access details are not in the record. The cabin rental is supported only by the June 2021 article; check current booking before publishing. The record has no built year; none is proposed as a correction. No corrections proposed. Not verified on site.

Build date (circa 1926) rests on NHLR and one 1926 newspaper item; Wikipedia's 1939 is a weaker later bound. Condition is from a single 2017 NHLR visit and Wikipedia's 2016 status. The repeater project was approved in 2010 and the tower was not removed (Wikipedia). The Reddit and FFLA items were not used: a 1988 transfer to the Forest Service is unverified. Access: hiking via a gate and 3/4-mile walk; no climbing.

Built year (1943) is supported by two sources. Removal is stated only as Removed (Forest Lookouts) and Tower Gone (index); no removal date found. No staffing history found for Bearden Knob. Access and present condition of the site are unknown; no photos added. Canaan Mountain cabin is a separate site (dismantled 1946) and is mentioned only as background. Brief record matched on name, county, coordinates, agency and 2008 registration; no corrections proposed.

Transfer to the Monongahela (1948) and 2017 registration are well supported. No built year appears in the sources; the 1926 Gazette item mentions a tower on Beaver Lick Mountain, which may be the state tower but is not confirmed. Removal date not found; the index is the only source saying Tower Gone. No access or present-condition information found. No photos added. Brief record matched on coordinates, elevation, agency and 2017 registration; no corrections proposed.

Removal is stated by the register only; no removal date found. Height conflicts (80 ft in 1936, 70 ft in 1976) and the 24.4 m record value is unconfirmed. Staffing documented 1947, 1948, 1962 and April 1976; later staffing unknown. The wvforestry article speaks for the state in general, not Bee Mountain specifically. Observer names appear only in source quotes and are left out of the story. No access or present-condition information found. No photos added. Brief record matched on coordinates, agency and 2008 registration; no corrections proposed.

The 1931 build and 1943 move agree across the Register, the Dolly Sods site record and the Forest Service history, so the history is well supported. Height is unresolved: 30-foot legs (Register) against about 70 feet (1956 station description quoted on the Forest Lookouts page); the record's 3.0 m matches neither, and the proposed 9.1 m is from the Register's legs and needs a human check. The cab collapse year is 2010 in two sources and before October 2015 in the Register. Current condition rests on the 2020 Register visit report and a 2013 travel post; not checked on site. Access (grassy road off Forest Road 19) comes from the 2013 travel post only. The Reddit and abandonedonline pages were not used. Nothing in the 1976 newspaper item was used beyond the employee's remark. No new photos with image URLs were added.

Only two sources, both lists or registers; no state disposal record was found. height_m is the 60-foot figure converted. The NHLR photo credit (Rocco Germani) has no stated license, so no photo was added. The visitor comment is an NHLR contributor's text, not an official record.

Brief record checked: coordinates, registration date and gone status match the sources; no corrections. The 1950-1960 staffing comes from reprinted newspaper notices (Raleigh Register and Beckley Post-Herald, as credited by Forest Lookouts); the originals were not checked. No build date, design, fires or removal date found. Story leaves access and visit facts out because no source states them.

Brief record checked: the 1933 build, 2015 NHLR registration, elevation and coordinates match the sources. Brief status note (cab gone) is supported by the FFLOS asterisk legend and the Register. The brief's access 'unknown' is now public (open platform). Decommissioning is dated only to the 1960s by the Gazette-Mail, so no closed event is recorded. Not used: a 2022 personal blog (stillsheroams.com) that says staffing was phased out by the 1970s; it conflicts in date with the Gazette-Mail's 1960s decommissioning and was not fetched or quoted. The Register's photo credits (1933 National Archives photo, Oct 2010 Brian Powell photo, 2017 Kristin Reynolds photo) have no image URLs here, so no photos were recorded. The first WebSearch returned the Register, Wikipedia and Gazette-Mail snippets; they were checked against fetched text before use.

Only one source describes this tower in detail (the FFLOS register). No build date, staffing or fire history turned up in the sources read; the easternuslookouts.weebly.com 'Big Mountain' section is a heading and a line only. The brief's removal event (2010) is the end of the register's 'between May 2008 and June 2010' window, so it is kept as approximate. The geocache page coord.info/GC6010 returned only its title, so it is not cited; the register names the cache. Access level is not given because no source says whether the site is public. Brief coordinates and elevation (700 m) match the register and FireLookout.org list, so no corrections are proposed.

Construction date and design are well supported by the register and a local site. Current condition rests on the 2021 register visit; no 2025-2026 report was found. Staffing history not found; the register's staffed field is blank. Hike length conflicts (2.6 vs 4 miles). A YouTube search snippet describes the tower as 60 ft (Aermotor MC-39); the fetched page had no description text, so this is not used. The Lost River State Park Wikipedia page does not mention the tower. No photos added; licenses not checked. Read budget ran about two pages over the cap.

Brief record checked: coordinates, registration date, gone status and elevation match the register; no corrections. The site is a public roadside overlook with a boardwalk, but no source describes the tower site itself or its access. The 1926 telephone note comes from a reprinted Charleston Gazette item, not the original. The 1930 fire is from a Forest Service marker and is not tied to the tower anywhere in the sources, so it is kept only as context in the story. The marker's 4,520 ft site elevation differs from the register's 4,548 ft.

Brief record checked: coordinates, registration date, agency and gone status match the sources; no corrections. The sources give no build date, design, staffing, fires, or removal date. Only 1926-27 telephone notes (reprinted from the Charleston Gazette and Raleigh Register) and a January 1987 photo date the tower. The FFLOS page is the only source naming the removal. Spelling of Sharples differs between the 1926 item (Sharplea) and the 1927 item (Sharples). A 1991 roadside marker reading Blair Mtn. Fire Tower Site Of Miners Battle appeared only in a search snippet; its WV History On View record returned HTTP 403, so it is not cited. The e-WV photo is cited as a page; no image URL was available, so no photos entry was added. Battlefield NRHP status is included as context and is not a tower event.

Record had no county; sources put the tower in Summers County inside Pipestem Resort State Park (Wikipedia notes the park straddles the Mercer/Summers line). Only OSM (way 611319752, which names it Bolar Lookout Tower, tower type observation) is in our record; the FFLA state list we checked has no Bolar or Pipestem entry. No build year, height or design found; the 2011 articles are the only dated sources. Status and climbability rest on present-tense or undated marker and guide text. Search snippets for a three-story wooden tower (athensweknew.net) were not fetched and are not used. A current check with WV State Parks would settle hours and access. Trail length conflict left open: ActionHub gives 0.2 miles one way (the story uses this); Turnbull's Pipestem Knob Trail entry gives 0.5 km, out-and-back (about 0.16 miles one way). The story does not resolve it.

No build year, designer or original station history found. The Nettie relocation rests on the FFLOS and firelookout.org entries, which share a register, plus a 2013 conference minutes note placing a Briery Knob tower behind the Nettie FD. No source dates the move. Access at Nettie and at the original summit is undocumented, so no access fact is recorded. The brief elevation (1376.8 m) differs from the 1916 figure (4,534 ft, about 1,382 m); see corrections. The FFLOS page has a 1914 photo but no image URL was captured, so none is added.

No source read gives a build date; the 1913-14 warden report is the earliest mention. The 1926 and 1938 newspaper items are only as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the originals were not checked. Only the FFLA list ties a standing tower to Nettie FD, and it conflicts with the Register's dismantled note. A photo of the Nettie FD tower would settle the status.

Thin record. The only history is two newspaper items (1957, 1960) quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. No construction date, removal date, description or photo was found in the pages read or in one web search. The brief's access 'unknown' is changed to private on the strength of the register's private-owner line; please confirm that is the level you want. Brief county Monroe matches the register; the Forest Lookouts header says Greenbrier/Monroe.

Two pages plus the state list were read, and one web search added nothing. No construction date and no removal date were found, so the story does not give either. The register credits a photo to Ronnie Scarbro, but no image URL appeared in the cached text, so no photo entry was made. The 1959 cabin is recorded as an announcement only.

The register and the Forest Lookouts page agree on the 1961 STEP erection. Only one incident (1963) was found. The 1963 account is the only design detail and it is from a newspaper quote on the Forest Lookouts page.

Only the clippings page, the FFLOS register entry and the FireLookout.org list describe this site. No removal date, cause or present condition found. The 1942 and 1954 clippings disagree about when a tower stood there. The state tower list PDF (wvenc-f5.wvnet.edu) could not be reached (DNS failure), so it was not checked and may hold more staffing detail. The WVU photo catalog entries returned 403 and were not used.

Only the FFLOS register entry and the FireLookout.org list describe this site. The Forest Lookouts Cabell page has a state header and no entries. Only the 1932 Gazette item (Forest Lookouts page), the FFLOS register entry and the FireLookout.org list describe this site. No build date, builder, staffing or removal date found. A WebSearch returned a Blair Mountain tower in Logan County; that is a different site and was not used. The state tower list PDF (wvenc-f5.wvnet.edu) could not be reached (DNS failure) and may hold more history. The WVU photo catalog entries returned 403.

Brief correction: the record's 1946 'built' is the move date; the original build was 1925 at Carlin Hill (firetower.org). A Facebook group post claims the tower stands 'on private land'; it was not used because it is unverified. Brief's record (kind ground, gone, built 1924, removed 1946) checks out; access was unknown and is now public per Mon Forest Towns. The FFLOS page calls it a tower; the Forest Service report says cabin, and the story follows the report. The 2008 footings photos and the 2026 outcrop-only description differ. No new photos added: FFLOS images have no verified image URLs here. The Mon Forest Towns guide's rules on removing artifacts from federal land are general, not site-specific.

Height (60 ft in brief, from a 1925 pre-construction item) is corrected to 80 ft per two later sources. Place name differs (Jacksonburg vs Smithfield), both Wetzel County. No new photos added (FFLOS photo credit to Shaun D. Kuhn has no image URL here).

No removal year or cause in any source read, so the story says only that the state list marks it gone. No source describes what remains on the site. Thin record. The Eastern lookouts Cottle page gives only the word Removed with no history. No build date, design, or staffing found in anything reachable. The 'moved to Pocahontas Co. Three sources only, one of them a list. No build date, staffing or fire history in any source read; two web searches added nothing usable. The move to Pocahontas Co. H.S. rests on a single FFLA list entry with no date. Register and FFLA agree the original is gone.

Core history is well sourced (built 1931, moved 1943, four sources agree on both). Thin on today: the only physical evidence is a September 2008 photo caption showing footings at the Plains site; no source says what is there now or whether the ground is open to visitors. The Bell Knob structure has its own record and story; this story stops at the move and summarises its state only. Build year not pinned. Clio gives only the 1930s. Two search snippets (livingnewdeal.org, sah-archipedia.org) point to a Camp Price CCC camp set up in 1935; neither page was read (SAH returned HTTP 403), so no year is claimed. Fetch livingnewdeal.org before stating a date. The archive photo (pocahontaspreservation.org item 577) is not added to photos because its rights line only says 'See Rights and Reproductions'. The state park history page had no tower mention. The waymarking.com page yielded no text. Record county and coordinates agree with FFLA and Wikipedia. Agency changed from the builder (CCC, per Clio; kept in events) to the managing agency, West Virginia State Parks, from the archive tags. Wikipedia's infobox lists the governing body as the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources; not used here.

Thin record. Status and coordinates come only from the FFLA list; no NHLR page for this tower is in the crawl cache. The Forest Lookouts page is the only source describing the tower itself, and it has no completion date or later history. Name and site are unclear: Forest Lookouts files it as Elk Horn Rock, FFLA as Elkhorn, and the Judy history uses Elk Horn Rock only as a boundary landmark. Check whether Elk Horn Rock and the Elkhorn tower are one site before merging records. The WV Division of Forestry article (wvforestry.com) does not name it. The Judy history's copyright line in the OCR text reads 'B, L, JUDY' while the title page reads 'E. L. JUDY'; the story uses E. L. Judy from the title page.

Thin record. The register page has no description, build date, staffing, or removal date. The only history is a 2022 Gazette-Mail column that names Foreman Knob among four Kanawha County towers, and the Forest Fire Lookout Association list marks it gone. The Forest Lookouts West Virginia page has no Foreman Knob entry. The Gazette page is a subscriber e-edition, but the column text was readable. The story is short (about 110 words) because nothing more is supported. A future pass could check West Virginia Division of Forestry records for a build or removal date.

Thin record. Standing status, county and coordinates come from the FFLA list only. Agency comes from the Forest Lookouts list. The 1930s build date, the house and the 1,439 ft elevation come from one personal blog. Mapcarta gives 1,411 ft. Not on the NHLR West Virginia list as crawled. Design, staffing, access and fires are unknown. No photos added (blog photos are personal with no license). A county, Forest Service or Division of Forestry record would firm up the build date.

Removal year is not in any source, so no removed event is recorded. Public status is inferred from the Forest Service listing of the campground as a developed recreation site; check seasonal access before any visit. The 1933 photo caption does not say it shows the tower itself. The brief's access 'unknown' can be updated to public. Sources differ on which towers survive (Bickle); this story does not depend on it.

Brief record fits the sources: gone, U.S. Forest Service, built 1936, registered 2008. Gaudineer's death date differs by one day across sources (April 27 vs 28, 1936), so the story says April 1936. The registry and Wikipedia disagree on when the tower began watching the forest. Tower height and design are not stated in any fetched source and are omitted. No staffing, fire, or rental records were found. Photo credits (May 2016 footings photo, Brian Powell; 1947 H. C. Frayer photo, National Archives) were noted but no image URLs were captured, so no photos are listed. A search snippet said a 1941 visitor saw the tower standing and that it was dismantled later; neither claim was on a page I could read, so neither is used.

Original build date and designer not found. Blaw-Knox appears only as the tower type on the Eastern lookouts and NHLR pages; no source ties the original Gauley tower to that firm, so design is recorded as the name used in the sources. Photos on the NHLR record (July 2010 photo by Brian M. Powell; relocation and October 2009 restoration shots by Andy FitzGibbon) have no image URLs or licence data captured, so none are added. NHLR says the Whittaker tower is administered by the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources; agency is recorded as the Division of Forestry for the original tower. Climbing rules are undocumented, so no visit fields are set. The story now calls the 2013 source minutes, not a trip report.

Two records share this tower: the Fayette County Gauley Mountain site (FFLOS US 1659, WV 50, gone) and the standing Whittaker Station tower at Cass (NHLR US 1176, WV 21). The brief's source path '../us-wv-gauley-mountain/' was not found; the Forest Lookouts Gauley Mountain page was used instead. Original erection year not found. The NHLR build field of 2009 is contradicted by the 1926 and 1928 items. Current visitor climbing rules not found; check the park. Used 1 WebSearch and about 7 page reads, over the per-tower read budget, to resolve the build-date conflict.

Very thin record. The register page has coordinates, elevation, registration date and a nominator, but no description, build date, staffing or removal date. A USGS-based topo listing calls it the Gay Knob Fire Tower (historical), which suggests an old tower name but is not proof a tower stood. The Association list marks it Unconfirmed, so the brief's gone status is not supported. Gay Knob is not in the Monongahela National Forest USDA fire tower history, and the Forest Lookouts West Virginia page has no entry for it. The story is short (about 90 words) because nothing more is supported. A future pass could check historical USGS Edray maps or Forest Service records.

Thin record. The register gives location, elevation, registration, nominator and administering agency, and the FFLOS index marks it gone. Two searches and the cached pages gave no build date, Grassy-specific staffing, removal date or current site description. The staffing account (source 3) is the state's general practice, not Grassy-specific, and the story says so. Record elevation 1333.8 m matches the register's 1,334 m. Access and current condition are unknown and the story says that plainly.

No construction date or builder was found. The earliest source is the November 1921 item. Trail distances differ across sources (see resolved_conflicts). The kind correction (ground to tower) is the main open question and should be checked against the FFLOS detail page for this site. The 2025 report describes a route that begins behind a closed fire gate, so the story does not suggest going past closures. No photos were captured. Searches for a construction date, builder, or removal date returned no usable page.

Current closure and rebuild plan are well documented (Gazette-Mail 2024, RealWV 2026, volunteer site). The history is less certain: the register's Built field (1997) contradicts its own description (1934), and rebuild dates differ across three sources. The 2020 report names the FFLA in its own title, so the publisher credit is no longer inferred. Elevation differs between the register and Gazette-Mail. Register photos (credited to Brian Powell and Victoria Oliver) were not added; licences not checked. The RealWV figure of $130,000 in donations was not used. The trail length (about one mile) is from RealWV and the Gazette-Mail (a mile-long trek); the Gazette-Mail's wording was not used for access. Read budget ran to about six page reads plus one search.

Very thin record. The register gives location, elevation, registration and nominator, and the FFLOS index marks it gone. Two searches and the register and state pages turned up no build date, staffing, removal date or current condition for this site. Source 3 is the state's general account of its towers and is labelled as general in the story. Coordinates: the register detail page (37.715278, -82.230556) matches the record; the index line (37.71539, -82.23078) is about 20 m away, which is minor. The agency correction is a typo in the register text, so a human should confirm before the record changes.

Unresolved: cabin size (14 x 13 ft per Bitter Southerner, 14 x 20 ft per USFS); distance from White Sulphur Springs (USFS gives 17 mi in its summary and 15 mi in its directions); road length (USFS about 4 mi, Bitter Southerner about 5 mi). The 2017 Charleston Gazette-Mail article (wvgazettemail.com, 'Renovated fire tower cabin converted into getaway') returned HTTP 429 twice; retry it for the rental details and the 1935 photo caption. Search snippets only, not cited: recreation.gov listing, USFS Facebook rental reminder, WCHS 'Traveling WV' piece (says USFS restored the cabin and it is now available to rent). Current gate status, rental status and any tower remains are unverified. No source gives who staffed the tower or any fires it watched. Record status 'gone' is right for the tower but the cabin stands, so the status note carries that. No corrections proposed. The 2020 caretaker account is one writer's first-person feature, so treat its access details as dated.

History is well sourced from 1936-37 newspaper transcriptions on Forest Lookouts. Current access is not documented in any source read, so no access level is recorded. The 2024 records request was marked granted but its outcome is not on the page. The Wriston article PDF (firelookout.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/pop-wriston-built-the-big-ones.pdf) returned no text through fetch_text and may name the tower model; unverified. No photos added (licenses not stated). A local history column (ptonline.net) mentions a family that owned land up to the knob top, including a former lookout tower; its date and scope are unclear, so it is not used.

No height in the brief; the 1952 'about 65 feet' figure may describe a later structure than the 1924 tower and is kept in design text, not height_m. The 1924 build and the 1916 predecessor rest on the register alone. The fire's date is not given in any source I could read. Current public access and ownership of the site are unknown. The 1987 Goldenseal article and the Wriston PDF linked from the register were not readable (the PDF returned no text). Reddit and POI Factory pages were not used as sources.

Record matches the register on location, elevation (4,347 ft) and kind (enclosed tower). Two sources disagree on elevation: the register gives 4,347 ft (1,325 m), while the transcribed 1916 warden report gives 4,388 ft; the story says so and does not pick one. The transcription page headers the report as c.1915 but dates the watchman entry 1916; the story follows the entry date. Build date rests on the register (1913-1914) and the 1913-14 lumber donation, which agree. Removal date, current site condition and access are not found in any source read. Only one search was run beyond the register pages.

Only two pages describe this tower in any detail: a 1929 newspaper report quoted on Forest Lookouts, and the registry entry. Removal date and present-day condition were not found in any fetched source, so the story says so. No staffing, fire, or rental records were found. Two search snippets mentioned a 73-foot tower and a $1,500 appropriation; they came from pages I could not open, so the figures are not used. The brief's height_m of 27.4 matches the 90-foot figure in the 1929 report. Do not confuse with the Whittaker Station tower, a relocated former Gauley Mountain tower.

Heights disagree: 75, 79, 85 and 88 feet across 1936-37 items and the Register; the story reports the spread and does not pick one. County disagrees: the Register and FFLOS list say Summers, a January 1937 item says Greenbrier. Elevation: Register 3,923 ft (1,196 m); 1937 items say 3,945 ft. The keeper is named 1936 in one item and appointed 1937 in another. Current condition rests on a May 2024 Hinton News article and the FFLOS list; no 2025-26 source found. No current access or staffing source found. Wikipedia Keeney's Knob read as a lead only (elevation 3,921 ft, transmitter site) and not cited.

The link between the register's tower site and Rich Mountain is an inference: the register's 2013 deck note and the MetroNews report describe the same deck at the former tower site, and the MetroNews report places that site on Rich Mountain. No build date, staffing or fire history found in the pages read; the story leaves those out. Do not confuse with the Buck Knob observation platform, which elkinsrandolphwv.com mentions separately in the same forest. Access and visit details are from a 2013 report and may be out of date. Records checked: firetower.org page (read twice), county table, MetroNews 2013, wvforestry.com, Wikipedia, wvencyclopedia, CCC camp page, wvstateparks search result only.

Thin record. No build year found: the register says the CCC built the 86-foot tower but gives no date, and two WebSearch queries found no construction history. Closure date conflicts: the register says 1991 for this tower, while the e-WV entry says the state's towers closed in 1990; the story reports both. The WV Division of Forestry district list (wvenc-f5.wvnet.edu PDF) could not be fetched (DNS error), so it was not used. The Eastern US Lookouts page has only a header (Wyoming County; WV Division of Forestry). The 2017 visit form also marks the tower not staffed, but the story does not use it. Pocahontas Land Corporation's role is not explained by any source read. Current access, staffing and condition are unknown; the story says so and advises against climbing. No new photos added. Height 26.2 m is converted from the register's 86 ft.

Build date and builder are not found in any source read (one web search, plus the FFLOS and Eastern pages). Elevation conflict left unresolved: FFLOS 2,927 ft (892 m), kept in the record; the 1916 state report says 3,075 ft. The record's elevation_m (892.1) is not corrected. County: the register says Barbour; the 1916 report puts the station on the Barbour-Randolph line, so no correction is proposed. The 1914 photo already in the record is from the state report; not re-checked. No source describes access or what stands at the site now. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the story's 'sat under a metal cover' wording was not in the source and was rewritten to 'a metal cover was provided against the weather'. The register is now named in full on first use. The removal wording 'by 1997' matches the register's Removed field.

Height not used in facts. The record's height_m 18.3 (60 ft) is not in the text read: the 1926 item proposes a 60-foot steel tower and the 1985 item says 50 feet. Opening date conflict: 1916 state report (completed that summer) vs 1921 (register and notice); the event is recorded as built 1921 with the conflict in the note. The 1985 item (3,250-ft ridge, 50-ft tower) does not match the 3,150-ft site and may describe another structure; the story says the link is unclear. County: the record and FFLA say Raleigh; some map sites say Fayette; sources describe the Raleigh/Fayette line. A firelookout.org PDF by Pop Wriston (pop-wriston-built-the-big-ones.pdf) turned up in search and may cover this tower; it is a scan with no text layer and was not read, so nothing from it is used. The FFLOS photo (credit Ronnie Scarbro, all rights reserved in record) is not added. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the story's 'join the station to the private line' wording went beyond the source (the source says the line connects with the Solvay private line) and was rewritten. The April 1926 item and the June 1921 American Forestry notice are now cited by their dates and attributions. Note: the April 9, 1926 item and the October 10, 1926 Charleston Gazette item both place the Kingston tower in Fayette County, while the 1916 report places it in Raleigh County; the story attributes Raleigh only to the 1916 report.

Thin record. The register's description is cut off mid-sentence in the cached page (ends 'from Kna'), so the story quotes only the part before the cut. No build date, staffing, fire history, removal date or site condition found after two searches and about four page reads. The Mon Forest Towns sentence is forest-wide context, not a claim that Little Mountain is one of the 22 towers. The story is about 125 words, near the 120-word floor. A Monongahela National Forest history or a Pocahontas County source would be the best next lookup.

Thin record. No build date, description or removal date found in the register or the Eastern list (one article, 1946). The 1929 date is only the caption of a Facebook photo post; the post body was not readable, and the caption is not a build date. Status comes from the FFLA county list. The 1946 article names the newspaper as Beckley Post-Herald. Next step if someone has time: Nicholas County newspapers or the state forestry annual reports for construction and removal dates. No site description is available, so the story says so. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the story now says 'about two weeks early' because the item gives two weeks and fourteen days, and March 8 to March 20 is 12 days. The 'unusually dry and windy' wording was paraphrased.

The brief's 'gone' status is wrong on the best evidence: two sources say never built, and the register's removal line is the outlier. Bill Spach is both the register's nominator and the person quoted on the trail page, so the conflict is within one person's accounts; asking him directly would settle it. The NPS page in the cache describes stone blockhouse foundations on the summit (1861). It is not confirmed that these are the same stonework as the footings on the trail page, so the story only raises the question. An earlier fetch of the same NPS URL returned an intro with more text (park acreage, trail) that the cache no longer returns; the checker reads the current cache, so only that text is quoted. Ownership of the footings is not confirmed. Clio's page returned no text in the fetch, so it is not used. Wikipedia's Loudoun Heights (Mountain) page had no tower mention. Two searches and about five page reads.

Construction and early history are consistent across the register and Forest Lookouts (1935 CCC build, 45-foot Blaw-Knox, 7 x 7 cab, stone quarters). Agency conflict, not resolved: the register names the WV Division of Natural Resources as administrator and the Division of Forestry as cooperator, while the Forest Lookouts header names the Division of Forestry. The record keeps the register's DNR value, and the story reports both. Closure: no Mann-specific date found; the e-WV statewide figure is 1990. The current status is only the undated Forest Fire Lookout Association listing ('standing'); no 2024 or later report was found, and the register has no visit report. The 1950 and 1961 items are quoted by Forest Lookouts from the Raleigh Register, not read from the newspaper itself. A TopoQuest snippet gives 3,356 ft for the summit; it was not read and is not used. Access and visiting rules are unknown. No new photos. Height 13.7 m converts the 45 ft tower height.

No source gives a build year, builder, or removal date for the tower, so none is in the story. Hunter's years of service are not dated; the Gazette-Mail says only 'for years'. A reader comment on richwooders.com calls him a retired fire warden and a Forest Service fire watcher, and disputes parts of the Hart legend; neither is used. Public access is inferred from national forest land and the Mon Forest Towns listing; no source gives a road or trail route or confirms the grave area is open. The Gazette-Mail feature carries photos of Hunter at the tower credited to the book Spruce Wind's Song; licence and rights are unknown, so none is added to photos. The record's elevation and coordinates agree with the register.

No source found gives a builder, owner, staffing, build year, or removal date for the McComas tower; two web searches and the register pages were checked. The two registers give coordinates a few tens of metres apart (FFLOS 37.390278, -81.299167; FFLA 37.39041, -81.29892); the record keeps the FFLOS point. The e-WV entry says both 'Less than a dozen remain standing today' and 'dozens of fire towers are still standing', which contradict each other, so the story avoids any count. The 1990 closure date comes from e-WV alone and may not apply to every tower.

The 1913 and 1916 texts are a transcription on a fan site quoting the state's biennial reports; the original report was not located. The 1916 station is three miles from Hambleton, but the register places the tower on the Parsons topographic quad; no source says whether these describe the same spot, so the link rests on the shared McGowan name and Tucker County. Record kind is still unknown: the 1916 source says 'station' with a watchman, and no source describes a tower structure. The 1916 elevation (3,354 ft, about 1,022 m) could fill the empty elevation_m field. No photos found; no record corrections proposed.

Brief status 'gone' understates that a tower stands at Thorny Mountain, but whether it is the 1924 structure is disputed across sources. The state forest page's 'still available for duty' is undated and conflicts with the 2015 rental. The state parks camping page does not itself mention the rental; the rental rests on Forest Lookouts and The Dyrt. No source describes the original summit today.

Second record for the same tower: us-wv-mikes-knob-tower-site-at-richwood-vfd already has a story and research file. Consider merging the two. The events entry in our record reads 'None relocated (The lookout was moved to Richwood VFD.)', which is garbled; the relocation event above replaces it. The 2008 FFLOS registration date that the other record cites did not appear in the Register page as cached, so it is not used here. The firetower.org Richwood VFD page returned 404. No staffing or fire history appears in the sources read.

Both Register photos are already in the record, so no new photos. No staffing or fire history found. Access rests on a 2024 blog post; the Richwood VFD was not contacted. The county conflict (Pocahontas vs Greenbrier) should be checked against the Forest Service or the Richwood station if the editor wants it settled.

No source newer than the Autumn 2018 article describes the tower's condition; standing status rests on the association list and that article. The article is a two-column PDF, so quotes were copied from pdftotext output and kept to single lines. The article also describes a 1960 killing at the site; it is omitted because it concerns private individuals and does not bear on the tower's history. Named observers and the 1958 fire's county official are not named. The microwave-tower date is not given in the source and is left undated.

Thin record: no build year, no removal date, no description of the site today, and no access information. Register gives 1,650 ft (503 m); a mapcarta peak elevation of 1,611 ft is for the summit and was not used. Brief's agency matches the register.

Built date conflicts with the 1949 column (about 1921 implied); register, Forest Lookouts and NHLR agree on 1928. Ranger district spelled Cheat (NHLR) vs Chert (Forest Lookouts). No source describes access or the site today beyond the October 2008 footings photo. Brief's agency matches the register.

Built year is consistent: 1939 in DC News Now and ICPRB, and the register says prior to 1941. The 1941 federal station description and the 1948 recovery note (name now Hampshire Tower) come from a single Forest Lookouts page that quotes the NGS record; the rename rests on that one note, and a search snippet claiming the same rename was not used. The DC News Now article is undated in the cache, so the late-1970s staffing and the 'oak steps missing' description are not dated precisely. The most recent condition evidence is the NHLR visit report of September 2021, which is not an access or status check. Access: the public WMA hike is roughly 4.5 miles round trip, and climbing is not permitted (ICPRB). The story does not describe any climb. Suggest considering 'Hampshire Tower' as an alternate name for other_names; this is not a correction. Status 'standing' is supported by the FFLA listing and the register. Photos: the record already has the NHLR 2016 and 2021 photos; no new ones added. Page-read budget: the two FFLA list pages and e-WV were read as shared context, so this tower used six distinct pages plus one WebSearch.

The register (North Fork Mountain, exact location unknown) and Eastern US Lookouts (North Mountain, south of US 33) disagree on the ridge; the register also lists coordinates, which conflicts with its own 'exact location is unknown' line. Do not present the point as a precise site. Forest Fire Lookout Association's North Fork Mountain entry (US 164, Pendleton) is a different tower. Army-funded tower count: Eastern says three, the forest history names two (Niges Cliff, Pigeon Roost). No staffing, fire or access history found in sources read; access left out. Eastern US Lookouts is a long index page; quotes come from its Niges Cliff section.

Thin record. No source gives a build year, builder, height, or removal date, so the story gives none. The steel replacement's date is not given either. No source describes what remains on the site or whether it is open to visitors; record access stays 'unknown'. A Mon Forest Towns guide lists a former fire tower site along the middle of the North Fork Mountain Trail but does not name it, so it is not linked here. Pike Knob (FFLA: US 1587, WV 21) is a separate record and was not merged. The record marks the two National Archives photos 'All rights reserved'; federal photos are often public domain, so check the licence before reuse.

Unresolved: agency (register says U.S. Forest Service; Eastern US Lookouts says WV Division of Forestry) and the 1929 date in Eastern US Lookouts. The forest history supports 1935 and lists the tower as a Monongahela tower, but describes no site. No source describes the site today; access left out. A search hit for a 1966 timber tower titled 'North Mountain Fire Lookout' (Ramblr) was not used: it could not be read and its description does not match this record. Register record name, location and status otherwise check out; no corrections proposed.

The FFLOS record gives October 12, 1939 as the first day in service, not a construction year, and no build year was found. Wikipedia's Coalwood article dates the Olga Coal Company name from a 1947 sale and rename, eight years after the 1939 date. The sources read do not say whether that is the same company, so the story reports the gap without resolving it. The 1986 Bluefield Daily Telegraph report, quoted on Forest Lookouts, names only the Olga Fire Tower and is not treated as a fact about No. 1; the same caveat is in us-wv-olga-no-2. No access or present-day site information was found. Wikipedia is used as a lead only; its own citations were not checked. The brief's coordinates, elevation and status agree with the sources; no corrections proposed.

No build year for Olga No. 2 was found. The 1986 Bluefield Daily Telegraph report on Forest Lookouts does not name which Olga tower it describes (No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3), so it is not treated as a fact about No. 2. Olga No. 1 facts are from its own site record and are marked as such. Olga and Huff Knob have no Wikipedia article at the titles tried. The Wriston article PDF may cover the Olga towers; fetch_text returned no text for it. Administrator Alawest is named only by the NHLR and the sister site records.

No build year, staffing period or removal date for No. 3 appears in any source read. The 1986 report names only the Olga Fire Tower and is not attributed to No. 3. The built-by and administrator statements come from the FFLOS No. 3 record. The three-tower statement comes from the NHLR entry for Olga No. 2, which does not name the other two. The 1947 Olga-name question in us-wv-olga-no-1 would matter for No. 3 only if its date were before 1947, and no date is given. The brief's coordinates and elevation agree with the sources; no corrections proposed.

Built date (1963, Backbone 1922) and elevation agree across the Forest Service, NHLR and Wikipedia. Current condition rests on one undated NHLR visit report. The register's staffing field has mixed visit answers ('No' on one visit, 'Sometimes' on a July 31, 2019 visit); both are now quoted and reported in the story. Access comes from the Forest Service page. One WebSearch via websearch.py; four page reads. No photos. No rental listed for Olson in the sources read.

Brief said access unknown; set to restricted from the 2013 Register visit report, the newest source found. That report is over 13 years old, so current access and condition are unverified. No watchers, staffing history or notable fires appear in the sources read. Build year, Blau-Knox type and state forest dates agree across sources. The Register spells it Blau-Knox; the Old Sentinel sources spell the maker Blaw-Knox. Used 3 page reads and 1 search. Stopped early because the sources are thin on history and nothing else turned up.

Only two sources were read: the FFLOS register page (fact-check 2026-10-09: only registry, date, nominator, location, coordinates, elevation and administrator fields; no build, removal or description text) and the FFA WV list. The WV Encyclopedia entry (wvencyclopedia.org/entries/2115) was checked with a grep for Parting, Godwin, Rich Mountain and Snowshoe and had no matching lines. The Godwin tower rests on a single list entry marked Private; no owner, build date, height, or move date was found. What, if anything, remains at the Parting Springs site is unknown. The WebSearch call for this tower was refused because the shared WebSearch budget for the run was already used up; websearch.py was not used to get around the limit. Re-search for the Parting Springs tower history and the Godwin tower before publishing.

Build year, builder, height and move date are not in any source read (two searches, register and association pages; the WV Division of Forestry list PDF host did not resolve). Godwin standing status rests on the Forest Fire Lookout Association list alone and is unverified on site. The Godwin name appears on that list above the relocated row. The list marks the location Private but does not state ownership, so ownership is unknown.

Only the FFLOS record and the FFLA list describe this site, and both mark it gone. The FFLA list gives the other name Holly River (Pickens); no source read explains the name. No build date, builder, staffing or removal date was found. A Wikipedia article on Holly River State Park was checked only in its matched lines, and no source read links it to this lookout, so it is not used. The Division of Forestry tower list PDF on wvnet.edu could not be fetched (DNS error). The e-WV entry is used for statewide context only. The brief's coordinates and elevation agree with the sources; no corrections proposed.

Only two register-type pages were read. Two web searches returned map and topo sites only, which were not read. No builder, construction date, staffing, removal date or site description found. A search snippet from topoquest.com gives 1,929 ft MSL, against the register's 1,950 ft; the story uses the register figure and does not mention the snippet.

Two coordinate sets disagree: register N 39.185767 W 079.217394 versus FFLA 39.18742 -79.22370. The record's conflict note says they 'share a register number', which does not describe the disagreement; the disagreement is the coordinates, and this research does not decide between them. The 2011 map label shows only that the name was on a USGS topo, not that a structure stands. Eastern US Lookouts says three Army-funded towers while the forest history names two; flagged in the story. The register gives the transfer as 1948 and the forest history as 1944 and 1948 for the pair. Access, staffing and fire history: none in sources read. No photos found.

No source gives a build year, so no built event was added; the 1930s and 90-foot height come from one 2026 hiking guide (cite 2) only. Agency conflict: the register names The Nature Conservancy; the Mon guide says the Forest Service and the Conservancy jointly manage the area; the eastern lookouts page header (easternuslookouts.weebly.com/pike-knob.html) reads 'National Forest'. The record's ownership 'federal' is not clearly wrong, since TNC's page says the old road reaches national forest land, but the site itself is in a TNC preserve; left for an editor. No staffing, fire or closure-date sources were found. The register photo (Brian Powell) is already in the record and was not re-added.

Build date, builder, design, height and staffing are not in any source read. Status conflicts: FFLA lists standing; Abandoned Online lists Closed with no date. Access is unknown; the story advises against climbing. Source 1 shows Closed on the line after the name; the evidence quote joins the two lines. Mindat returned 403. Unread leads: e-WV Fire Towers (wvencyclopedia.org/entries/2115), e-WV Flat Top Mountain (entries/2123), Wikipedia Flat Top Mountain (West Virginia). Search summaries claiming a 1990 statewide closure and a separate Pilot Knob in Wyoming County were not verified and are not used. The NHLR photo is all rights reserved, so no new photos were added. Page-read budget: about 6 successful fetches, the brief's limit.

Thinnest of the three. No source gives a build date, staffing, a closure date or a description of the site. The story's statewide sentences (cite 4, Beanblossom op-ed) describe West Virginia towers in general and are not about this tower; a human may want to cut them. Agency comes only from the eastern lookouts page header (cite 3); the register page names no administrator. Record elevation 598.9 m agrees with the register's 599 m.

Build year conflicts: the NHLR says 1925 (WV Conservation Commission); the 1973 Charleston Gazette, quoted by Forest Lookouts, says the tower was originally built to 60 feet in 1927. Both kept as events. Elevation conflicts: NHLR 3,364 ft (matches record elevation_m 1025.3); the 1973 article says 3,500 ft; the 1916 report quoted by Forest Lookouts says 3,550 ft. Not reconciled. Record height_m 30.5 matches the NHLR's 100-foot total height, so it is kept. Registration correction: FFLOS US 1692 ('Potato Hill Tower Site', registered 2017) gives its location as unknown in Webster County with coordinates unlisted, and Forest Lookouts uses the name Potato Hill as a historic name for this site. Whether the FFLOS tower is this one is not established; the correction proposes unlinking, and the 2017 fflos_registered event was left out of this tower's events for that reason. Access and current condition: the newest sources are the NHLR (undated) and the firelookout.org list; the NHLR links to a 2015 video of a climb; no source read says whether the public may visit or climb now. Searches found no 2024-2025 access notice. The WBOY article on climbable WV towers does not mention Point Mountain. Ownership: the NHLR names the WV Division of Forestry as administrator; the Monongahela National Forest list in a search summary was not read and was not used. Budget: four fetch_text page reads (NHLR, FFLOS, firelookout WV list, WBOY), one failed fetch of a WV tower list PDF (DNS error), two WebSearch calls, and one local read of the cached Forest Lookouts page (eastern_us_lookouts/point-mountain.html). No photos added.

Only two register-type pages were read: the FFLOS detail page, which has no description, and the FFLA county list, which gives the status. Two web searches returned topo map sites only, which were not read. No builder, construction date, staffing or removal details found. The record's 550.8 m elevation matches the register's 551 m.

Only two register-type pages were read: the FFLOS detail page, which has no description, and the FFLA county list, which gives the status. Two web searches returned topo map and cemetery pages only, which were not read. No builder, construction date, staffing or removal details found. The record's 527 m elevation matches the register.

No source gives a build date or the tower's design. The height (80 ft, 24.4 m) and the 1974 staffing come from one newspaper item quoted on the eastern lookouts page (cite 3); 24.4 m matches the record. Agency conflict: the register names the WV Division of Forestry; the eastern lookouts page header names the WV Department of Natural Resources. Left unresolved for an editor. The statewide closure sentence (cite 4) is context, not a closure date for this tower. The 1974 observer is named in the source and is a historical figure; no living person is identified.

Current use is well sourced by the Forest Service release of September 8, 2026: the cab and campsite are open for rental, booked on Recreation.gov, with the 2027 season April 15 to November 30. The Recreation.gov listing itself was not read, so check rates and dates there before publishing. Open disagreements, left in the story: location (register says east of Cowen; Forest Service says about 12 miles south of Cowen) and cab size (register 14 by 14 ft; 2023 news 12 by 13 ft). The register's 80-foot height is also used by the 2023 news report, so it is treated as settled. The record's access 'unknown' is now given as public (rental). No corrections proposed. No photos added: the register's May 2022 photo is credited to an individual with no licence shown. The rental release does not say whether the tower itself may be climbed, so the story does not advise climbing it.

The link between the Red Spruce Knob trail guide's fire tower site and the register's Red Spruce Tower Site is inferred from the matching names only; the register coordinates were not checked against the knob. Not used: a Facebook post in search results saying 'Red Spruce Knob ... Removed in 1968' (social post, unverified, possibly a different site). The exact year the tower came down is not in any source read. The guide has photos of the remains that were not downloaded.

Only the FFLOS register page, the FFLOS county list, one Mon Forest article and the NHLR Snowshoe page were usable; two searches added nothing about this site. No build date, staffing, fire or access source found, so access is omitted. The brief's status 'gone' matches the county list. The Randolph County Rich Mountain (FFLOS US 1690, listed Tower Gone) is a separate record and was not researched here. No photos found.

Four sources read: the FFLOS register page for the Randolph County site, the NHLR page for the Snowshoe tower, the Eastern US Lookouts Snowshoe page, and the FFA WV list. The 1999 sale is described two ways. The register says it was sold to Snowshoe Mountain, Inc.; the Eastern US Lookouts page says the Department of Natural Resources sold it for one dollar. The register does not name the seller, so the two are not in conflict. The 80-foot height is from the Eastern US Lookouts page only and may be overall height rather than cab-floor height, so facts.height_m is omitted. Nothing is known about the Randolph County site beyond the 2022 photo captions (site and footings) and the association's Tower Gone; no owner or access found. A newspaper account of the 1999 sale would help. Fact-check 2026-10-09: the NHLR Snowshoe page lists 'Built 1999' under Lookout Details, which differs from the FFLOS 'Built by 1925' for the original Randolph County tower; the story does not use NHLR's build date, so an editor should decide whether to note the difference. The story's 'The register' now refers only to the FFLOS register, and NHLR is named where it is cited.WebSearch was refused for this tower because the shared run budget was already spent, and websearch.py was not used to get around the limit. Re-search before publishing.

Build date 'by 1925' comes from the FFLOS Randolph County record; NHLR's Built 1999 is the relocation year. The record's events list 1999 as built and should be corrected. A WBOY search snippet places the tower 'on top of Cheat Ridge' in Pocahontas County; the page was not read, so the Snowshoe Mountain location rests on NHLR. The 80-foot height is from one history page only. Access: private resort ground; no climbing.

Brief height 22.9 m reflects the planned 1928 height; the built height is 60 ft per two sources. Brief removal year 1980 is not in the register, which says only 1980s. The 1928 and 1962 newspaper passages were read as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, not from the original newspapers. No source found about the site today, including after a web search. The register and Forest Lookouts pages disagree on elevation and the agency at build time.

Only the FFLOS detail page, the FFLOS county list and the e-WV encyclopedia article were usable. Two searches found nothing about the tower's construction, staffing or fires. The 1942 postcard and 2008 foundation photo are described by caption only; their image URLs were not captured, so no photos entry. Access is unknown and omitted. The register does not date the removal.

The status is unknown, not gone: the register's former-site listing and the forest-wide razing statement do not say this tower was removed, and no source read gives a removal date or the site's condition. No web search turned up a Sharp Knob trail or site description. The 1947 National Archives photo is credited on the register page and in the Forest Service history, but its image URL was not captured, so no photos entry. The 2016-2017 brief dates are consistent with the register.

Thin record. The register and the FFLA county list agree the tower is gone, but no source gives a build date, design, height, or what remains. The 1939 watchman search has no outcome in our sources. Access is not stated. Search hits for 1930s CCC towers at Shawnee National Forest (IL) and Shawnee State Forest (OH) are different places and were not used. A Division of Forestry or McDowell County history check would help.

Register and county list agree on Tower Gone. The Forest Lookouts page's 1923 date and its 'Fulton and Bedford counties' text belong to a Pennsylvania tower on the same ridge name, so the story only uses that page to say they are different. The WBOY 'five former fire towers' article returned 403 and was not read. No staffing or fire source found. Access unknown and omitted. No photos found.

Stub-level record. Standing status and coordinates come from the FFLA list. The name match to Mapcarta's Slaty Lick Knob Lookout Tower is inferred from the coordinates, not confirmed by any agency. The local GNIS peaks file lists Slate Lick Knob at 39.4223, -78.7903; it is not cited because the GNIS page fetched without usable text. Slate Lick does not appear on the Forest Lookouts or NHLR West Virginia lists as crawled. Build date, design, builder, staffing, access and fires are unknown. Mapcarta's 'Slaty' spelling should be checked against a county or Forest Service source before the name is changed.

Gone tower with thin sourcing: the build, scrap and registration facts come from two registers, and the 1948 and 1950 notices are secondhand quotes on Forest Lookouts, not checked against the newspapers. Removal date and buyer are not in any source; the Division of Forestry was not contacted. No access level is given because the sources say nothing about whether the tower spot is open to visitors, and no source describes the site today. The brief's county (Morgan) is kept, with the conflict noted. Source pages carry a zero-width space before the agency name; the quote avoids it.

The register and Forest Lookouts agree on 1928 and last staffing in 1950. The hiking guide is the only source for what is at the site now, and it says parking is nonexistent on site, and gives room for two or three cars on Forest Service Road 54 off WV 28 (it names FR 58 for the forest road up the mountain). Check current access with the Monongahela NF Greenbrier Ranger District before publishing visit advice. The record's 9.1 m height matches the 30-foot figure. The register photos are already in the record, so no new photos were added.

Source conflict on ownership (1926 joint vs register's Maryland). The register gives the 1980s both as the fire year and as the removal date; the Forest Lookouts page gives no end date. The 1980 event year is a placeholder for the decade. A Maryland DNR fire tower poster appeared only in a search snippet (the fetch returned 404), claiming a wooden 1940s tower; that conflicts with the 1925 steel-tower reports, so it is not used. The FFLA Maryland list has a separate Snaggy Mountain (Pitch Pine Rock) entry in Garrett County with unknown coordinates, marked gone; check whether it is this tower before merging. The 60-foot height is the 1925 announced height. The register photos are already in the record.

No build year and no removal date appear in any source read. The 1926 item is the earliest found. The Forest Lookouts page carries a bare Removed heading with no date. Access is unknown; the brief's access field is not set. Two WebSearch queries were run; nothing new beyond the register and the Forest Lookouts page. The register and state list both show WV 28 for Sleepy Creek, so the WV number alone does not identify a site.

Date the wooden lookout came down is not found, so no removal event is recorded. Whether the 1969 observation tower replaced it is inferred from the register wording and not stated outright in any fetched source. The brief's elevation (1482.2 m) is the summit height, not a tower height; no height key is given. Brief status corrected: the FFLA list reads Gone. Two WebSearch results (a Monongahela guide saying the stone tower stands on a former wooden tower site, and a 1938 photo of a fire tower) were not fetched, so they are not used. The FFLA list's Gone status and the register's wording fit together, so the record is not contradictory once the observation tower is separated from the fire lookout. Used 2 WebSearch calls and 6 page reads.

The register's relocation to Peters Mountain is not tied to a structure: neither the register nor the state list names the tower now there. The state list has a separate row, Peters Mountain, Monroe County, Tower, Gone, with no register number; it may be connected but no source says so. The relocation has no year in any source, so it is not in events; fact status carries it. The register misspells the agency name (corrections). The brief's status gone is corrected to relocated by the register text. Access is unknown; no access field set. Two WebSearch queries were run; no new Stop Knob sources surfaced.

No construction date found for the current tower; the earliest dated references are a 1916 station with a watchman and a 1926 tower on telephone lines. Staffing is recorded as unknown: the 1947 'in charge' item is not evidence of current staffing. County conflicts (Greenbrier per NHLR; Nicholas per the lookout list and the forest-lookout site). Elevation also differs: NHLR gives 3,112 ft (949 m), while the 1916 report gives 3,158 ft for the station. A Facebook post in search results (WV fire lookouts) asks whether the tower was removed; only its title could be read (login wall), so it is not used. Check status before publishing. Search results also return a different Sugar Grove tower in Berne Township, Fairfield County, Ohio (110 ft, Lancaster Eagle-Gazette, 2017); it is not this tower and must not be merged into this record.

Access and visiting status unknown; the register says emergency use only on Beaver Coal Company land, and no public visiting or rental information was found. The newspaper clippings are secondhand, transcribed on the Forest Lookouts site, not checked against the original papers. The build year conflicts (register 1934, clippings Jan 1935). A Facebook group post claiming a 2012 observation could not be read, so it is not used. Mapcarta gives 2,654 ft elevation against the register's 2,637 ft; not used. No record corrections proposed.

The NHLR says originally built in the 1920s by the CCC; the state history credits the Civilian Conservation Corps with forest work but places a 1924 tower on Michael Mountain. Search snippets from theclio.com/entry/45123 and wvencyclopedia.org credit the CCC with building the 1935 tower, but those pages were not opened and no quote was recorded. Read on the 2026-10-08 fact-check, easternuslookouts.weebly.com/thorny-mountain.html (not cited in the story, not an NHLR or state source): a '1935' entry says the lookout duties were transferred to this site from Michael Mountain, which bears on the 'Michael Mountain link is not confirmed' sentence; a November 28, 1937 Bluefield Daily Telegraph item says a new tower with observer's cabin atop a '40-foot steel framework' was 'completed recently' on Thorny Mountain, built by CCC labor. The story does not use either item. The editor should decide whether the 1935 date, the 'not confirmed' sentence, or the height note needs them. Staffing not recorded: the NHLR shows 'Staffed? No' but the quote is split across lines. Six page reads used. No photos recorded. Elevation on the NHLR page is 3,385 ft (1,032 m), consistent with the brief.
