Built year conflicts: register 1937 vs park page and trail blog 1935; the January 1937 item supports 1937 (described as yet to be erected). Access conflicts: park wording 'open' vs register fence and trail blog 'not open for climbing'; recorded as restricted. No fire or staffing history found. easternuslookouts tick-ridge1.html covers a different Tick Ridge in Carter County and was excluded. A Facebook group post and a Historic Wayne County post could not be read in full, so they are not used. The record's 80-foot height and 1,367 ft elevation fit the sources; no record corrections proposed.

Thin record: one dated 1930s item, and the state list is the only fate source. No staffing source found, so staffing is omitted. The register's 1937 photo (courtesy of Jim Foster) has no image URL in the text we read, so it is not in photos. Two WebSearch queries were run; no new White Oak sources surfaced. The brief's conflict note is explained: WV 26 is shared with Sugar Grove (US 1678). Wharton-area and Boone County newspapers were not searched and could fill the staffing and fate gaps.

Thin record: no build date, design, height or staffing found in the sources read. The 1926 item is cited through the Forest Lookouts transcription; the Charleston Gazette itself was not read. Worth a newspaper search or state survey before expanding; the story says nothing on current condition beyond what the sources give.

Brief record matches the FFLOS entry. The story says no source describes the site today. The 1951 staffing is a newspaper plan, not a confirmed record of operation. The 'replaced an earlier tower' claim is unconfirmed (see resolved_conflicts). The 1951 PDF by Robert Beanblossom on Pop Wriston did not extract text and was not used.

No removal year, cause or current-site description found in the sources; the Gone status rests on the FFLA inventory alone. A 1941 Jackson Hole Courier item about four new Teton lookout houses does not name Baldy, so it is not used. The NRHP nomination is for Huckleberry Mountain Lookout and mentions Baldy only as one of the six sites. firelookout.com gives the agency as Bridger-Teton. A records check with the Bridger-Teton National Forest would be the next step for a removal date.

The brief's record also carries a second coordinate pair (41.30083, -106.49806, labelled west_us_lookouts); the FFLA inventory gives 41.32657, -106.52627, which is used here. The second pair's source was not checked. The 1918 and 1921 entries come from the Saratoga Sun and Laramie Republican reprints on the weebly page, and the 1930 entry from the Casper Tribune-Herald item quoted on the Adventr blog. No removal year, description or current-site detail was found.

1937 newspaper wording is read through the Forest Lookouts transcription; original papers were not checked. The Forest Lookouts page has a 'Removed' heading with no text, so removal date is unknown. 'Gone' rests on the FFA and firelookout.com lists. The NPS rephotography finding aid mentions a 1935 Bechler River panorama but does not describe the site, so it was not used. A 1937 photo is captioned on the FFLOS page but no image URL was captured, so no photo entry was added. The access level 'public' reflects Yellowstone National Park land only.

Only two sources. The weebly page is titled Little Sheep Mountain and gives no structure, staffing or removal detail. The FFLA inventory lists the site as Big Bend (Little Sheep) with type Unknown and status Gone. A TopoQuest entry for a Big Bend in Sublette County (N43.366335, W109.987945, 7,805 ft) lies roughly 6 km from the inventory point; it was not used and is not confirmed as the same site. The fire of 1912 is not named in the source.

Closure and access are well supported by the 2025 news report, which is a Wyoming News Exchange piece; the Forest Service order itself was not read. Build year is disputed (1939 vs. completion October 1940). Elevation differs between NHLR (9,383 ft) and firelookout.com (9492'). The 2014 report says Historic Core; the 2025 article says HistoriCorps; the story treats them as the same group but that is not confirmed. Not read: Living New Deal (403 error), a Sheridan Press closure article and a 2024 Cowboy State Daily piece (search snippets only). No last-watch date found; the 1980 end date comes from the 2025 article. No photos added; NHLR photo credits not checked.

Thin on history: only three pages read and no fire or rental record found. Do not confuse with the Bighorn Mountains Black Mountain (Sheridan County, BHNF, built 1939 by the CCC, now boarded up); the Sheridan travel-history article and the Road Trip Ryan page describe that tower. Staffing dates in the register come from the 2018 visit and may have changed. Personal names of past lookouts are kept to the published lists.

No source checked actually states a 1950 build year for the current tower; both NHLR and Recreation.gov agree on 1963, so the earlier draft's claimed 1950/1963 discrepancy was unsupported and has been removed. No clear record of when active staffing ended beyond NHLR's '25 years then standby' note, and no date given for when that standby period began.

The climbing guide and the NRHP form give only 'the 1930s' for construction, so no build event is recorded. Elevation 7694 ft (about 2,345 m) per firelookout.com; the record has none. Removal date and cause unknown. The guide asks for pictures of the footings only; none found in our reads. The 1951 date comes from a Rigby Star item quoted on westlookouts.weebly.com, not the newspaper itself.

Two searches and the cached pages gave no construction, staffing or removal history. Elevation 8311 ft (about 2,532 m) per firelookout.com; the record has none. The record's ownership is 'unknown'; firelookout.com's location line puts the site on the Wind River Indian Reservation, which a human should weigh before filling ownership. The 2017 notice credits two named people with arranging the permission; check before any site visit.

Key open question is current condition: the sources conflict and none is recent. Access rests on one family blog of unknown date; verify with the Shoshone National Forest before publishing access wording. Brief record 'gone' is contested. Blog quote about 23 miles is for the trailhead, firelookout.com's 18 miles for the lookout (unconfirmed).

Thin record. Read: the firelookout.com page, the FFLA Wyoming list and the Wikipedia article on the reservation. Two web searches found nothing on build date, design, staffing or fires. The access level 'permission' is carried over from the record; no source states a visiting rule. The record's 'tribal' ownership is not stated in any source read. Agency correction proposed.

firelookout.com's page is headed as a fire lookout, while the Forest Fire Lookout Association inventory files the site among lookout sites and non-lookout structures with type unknown. The sources disagree and we did not settle it. Elevation 9292 ft (about 2,832 m) per firelookout.com; the record has none. Two searches found no build, staffing, access or removal history. Unverified lead: a 2003 Forest Service report, Lookouts, Latrines, and Lodgepole Cabins, cited by a Living New Deal entry for another Bridger-Teton lookout; it may not cover this peak.

Build year is the open point. The register says 1925, but a 1921 newspaper item describes a lookout house on the peak, and the 1911 papers only report a plan. The story reports both and proposes no date. Public access is inferred from two trip reports; no official statement was found. Newspaper items are quoted from westlookouts.weebly.com, which reprints them; the original papers were not read. The register's registration date (January 1, 2026) was confirmed on the page. No photo was added; no licensed image source was found. The record's 1960 removal year is approximate, since the register says only 1960s.

Thin record: one 1940 newspaper item, read through westlookouts, which reprints it (the Tribune original was not read), and two lists that say gone with no date. The source spells the place 'Mammath'; the story uses the correct spelling and quotes nothing with the typo. A social post by Yellowstone Wildlife Profiles on Facebook says the 1988 North Fork Fire moved across Bunsen Peak toward Mammoth; it is not used, since it is a social post. The NPS 1988 fires page (https://www.nps.gov/yell/learn/nature/1988-fires.htm) turned up in search but was not read, and may say whether the lookout was involved. The access level rests on the NPS trail page, not on any statement about the lookout site. No photo added: firelookout.com credits the National Park Service Archives but gives no image URL.

Build year 1941 rests on the register alone; the KINGFM CCC attribution is a hiking video's narration quoted second-hand and is unverified. The 'standing' status comes from the firelookout.org index, not the register text. The access level 'public' is inferred from the hiking account, not stated by any source. Brief record checked: name, county, elevation, agency and 2022 registration match the register, so no corrections. Not reached: Bridger-Teton lookout records or a Forest Service page on current status; a 2022 Wyoming fire report mentioning the Cabin Creek lookout cabin appeared in search but was not read. The story does not claim a current site check.

Could not fetch the bhpioneer.com newspaper article (HTTP 429, too many requests) within the read budget, so staffing/anecdote detail rests on NHLR and the brochure PDF plus firelookout.com's personnel list; worth a retry later for any additional staffing or incident detail. Did not verify current rental/public-access specifics (e.g. whether the tower cab itself is open to visitors) beyond the brief's existing 'public' access level. 2026-10-04 fact-check: the story originally said the lookout straddles the Wyoming-South Dakota line; no source supports that, and firelookout.com (source 2) instead places it in Crook County, Wyoming, about a mile from the state line. Fixed the story wording and citation accordingly.

Height_m taken from Wikipedia's 26.25 ft (8.00 m) structure height, not from ground elevation. Material conflict (wood vs concrete) flagged but not independently resolved beyond preferring the NRHP-sourced Wikipedia account.

Built 1940 and gone are consistent across the register, the Wyoming list and the trail guide. Staffing, the removal date and the summit's condition today are not in any source read, so they are left out. The 1940 Shoshone report is read only as quoted on the register page. The register's '20 timber tower' looks garbled, so no height is given. Access is marked public from the trail guide and the designation; no closure was found.

No build date, builder, design or removal date appears in any source read. The 1955 dedication is a reprint in a 'Twenty Years Ago This Week' column, so the event year of about 1935 is inferred and the story says 'probably'. The Forest Service history (Report BT-02-637, hosted by the NPS History E-Library) treats the 1954 Pinedale lookouts as uncertain, while the 1955 item calls Crow's Nest a lookout on a summit; the story reports both. The Pastmaps page is a site description: its map label, the portrayed date (1968) and the published date (1973) are the parts relied on. The record's coordinates (42.65022, -109.21911) were not checked against any source. The original 1955 Pinedale Roundup was not read.

Build date is disputed: NHLR circa 1940; county page and brochure 1941 (CCC role claimed on the county page, possible but undocumented per the brochure). The brochure says the cab was moved from Red Castles on Bare Pass before 1955, which the NHLR record does not mention. Restoration start: August 2015 (Pinedale) vs 2016-2019 (brochure). Unread leads: a 2020 Pinedale Online piece says built around 1941 by the CCC; a search snippet from npshistory.com (Lookouts, Latrines, and Lodgepole Cabins, hcs-2.pdf) says the lookout is recommended not eligible for the National Register; neither was read or verified. Road access is from a 2019 brochure; check current conditions with the Big Piney Ranger District before publishing visit advice.

The 1941 build year is supported by the register, firelookout.com and a 1941 newspaper item reprinted on West Lookouts, which is a secondary transcription. The 1940 telephone-line item calls the site a fire lookout before the 1941 build report; I could not settle whether an earlier structure stood there. The abandonment claim comes from a hiking listing, not an agency record. No staffing, fire or current access source was found, so none is stated. Brief record checked: the name, elevation, agency and 2022 registration match, so no corrections were needed. Not reached: Bridger-Teton or Bridger NF lookout records, and the NHLR nomination file for WY 21.

No build date, builder or design source beyond firelookout.com's 'log and frame cabin'. Do not merge this lookout with the CCC-era Deer Creek Guard Station named in the Forest Service history, which is a different building, nor with the rentable Deer Creek Cabin on Recreation.gov (a guard station near Alpine on the Greys River district). The Deer Creek name in the 1954 item and the Forest Service photo caption 'Deer Creek Lookout near Goosewing Guard Station' are taken to be the same site; the story states this as an inference, not a fact. The photo caption supports the location but gives no coordinates. The record's coordinates (43.61512, -110.19102) match firelookout.com. The 1956 items name a worker; the story omits the name. No photo added: the caption credits a USFS photo, but no image URL was retrieved. The history's abandonment and burning dates are given as 'by 1970' and 'mid-1970s'; the 1975 year on the burned event is approximate.

No source read gives the build year, and no staffing dates were found, so neither is in the story or facts. The Yellowstone manned-lookout claim is from a 2018 quote by a Mount Washburn lookout, not a dated record. Elevation: FFLOS gives 8,771 ft (2,673 m) and firelookout.com gives 8750'; the record keeps the FFLOS figure. The FFLOS list marks it as removed in 1991, and the firelookout.org list marks it Tower Gone. The Facebook post about Divide could not be read, so it is not cited. The firelookout.com page has a photo credited to NPS Archives, but no image URL was retrieved, so no photo is listed.

Sources conflict on whether the structure is a tower or a cabin. The 2007 fire item is quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; its original publisher, Teton Valley News, was not opened. The Buckrail article speaks of towers and may not cover this site. The brief's elevation (2596 m) was not checked against a source we read; 'Ground' matches the FFLA list. Do not confuse this with the Elk Mountain Fire Lookout in the Black Hills National Forest, South Dakota, which appeared in search results only and is not cited. Access and staffing are unknown.

The 1940 build year is a planned summer completion from a June 1940 newspaper item quoted on westlookouts; no source confirms the finished date. The 1952 and 1940 newspaper items are second-hand quotes on the westlookouts page and were not checked against the originals. Both lookout pages say gone or removed but give no removal date, so the timeline has no fate event. No source describes the site today or its access.

The steel tower date is in conflict between the directory (1953) and the newspaper report (erected by February 1954); the story gives both. The newspaper items are second-hand quotes on the westlookouts page and were not checked against the originals. No source gives the wooden tower's build date, the tower height, or what remains at the site today.

Record was thin: the NHLR page is the only substantive source, and the other two are short. No staffing, fire or current-condition source was found. The brief's height_m 36.6 (120 ft) traces to the Stumpy Point, NC tower on the same ranch (westlookouts), so it is corrected to 30 ft from firelookout.com. Agency conflict is left unresolved. Two leads were not used: a Deadwood history Facebook post (search snippet only, page did not load) says the Moskee Fire burned more than 7,000 acres in 1936; and ghosttowns.com's Moskee page gives 1921 for Homestake's involvement, not 1922. Access is set to permission from both NHLR and westlookouts. No photos added: the NHLR credits Dixie Boyle but gives no license.

Thin record. Sources give only location, agency, kind (ground site), status and a summit height; no source gives a build date, staffing, a removal date or what remains at the summit. The story is short because the evidence is short. Elevation figures differ slightly between Komoot and the trail description. The Targhee attribution is confirmed by both lookout pages; the wilderness claim rests on the Komoot listing alone.

Thin record: three web entries, and the two lookout pages hold no history beyond location and status. Two searches found nothing more about construction, staffing or fires, so the story is short by design. elevation_m is null in the record; the cited 7,932 ft is about 2,417.7 m if the editor wants to fill it. The kind field stays unknown because no source names the structure type. Agency and county agree across sources.

Build year 1938 is supported by three sources, but a 1942 newspaper item (quoted on westlookouts) calls Huckleberry a permanent station that year; not resolved. Current status is unconfirmed: the newest dated text read is the register entry (2011 registration; 'slated for restoration') and firelookout.com 'Standing'. Elevation conflict (7,209 ft register vs 9,615 ft nomination and firelookout) is proposed as a correction for human review. Page budget was used up before reading the Wyoming SHPO page, the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort page or the Hiking Project page; search snippets claim restoration and overnight use, but those were not read or cited, so check them before any access statement is changed. No new photos.

History comes from one compiled page (Forest Lookouts) that quotes a 1939 fire report, a History of the Bighorn National Forest, a CCC inspection memo and regional forester memos. Those primary documents were not checked directly. The 1939 fire refers to the Hunter Mesa LO location before the 1940 tower, so the site may have been in use before the tower; the sources do not say. Distance: firelookout.com says 10 miles west of Buffalo; a Living New Deal page, which could not be fetched, is reported to give 12.75 miles, so it is not cited. Living New Deal also says it is unsure the structure still stands; that could not be checked. Removal date not found. The record says kind tower and that matches. Access level unknown.

The 1912-1914 history comes from Park County Enterprise items as quoted on the westlookouts page; the original paper was not checked. Staffing is planned in the 1913 items and only one 1914 item (Arthur Braten, who left for Crandall Creek to take the work at a Lookout Station) suggests staff; that item does not name the peak, so the staffed event is hedged. A Cody Journal biography of Evelyn Braten covers Windy Mountain, not this peak, and was not used. No removal date and no description of the site today were found. Dimensions conflict between the 1913 paper and firelookout.com (see resolved_conflicts). The elevation 9,037 ft on firelookout.com could fill elevation_m if the editor wants it.

Elevation conflict left unresolved: register 9,395 ft (2,864 m, matches the record's 2863.6 m) vs Forest Service 9,477 ft. NRHP listing date: register says December 2016, Wikipedia says November 15, 2016. Footprint: register and Wikipedia give 14 ft square, the nomination gives a 20 ft exterior footprint. The Forest Service page spells the name 'James Torrey Saban'; the register says 'James T.', so the story keeps 'James T.' and does not expand it. Current staffing and access come from the Forest Service page (last updated May 13, 2025), not a site visit. A search snippet about an overnight rental concerned Sheep Mountain, a different lookout, and was not used. The nomination gives no date for the restoration work. No new photos.

Brief kind 'platform' matches the listing, but the 1930 steel tower is not in the brief's record. The 1930 article is credited to the Casper Tribune-Herald on westlookouts; the FFLOS Somber Hill page (firetower.org/lookouts/us/wy/somber-hill-lookout-site/) credits the same article to the Casper Star-Tribune, and the story cites westlookouts only. No removal date and no site-today description found; sites in this record were not described beyond the listing. Search budget: two websearch.py fallback queries; six page reads.

Brief height_m 202.7 has no source support; see corrections. Agency in the brief (BLM) is what the listings say, but the 1938 order reserved the land for the Forest Service; the story reports both. The Facebook post (FFLA, 1941 photo, 'likely built in the mid-1930's') appeared only in a search snippet and is not used. The 1953 9,665 ft figure conflicts with 9,656 ft; both are reported. No new photos recorded. Search budget: one websearch.py fallback query; four page reads.

The brief's 1969 build date is contradicted by three sources (1964); Wilma Perue's 1969-1971 tenure may be the source of the mix-up. Rental fee comes from a Forest Service page last updated June 6, 2025; confirm before publishing. The record's kind 'two_story' is not supported by any source read: the NHLR describes a single R-6 cab with an interpretive site on a lower level. No fire or move history found; the CCC-era cab is undated beyond the 1930s.

Good newspaper record of staffing and fires from the Forest Lookouts page, but those clippings are secondhand transcriptions and were not checked against the newspapers. The fate is unclear: two lists say gone, and the only mention of burning is a bare caption on Forest Lookouts with no date or structure. The brief's height_m of 152.4 has no source; corrected above. The valhikes blog is outside the brief's source list; it was found by search and is a 2022 trip report, the only current-condition source. The Just Trails page is suspended (its account is closed), so its claims could not be checked. The register's Photo courtesy of American Heritage Center credit has no image URL, so no photo entry was added. The staffing notes stop at 1936; no source read says when the post ended. Access is marked public on the strength of national forest land and the 2022 trip report, not a closure or access notice.

The 1941 CCC build and precut log method rest on the USFS survey (Volume II evaluations, cover photo credited to the USFS). Current status rests on firelookout.com's undated 'Still there'. Not read: a Flickr photo page (search snippet calls it abandoned; not used), and the Living New Deal page (403 Forbidden). The westlookouts 1941 item describes four CCC lookout houses, 12 feet square; the story does not tie those to this site, and the survey supports the 1941 build on its own. The record has no height_m for this site, and none was found in these sources. No staffing after 1954 was found. No photos added: the NHLR credits SingleTracks.com but gives no license.

Build year conflict: the two registers say 1930; the park's 2019 press release (as reported by MTPR/YPR) and firelookout.com say 1931. The story reports both and does not settle it. Elevation: the registers say 10,256 ft (3,126 m), matching the record; firelookout.com says 10,336 ft and the 1935 Pinedale Roundup says about 10,300 ft. The record's elevation_m (3126) follows the register. The park's own press release on nps.gov (news/071719.htm) returned HTTP 404 to fetch_text; the story relies on the MTPR/YPR report that quotes it. The 2004 register entry was nominated by James Muhn; the 2020 FFLOS entry has the same nominator. The Wikidata entry links a 2012 photo on Wikimedia Commons (file 48310419056) but its licence was not checked, so no photo is proposed. The record's access field is 'unknown'; the 2019 closure is the only access statement found and is dated. Per the record's conflict note, firelookout.com does not list it on its map of standing lookouts, which matches the 2019 fire.

Built year and register data are well sourced. The 1926 build date (Outside Bozeman) is unresolved and reported as a conflict. Jim McCown (1963-1987) rests on one listing and is not confirmed; the 1975 visitor's Jim is unnamed, so the story does not link them. Current condition is inferred from a standing listing and a photo caption; no recent condition report was read. A search summary attributed a 1991 removal to this lookout, but the Outside Bozeman article's 1991 removal concerns Divide Lookout, not Sheridan, so it is not used. Blueprint location conflicts: WillhiteWeb says the Montana State Library holds them; Montana History Portal item 93097 credits the Yellowstone National Park Heritage and Research Center. Access level is unknown; no source read says whether the cabin can be entered. Height is not stated in any source; elevation_m is from the register. The record's Park County is supported; the Teton County listing is the only conflict.

Build date is contested: the NHLR Built field and HABS say 1941, but the NHLR narrative says construction began June 1939 and was completed summer 1940. The record keeps 1941; the story reports both. The 1921 stone lookout (Willhite, HABS, NHLR) is treated as the predecessor. The NPS page is undated; its staffing statement is in the present tense. Drive-up status rests on HABS (a parking area north of the building; the lookout described as the only Yellowstone fire lookout facility accessible by vehicle) plus two NPS hiking trails. Road seasonality and whether the upper floors are open to visitors were not checked. No fire events beyond the staffing history and the 1980 modification appear in the sources read. No climbing advice is given.

Brief status 'gone' should read 'moved': the steel tower went to Seth Bullock Lookout in Pennington County, South Dakota, in 1966. That South Dakota site is a separate lookout and may need its own record. Build year 1940 vs 1941 is unresolved; the story gives both. Whether any 1957 Pisgah steel stands in the current Seth Bullock tower is disputed between the register, firelookout.com and the NHLR. No source describes the Wyoming summit today, and Wyoming access is unknown. Living New Deal and Facebook or Instagram posts appeared only as search snippets and were not read, so they are not cited. Newspaper items are quoted via westlookouts.weebly.com, which reprints them.

No source gives a year for the mid-1970s burn, so the destroyed event is recorded with year null; the story says mid-1970s. The Forest Lookouts page is cited for the 1936-1954 record. The Forest Lookouts and FFLA sources name the agency Bridger-Teton National Forest, which matches the brief. The NPS-hosted PDF's publisher was checked on the title page (Bridger-Teton National Forest, 1904-1955; USDA Forest Service). The FS area page does not describe the summit. Search budget: three websearch.py fallback queries, one over the two-per-tower budget; six page reads.

NHLR is the main source for the 1939 build, the CCC help, the secondary-lookout purpose and the 2021 registration. Current use and public access are not stated in any source read: the NPS trail page covers the hike only, so the access level is left out of facts. Staffing is not documented; the slide-file captions only label the structure as a lookout (1964) and a lookout station (1975). Unread leads, from search snippets only and not used: a Parkwolf trail page calls the summit lookout 'historic (typically closed)', and a SummitPost Cascade Lake page says an old summit structure is 'apparently no longer in use'. Both should be checked before any statement about current use. Elevation 9,402 ft matches the record's elevation_m 2865.7. No height_m in any source read. No photos added: the NHLR photos lack licence terms and the NPS slide-file image URLs were not captured.

Built, staffing and registration rest on the NHLR page. The 1937 newspaper wording is quoted second-hand on the Forest Lookouts page; the newspapers themselves were not checked. Access and hike details come from one personal visitor account, which is undated, so treat them as indicative. No specific fires are named in the sources. The brief's access 'unknown' could become 'restricted' once the NPS status is confirmed. No photo URLs were added.

No build date, design, height or removal date appears in any source read. Staffing rests on a secondhand 1965 interview as quoted by Forest Lookouts. The Wikipedia article on Pinnacle Buttes covers the mountain, not the lookout. Two web searches found no other lookout history. Guessed firetower.org registry URL returned 404; no registry entry was located. Brief's agency entry (Washakie National Forest) matches only one of the two names in sources; the story reports both. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the Lander High School wording was added to evidence, and the Collom sentence was reworded so it no longer copies the quote.

Build year (1941) and staffing are consistent across NHLR and the 1941 newspaper items as transcribed on Forest Lookouts; the original newspaper scans were not read. Current access, rental status and condition are not established beyond the July 2025 FFLA post. A June 2025 Pinedale Online / geolconsulting article on protecting the tower could not be read (SSL certificate errors from both fetch_text and WebFetch), so the wrap and fire details rest on the FFLA post alone. Elevation differs between NHLR (9,665 ft) and firelookout.com (9642'). Access is omitted because no level could be supported. No photos added.

A travel-blog page (roadtripryan.com) and the WebSearch AI summary both offered a vivid, specific narrative - an 1922 primitive fire watch predecessor and a 1938 lightning strike that set the lookout's bed on fire - that appears nowhere in the NHLR register, the FFLA register, or the Forest Service's own Bighorn lookouts history page. I did not use any of that material; it has the hallmarks of AI-generated filler rather than sourced history, and a human may want to track down the roadtripryan.com page's own citations if any exist. Note that the CCC-construction claim itself is NOT part of that invented narrative - Recreation.gov and the Rocket-Miner newspaper piece (sources 4 and 6, both used in the story) independently and directly state the lookout was 'Constructed in 1950 by the Civilian Conservation Corps,' so that part is sourced, just flagged in the story as doubtful because the CCC was disbanded in 1942. A footnote error was also fixed: the story had attributed the 'Emergency' staffing status to 'the Forest Fire Lookout Association's own register,' but that fact actually comes from firelookout.com, an independent reference site by Rex Kamstra, not from FFLA's own site (firelookout.org, source 3) - the FFLA page for Wyoming is just a name/county/status table with no staffing field for this lookout. Text corrected; footnote [^2] was already pointing at the right source. The record's elevation_m (2911.8m / ~9554ft) runs a little low against the 9600-9610ft the registers give; likely just rounding/survey differences, not flagged as a correction. No other conflicts found worth a formal correction.

No removal year appears in any source; Forest Lookouts marks it Removed without a date. No source describes remains or current public access. Staffing and elevation conflicts are recorded in resolved_conflicts. The 1955 USGS map caption on the Willhite page was not used. Willhite Web has photos of the lookout but no direct image URL was captured, so no photos are listed. One web search used. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the August 9, 1951 date belongs to the Jackson's Hole Courier item (August 9, 1951 was a Thursday) and the strike is reported as Sunday night with no strike date, so the story no longer dates the strike to August 9. The 7,000-register item is dated January 25, 1939. The drive-up note was reworded so it does not imply the site is open to the public.

Brief record checks out: relocated status, Carbon County, coordinates and elevation (2,918 m) match the Register, and the FFLOS registration date of January 1, 2026 is confirmed. No record errors found, so no corrections. Original site: no source describes remains or access, and it was not visited. Museum tower: standing per the Firelookout.org index; access rests on one visit report, and the museum's own page was not read, so hours and whether the tower can be entered are unverified. The Register's agency line is used for agency. Budget: 2 WebSearch and about 5 page reads, within limits.

Museum hours and the tower's presence at the museum come from undated tourism and visitor-tip pages; confirm with the museum (gemuseum.com) before publishing. Climbing status is not confirmed. Height 15.2 m converts the 50-foot figure from firelookout.com. The 1986 move year comes from the register alone. The record's agency is null; the Forest Service entry refers to the original site.

No new photos found beyond those already on the tower record. The exact abandonment year is unknown (NHLR hedges with 'most probably ... mid to late 1940's'); I used 1945 as a placeholder year for the 'abandoned' event rather than inventing precision. The kind correction (tower -> shelter) is worth a human look since 'tower' vs 'shelter' is partly a classification judgment, not a hard fact.

The brief's height of 18.3 m matches the 60-foot steel tower reported in the 1927 item. The register's 'Removed 1960s' appears as 1960 in the events list; that year is approximate. The 1911 event refers to a wooden platform, not a tower. Staffing after 1932 is not documented in the sources read. The newspaper items come from westlookouts.weebly.com, which reprints them; the originals were not read. Access is unknown and no remains are described, so the story says so. No photo added.

No build date and no removal date in any source read. An NPS Grand Teton history chapter (search snippet: 'Spaulding Bay fire lookout, built c. 1940') could not be used: the cache returns an unrelated NPS page for that URL, so the c. 1940 date is not cited and should be checked by hand. Willhite Spalding Bay page URL not located (guessed URL 404). Guessed firetower.org registry URL returned 404. Two web searches used. Only one dated staffing item was found. Fact-check 2026-10-10: the story text was checked claim by claim and needed no change; evidence entries were added for the Teton County, Sunday-guest and Wyoming list type claims.

Height_m in the record (9.1 m / ~30 ft) likely describes the original 1930s pole tower rather than the current 41-55 ft structure; worth checking against a primary USFS record before correcting. Exact year of the tower replacement (after the original 1938 build) is not pinned down by any source consulted.

Sources disagree on distance from Dubois: 10 miles west (1928 newspaper quoted on westlookouts) vs 7 miles WNW (firelookout.com). Record coordinates left as they are. Elevation differs slightly: 9,530 ft (register) vs 9518 ft (firelookout.com). Removal date and any later fate are unknown. A YouTube page seen only in search results says the tower was built in the 1930s and burned in 1987; that conflicts with 1927 and with the register's unknown removal date, could not be verified on a readable page, and is not used. A County10 Dubois history article returned HTTP 403 on fetch and is not used. No access status found, so access is omitted. Staffing evidence is the 1958 memos only. The Dubois museum Facebook photo was not fetched and no photo license was checked.

History is well sourced across the Forest Service, NHLR and Wikipedia. Access and restroom details rest on Hiking Project, a third-party listing that may be out of date. The brief's design L-4 most likely describes the 1938 cab, so it is corrected. The first lookout's name is unresolved: NHLR says Mert Ellsbury, firelookout.com says Lyman Ellsbury for 1939. The story reports both. Staffing source is NHLR undated text, so as_of is undated. Brief elevation 2028.7 m matches NHLR 6,656 ft; Wikipedia says 6,640 ft. Sundance AFS radar claim is from the Forest Service page and was not separately checked. No photos added.

Only four pages describe this lookout, and none gives a staffing record, so staffing is omitted; two web searches found nothing more. Elevation differs slightly: 10,276 ft (register, matches record 3,132 m) vs 10,267 ft (firelookout.com). Firelookout.com says '20' wooden L-4 tower' where the register says the cabin 'appears to be' a modified L-4 on an open timber tower; both are compatible. Height to cab floor is not stated, so height_m is omitted. The 1940 brochure says '6 miles' and the handbook (printed 1941) says 'about 6 miles' from the Crandall Ranger Station. Access status is not found, so access is omitted. Crandall Ranger Station restoration articles surfaced in search but do not mention this lookout and were not used.

Status is likely wrong in the tower record (see correction) and should be fixed by an editor, not auto-applied. Build year is fuzzy (1932 vs. ~1934) because NHLR's stated span and the Buckrail piece's '23 years of service ending 1957' don't quite agree; left unresolved rather than guessed. No NRHP nomination form or newspaper coverage was found for this one — the two non-register sources (firelookout.com, Buckrail) carried the real narrative detail (staff names, prior tent/stone camp). Fact-check correction (2026-10-04): a draft version of the story attributed a 2000 near-miss wildfire to Wyoming Peak, citing the Buckrail article; that passage in Buckrail is actually about Deadman Fire Lookout, a different lookout covered in the same article, and has been removed.
